## Abstract
Abstract—The study used ClinicalBERT to predict body system categories based on clinical notes from the first three days of admission, using the MIMIC-III dataset. After data preprocessing, including the extraction of admission details, clinical notes, and diagnoses, the dataset comprised 510,956 notes associated with 44,270 unique hospitalizations. Discharge diagnoses were categorized into body systems, and the ClinicalBERT model was fine-tuned to predict associations with these diagnoses, resulting in 19 classification models - one for each body system. Around 80% of the models achieved F1 scores exceeding 0.7. Models for diseases of the circulatory, infectious and parasitic, respiratory, nervous, digestive, and genitourinary systems had F1 scores surpassing 0.8. Conversely, models for congenital malformations, eye and adnexa diseases, and ear and mastoid process diseases showed notably lower F1 scores. To explore model robustness, a comparison between three days and one day of notes per patient was conducted. While F1 scores generally decreased, a significant finding was that most body system models maintained satisfactory performance due to the statistical distribution similarities in note types and lengths between one and three days. This suggests the potential for ClinicalBERT's adaptability to varied data availability scenarios. Future studies could delve into developing a multiple notes model, testing its flexibility and robustness across different prediction durations, thereby potentially reducing the time and effort associated with model implementation in diverse clinical settings. Keywords—Large Language Models, diagnostic uncertainty, emergency department I.

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION Diagnostic errors in the emergency department represent a serious challenge in improving urgent patient care [1-2]. According to a recently conducted systematic review, 5.7% of the 130 million emergency department visits in the United States result in misdiagnosis [1]. This translates to approximately 7.4 million patients being misdiagnosed every year. The same review also found that 2.0% of these patients suffer an adverse event as a result of the misdiagnosis, and about 0.3% suffer serious harm [1]. Other studies described clinical reasoning and decision-making strategies used by emergency medicine physicians and contributing factors to diagnostic errors occurring in emergency medicine (e.g., overconfidence, cognitive stress, anchoring bias), and strategies to address the risk of error based on reduction of diagnostic uncertainty [3-4]. Diagnostic uncertainty is one of the largest contributory factors to the occurrence of diagnostic errors across most specialties in clinical care, especially in emergency medicine due to the undifferentiated symptoms with which emergency department physicians are often presented [5]. Physicians can respond to diagnostic uncertainty in various ways through the interplay of a series of cognitive, emotional, and ethical reactions. The consequences of such uncertainty, however, can impact negatively upon physicians, their patients, and the wider healthcare system [6-7]. Diagnostic uncertainty is inherent in the practice of emergency medicine [9-10]. Patients often present with a broad spectrum of overlapping symptoms characteristic of different health conditions, making it difficult for clinicians to identify a root cause for the emergency department (ED) visit [11-13]. In addition to the patient presentation, time constraints in emergency care, complexity of differential diagnostics, and limitations in cognitive processing all influence clinical decisions amid diagnostic uncertainty [14-16]. Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown promise in reducing diagnostic uncertainty in medicine [8]. AI can help expand the differential diagnosis and reduce cognitive stress on physicians [17]. Recent studies found that an AI program performed about as well as clinicians in diagnosing patients when given the same clinical information [18-19]. Another study evaluated the use of an electronic differential diagnosis generator (EDDG) in the high-acuity area of a tertiary care emergency department [8]. The EDDG was used by residents evaluating each patient in the area, and it led to a diagnosis not initially considered in 47% of cases and led to additional diagnostic testing in 4% of cases. Developing a clinical decision support system (CDS) for differential diagnosis in the emergency department using AI is a complex iterative task that requires a multidisciplinary team of experts [20]. The first step is to define the problem that the CDS will address. This involves identifying the types of diagnoses that are most commonly missed or delayed in the emergency department and determining how AI can assist in the diagnostic process. Once the data has been collected, the AI algorithms can be developed. This involves selecting the appropriate machine learning algorithms and training them on the collected data. The CDS should be integrated into the clinical workflow to ensure that it is used effectively. METHOD A. Dataset Creation The dataset used was MIMIC-III (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III). MIMIC-III contained de-identified health records from patients admitted to ICU at Beth Israel Deaconess Hospital between 2001 and 2012. The dataset 19 information tables represented admission information, patient demographics, lab results, ICU stay information, notes, and diagnoses among other comprehensive stay details. The note types included were clinical notes, vital signs, laboratory results, and imaging reports. With over 58,000 hospital admissions, it served as a valuable resource for medical research, enabling investigations into patient outcomes, disease patterns, and treatment efficacy. We identified all patients with clinical notes and discharge diagnoses and excluded children and those cases without clinical notes or valid discharge diagnoses. After evaluating note types and note length, we further excluded notes that were less than 10 words and discharge summary notes. We extracted admission id, patient id, admission time and discharge time from the ‘admissions’ table. The duration of the patient’s stay was found by subtracting admission time from discharge time. Clinical notes were found in the ‘noteevents’ table. Diagnoses were found in the ‘diagnoses_icd’ table. All tables were joined through the unique admission identifier (HADM_ID) and the unique patient identifier (SUBJECT_ID). The entries in the ‘diagnoses_icd’ table were discharge diagnoses and ICD codes were generated for billing purposes at the end of the hospital stay. Since the diagnoses were in ICD-9CM, we first converted them into ICD-10-CM and then used the Clinical Classifications Software Refined (CCSR) to categorize all diagnoses into their associated CCSR default category for inpatient diagnoses. The Clinical Classifications Software Refined is part of the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP), a Federal-State-Industry partnership sponsored by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). CCSR categorizes ICD-10-CM into clinically relevant categories. CCSR contains over 530 clinical categories across 22 body systems to classify more than 70,000 ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes. The body system associated with the default category was the first 3 characters of the category code (Figure 1). The MIMIC-III data for was associated with 19 of the 22 CCSR body systems. External causes of morbidity (EXT), certain conditions originating in the perinatal period (PNL), and dental diseases (DEN) were not found. We further filtered to include only the first 3 days of notes since admission, by calculating the time difference between the note date and the admission date. Since multiple notes could be generated for each stay, the text from the notes from a unique stay was concatenated. This text was then processed to remove characters that might create problems for the model (e.g., brackets added in the note deidentification process, decimals within numbers, dashes, underscores, and equals signs). Abbreviations for doctors were expanded. Figure 1. Example of obtaining a body system. 237 Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:28:07 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. The maximum input size for the ClinicalBERT model we used was 512 tokens. The model uses sub-word tokenization, which breaks words into pre-fix, stem, and post-fix, where possible. These breaks result in an increased number of tokens. To accommodate these issues, the concatenated note text was broken into 318-word groups. All 318-word groups for a single patient stay were associated with the same document ID and an output label. We created train, validation, and test data sets for the 19 body systems separately. For each body system, the output label was 1 if the body system occurred in the discharge diagnoses and 0 if it did not. Balanced datasets were created by sub-sampling the majority class to have a similar number of stays as the minority class. Eleven body systems had more than 10,000 unique stays for the minority class. To reduce the training time, we subsampled both classes to have no more than 10,000 unique stays for each class. We split each dataset into 80% training, 10% validation and 10% test. B. Model training The model we used was ClinicalBERT trained by Huang et al. (2020). They started with BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), which is a pre-trained natural language processing model introduced by Google. BERT is bidirectional because it uses both left and right context of words. Their goal in developing BERT was to understand context and semantics. BERT was trained on a combination of the English Wikipedia and the BookCorpus dataset. ClinicalBert was built by further training with MIMIC-III notes, using both masked language modeling and consecutive sentence classification, at the same time. The ClinicalBERT objective function is the log-likelihood of the predicted masked tokens combined with the log-likelihood of the binary consecutive sequence decision. The goal of ClinicalBERT is expand the understanding of context and semantics to clinical text. We fine-tuned the Huang, et al. (2020) ClinicalBERT model to predict whether a body system will be associated with a patient’s discharge diagnoses. We created 19 classification models. One for each body system. Each fine-tune consisted of one training epoch run over the ClinicalBERT model. Training ClinicalBERT involves configuring the input lines (i.e., tokenizing, adding [CLS] and [SEP] tokens, and converting to token ids). Token ids identify which vocabulary item is associated with each token. The input lines were trained to produce the output label. After the training epoch, we evaluated the system performance by running the model over each test item. We then used the document ID to gather the predicted labels for each 318-word section of the note text. We then used the Huang et al. (2020) probability metric to determine the final label. We evaluated each individual model using AU-ROC, precision, recall, F1 score and accuracy. III. RESULT A. Demographics There were 510,956 notes and 44,270 unique hospitalizations in the analytic dataset. Over 80% of visits were emergency admissions. 47% of the hospitalizations were admitted from the emergency room, followed by 18% from clinic referrals, 17% from physicians’ referrals and 16% from transfers from hospitals. In addition, the average hospital length of stay was 9.83±9.59 days and the average ICU length of stay was 4.90±9.60 days. Table II. As shown in Table II, the average age at hospitalization was 63.93±17.31 years old. 14% of patients were young adults (between 18 and 45 years old), 31% of patients were middleaged adults (between 46 and 64) and 54% of patients were older adults (> 64 years old). There was a significantly higher (p <0.05) proportion of male adults (56%) than female adults (43%) in the dataset. In terms of race and ethnicity, 72% of patients were White, followed by 9% Black or African American patients and 3% of Hispanic or Latino patients. B. Diagnoses In the method section, we described how body systems were obtained using discharge diagnoses. There were 19 body systems identified in the analytic dataset. The discharge diagnosis for each hospital stay was associated with on average 5.70 ± 2.55 body systems (Figure 2). The diseases of the circulatory system (CIR) were most often associated with discharge diagnoses. 80% of patients had diagnoses associated with this body system. The top 5 most frequently diagnosed body systems were diseases of the circulatory system (81%), endocrine, nutritional, and metabolic diseases (67%), diseases of the respiratory system (47%), diseases of the genitourinary system (47%) and diseases of the digestive system (43%). C. Clinical notes There were 510,956 clinical notes in the dataset. The top 6 most frequent note types were radiology notes (n = 151,147), nursing/others notes (n = 111,850), nursing notes (n = 85,345), ECG notes (n = 74,163), physician notes (n = 54,281) and Echo notes (n = 17,733). These notes constituted over 95% of all notes. Table III compares the average number of notes per patient between the first day and the first 3 days of hospital admission. There were on average 4.11±3.24 notes for the first day and 11.54±9.45 notes per patient during the 3-day period. When categorized by the note author, there were 0.71±1.35 nursing notes, 1.73±1.89 radiology notes and 0.99±0.96 ECG notes on the first day of admission. Nursing notes increased the most in the 3-day period. When exploring note length, the average note length was 439.17±641.22 words. Physician notes contained significantly more words (mean: 2071.99, std 678.07), and ECG notes significantly fewer (mean 27.28, std 13.72) than the other than those authored by nurses, ECHO cardiologists, and radiologists, which were all around 200 to 300 words. Table III. 1 day and 3 days comparison of average number of notes per patient. D. Model Results We constructed 19 independent ClinicalBERT models, one for each body system. Table V showed the evaluation for each model. Fifteen models (79%) achieved F1 scores over 0.7. Pregnancy childbirth and puerperium (PRG) performed the best, all stays had the body system associated with the discharge diagnosis correctly predicted (F1: 1, AU-ROC:1). However, the training and test data sets for this body system were very small 158 stays and 63 stays, respectively. The models for diseases of the circulatory system (F1: 0.88, AU-ROC: 0.85), certain infectious and parasitic diseases (F1: 0.88, AU-ROC: 0.88), neoplasms (F1: 0.85, AU-ROC: 0.87), diseases of the respiratory system (F1: 0.84, AU-ROC: 0.83), diseases of the nervous system (F1: 0.82, AU-ROC: 0.83), diseases of the digestive system (F1: 0.80, AU-ROC: 0.81) and diseases of the genitourinary system (F1: 0.80, AU-ROC: 0.82) performed well and had F1 scores higher than 0.8. In contrast, models for congenital malformations, deformations and chromosomal abnormalities (F1: 0.32, AUROC: 0.60), diseases of the eye and adnexa (F1: 0.20, AU-ROC: 0.55) and diseases of the ear and mastoid process (F1: 0.19, AUROC: 0.55) had very low F1 scores. These body systems could have been predicted to perform badly because the numbers of positive examples in their training and test data sets were small. MAL train and test positive examples were (1539, 516), EYE (1856, 563), EAR (490, 214). Conversely, the training and test set positive example sizes for the well performing models were as follows: CIR (6217, 848), END (5962, 837), RSP (5425, 811), GEN (5336, 837), and DIG (5189, 811). We further tested the model trained using 3 days of notes, with a data set containing only 1-day of notes per patient. The results are shown in Table V. Each F1 score decreased, however, 9 out of 13 (70%) body system models had F1 score above 0.7. Figure 2. DISCUSSION The demographic and clinical characteristics of the dataset provided valuable context, highlighting a predominantly older adult population with various admission sources and a significant prevalence of diseases of the circulatory and endocrine systems. The ClinicalBERT model, pre-trained by Huang et al. (2020) and fine-tuned for each body system, demonstrated promising performance across various evaluation metrics. Our study focused on 19 separate body systems which allowed for a comprehensive analysis of model effectiveness. Considering the average length of hospital stay in the analyzed dataset was approximately 9.83 days, with an average ICU stay of 4.90 days, the utilization of clinical notes from the first three days for predicting final discharge diagnoses appears to be a sensible choice. This choice aligned with the real-world practicality of capturing crucial information early on in a patient's admission. In addition, the results indicated high F1 scores for several body systems, particularly those associated with common medical conditions, such as diseases of the circulatory and respiratory systems. However, some body systems, such as congenital malformations and diseases of the eye and ear, exhibited lower F1 scores, potentially due to limited positive examples in the training and test datasets. This highlighted the challenge of predicting less common medical conditions with smaller representation in the data. In exploring the model's robustness, a comparison was made between the model trained on three days of notes and a dataset containing only one day of notes per patient. While F1 scores generally decreased, a noteworthy finding was that the majority of body system models still maintained satisfactory performance due to the similarities of the statistical distribution of note types and note length between one day and three days. It was important to understand that the training set for the three-day note model inherently included information from the one-day notes, further emphasizing the model's ability to generalize across different timeframes. In future studies, there is an opportunity to explore the development of a multiple-day notes model, testing its flexibility and robustness in predicting discharge diagnoses across various durations. By training a single model that can be applied to different timeframes, there is a potential reduction in time and effort, streamlining the implementation of ClinicalBERT in diverse clinical settings. In our previous work [28], using unstructured patient information extracted from the notes documented at the very first hours of admission to the hospital, four machine learning models were developed and tested. The random forest model demonstrated the best performance with an F1 score of 93% for differential diagnosis of a single condition (COPD). The current work demonstrates that using LLM shows significant promise for scalable and accurate differential diagnosis across multiple conditions [29]. In future studies, we plan to delve into developing a multiple notes model, testing its flexibility and robustness across different prediction durations, thereby potentially reducing the time and effort associated with model implementation in diverse clinical settings. V.

## Conclusion
CONCLUSION In conclusion, the study successfully applied CinicalBERT to predict body system categories using MIMIC-III data. The results showcased high F1 scores for numerous body systems, particularly those associated with prevalent medical conditions, such as diseases of the circulatory and respiratory systems. However, certain body systems, including congenital malformations and diseases of the eye and ear, displayed lower F1 scores, possibly due to limited positive examples in the datasets. The robustness analysis, comparing model performance between three days and one day of notes, yielded insightful findings. While F1 scores experienced a decrease, most body system models demonstrated reasonable performance, highlighting the adaptability of the ClinicalBERT model. Further research can build upon these findings to enhance model generalization and applicability in real-world healthcare scenarios. VI.

DISCUSSION The demographic and clinical characteristics of the dataset provided valuable context, highlighting a predominantly older adult population with various admission sources and a significant prevalence of diseases of the circulatory and endocrine systems. The ClinicalBERT model, pre-trained by Huang et al. (2020) and fine-tuned for each body system, demonstrated promising performance across various evaluation metrics. Our study focused on 19 separate body systems which allowed for a comprehensive analysis of model effectiveness. Considering the average length of hospital stay in the analyzed dataset was approximately 9.83 days, with an average ICU stay of 4.90 days, the utilization of clinical notes from the first three days for predicting final discharge diagnoses appears to be a sensible choice. This choice aligned with the real-world practicality of capturing crucial information early on in a patient's admission. In addition, the results indicated high F1 scores for several body systems, particularly those associated with common medical conditions, such as diseases of the circulatory and respiratory systems. However, some body systems, such as congenital malformations and diseases of the eye and ear, exhibited lower F1 scores, potentially due to limited positive examples in the training and test datasets. This highlighted the challenge of predicting less common medical conditions with smaller representation in the data. In exploring the model's robustness, a comparison was made between the model trained on three days of notes and a dataset containing only one day of notes per patient. While F1 scores generally decreased, a noteworthy finding was that the majority of body system models still maintained satisfactory performance due to the similarities of the statistical distribution of note types and note length between one day and three days. It was important to understand that the training set for the three-day note model inherently included information from the one-day notes, further emphasizing the model's ability to generalize across different timeframes. In future studies, there is an opportunity to explore the development of a multiple-day notes model, testing its flexibility and robustness in predicting discharge diagnoses across various durations. By training a single model that can be applied to different timeframes, there is a potential reduction in time and effort, streamlining the implementation of ClinicalBERT in diverse clinical settings. In our previous work [28], using unstructured patient information extracted from the notes documented at the very first hours of admission to the hospital, four machine learning models were developed and tested. The random forest model demonstrated the best performance with an F1 score of 93% for differential diagnosis of a single condition (COPD). The current work demonstrates that using LLM shows significant promise for scalable and accurate differential diagnosis across multiple conditions [29]. In future studies, we plan to delve into developing a multiple notes model, testing its flexibility and robustness across different prediction durations, thereby potentially reducing the time and effort associated with model implementation in diverse clinical settings. V. CONCLUSION In conclusion, the study successfully applied CinicalBERT to predict body system categories using MIMIC-III data. The results showcased high F1 scores for numerous body systems, particularly those associated with prevalent medical conditions, such as diseases of the circulatory and respiratory systems. However, certain body systems, including congenital malformations and diseases of the eye and ear, displayed lower F1 scores, possibly due to limited positive examples in the datasets. The robustness analysis, comparing model performance between three days and one day of notes, yielded insightful findings. While F1 scores experienced a decrease, most body system models demonstrated reasonable performance, highlighting the adaptability of the ClinicalBERT model. Further research can build upon these findings to enhance model generalization and applicability in real-world healthcare scenarios. VI. REFERENCES 1. Newman-Toker DE, Peterson SM, Badihian S, et al. ## Abstract
ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced the classification and management of speech and language disorders, by learning diagnostic patterns from acoustic, prosodic, and linguistic signals. Speech production relies on coordinated respiratory, phonatory, articulatory, and cognitive mechanisms. Disruptions in these systems, particularly due to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and dysarthria, can lead to speech impairments affecting clarity, fluency, and timing. This systematic literature review synthesizes insights from 231 studies (2007–2024) on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques for classifying and analyzing 16 distinct speech and language disorders, with emphasis on neurodegenerative conditions. This review highlights the progression from traditional ML approaches, such as support vector machines, to advanced DL architectures, including convolutional and recurrent neural networks, and explores the potential of hybrid and multimodal models. ## Introduction
INTRODUCTION Speech and language disorders refer to difficulties in communication, but they differ in nature. Speech and language 177136 2025 The Authors. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License. For more information, see VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders disorders comprise developmental, acquired, and neurodegenerative conditions; some progress over time (e.g., Parkinson’s Disease), while others are non-progressive (e.g., developmental stuttering. Language disorders involve problems in understanding (receptive) or producing (expressive) language, affecting grammar, meaning, and other linguistic aspects. Speech disorders, on the other hand, involve difficulties in producing speech sounds correctly, including issues with voice, articulation, and fluency. While language disorders affect both spoken and written communication, speech disorders mainly impact the vocal expression of language [1], [2]. Frequently observed disorders include stuttering, apraxia of speech, dysarthria, phonological disorders, aphasia, and various voice disorders. The etiology of these disorders may involve genetic predispositions, neurological dysfunctions, physical trauma, or developmental anomalies [3], [4], [5]. Neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis markedly hinder communicative ability and diminish quality of life by disrupting both motor and cognitive systems, thereby resulting in articulation impairments, dysarthria and speech-related challenges [6]. Individuals with these conditions may encounter substantial challenges in articulating words, sustaining fluent speech, or modulating vocal qualities, which adversely affects their social interactions, educational development, and overall quality of life. In parallel with the growing clinical challenges, there has been a marked global increase in the demand for assistive technology (AT). Assistive technology (AT) is an umbrella term encompassing assistive products, their related systems, and services. Assistive products help maintain or improve an individual’s functioning related to cognition, communication, hearing, mobility, self-care, and vision, thus enabling their health, well-being, inclusion, and participation [7]. The World Health Organization estimates that approximately 2.5 billion individuals globally require assistive technology (AT). Projections suggest that this figure may increase to approximately 3.5 billion by 2050 [7]. However, access to appropriate and specialized speech-related AT remains limited in many settings. Proficient assessment and classification of speech and language disorders are pivotal for prompt diagnosis and intervention, thereby assisting individuals in the restoration of communicative capabilities and enhancement of their daily functional activities [8]. A study conducted in China analyzed the service delivery and satisfaction levels of assistive devices among 872 individuals with disabilities via the World Health Organization’s Rapid Assistive Technology Assessment (rATA) questionnaire and revealed that AI-enhanced assistive solutions have demonstrated promising outcomes in improving the accuracy, accessibility, and personalization of diagnostic and intervention tools, enhancing the communicative abilities and autonomy of affected individuals [9]. Artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced transformative possibilities for addressing speech and language disorders and developing assistive tools. Traditional methods of speech assessment have typically relied on clinical evaluations conducted by speech-language pathologists [9]. However, these processes can be subjective, time-consuming, and imprecise. To address these challenges, automated speech assessment tools based on machine learning (ML) [10], [11] and deep learning (DL) models [12] have evolved, providing more objective, scalable, and efficient solutions. These tools often rely on biomedical signal processing techniques to extract meaningful acoustic and physiological information from speech data. Machine learning could enable data to be used more efficiently to provide insights into disease mechanisms and to help with earlier diagnosis, prognosis, patient stratification and development of new therapies [13]. In addition to classification, speech enhancement techniques have emerged as a complementary avenue to address signal distortion and improve intelligibility before diagnosis. Recent research has introduced noise-aware deep learning models [14], multi-scale fusion architecture (e.g., MFFR-net) [15], and neuromorphic or low-power transformer-based systems [16] that aim to refine degraded or pathological speech. For instance, models like Noise-Aware VAE, LangChainenhanced AAC devices [17], and ultrasound-tongue-based reconstruction networks [18] enhance disordered speech signals, enabling more reliable input for subsequent classification or therapeutic interpretation. These enhancement techniques contribute not only to assistive communication but also to more robust downstream applications in AI pipelines, particularly in real-world noisy conditions or with low-quality input from impaired speakers. However, the efficacy of automated tools [8], [19] is determined by the model’s ability to handle a range of disorders and adapt to different speech features [20], [21] and linguistic contexts. These tools employ sophisticated algorithms to analyze vocal characteristics, including acoustic, prosodic, and linguistic components, thus enabling the precise categorization of different speech and language disorders. The classification of speech and language disorders is critical not only for identifying a particular disorder but also for developing customized therapeutic strategies. Recent developments in multimodal AI frameworks that integrate features from different modalities, including acoustic signals, linguistic cues, and physiological data, offer a unique approach path for addressing the complexities related to neurodegenerative speech and language disorders. Loss of speech after paralysis is devastating, but circumventing motor pathway injury by directly decoding speech from intact cortical activity has the potential to restore natural communication and self-expression [22]. Despite the considerable global prevalence of conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (∼35–100 per 100,000) [23], Lewy body dementia (LBD) (∼1% of individuals over 65) [24], and myasthenia gravis (∼14–20 per 100,000) [25], research focusing on speech manifestations is disproportionately scarce in comparison with that of individuals with VOLUME 13, 2025 177137 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. Moreover, gaps remain in dataset diversity, generalizability, and real-world applicability of AI-driven assistive solutions. To bridge these gaps, this study offers a comprehensive overview of research on speech and language disorders, employing diverse AI techniques for diagnosis and monitoring through voice samples. Additionally, this review incorporates recent advances in speech enhancement, examining how signal processing and deep neural methods are being used to improve disordered speech quality prior to classification. By offering a comprehensive synthesis of the current state of research on various speech and language disorders and classification methods, this review contributes to a better understanding of the advancements and challenges associated with the automated classification and enhancement of speech and language disorders. We aim to address the following research questions: RQ1: What speech and language disorders have been addressed by AI models, including neurodegenerative conditions? RQ2: What corpora are used, and how do they support diverse, longitudinal, and multimodal analyses? RQ3: What methods, feature selection methods, and metrics are used for classifying different speech and language disorders? RQ4: What are the real-world applications, limitations and future opportunities for improving AI-based speech and language disorder classification? RQ5: What are the recent advancements in speech enhancement methods supporting downstream classification tasks? This paper makes several key contributions to the literature on artificial intelligence (AI) applications for speech and language disorder diagnosis, classification and enhancement. First, it synthesizes findings from a broad corpus of studies, providing a comparative analysis of AI applications across neurodegenerative and other speech-affecting conditions. This includes both classification-focused models and enhancement techniques that improve speech intelligibility prior to analysis. Second, it identifies critical research gaps, emphasizing the limited focus on certain high-prevalence conditions despite their clinical importance as well as the underutilization of enhancement frameworks in clinical pipelines. Third, the study highlights challenges in dataset availability, diversity, and longitudinal scope, suggesting the need for more comprehensive resources to address these limitations. Finally, it explores advancements in AI methodologies, emphasizing the need for personalized, explainable, and clinically integrated models to address the unique complexities of speech and language disorders. The remaining sections of this paper are organized as follows. The Background section highlights the need for this literature review by comparing it with the previous studies. The speech and language disorder classification architecture outlines a foundational framework for classifying such disorders. ## Methodology
methods—acoustic, prosodic, and linguistic—are analyzed for their ability to capture speech complexities, whereas multimodal frameworks that integrate acoustic, linguistic, and physiological signals show promise for increased diagnostic accuracy. In addition to classification, emerging work has focused on deep learning-based speech enhancement methods aimed at improving intelligibility and signal quality for pathological speech. Techniques such as multi-scale feature fusion and attentive recalibration network (MFFR-net), noise-aware variational autoencoders, LLM (Large language models)-integrated communication aids, and ultrasound-guided reconstruction for impaired articulation are enhancing the clarity of speech inputs for downstream diagnostic tasks. These approaches are especially beneficial for noisy environments and low-resource users, providing improved preprocessing pipelines for classification systems. The key challenges identified include the lack of longitudinal and cross-cultural datasets and the limited explainability of artificial intelligence (AI) models in clinical contexts. LLMs and adaptive techniques are identified as opportunities to enable disorder-agnostic frameworks and personalized care. Future research should prioritize multimodal feature integration, disorder-specific modeling, joint modeling of enhancement and classification and the creation of more comprehensive datasets to increase the accuracy, generalizability, and clinical adoption of AI-based speech and language disorder classification systems. ## Results
Results section examines different speech and language disorders based on their prevalence within the realm of AI research, analyzes the datasets and methodologies applied, and explains emerging themes and shortcomings. The Discussion section correlates the findings with both theoretical and practical implications, suggesting strategies that could mitigate the identified gaps. The Conclusion summarizes the contributions of the study and delineates potential research directions, emphasizing the importance of better AI frameworks for clinical applications in the management of speech and language disorders. II. BACKGROUND In recent years, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques for identifying speech and language disorders has increased, particularly through advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. ASR has evolved with the adoption of deep learning architectures, enabling improved robustness in noisy, real-world, and low-resource environments. Kheddar et al. [26] provided a survey on the role of deep transfer learning in ASR, demonstrating how pre-trained models can be fine-tuned to improve performance in low-resource, mismatched, and speaker-variable conditions, thus enhancing generalization across domains. Complementing this, Hamza et al. [27] provided a comprehensive survey of advanced deep learning approaches in ASR, emphasizing the use of transformers, deep reinforcement learning, and federated learning to enhance speech recognition accuracy under varying conditions. The study [28] provides a comparative analysis of three prominent speech recognition frameworks—SpeechBrain, OpenAI’s Whisper, and Facebook’s Wav2Vec2—evaluating their performance across various datasets and languages. This work is particularly relevant for speech disorder research as it highlights the models’ generalization capabilities, robustness to noise, and potential suitability for clinical and assistive applications involving impaired speech. This section highlights the importance of this literature review relative to prior studies, emphasizing its broader scope and the unique contributions it makes beyond existing reviews. The matrix in Fig.1 compares speech and language disorders addressed by this work with those reported in prior review articles. Brahmi et al. [29] reviewed different ML assistive technologies for speech and language disorders. Hamza et al. [27] focused on machine learning frameworks for dysarthria severity classification, analyzing feature extraction, model performance, and benchmark comparisons on clinical datasets such as TORGO and UA-Speech. Thirtythree studies on speech-based deep learning approaches for Parkinson’s disease classification published between January 2020 and March 2024 reviewed and discussed the limitations of publicly accessible speech-based PD datasets due to privacy concerns [30]. A review by Lounis et al. [31] highlights the growing interest in using advanced techniques such as deep neural networks (DNNs) for mispronunciation detection 177138 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders and diagnosis (MDD) in language learning and highlights the need for diverse and comprehensive datasets, especially for tonal languages such as Mandarin. Across these fields, one of the most pervasive challenges is the lack of comprehensive and standardized datasets, particularly for uncommon or specialized voice disorders. The study performed by Sindhu et al. [20] emphasized the absence of universally accepted assessment tools, and the scarcity of studies applying unsupervised methods hinders progress in speech and disorder detection research. Moreover, studies on speech assessment in children, particularly infants under 24 months, highlight the difficulty of early diagnosis [8], with future work necessitating the development of automated tools for quantifying speech patterns to improve diagnostic efficiency. Parkinson’s disease (PD) has been a significant focus in [32], with research highlighting the development of intelligent systems to detect and monitor the disease through different algorithms. In a systematic review, Sonawane and Sharma [33] reinforced the role of these systems, especially in detecting voice disorders related to PD, such as dysphonia and dysarthria, pointing toward the need for automated tools owing to the limitations associated with manual and subjective evaluation. However, the current literature on predicting PD severity through speech analysis remains limited and requires more advanced machine learning techniques to fill this gap [33]. Recent advancements in stuttering detection with AI were reviewed by Alnashwan et al. [34], but many challenges still need to be solved due to the unavailability of diverse datasets and class imbalance, which significantly affects model generalizability. According to researchers, in existing methods, essential speech features are often altered, and more sophisticated augmentation techniques must be used to increase accuracy in real-world applications [34]. Another growing area of research is the detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) from spontaneous speech. The gap identified across multiple studies reviewed by Qi et al. [35] is that longitudinal datasets are needed to track the progression of the disease. Current systems have focused mainly on short recordings, which limit their effectiveness in real-time AD detection. Moreover, [35] emphasized the integration of multimodal data with interpretable neural networks to improve the dependability of the model. Moreover, the review by Idrisoglu et al. [36] focused mainly on individual disorders, with limited research on unified frameworks that handle overlapping symptoms across multiple disorders. The relevance of using voice data for broader disorder detection has also been underlined, emphasizing the inclusion of voice-affecting disorders such as dementia, multiple sclerosis, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis [36]. Within the field of voice disorders unrelated to neurological diseases, the primary limitation is the overreliance on supervised learning techniques, with the underutilization of available databases such as the Arabic Voice Pathology (AVPD) database. After a meta-analysis of 45 studies on voice disorders, Syed et al. [37] reported that despite many datasets suffering from imbalance and a lack of global representation due to language restrictions, machine learning algorithms, especially support vector machines (SVMs), were common. The importance of CNN and RNN architecture is discussed in [38]. In addition to classification, this review also encompasses recent advancements in speech enhancement—a crucial aspect of assistive communication tools. Deep learning-based speech enhancement models have shown significant potential in recovering intelligible speech from noisy or distorted signals, making them valuable in both clinical and realworld environments. As reported by [39], the evolution of deep learning architectures—from traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNN) to convolutional neural networks (CNN) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)—has outperformed classical methods like Wiener filtering or spectral subtraction in handling non-stationary noise. Similarly, [40] emphasizes that modern speech enhancement methods must balance intelligibility and naturalness, with neural models offering promising directions but still lacking phonetic specificity, such as formant preservation. The review by [41] underscores the value of multimodal and attention-based architectures, particularly those leveraging transformer models, in refining speech signals across diverse acoustic conditions. Nevertheless, these studies tend to remain theoretical or noise-focused, often overlooking the specific challenges posed by disordered speech. More recent contributions have attempted to address these limitations by contextualizing speech enhancement within clinical and assistive domains. The review article [42] explores the use of Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNNs) and attention-based recalibration techniques for low-latency, low-power applications, including preliminary work on speech-impaired populations. While promising, the lack of clinical benchmarking limits its practical impact. A comparative evaluation of various DL architectures, with specific attention to speaker-independence and medical applicability was identified in [43]. Despite its strengths, the study remains reliant on synthetic datasets. Collectively, these reviews underscore the rapid progress in DL-based speech enhancement while also illuminating the need for clinically validated models, ethically sound deployment, and inclusive dataset development—particularly when targeting individuals with speech and language disorders. Therefore, by including both classification and enhancement approaches in our analysis, this survey offers a more holistic perspective on the use of AI in the domain of speech and language disorders, supporting both accurate diagnosis and improved communication efficacy. While previous studies provide valuable insights, this survey distinguishes itself from previous reviews by offering a comprehensive analysis of 16 distinct speech and language disorders. Unlike previous reviews that have summarized existing methodologies, the survey identifies critical research gaps and proposes concrete future directions, such as enhancing multimodal feature integration, developing inclusive and representative datasets, and leveraging large language models (LLMs) to improve disorder classification. By providing a forward-looking perspective, this review not only consolidates current research but also lays the groundwork for the development of more effective, personalized, and ethically responsible AI-driven solutions for speech disorder classification. In the pediatric context, automated speech tools can outperform traditional evaluations, supporting early assistive interventions [8]. Speech-based methods are cost-effective, noninvasive assistive technologies for managing Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, respectively [29] and [38]. In parallel, recent literature on speech enhancement has advanced the development of intelligent pre-processing modules that improve speech intelligibility and quality in noisy, resourceconstrained, or pathological speech settings. Reviews by [39] and [41], and others have underscored the importance of deep learning architectures—such as CRNNs, GANs, and Stacked Encoder-Decoder Architecture (SEGAN)—in enabling real-time and low-power enhancement pipelines that can be embedded in assistive systems. These enhancement models not only facilitate clearer speech perception for listeners and AI systems but also improve the accuracy of downstream classification tasks. III. SPEECH AND LANGUAGE DISORDER CLASSIFICATION ARCHITECTURE A typical comprehensive speech and language disorder classification model [35] has a three-stage architecture: data collection, feature extraction, and classification, as shown in Fig. 2. In the data collection stage, diverse speech samples from individuals with and without speech and language disorders are gathered. The datasets gathered must cover various disorders, such as stuttering, dysarthria, and apraxia, to capture the unique characteristics of each condition. Speech recordings are commonly complemented with multimodal data [44], such as video for facial movements or physiological data, to capture the full range of disordered speech behaviors. Multimodal data further allow deep insight into complex patterns of speech, thus justifying robust models for real applications. After the data are collected, preprocessing techniques such as noise reduction, volume normalization, and segmentation are applied to enhance the VOLUME 13, 2025 177141 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders input for later stages [45]. Speech recordings, along with multimodal data such as video for facial movements or physiological signals, can improve model robustness for real-world applications [44]. The feature extraction stage transforms the raw speech data into a numerical format that can be interpreted via machine learning algorithms. Commonly used features include Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) [20], pitch, formants, and prosodic elements such as rhythm and intonation [20]. These features capture the acoustic [46] and temporal [47] properties of speech that are disrupted in various disorders. Once the features are extracted, they are fed into the classification stage, where machine learning (ML) or artificial intelligence (AI) models such as support vector machines (SVMs) [48], random forests [49], or more advanced deep neural networks (DNNs) [50] are employed. Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for spectrogram analysis [51] and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for temporal speech patterns [52], have proven effective in classifying different types of speech and language disorders. The classification stage assigns labels to the speech data, identifying both whether a speech and language disorder is present and, if so, specifying the type of disorder. IV. ## Conclusion
conclusions about the question under consideration [53]. ‘‘Systematic reviews are undertaken to clarify the state of existing research and the implications that should be drawn from this’’ [54]. The summarization process encompasses the identification, compilation, evaluation, and synthesis of high-quality research evidence within the purview of the research inquiry by adhering to a predetermined protocol [55]. The objective of an SLR is to provide insight into contemporary research so that policymakers may capitalize on current knowledge and rectify the deficiencies that can serve as a foundation for novel research. The predetermined protocol delineates the methodology to be adhered to, articulates the research inquiry, and encompasses information regarding inclusion/exclusion criteria and quality evaluation [53]. All the information pertaining to the methodological approach that steered the implementation of this SLR is predicated on the prespecified SLR protocol [36]. A. SEARCH STRATEGY A search string was formulated through the application of the most frequently utilized terminologies to identify pertinent scholarly articles; the retrieved articles, along with their references within the domain, were subsequently employed to unearth additional suitable keywords [56], [57]. By incorporating the newly identified keywords into the search string, a thorough search string was established, as shown in Table 3 in supplementary material C. A tailored variant of the search string was employed in databases such as Web of Science (WoS), PubMed, and Scopus to locate all pertinent peer-reviewed primary journal articles published between 2007 and 2024. Exclusion criteria prioritized clinical specificity, eliminating studies without detailed pathological focus to ensure relevance to speech and language disorder classification. The search string for AI-driven speech and language disorder classification encompasses diverse studies across various domains and methodologies. It comprises terminology related to speech and voice features, speech and language disorders, AI and computational methods, as well as speech processing and applications. RQ1 addresses a spectrum of speech and language disorders, integrating AI-specific terminology. RQ2 includes multimodal features and implicitly refers to longitudinal corpora through phrases such as ‘‘automatic assessment.’’ RQ3 reflects a range of computational methods and feature selection tactics using AI-related terminology. RQ4 emphasizes terms that showcase practical applications and prospective enhancements. RQ5 expands the scope by incorporating terminology related to speech enhancement, signal restoration, intelligibility improvement, and denoising, thereby ensuring that enhancement-focused studies are captured alongside classification-oriented research. The search string is comprehensive and inclusive, harmonizing precision with breadth and targeting both foundational and advanced research in AI-driven speech and language disorder classification. The integration of both general and specialized terms guarantee thorough coverage of AI-based speech and language disorder classification and enhancement. B. STUDY SELECTION PROCESS The PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) flowchart [58] pertinent to the present investigation is illustrated in Fig. 3. The automated search yielded a cumulative total of 2360 scholarly articles from the databases, specifically Scopus (2180), Web of Science (158), and PubMed (22). After eliminating duplicate entries, 2324 articles were evaluated through title and abstract screening. Ultimately, 295 manuscripts were incorporated into the full-text reading cohort. A total of fourteen articles could not be accessed. During the comprehensive reading of 281 papers, 50 articles were deemed outside the scope of this research for various reasons: relevance to classification as review papers (n=10), and nonalignment with the classification category (n=40). Consequently, the final compilation consisted of 231 articles that were utilized for data classification. Inclusion criteria • Peer-reviewed Journal articles • Studies written in English • Studies published from 2007 onward • Research aims to diagnose speech and language disorder and speech enhancement. RQ1: SPEECH AND LANGUAGE DISORDERS ADDRESSED Understanding the range of speech and language disorders addressed by AI classification methods is crucial for identifying the scope and impact of technological advancements in speech and language disorder diagnosis and treatment. RQ1 seeks to categorize the disorders and explore how AI technologies have been utilized to identify, analyze, and classify them. A total of 16 disorders, shown in Table 1, were addressed in this paper, which were classified with machine learning or deep learning models. Most of these studies focused on Parkinson’s disease, dysarthria, and different voice disorders. Distribution of speech and language disorders classified with machine learning or deep learning models, with Parkinson’s disease, dysarthria, and different voice disorders accounting for 77.5 % of the total. Interestingly, several high-prevalence conditions, including multiple sclerosis (MS) and Lewy body dementia (LBD), are notably absent in AI research despite their significant impact on speech. MS, with a prevalence of ∼35–100 per 100,000 people [23], often causes mixed dysarthria but is overshadowed by more common disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease.
