RQ3: AI TECHNIQUES AND METHODS AI-driven speech and language disorder classification requires advanced computational methods, feature selection techniques, and evaluation metrics. RQ3 identifies algorithms and techniques used for the detection and classification of speech and language disorders based on acoustic, linguistic, and multimodal features. It also analyzes the criteria used for feature selection as well as model performance. 1) FEATURE EXTRACTION AND SELECTION METHODS Feature extraction converts raw speech into key features for detecting speech and language disorders, whereas feature selection isolates the most relevant features for classification. Features are typically categorized into three primary types: acoustic features derived from audio signals, linguistic features from transcripts, and auxiliary features that further enrich the analysis. Fig. 5 highlights the three primary feature categories and associated methods for effective classification and analysis. SelectKBest [68] is a univariate filter that ranks features that can be used with acoustic, linguistic, and auxiliary features, and combined with cross-validated model selection in clinical speech pipelines. It selects the top k features based on statistical tests that assess the relationship between each feature and the target variable. The stacked based ensemble [10] is one of the machine learning models used to rank and select the most important features. Acoustic features are vital for audio-heavy tasks, whereas linguistic features excel in language structure analysis. Auxiliary methods enhance the overall model precision and computational efficiency. i) Acoustic features: Acoustic attributes reflect physiological and cognitive changes caused by speech and language disorders, affecting articulation, pitch, fluency, and intelligibility. • Cepstral features: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) [69] and their variants, such as gamma cepstral coefficients (GTCCs) [70] and power-normalized cepstral coefficients (PNCCs) [67], increase sensitivity and noise robustness. • Wavelet transforms: Methods such as the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) [71] and wavelet scattering VOLUME 13, 2025 177145 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders FIGURE 5. Feature extraction and selection in speech and language disorder detection. transform (WST) [70] analyze signals across multiple resolutions. • Time-frequency representations: Tools such as shorttime Fourier transform (STFT) [59] and melspectrograms [72], derived from mel-filter banks, focus on speech-relevant frequencies. • Acoustic feature extraction tools such as OpenSMILE (Speech and Music Interpretation by Large-Space Extraction) [48], Praat [73], and Surfboard extract low-level descriptors (LLDs) [74], such as pitch, jitter, shimmer, and the Harmonics-to-Noise Ratio (HNR), for clinical analysis. • Deep acoustic features: Advanced neural models such as Wav2Vec 2. 0 [21], [75] and VGGish [76] extract high-level embeddings that integrate phonetic and prosodic data for sophisticated analysis. ii) Linguistic features: Linguistic features analyze lexical, syntactic, and semantic aspects, revealing impairments in vocabulary, syntax, and coherence. • Lexical/syntactic features: Unigrams, bigrams, and trigrams capture structural elements, whereas natural language processing (NLP) models evaluate grammar and sentence patterns. • Deep linguistic features: Pretrained transformers such as BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) [48] and BETO (a Spanish variant of BERT) offer embeddings for syntax, semantics, and discourse analysis. • Feature fusion: Combining acoustic and linguistic data (e.g., MFCCs with BERT embeddings) enhances classification accuracy by creating comprehensive representations. iii) Auxiliary features: Auxiliary features streamline data, improving accuracy and efficiency through feature selection and dimensionality reduction techniques. • Filter methods: Statistical techniques, such as chisquare tests, analysis of variance (ANOVA) [49], and F-ratios [77], are used to identify relevant features. Methods such as correlation-based feature selection (CFS) [77] and maximum-relevance minimumredundancy (mRMR) [78] maximize relevance and minimize redundancy. • Wrapper/embedded methods: Algorithms such as recursive feature elimination (RFE) [65], [79] and genetic algorithms (GA) [80] refine features iteratively. Regularization techniques, such as least absolute shrinkage [71], the selection operator (Lasso) [71], and ElasticNet [81] optimize feature sets. • Dimensionality reduction: Techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA) [82], linear discrimi177146 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders nant analysis (LDA) [45], and T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) [83] simplify data while preserving variance or class separability. • Optimization algorithms: Advanced techniques such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [73], [84], the Adaptive Controlling Parameter-based African Vultures Optimization Algorithm (ACP-AVOA) [85], and the Multi-Agent Salp Swarm Algorithm (MASS) [46] optimize high-dimensional feature spaces to improve model performance. 2) ALGORITHMS FOR CLASSIFICATION AND SCREENING Table 5 in Supplementary Material E categorizes speech and language disorders, the datasets used, and the corresponding algorithms, highlighting advancements in leveraging AI for identifying and classifying diverse impairments. Support vector machines (SVMs) [86], random forests (RFs) [87], [88] and k nearest neighbors (KNNs) [89] are effective for smaller datasets and less complex tasks. For example, SVMs [86] perform well with datasets such as NEMOURS for dysarthria, whereas RF and KNN [90] are commonly used for articulation [91] and pronunciation disorders. Deep learning architecture, including deep neural networks (DNNs) [92], convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [93], [94], and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), dominate speech and language disorder classification. For example, DNNs and CNNs effectively extract high-dimensional features for dysarthria classification via datasets such as TORGO and UA-Speech. Advanced techniques such as bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) networks and transformer-based models have been applied to neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease. Hybrid models and ensemble methods increase robustness and generalizability. Combining stacked ensembles with ML [10] and DL [95] algorithms is used for Parkinson’s and vocal cord disorders, which perform better for classification. Hybrid ANN-HMM and hybrid deep ensemble models have been employed for stuttering and fluency disorders. These methods exploit the advantages of different algorithms by integrating them into the same system. This technique improves accuracy by combining the temporal features captured by the RNNs and the spatial features extracted by CNNs. Other methods, such as the mixture-of-experts (MoE) [96], transfer learning and goodness-of-pronunciation (GoP) [97] methods with neural networks, have demonstrated potential in conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and dysarthria. The trend toward deep learning approaches reflects their adaptability in handling high-dimensional data, which is beneficial for complex disorders. Emerging multimodal techniques leverage diverse inputs, such as spectrographic data, linguistic annotations, and articulatory signals, to better capture the multidimensional aspects of speech impairments. Spatial convolutional neural networks (SCNNs) with multihead attention transformers (MHATs) [98] and graph-based learning are promising for multimodal datasets. Results and trends from Table 5 of Supplementary Material E: Analysis of methodologies across disorders and datasets reveals key trends: i) Dysarthria: Neural network models such as CNNs, DNNs, and LSTMs are widely used, leveraging the temporal nature of symptoms with datasets such as TORGO and UASpeech. ii) Parkinson’s Disease: Methods range from traditional ML models such as SVM to transformer-based sequence-tosequence models, supported by datasets such as PC-GITA and EEG. iii) Stuttering: CNN-BiLSTM combinations and hybrid models effectively capture spatial and temporal variations via datasets such as FluencyBank and SEP-28k. iv) Alzheimer’s Disease: SVM and DNN models dominate, particularly with datasets such as NCMMSC2021, efficiently identifying acoustic features linked to cognitive decline. v) Pronunciation and Articulation Disorders: Articulation datasets such as TCC-300 rely on simpler methods such as Apriori, whereas pronunciation error detection benefits from GRU-RNN architectures. vi) Voice Disorders: CNNs, SL-RANs, and light CNNs analyze datasets such as MEEI and Saarbruecken, reflecting the complexity of these conditions. vii) Fluency and Speech Intelligibility: Fluency disorders benefit from time-delay neural networks (TDNNs) and hybrid classifiers, whereas intelligibility classification leverages DNNs and SVMs with datasets such as UA-Speech. viii) Emerging conditions: Although the primary focus of this review is on AI techniques across general speech and language disorders, we recognize the growing relevance of pediatric conditions such as Specific Language Impairment (SLI). Several recent studies have explored age-aware and hybrid deep learning models—like SLINet and CNN-LSTM architectures—which achieved high diagnostic accuracies on child speech datasets such as LAANA. These efforts highlight the applicability of AI methods in addressing developmental variability and early screening challenges in pediatric populations. 3) EVALUATION METRICS To evaluate model performance in speech processing and classification tasks, a wide range of metrics are employed, each offering insights based on specific goals, data characteristics, and application contexts. These metrics include accuracy measures, error rates, and correlation-based metrics. Accuracy-based metrics evaluate the proportion of correctly predicted instances and are widely used for binary and multiclass classification tasks. Accuracy measures the ratio of true positives and true negatives to the total number of predictions, making it a standard metric, although metrics such as unweighted accuracy are needed for imbalanced datasets [67]. Classification accuracy is commonly used in VOLUME 13, 2025 177147 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders tasks such as speech recognition, providing an overall measure of model performance [99]. The recognition rate further refines this evaluation by focusing on the percentage of accurately identified speech units, highlighting a model’s precision in specific recognition tasks [51]. Error rates are critical for assessing transcription accuracy and intelligibility. The word error rate (WER) calculates insertion, deletion, and substitution errors at the word level, making it a key metric for transcription tasks [50]. Similar metrics include the phoneme error rate (PER) and the character error rate (CER), which focus on phonemes and characters, respectively, and are particularly useful for languages with complex structures [100], [101]. The syllable error rate (SER) measures errors per syllable and can be used to evaluate intelligibility and clarity, especially in rehabilitation applications [102]. The precision, recall, and F1 score are critical evaluation metrics for classification models. The precision is the number of true positives compared with all the predicted positive cases. This is significant in applications where the occurrence of false positives must be minimized, such as in diagnostics [62]. Recall, known as sensitivity, is defined as the fraction of true positives out of all actual positive cases to avoid missing cases [62]. The F1 score, which is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, provides a balanced measure that is especially useful in imbalanced datasets [48], [82]. Specificity and balanced metrics provide improved evaluations of model performance. Specificity measures the proportion of correctly identified negatives, complementing sensitivity to assess discriminatory power [71]. Balanced accuracy (BAC) averages sensitivity and specificity, mitigating the effects of class imbalance and providing a more equitable measure of performance [74]. Similarly, G-Mean balances sensitivity and specificity through a geometric mean, making it valuable for evaluating imbalanced datasets [103]. The area under the curve (AUC) metrics assesses a model’s ability to distinguish between classes across thresholds. AUC-ROC evaluates this distinction by plotting true positive rates against false positive rates, with higher values indicating robust performance [104]. AUCPRC focuses on precision and recall, providing additional insights into scenarios where these measures are prioritized [80]. Correlation-based metrics assess the relationship between the predicted and actual values. In continuous or ordinal predictions, Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients are widely used, as they show linear and monotonic relationships [75]. For binary classification problems, the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) is used. It considers all true and false predictions and is a well-known measure in an imbalanced dataset [105]. Mean error metrics are applied in regression tasks to quantify the average magnitude of errors. The mean absolute error computes the average of the absolute differences between the predictions and the actual values, whereas the root mean square error (RMSE) penalizes large deviations, making it a better choice for applications in which large errors are undesirable [78], [106]. The average mean absolute error (AMAE) is an improvement that considers different contexts of prediction [78]. Other metrics and ratios provide specialized insights for speech processing. Unweighted average recall (UAR) calculates recall across all classes without weights for class frequency, making it valuable for multiclass and imbalanced datasets [61]. The penalized expected deviance (PED) and detection cost function (DCF) are commonly applied in security and authentication tasks to penalize errors on the basis of application risk [107], [108] Confusion matrix derivatives, such as the true positive rate (TPR), false positive rate (FPR), and equal error rate (EER), are used to evaluate biometric and security applications where a balance between false positives and negatives is critical. D. RQ4: APPLICATIONS AND ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGIES RQ4 explores current applications of AI-based speech and language disorder classification in various domains with their limitations. This review identifies different applications, such as telediagnosis and telemonitoring systems, early detection and noninvasive screening [46], assistive technology for speech impairments [49], multimodal and advanced diagnostic tools [48], telehealth and real-time monitoring [50], automated pathology detection and classification [38], language learning and pronunciation training [85], [109], therapeutic tools and speech rehabilitation [110], smart healthcare and edge computing applications [111], clinical decision support systems [70], mobile health [112] and low-cost diagnostic solutions [87]. For Parkinson’s disease, telediagnosis [69] and telemonitoring [96] reduce outpatient visits while supporting real-time monitoring and therapy adjustments. Dysarthria-focused tools improve communication through assistive systems and early diagnosis [59], [60]. Voice disorders benefit from diagnostic tools in mobile and real-time settings [99], [112]. Tools for stuttering, SLI (Speech Language Impairment), and aphasia provide targeted assessments, aiding therapy [63]. E. RQ5: SPEECH ENHANCEMENT METHODS Table 6 in supplementary material F summarizes recent speech enhancement studies focused on improving intelligibility, quality, and downstream processing of speech in noisy or impaired conditions. These studies deploy diverse AI models across multiple datasets and real-world scenarios. One of the prominent contributions is the MFFR-Net model [15], which combines multi-scale feature fusion with attention recalibration. Evaluated on the TIMIT and LibriSpeech datasets, this model yielded a 17.3% improvement in STOI, illustrating the benefits of integrating spectral and temporal features for intelligibility enhancement. The SRU-based lightweight recurrent model [113] leverages simplified recurrent units to support real-time deployment, achieving an improvement of +0.69 in Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) and +0.19 in Short-Time 177148 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders Objective Intelligibility (STOI). This model demonstrates that low-latency solutions can maintain high enhancement accuracy, particularly for embedded or mobile speech applications. In parallel, the Spiking-FullSubNet [16] introduces neuromorphic computing into speech enhancement by integrating self-organizing maps and spiking neural networks (SOM-SNN). Evaluated using Scale-invariant signal-todistortion ratio (SI-SDR) and Deep Noise Suppression Mean Opinion Score (DNSMOS), it targets ultra-low-power use cases such as hearing aids and assistive communication devices. Other models adopt self-supervised learning or spatial awareness techniques. For example, the Noise-Aware SelfSupervised Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [14] enhances intelligibility using NISQA and STOI-NET metrics, while the SINA-MOnaural model [114] exploits spatial information to boost quality in monaural speech enhancement contexts. The Nested U-Net with channel attention [115] employs convolutional architectures to optimize performance under unseen noise conditions, showing robustness in practical deployment scenarios. Importantly, one study applied GAN-based architectures [116] to convert whispered to voiced speech for laryngeal patients, extending enhancement beyond noise removal to functional speech restoration. Similarly, a hybrid dysarthric speech enhancement model [117] focused on correcting articulation distortions, directly targeting communication impairments in speech disorders. Across these studies, common evaluation metrics included PESQ, STOI, SI-SDR, and DNSMOS. However, a critical observation is the limited validation of these enhancement methods on disordered or pathological speech corpora— most being trained on generic or synthetically noisy datasets. Despite this, the performance improvements and versatility across applications (e.g., hearing aids, voice assistants, speech therapy tools) affirm the relevance of enhancement techniques in AI-based assistive systems. VI. DISCUSSION In RQ1, speech and language disorders encompass a wide spectrum of conditions, each with distinct challenges for AI-driven classification and diagnosis. Among the 16 disorders reviewed, Parkinson’s disease and dysarthria emerged as the most studied, accounting for 67 and 37 papers, respectively. This focus likely reflects the availability of well-structured datasets, the prevalence of these conditions, and the clear clinical need for advanced diagnostic and monitoring tools. Similarly, voice disorders, addressed in 75 papers, demonstrate the field’s emphasis on improving voice pathology assessments and noninvasive diagnostic solutions. Neurodegenerative disorders differ fundamentally from other speech and language disorders because of their progressive nature, leading to significant temporal variability in speech patterns. This deterioration significantly impacts the design and application of AI models, datasets, and practical implementations for speech and language processing. This multifaceted nature complicates speech modeling. Disease progression varies significantly between individuals and is influenced by factors such as age, comorbidities, and treatment interventions. The progressive nature of neurodegenerative disorders requires AI systems that go beyond static classification to support continuous monitoring and adaptation. The variability in individual disease trajectories, influenced by age, comorbidities, and treatment responses, can be assisted by personalization. In response to RQ2, the predominant obstacle encountered in the classification process is the insufficiency of accessible speech corpora, as the majority are proprietary, thereby impeding researchers from effectively training and evaluating their frameworks. Among the 231 scholarly articles selected, 32 pertained to English corpora, and 20 addressed corpora in other languages. Table 7 in supplementary material G shows that neurodegenerative research is limited by a lack of diverse, longitudinal datasets, which are critical for tracking disease progression, whereas studies of other disorders face issues such as data imbalance and overlapping symptoms. This comparison highlights RQ3, the need for adaptive and explainable AI for neurodegenerative disorders and broader dataset development for other disorders. Visual cues such as facial expressions, lip movements, and gestures are crucial, especially in conditions such as dysarthria, Parkinson’s disease, or aphasia, where motor and articulatory symptoms are evident in both audio and visual modalities. Therefore, integrating video features with speech [118] could improve performance in classification tasks and enhance interpretability by revealing how visible speech cues are related to detected disorders. While answering RQ3, Table 7 in supplementary material G shows that for neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and dysarthria, advanced methods such as CNNs, LSTMs, and DNNs are more frequently employed. These techniques effectively address the temporal and multimodal complexities of progressive speech impairments. In contrast, some disorders, such as stuttering, articulation disorders, and fluency disorders, have a broader distribution of approaches, and some of them rely on simpler methods, such as KNN, SVM, and decision trees. These methods align with the static nature of these conditions and the availability of focused datasets. Feature extraction/selection algorithms enhance model accuracy by reducing overfitting, training time and dimensional space. Section IV lists the different feature extraction and selection algorithms for extracting acoustic, linguistic, and auxiliary features. The reviewed studies demonstrate that both machine learning and deep learning algorithms are widely used for classification tasks. Machine learning techniques are widely applied when datasets are limited. These models are generally shallow (limited layers or complexity) and rely on human-engineered features such as acoustic measurements or linguistic scores. They often offer faster training and more transparent decision-making than deep learning models do, although they may not capture complex VOLUME 13, 2025 177149 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders patterns as effectively. Among machine learning algorithms, the support vector machine (SVM) [90] model stands out for its robust performance. SVMs achieve high accuracy, on the order of ∼85–95% in binary classification tasks, given quality features and balanced data. A linear SVM [119] can offer moderate interpretability by highlighting which features contribute most to the decision boundary. However, nonlinear SVMs act as Less Interpretable Models, making their decisions less transparent to clinicians. Overall, traditional ML models excel when feature engineering is strong and data are limited, offering faster deployment and some level of transparency at the expense of the highest possible accuracy. In the realm of deep learning, several architectures have shown high accuracy in classifying different speech and language disorders, as they automatically learn feature representations from raw data. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [120] are used for analyzing acoustic signals by converting them to time-frequency representations such as spectrograms. CNNs learn local patterns such as formant structures or turbulence noise that are indicative of disorders. CNN-based architecture has shown high accuracy, often reaching 90% accuracy in distinguishing disordered vs. healthy speech in controlled settings; however, CNNs remain Less Interpretable Models for clinicians. RNNs are designed to capture temporal dependencies in sequential data. In speech disorder tasks, RNN models [121] are used to analyze time series of acoustic features or sequences of words/phonemes. An RNN can learn the progression of a speaker’s articulation through a sentence or the pattern of sound repetitions in stuttering. These models are deep when stacked in multiple layers, can also be combined with CNNs, and yield improved accuracy by capturing both spectral and temporal cues. However, RNNs suffer from low interpretability. The learned memory states and gating values do not map cleanly onto human-understandable features. Transformer-based architectures use self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in data. In speech disorder classification, transformers are being explored in two main ways: (1) Audio transformers, such as spectrogrambased transformers, and (2) Language transformers applied to speech transcripts or linguistic features. The model can be combined with a CNN, which performs well in classification. As the models are very deep, they require large datasets or pretraining. The attention mechanism in transformers does offer a crumb of interpretability; one can inspect attention weight distributions to determine which parts of the input the model focuses on. As shown in Table 2, the shallow models such as SVM and RF depend on carefully chosen acoustic/linguistic features and tend to be easier to interpret, whereas deep models such as CNNs, RNNs, and transformers automatically learn complex patterns from data and often reach higher accuracy in terms of interpretability. There is a clear trade-off between model complexity and transparency. The choice of model also correlates with the disorder type and data modality. A static classification such as ‘‘PD vs healthy’’ from a sustained vowel might be effectively handled by an SVM on a small feature set, whereas a nuanced task such as ‘‘assess dysarthria severity from a continuous speech passage’’ may benefit from a deep CNN-LSTM that captures subtle spectro-temporal cues. Notably, models incorporating the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) with layered convolutional neural networks (CNNs), standalone CNNs, hybrid models combining artificial neural networks (ANNs), multilayer long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) models have proven effective. Transfer learning approaches that use LSTM and GRU models, along with customized CNN architectures, achieve high accuracy across various speech and language disorder classification tasks. Table 3 illustrates the key insights from our findings that can be used in future research and clinical applications in AI-driven speech disorder classification. This table captures novel perspectives that emerged across model families. Foundational metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC-ROC were widely reported across the reviewed studies, reflecting their utility in general classification tasks. For specific challenges, such as imbalanced datasets in neurodegenerative disorders, metrics such as the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) [122] allow balanced evaluation across classes. Additionally, tasks involving transcription accuracy, such as fluency and intelligibility assessments, use metrics such as the word error rate (WER). As stated in RQ4, AI-driven speech assistive technology can enhance communication capabilities for individuals with speech and language disorders through adaptive automatic speech recognition systems. AI-based classification approaches for speech and language disorders have been deployed across a range of application domains, including telediagnosis [123], telemonitoring [69], early detection, and therapeutic intervention. These systems facilitate noninvasive, real-time assessment, improve accessibility to care, and alleviate the demands on clinical infrastructure, particularly in underserved or resource-limited settings. Assistive technologies have demonstrated substantial utility in enhancing communicative abilities among individuals with disorders such as dysarthria, stuttering, and aphasia while also contributing to rehabilitation and the delivery of personalized therapeutic strategies. Nevertheless, key challenges persist in the areas of model generalizability, effective multimodal integration, and rigorous clinical validation. While multimodal approaches offer promise, their effectiveness is constrained by the need for standardized and annotated multimodal datasets. Future efforts must address these limitations to enable robust modeling and generalizability across disorders. The review identified a notable gap in the use of spontaneous speech data for diagnosing speech disorders. Most of the reviewed papers highlighted the need to develop and share standardized, high-quality pathological voice databases to encourage reproducibility 177150 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders TABLE 2. Structured comparison of representative model. and collaborative progress across research teams. Moreover, several studies highlight the need to generalize models to real-life settings by validating their performance on unseen data and addressing language-dependent acoustic variations. The incorporation of personalized assistive systems for various conditions can also enhance practical usability. The review discussed the need to incorporate a broader range of acoustic features, such as prosody, pitch, and timbre, alongside advanced spectro-temporal features, to improve detection accuracy. The integration of wearable sensors and cloud-based platforms was also emphasized as a promising direction for continuous voice monitoring, especially in telemedicine and remote assessments. Addressing linguistic and cultural diversity remains critical, with a gap in models that are cross linguistically validated. Additionally, leveraging large language models (LLMs) could enable disorder-agnostic frameworks, providing a unified approach to manage diverse speech pathologies while addressing crosslinguistic variability. In addition to performance accuracy, computational efficiency and real-time feasibility are essential for integration into assistive technologies, especially for mobile health applications and edge devices. While some models, such as STFT-layered CNNs, achieve high accuracy (up to 99.89%) and BiLSTM (94.1%), their computational complexity and memory requirements may restrict deployment on low-power devices. In contrast, approaches utilizing GMM-HMM, SVM, or hand-crafted features such as MFCCs offer faster inference with lower energy consumption, although often with slightly reduced accuracy. Few studies reported metrics like inference latency, model size, or energy usage, indicating a gap in evaluating deployability trade-offs. Deep spectro-temporal models and Transformers offer excellent recognition performance but typically require cloud support or GPU acceleration. Optimizing models through compression, quantization, or lightweight architectures remains critical for achieving real-time, ondevice applications. VOLUME 13, 2025 177151 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders TABLE 3. Key insights and implications from comparative analysis of classification models. This review identified that AI models have shown significant promise in advancing classification, diagnosis, and therapeutic support for individuals with speech and language disorders. Across the reviewed papers, it is evident that while classification remains a primary focus, speech enhancement is emerging as a critical complementary area, particularly in the context of real-world and clinical deployment. RQ5 underscores the growing role of AI-driven speech enhancement techniques in improving the intelligibility and perceptual quality of disordered or noisy speech. Enhancement methods such as multi-scale feature fusion networks (e.g., MFFR-Net), spiking neural networks (SpikingFullSubNet), lightweight recurrent units (SRU), and GANbased whispered-to-voiced conversion models not only contribute to improved user experience but also enable more accurate downstream classification in systems designed for disorder detection and monitoring. However, one key observation is that many enhancement models are trained predominantly on clean or artificially corrupted corpora, with limited validation on pathological or clinically diverse datasets. This discrepancy highlights the need for enhancement models to be adapted or retrained for real-world pathological speech conditions to ensure robust clinical application. From a clinical translation perspective, integrating enhancement models as a preprocessing step in speech disorder diagnostic pipelines offers tangible benefits, such as reduced background noise, improved clarity for ASR engines, and enhanced patient–clinician interaction, particularly in telemedicine and assistive contexts. Despite promising advances, speech enhancement remains underrepresented in current literature when compared to classification. As AI-enabled speech interfaces increasingly enter clinical and home-based settings, enhancement will be critical for generalizability, usability, and accessibility, especially for individuals with severe impairments or speech affected by environmental factors. Furthermore, embedding enhancement architectures in real-time, low-latency systems, such as mobile health platforms or wearable devices, aligns well with trends toward continuous monitoring and edge computing. Lightweight models such as Simple Recurrent Unit (SRU) or transformer-based speech enhancement architectures, when optimized for energy efficiency and response time, can support a broader ecosystem of AI-enabled assistive technologies. In the future, combining enhancement and classification in a unified multimodal framework will provide an end-to-end, robust solution for diagnosing and managing speech and language disorders. In summary, the discussion of RQ5 highlights that while classification remains the cornerstone of current AI research, speech enhancement plays a critical role in improving diagnostic performance, communication quality, and user engagement—thus serving as both a complementary and enabling technology in the broader AI-driven speech disorder landscape. To support deployable pipelines, enhancement should be co-optimized with classification (shared loss or curriculum training) so that clinically salient cues (e.g., formant structure, jitter/shimmer) are preserved while intelligibility improves. 177152 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE AND POLICY The following can be used to help build AI systems that are more adaptive, inclusive, and ethical, addressing the needs of patients, clinicians, and researchers: 1) DYNAMIC AI MODELS FOR EVOLVING NEEDS AI systems designed for neurodegenerative disorders must be capable of adapting to the progressive nature of these conditions. Techniques such as lifelong learning and adaptive modeling help models remain effective as patients’ symptoms evolve, while incorporating explainability ensures that clinicians can trust and understand AI decisions, particularly in monitoring disease progression. 2) LIMITED DATASETS A significant obstacle in tackling illnesses such as MS and LBD is the scarcity of publicly accessible and longitudinal datasets. In contrast to PD, which has advantages over well-organized datasets such as PC-GITA and the UCI repository, MS and LBD encounter difficulties in dataset development due to episodic symptoms and overlapping speech impairments, emphasizing the necessity for teamwork to create multimodal datasets that accurately reflect complicated illness development. Moreover, AI models for illnesses such as myasthenia gravis must consider symptom variability affected by treatment responses, introducing an additional layer of complexity. 3) LONGITUDINAL DATASETS Documenting temporal alterations in speech resulting from neurodegeneration necessitates varied and longitudinal datasets. These datasets must include consistent recordings of natural speech and task-specific prompts from the same participants for longitudinal progress analysis. Moreover, to enhance generalizability, datasets should encompass varied linguistic and cultural contexts to facilitate cross-cultural and multilingual applications. 4) PERSONALIZATION FOR PATIENT-SPECIFIC CARE The advancement of neurodegenerative diseases differs markedly among individuals, requiring customized AI systems. Multimodal methodologies that integrate acoustic and linguistic characteristics are inadequately employed in certain illnesses, such as specific language impairment (SLI) and stuttering, which could benefit from tailored instruments for improved results. These systems must incorporate carer and physician feedback to customize interventions, whereas mobile and telehealth platforms are employed for real-time progress monitoring and adaptive treatment modification. 5) MANAGING ETHICAL CHALLENGES WITH PUBLIC DATASETS Publicly available datasets are vital for advancing AI research in neurodegenerative disorders but raise significant privacy and security concerns. Ensuring privacy and minimizing bias in speech data remain significant challenges owing to the scarcity of publicly accessible, well-annotated datasets. Anonymization techniques such as differential privacy or synthetic data, tiered access models, and dynamic consent systems can safeguard patient identities and empower them to control their data, ensuring ethical and effective research. 6) EXPLAINABLE AND ETHICAL AI IN PRACTICE Models used for integrating AI into clinical workflows need to be both explainable and ethical. Transparent systems build trust with clinicians and facilitate sensible decisions. Enforcing ethics committees can ensure that datasets and models are developed based on high standards of privacy and inclusivity. We recommend integrating post-hoc explanations (e.g., SHAP/LIME/Grad-CAM) into model-selection criteria to support clinical auditability and stakeholder trust. B. FUTURE WORK To address the challenges and gaps identified in this review, the following areas represent future directions for advancing AI in speech and language disorder classification. 1) CREATING COMPREHENSIVE DATASETS Future research needs longitudinal, multimodal datasets capturing the temporal progression of speech impairment across diverse demographics and languages. The lack of multimodal datasets represents a significant research gap and an opportunity for interdisciplinary collaboration. Future work should prioritize collecting and curating such datasets while ensuring ethical data handling, anonymization, and accessibility. Cross-cultural datasets enhance AI generalizability, ensuring inclusive diagnostics, whereas variations in speaking styles and noise conditions improve adaptability to real-world scenarios. 2) DEVELOPMENT OF ADAPTIVE AI SYSTEMS speech and language disorders, particularly neurodegenerative disorders, show variability and progression; therefore, adaptive AI models are needed. Techniques such as lifelong learning and transfer learning can be pursued to allow AI systems to adapt dynamically to individual patient trajectories, enhancing clinical relevance and personalization. Moreover, reinforcement learning can be used to train interactive AI models that refine their predictions based on clinician feedback, thus creating a dynamic loop between the AI system and medical experts. 3) INTEGRATION OF MULTIMODAL DATA Future research should use wearable sensors that encompass acoustic, linguistic, and physiological data alongside real-time speech processing. The multimodal framework facilitates a comprehensive understanding of speech and language impairments, enhancing diagnosis and therapeutic strategies. Advanced multimodal fusion techniques, such as attention-based transformers or joint embedding spaces, VOLUME 13, 2025 177153 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders should be explored to enhance heterogeneous data type integration. 4) EXPLAINABLE AND ETHICAL AI Explainability is critical for integrating AI into clinical workflows. Future studies should focus on developing transparent models that clinicians can interpret and trust. Several explainable AI techniques have been developed to address these concerns, including: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) which provides feature-level explanations based on cooperative game theory, indicating the contribution of each input feature to a model’s output. It is particularly useful for understanding acoustic or articulatory features that influence classification decisions. LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) perturbs the input space locally to approximate the behavior of Less Interpretable Models, making it suitable for model-agnostic interpretability in speech-based classification tasks. Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) helps visualize the spatial importance of spectrogram features in classification tasks related to voice disorders. In addition, ethical considerations such as privacy, informed consent, and equitable dataset usage should be the guiding principles in advancing AI to ensure responsible deployment. 5) EXPANDING RESEARCH ON UNDERREPRESENTED CONDITIONS high incidence but underrepresented disorders such as multiple sclerosis, Lewy body dementia, and myasthenia gravis, and therefore, research must be focused. The development of condition-specific datasets and AI models will help to fill the gap in the current literature and provide tools for diagnosing and managing those conditions. Using unsupervised pretraining methods under data-scarce conditions improves model performance with a decrease in dependence on large, annotated datasets. 6) VALIDATION ACROSS LANGUAGES AND CULTURES Validation across languages and cultures: AI systems need to be rigorously cross linguistically and culturally validated to ensure their effectiveness in diverse populations. This approach will enhance the global applicability of speech and language diagnostic tools, addressing disparities in healthcare access. Transfer learning and federated learning can be particularly effective for adapting models to low-resource languages without requiring extensive local datasets. 7) ADVANCING CLINICAL APPLICATIONS the integration of AI systems into clinical practice should focus on telemonitoring, assistive technologies, and rehabilitation tools. This will ensure that practical and scalable solutions for managing speech and language disorders are developed through collaborative partnerships between researchers, clinicians, and industry stakeholders. Real-time speech monitoring tools using edge computing can reduce latency and make AI systems function effectively in resourceconstrained environments. 8) AI TECHNIQUES Transformer architectures and large pretrained models incorporate knowledge learned from massive datasets, which can be fine-tuned to detect subtle anomalies in disordered speech. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Whisper are increasingly being applied to extract higher-level semantic and syntactic patterns from speech. For instance, LLMs can be leveraged to generate dynamic speech transcripts for clinical documentation or interact with patients as real-time dialogue agents for preliminary screening. These systems can also support symptom progression monitoring by correlating temporal linguistic features with disease trajectories. 9) DEVELOPMENT OF PATHOLOGY-SPECIFIC ENHANCEMENT MODELS Current enhancement techniques are predominantly trained on general-purpose or synthetic noise datasets. Future research should prioritize training and validating enhancement models on pathological speech corpora to ensure performance generalization across diverse disorder types such as dysarthria, stuttering, or aphasia. These models must be sensitive not only to background noise but also to the unique spectral distortions introduced by vocal pathologies. 10) FUSION OF ENHANCEMENT WITH CLASSIFICATION FRAMEWORKS Instead of treating enhancement and classification as independent modules, future systems should adopt end-to-end architectures that jointly optimize enhancement and classification. This co-training can ensure that the enhancement process preserves clinically relevant features while improving clarity and intelligibility, particularly for ASR-based diagnostic systems. 11) LOW-RESOURCE AND REAL-TIME ENHANCEMENT SYSTEMS There is a critical need for lightweight and energy-efficient enhancement models suitable for deployment on mobile or embedded devices. Architectures such as Spiking Neural Networks, efficient transformers, and quantized RNNs show potential for use in low latency telemonitoring and wearable platforms, enabling real-time feedback in remote care scenarios. 12) MULTIMODAL ENHANCEMENT STRATEGIES Future work should explore multimodal enhancement, where visual cues (e.g., lip movement, facial expressions) complement degraded audio signals to improve restoration accuracy. This is particularly valuable for disorders with articulatory disruptions, such as apraxia or severe dysarthria. Multimodal architectures like SpeechT5 and CLIP illustrate the ability to 177154 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders align audio, visual, and textual inputs, which is particularly useful for disorders involving articulatory impairments or facial motor dysfunctions. Innovative approaches such as graph neural networks and federated learning provide effective solutions for handling intricate, distributed information while maintaining privacy and security. Moreover, self-supervised learning and generative models, including diffusion models, can improve performance by utilizing unlabeled speech data and generating synthetic data to address the insufficiency of databases for uncommon illnesses. VII. CONCLUSION The synthesized research on AI applications for speech and language disorder classification addressed key research questions, highlighting gaps and advancements in the field. For RQ1, a disproportionate focus on specific conditions, such as Parkinson’s disease, is driven largely by the availability of datasets tailored to these disorders. In contrast, high incidence yet underrepresented conditions, including multiple sclerosis and Lewy body dementia, remain insufficiently studied, highlighting a misalignment between research focus and clinical need. Addressing this imbalance is essential for advancing equitable AI applications in speech pathology. For RQ2, dataset limitations emerged as a critical barrier. Current datasets often lack longitudinal, multimodal, and crosslinguistic diversity, constraining the generalizability of AI models. The review emphasized that future advancements in dataset creation must focus on capturing the temporal progression of speech impairments across diverse populations and environments. Inclusive datasets from diverse languages, such as speech and language disorders, will help generalize applications to various populations. For RQ3, the identification and classification of speech and language disorders constitute a highly dynamic domain of research. However, there is notable reliance on CNN and DNN models, along with traditional features such as MFCCs. Few studies have used multimodal and advanced deep learning approaches. Neurodegenerative disorders pose unique challenges due to their progressive nature. Future research requires dynamic AI models such as self-supervised learning capable of tracking temporal changes in speech patterns and adapting to individual progression. For RQ4, the applications of AI in speech and language disorders are promising, particularly in diagnostics, telemonitoring, and rehabilitation. However, challenges in clinical adoption remain, including the limited interpretability of models and the need for real-world validation. Addressing these issues requires the integration of explainable AI techniques, such as SHAP values and counterfactual explanations, alongside ethical frameworks to ensure privacy, transparency, and equitable deployment. For RQ5, speech enhancement has emerged as a crucial yet underrepresented area in the domain of AI-based speech disorder systems. Enhancement techniques, particularly those employing deep learning architecture such as CNNs, BiLSTM, and transformer-based models, have shown potential in improving speech clarity and intelligibility in pathological speech. These methods are especially valuable when used as preprocessing modules to improve classification accuracy or are integrated into real-time assistive technologies. However, few studies address the pathology-specific nuances required for effective enhancement, signaling the need for disorder-adapted enhancement models and better evaluation metrics tailored to impaired speech. Future systems should prioritize the co-optimization of enhancement and classification tasks in a unified pipeline to better reflect real-world deployment scenarios. AI has transformative potential in diagnosing, monitoring, and managing neurodegenerative speech and language disorders. Leveraging advanced AI techniques and multidisciplinary collaboration can yield highly accurate, personalized, accessible diagnostic and assistive technologies, thereby substantially improving quality of life. Addressing the key challenges of data availability, model interpretability, and privacy concerns is crucial for fully realizing the benefits of AI in clinical practice. The findings highlight the need for a shift in AI research for speech and language disorders, prioritizing the creation of comprehensive datasets, the development of adaptive and multimodal models, and the application of novel AI techniques to underrepresented conditions and the integration of speech enhancement as a foundational step in building reliable speech technology for impaired populations. III. SPEECH AND LANGUAGE DISORDER CLASSIFICATION ARCHITECTURE A typical comprehensive speech and language disorder classification model [35] has a three-stage architecture: data collection, feature extraction, and classification, as shown in Fig. 2. In the data collection stage, diverse speech samples from individuals with and without speech and language disorders are gathered. The datasets gathered must cover various disorders, such as stuttering, dysarthria, and apraxia, to capture the unique characteristics of each condition. Speech recordings are commonly complemented with multimodal data [44], such as video for facial movements or physiological data, to capture the full range of disordered speech behaviors. Multimodal data further allow deep insight into complex patterns of speech, thus justifying robust models for real applications. After the data are collected, preprocessing techniques such as noise reduction, volume normalization, and segmentation are applied to enhance the VOLUME 13, 2025 177141 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders input for later stages [45]. Speech recordings, along with multimodal data such as video for facial movements or physiological signals, can improve model robustness for real-world applications [44]. The feature extraction stage transforms the raw speech data into a numerical format that can be interpreted via machine learning algorithms. Commonly used features include Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) [20], pitch, formants, and prosodic elements such as rhythm and intonation [20]. These features capture the acoustic [46] and temporal [47] properties of speech that are disrupted in various disorders. Once the features are extracted, they are fed into the classification stage, where machine learning (ML) or artificial intelligence (AI) models such as support vector machines (SVMs) [48], random forests [49], or more advanced deep neural networks (DNNs) [50] are employed. Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for spectrogram analysis [51] and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for temporal speech patterns [52], have proven effective in classifying different types of speech and language disorders. The classification stage assigns labels to the speech data, identifying both whether a speech and language disorder is present and, if so, specifying the type of disorder. IV. METHODOLOGY A systematic literature review (SLR) is an independent academic method that aims to identify and evaluate all relevant literature on a topic to derive conclusions about the question under consideration [53]. ‘‘Systematic reviews are undertaken to clarify the state of existing research and the implications that should be drawn from this’’ [54]. The summarization process encompasses the identification, compilation, evaluation, and synthesis of high-quality research evidence within the purview of the research inquiry by adhering to a predetermined protocol [55]. The objective of an SLR is to provide insight into contemporary research so that policymakers may capitalize on current knowledge and rectify the deficiencies that can serve as a foundation for novel research. The predetermined protocol delineates the methodology to be adhered to, articulates the research inquiry, and encompasses information regarding inclusion/exclusion criteria and quality evaluation [53]. All the information pertaining to the methodological approach that steered the implementation of this SLR is predicated on the prespecified SLR protocol [36]. A. SEARCH STRATEGY A search string was formulated through the application of the most frequently utilized terminologies to identify pertinent scholarly articles; the retrieved articles, along with their references within the domain, were subsequently employed to unearth additional suitable keywords [56], [57]. By incorporating the newly identified keywords into the search string, a thorough search string was established, as shown in Table 3 in supplementary material C. A tailored variant of the search string was employed in databases such as Web of Science (WoS), PubMed, and Scopus to locate all pertinent peer-reviewed primary journal articles published between 2007 and 2024. Exclusion criteria prioritized clinical specificity, eliminating studies without detailed pathological focus to ensure relevance to speech and language disorder classification. The search string for AI-driven speech and language disorder classification encompasses diverse studies across various domains and methodologies. It comprises terminology related to speech and voice features, speech and language disorders, AI and computational methods, as well as speech processing and applications. RQ1 addresses a spectrum of speech and language disorders, integrating AI-specific terminology. RQ2 includes multimodal features and implicitly refers to longitudinal corpora through phrases such as ‘‘automatic assessment.’’ RQ3 reflects a range of computational methods and feature selection tactics using AI-related terminology. RQ4 emphasizes terms that showcase practical applications and prospective enhancements. RQ5 expands the scope by incorporating terminology related to speech enhancement, signal restoration, intelligibility improvement, and denoising, thereby ensuring that enhancement-focused studies are captured alongside classification-oriented research. The search string is comprehensive and inclusive, harmonizing precision with breadth and targeting both foundational and advanced research in AI-driven speech and language disorder classification. The integration of both general and specialized terms guarantee thorough coverage of AI-based speech and language disorder classification and enhancement. B. STUDY SELECTION PROCESS The PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) flowchart [58] pertinent to the present investigation is illustrated in Fig. 3. The automated search yielded a cumulative total of 2360 scholarly articles from the databases, specifically Scopus (2180), Web of Science (158), and PubMed (22). After eliminating duplicate entries, 2324 articles were evaluated through title and abstract screening. Ultimately, 295 manuscripts were incorporated into the full-text reading cohort. A total of fourteen articles could not be accessed. During the comprehensive reading of 281 papers, 50 articles were deemed outside the scope of this research for various reasons: relevance to classification as review papers (n=10), and nonalignment with the classification category (n=40). Consequently, the final compilation consisted of 231 articles that were utilized for data classification. RQ3: AI TECHNIQUES AND METHODS AI-driven speech and language disorder classification requires advanced computational methods, feature selection techniques, and evaluation metrics. RQ3 identifies algorithms and techniques used for the detection and classification of speech and language disorders based on acoustic, linguistic, and multimodal features. It also analyzes the criteria used for feature selection as well as model performance. 1) FEATURE EXTRACTION AND SELECTION METHODS Feature extraction converts raw speech into key features for detecting speech and language disorders, whereas feature selection isolates the most relevant features for classification. Features are typically categorized into three primary types: acoustic features derived from audio signals, linguistic features from transcripts, and auxiliary features that further enrich the analysis. Fig. 5 highlights the three primary feature categories and associated methods for effective classification and analysis. SelectKBest [68] is a univariate filter that ranks features that can be used with acoustic, linguistic, and auxiliary features, and combined with cross-validated model selection in clinical speech pipelines. It selects the top k features based on statistical tests that assess the relationship between each feature and the target variable. The stacked based ensemble [10] is one of the machine learning models used to rank and select the most important features. Acoustic features are vital for audio-heavy tasks, whereas linguistic features excel in language structure analysis. Auxiliary methods enhance the overall model precision and computational efficiency. i) Acoustic features: Acoustic attributes reflect physiological and cognitive changes caused by speech and language disorders, affecting articulation, pitch, fluency, and intelligibility. • Cepstral features: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) [69] and their variants, such as gamma cepstral coefficients (GTCCs) [70] and power-normalized cepstral coefficients (PNCCs) [67], increase sensitivity and noise robustness. • Wavelet transforms: Methods such as the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) [71] and wavelet scattering VOLUME 13, 2025 177145 M.
