Support vector machines (SVMs) [86], random forests (RFs) [87], [88] and k nearest neighbors (KNNs) [89] are effective for smaller datasets and less complex tasks. For example, SVMs [86] perform well with datasets such as NEMOURS for dysarthria, whereas RF and KNN [90] are commonly used for articulation [91] and pronunciation disorders. Deep learning architecture, including deep neural networks (DNNs) [92], convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [93], [94], and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), dominate speech and language disorder classification. For example, DNNs and CNNs effectively extract high-dimensional features for dysarthria classification via datasets such as TORGO and UA-Speech. Advanced techniques such as bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) networks and transformer-based models have been applied to neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease. Hybrid models and ensemble methods increase robustness and generalizability. Combining stacked ensembles with ML [10] and DL [95] algorithms is used for Parkinson’s and vocal cord disorders, which perform better for classification. Hybrid ANN-HMM and hybrid deep ensemble models have been employed for stuttering and fluency disorders. These methods exploit the advantages of different algorithms by integrating them into the same system. This technique improves accuracy by combining the temporal features captured by the RNNs and the spatial features extracted by CNNs. Other methods, such as the mixture-of-experts (MoE) [96], transfer learning and goodness-of-pronunciation (GoP) [97] methods with neural networks, have demonstrated potential in conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and dysarthria. The trend toward deep learning approaches reflects their adaptability in handling high-dimensional data, which is beneficial for complex disorders. Emerging multimodal techniques leverage diverse inputs, such as spectrographic data, linguistic annotations, and articulatory signals, to better capture the multidimensional aspects of speech impairments. Spatial convolutional neural networks (SCNNs) with multihead attention transformers (MHATs) [98] and graph-based learning are promising for multimodal datasets. Results and trends from Table 5 of Supplementary Material E: Analysis of methodologies across disorders and datasets reveals key trends: i) Dysarthria: Neural network models such as CNNs, DNNs, and LSTMs are widely used, leveraging the temporal nature of symptoms with datasets such as TORGO and UASpeech. ii) Parkinson’s Disease: Methods range from traditional ML models such as SVM to transformer-based sequence-tosequence models, supported by datasets such as PC-GITA and EEG. iii) Stuttering: CNN-BiLSTM combinations and hybrid models effectively capture spatial and temporal variations via datasets such as FluencyBank and SEP-28k. iv) Alzheimer’s Disease: SVM and DNN models dominate, particularly with datasets such as NCMMSC2021, efficiently identifying acoustic features linked to cognitive decline. v) Pronunciation and Articulation Disorders: Articulation datasets such as TCC-300 rely on simpler methods such as Apriori, whereas pronunciation error detection benefits from GRU-RNN architectures. vi) Voice Disorders: CNNs, SL-RANs, and light CNNs analyze datasets such as MEEI and Saarbruecken, reflecting the complexity of these conditions. vii) Fluency and Speech Intelligibility: Fluency disorders benefit from time-delay neural networks (TDNNs) and hybrid classifiers, whereas intelligibility classification leverages DNNs and SVMs with datasets such as UA-Speech. viii) Emerging conditions: Although the primary focus of this review is on AI techniques across general speech and language disorders, we recognize the growing relevance of pediatric conditions such as Specific Language Impairment (SLI). Several recent studies have explored age-aware and hybrid deep learning models—like SLINet and CNN-LSTM architectures—which achieved high diagnostic accuracies on child speech datasets such as LAANA. These efforts highlight the applicability of AI methods in addressing developmental variability and early screening challenges in pediatric populations. 3) EVALUATION METRICS To evaluate model performance in speech processing and classification tasks, a wide range of metrics are employed, each offering insights based on specific goals, data characteristics, and application contexts. These metrics include accuracy measures, error rates, and correlation-based metrics. Accuracy-based metrics evaluate the proportion of correctly predicted instances and are widely used for binary and multiclass classification tasks. Accuracy measures the ratio of true positives and true negatives to the total number of predictions, making it a standard metric, although metrics such as unweighted accuracy are needed for imbalanced datasets [67]. Classification accuracy is commonly used in VOLUME 13, 2025 177147 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders tasks such as speech recognition, providing an overall measure of model performance [99]. The recognition rate further refines this evaluation by focusing on the percentage of accurately identified speech units, highlighting a model’s precision in specific recognition tasks [51]. Error rates are critical for assessing transcription accuracy and intelligibility. The word error rate (WER) calculates insertion, deletion, and substitution errors at the word level, making it a key metric for transcription tasks [50]. Similar metrics include the phoneme error rate (PER) and the character error rate (CER), which focus on phonemes and characters, respectively, and are particularly useful for languages with complex structures [100], [101]. The syllable error rate (SER) measures errors per syllable and can be used to evaluate intelligibility and clarity, especially in rehabilitation applications [102]. The precision, recall, and F1 score are critical evaluation metrics for classification models. The precision is the number of true positives compared with all the predicted positive cases. This is significant in applications where the occurrence of false positives must be minimized, such as in diagnostics [62]. Recall, known as sensitivity, is defined as the fraction of true positives out of all actual positive cases to avoid missing cases [62]. The F1 score, which is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, provides a balanced measure that is especially useful in imbalanced datasets [48], [82]. Specificity and balanced metrics provide improved evaluations of model performance. Specificity measures the proportion of correctly identified negatives, complementing sensitivity to assess discriminatory power [71]. Balanced accuracy (BAC) averages sensitivity and specificity, mitigating the effects of class imbalance and providing a more equitable measure of performance [74]. Similarly, G-Mean balances sensitivity and specificity through a geometric mean, making it valuable for evaluating imbalanced datasets [103]. The area under the curve (AUC) metrics assesses a model’s ability to distinguish between classes across thresholds. AUC-ROC evaluates this distinction by plotting true positive rates against false positive rates, with higher values indicating robust performance [104]. AUCPRC focuses on precision and recall, providing additional insights into scenarios where these measures are prioritized [80]. Correlation-based metrics assess the relationship between the predicted and actual values. In continuous or ordinal predictions, Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients are widely used, as they show linear and monotonic relationships [75]. For binary classification problems, the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) is used. It considers all true and false predictions and is a well-known measure in an imbalanced dataset [105]. Mean error metrics are applied in regression tasks to quantify the average magnitude of errors. The mean absolute error computes the average of the absolute differences between the predictions and the actual values, whereas the root mean square error (RMSE) penalizes large deviations, making it a better choice for applications in which large errors are undesirable [78], [106]. The average mean absolute error (AMAE) is an improvement that considers different contexts of prediction [78]. Other metrics and ratios provide specialized insights for speech processing. Unweighted average recall (UAR) calculates recall across all classes without weights for class frequency, making it valuable for multiclass and imbalanced datasets [61]. The penalized expected deviance (PED) and detection cost function (DCF) are commonly applied in security and authentication tasks to penalize errors on the basis of application risk [107], [108] Confusion matrix derivatives, such as the true positive rate (TPR), false positive rate (FPR), and equal error rate (EER), are used to evaluate biometric and security applications where a balance between false positives and negatives is critical. D. RQ4: APPLICATIONS AND ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGIES RQ4 explores current applications of AI-based speech and language disorder classification in various domains with their limitations. This review identifies different applications, such as telediagnosis and telemonitoring systems, early detection and noninvasive screening [46], assistive technology for speech impairments [49], multimodal and advanced diagnostic tools [48], telehealth and real-time monitoring [50], automated pathology detection and classification [38], language learning and pronunciation training [85], [109], therapeutic tools and speech rehabilitation [110], smart healthcare and edge computing applications [111], clinical decision support systems [70], mobile health [112] and low-cost diagnostic solutions [87]. For Parkinson’s disease, telediagnosis [69] and telemonitoring [96] reduce outpatient visits while supporting real-time monitoring and therapy adjustments. Dysarthria-focused tools improve communication through assistive systems and early diagnosis [59], [60]. Voice disorders benefit from diagnostic tools in mobile and real-time settings [99], [112]. Tools for stuttering, SLI (Speech Language Impairment), and aphasia provide targeted assessments, aiding therapy [63]. E. RQ5: SPEECH ENHANCEMENT METHODS Table 6 in supplementary material F summarizes recent speech enhancement studies focused on improving intelligibility, quality, and downstream processing of speech in noisy or impaired conditions. These studies deploy diverse AI models across multiple datasets and real-world scenarios. One of the prominent contributions is the MFFR-Net model [15], which combines multi-scale feature fusion with attention recalibration. Evaluated on the TIMIT and LibriSpeech datasets, this model yielded a 17.3% improvement in STOI, illustrating the benefits of integrating spectral and temporal features for intelligibility enhancement. The SRU-based lightweight recurrent model [113] leverages simplified recurrent units to support real-time deployment, achieving an improvement of +0.69 in Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) and +0.19 in Short-Time 177148 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders Objective Intelligibility (STOI). This model demonstrates that low-latency solutions can maintain high enhancement accuracy, particularly for embedded or mobile speech applications. In parallel, the Spiking-FullSubNet [16] introduces neuromorphic computing into speech enhancement by integrating self-organizing maps and spiking neural networks (SOM-SNN). Evaluated using Scale-invariant signal-todistortion ratio (SI-SDR) and Deep Noise Suppression Mean Opinion Score (DNSMOS), it targets ultra-low-power use cases such as hearing aids and assistive communication devices. Other models adopt self-supervised learning or spatial awareness techniques. For example, the Noise-Aware SelfSupervised Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [14] enhances intelligibility using NISQA and STOI-NET metrics, while the SINA-MOnaural model [114] exploits spatial information to boost quality in monaural speech enhancement contexts. The Nested U-Net with channel attention [115] employs convolutional architectures to optimize performance under unseen noise conditions, showing robustness in practical deployment scenarios. Importantly, one study applied GAN-based architectures [116] to convert whispered to voiced speech for laryngeal patients, extending enhancement beyond noise removal to functional speech restoration. Similarly, a hybrid dysarthric speech enhancement model [117] focused on correcting articulation distortions, directly targeting communication impairments in speech disorders. Across these studies, common evaluation metrics included PESQ, STOI, SI-SDR, and DNSMOS. However, a critical observation is the limited validation of these enhancement methods on disordered or pathological speech corpora— most being trained on generic or synthetically noisy datasets. Despite this, the performance improvements and versatility across applications (e.g., hearing aids, voice assistants, speech therapy tools) affirm the relevance of enhancement techniques in AI-based assistive systems. VI. DISCUSSION In RQ1, speech and language disorders encompass a wide spectrum of conditions, each with distinct challenges for AI-driven classification and diagnosis. Among the 16 disorders reviewed, Parkinson’s disease and dysarthria emerged as the most studied, accounting for 67 and 37 papers, respectively. This focus likely reflects the availability of well-structured datasets, the prevalence of these conditions, and the clear clinical need for advanced diagnostic and monitoring tools. Similarly, voice disorders, addressed in 75 papers, demonstrate the field’s emphasis on improving voice pathology assessments and noninvasive diagnostic solutions. Neurodegenerative disorders differ fundamentally from other speech and language disorders because of their progressive nature, leading to significant temporal variability in speech patterns. This deterioration significantly impacts the design and application of AI models, datasets, and practical implementations for speech and language processing. This multifaceted nature complicates speech modeling. Disease progression varies significantly between individuals and is influenced by factors such as age, comorbidities, and treatment interventions. The progressive nature of neurodegenerative disorders requires AI systems that go beyond static classification to support continuous monitoring and adaptation. The variability in individual disease trajectories, influenced by age, comorbidities, and treatment responses, can be assisted by personalization. In response to RQ2, the predominant obstacle encountered in the classification process is the insufficiency of accessible speech corpora, as the majority are proprietary, thereby impeding researchers from effectively training and evaluating their frameworks. Among the 231 scholarly articles selected, 32 pertained to English corpora, and 20 addressed corpora in other languages. Table 7 in supplementary material G shows that neurodegenerative research is limited by a lack of diverse, longitudinal datasets, which are critical for tracking disease progression, whereas studies of other disorders face issues such as data imbalance and overlapping symptoms. This comparison highlights RQ3, the need for adaptive and explainable AI for neurodegenerative disorders and broader dataset development for other disorders. Visual cues such as facial expressions, lip movements, and gestures are crucial, especially in conditions such as dysarthria, Parkinson’s disease, or aphasia, where motor and articulatory symptoms are evident in both audio and visual modalities. Therefore, integrating video features with speech [118] could improve performance in classification tasks and enhance interpretability by revealing how visible speech cues are related to detected disorders. While answering RQ3, Table 7 in supplementary material G shows that for neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and dysarthria, advanced methods such as CNNs, LSTMs, and DNNs are more frequently employed. These techniques effectively address the temporal and multimodal complexities of progressive speech impairments. In contrast, some disorders, such as stuttering, articulation disorders, and fluency disorders, have a broader distribution of approaches, and some of them rely on simpler methods, such as KNN, SVM, and decision trees. These methods align with the static nature of these conditions and the availability of focused datasets. Feature extraction/selection algorithms enhance model accuracy by reducing overfitting, training time and dimensional space. Section IV lists the different feature extraction and selection algorithms for extracting acoustic, linguistic, and auxiliary features. The reviewed studies demonstrate that both machine learning and deep learning algorithms are widely used for classification tasks. Machine learning techniques are widely applied when datasets are limited. These models are generally shallow (limited layers or complexity) and rely on human-engineered features such as acoustic measurements or linguistic scores. They often offer faster training and more transparent decision-making than deep learning models do, although they may not capture complex VOLUME 13, 2025 177149 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders patterns as effectively. Among machine learning algorithms, the support vector machine (SVM) [90] model stands out for its robust performance. SVMs achieve high accuracy, on the order of ∼85–95% in binary classification tasks, given quality features and balanced data. A linear SVM [119] can offer moderate interpretability by highlighting which features contribute most to the decision boundary. However, nonlinear SVMs act as Less Interpretable Models, making their decisions less transparent to clinicians. Overall, traditional ML models excel when feature engineering is strong and data are limited, offering faster deployment and some level of transparency at the expense of the highest possible accuracy. In the realm of deep learning, several architectures have shown high accuracy in classifying different speech and language disorders, as they automatically learn feature representations from raw data. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [120] are used for analyzing acoustic signals by converting them to time-frequency representations such as spectrograms. CNNs learn local patterns such as formant structures or turbulence noise that are indicative of disorders. CNN-based architecture has shown high accuracy, often reaching 90% accuracy in distinguishing disordered vs. healthy speech in controlled settings; however, CNNs remain Less Interpretable Models for clinicians. RNNs are designed to capture temporal dependencies in sequential data. In speech disorder tasks, RNN models [121] are used to analyze time series of acoustic features or sequences of words/phonemes. An RNN can learn the progression of a speaker’s articulation through a sentence or the pattern of sound repetitions in stuttering. These models are deep when stacked in multiple layers, can also be combined with CNNs, and yield improved accuracy by capturing both spectral and temporal cues. However, RNNs suffer from low interpretability. The learned memory states and gating values do not map cleanly onto human-understandable features. Transformer-based architectures use self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in data. In speech disorder classification, transformers are being explored in two main ways: (1) Audio transformers, such as spectrogrambased transformers, and (2) Language transformers applied to speech transcripts or linguistic features. The model can be combined with a CNN, which performs well in classification. As the models are very deep, they require large datasets or pretraining. The attention mechanism in transformers does offer a crumb of interpretability; one can inspect attention weight distributions to determine which parts of the input the model focuses on. As shown in Table 2, the shallow models such as SVM and RF depend on carefully chosen acoustic/linguistic features and tend to be easier to interpret, whereas deep models such as CNNs, RNNs, and transformers automatically learn complex patterns from data and often reach higher accuracy in terms of interpretability. There is a clear trade-off between model complexity and transparency. The choice of model also correlates with the disorder type and data modality. A static classification such as ‘‘PD vs healthy’’ from a sustained vowel might be effectively handled by an SVM on a small feature set, whereas a nuanced task such as ‘‘assess dysarthria severity from a continuous speech passage’’ may benefit from a deep CNN-LSTM that captures subtle spectro-temporal cues. Notably, models incorporating the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) with layered convolutional neural networks (CNNs), standalone CNNs, hybrid models combining artificial neural networks (ANNs), multilayer long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) models have proven effective. Transfer learning approaches that use LSTM and GRU models, along with customized CNN architectures, achieve high accuracy across various speech and language disorder classification tasks. Table 3 illustrates the key insights from our findings that can be used in future research and clinical applications in AI-driven speech disorder classification. This table captures novel perspectives that emerged across model families. Foundational metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC-ROC were widely reported across the reviewed studies, reflecting their utility in general classification tasks. For specific challenges, such as imbalanced datasets in neurodegenerative disorders, metrics such as the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) [122] allow balanced evaluation across classes. Additionally, tasks involving transcription accuracy, such as fluency and intelligibility assessments, use metrics such as the word error rate (WER). As stated in RQ4, AI-driven speech assistive technology can enhance communication capabilities for individuals with speech and language disorders through adaptive automatic speech recognition systems. AI-based classification approaches for speech and language disorders have been deployed across a range of application domains, including telediagnosis [123], telemonitoring [69], early detection, and therapeutic intervention. These systems facilitate noninvasive, real-time assessment, improve accessibility to care, and alleviate the demands on clinical infrastructure, particularly in underserved or resource-limited settings. Assistive technologies have demonstrated substantial utility in enhancing communicative abilities among individuals with disorders such as dysarthria, stuttering, and aphasia while also contributing to rehabilitation and the delivery of personalized therapeutic strategies. Nevertheless, key challenges persist in the areas of model generalizability, effective multimodal integration, and rigorous clinical validation. While multimodal approaches offer promise, their effectiveness is constrained by the need for standardized and annotated multimodal datasets. Future efforts must address these limitations to enable robust modeling and generalizability across disorders. The review identified a notable gap in the use of spontaneous speech data for diagnosing speech disorders. Most of the reviewed papers highlighted the need to develop and share standardized, high-quality pathological voice databases to encourage reproducibility 177150 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. S. Moreover, several studies highlight the need to generalize models to real-life settings by validating their performance on unseen data and addressing language-dependent acoustic variations. The incorporation of personalized assistive systems for various conditions can also enhance practical usability. The review discussed the need to incorporate a broader range of acoustic features, such as prosody, pitch, and timbre, alongside advanced spectro-temporal features, to improve detection accuracy. The integration of wearable sensors and cloud-based platforms was also emphasized as a promising direction for continuous voice monitoring, especially in telemedicine and remote assessments. Addressing linguistic and cultural diversity remains critical, with a gap in models that are cross linguistically validated. Additionally, leveraging large language models (LLMs) could enable disorder-agnostic frameworks, providing a unified approach to manage diverse speech pathologies while addressing crosslinguistic variability. In addition to performance accuracy, computational efficiency and real-time feasibility are essential for integration into assistive technologies, especially for mobile health applications and edge devices. While some models, such as STFT-layered CNNs, achieve high accuracy (up to 99.89%) and BiLSTM (94.1%), their computational complexity and memory requirements may restrict deployment on low-power devices. In contrast, approaches utilizing GMM-HMM, SVM, or hand-crafted features such as MFCCs offer faster inference with lower energy consumption, although often with slightly reduced accuracy. Few studies reported metrics like inference latency, model size, or energy usage, indicating a gap in evaluating deployability trade-offs. Deep spectro-temporal models and Transformers offer excellent recognition performance but typically require cloud support or GPU acceleration. This review identified that AI models have shown significant promise in advancing classification, diagnosis, and therapeutic support for individuals with speech and language disorders. Across the reviewed papers, it is evident that while classification remains a primary focus, speech enhancement is emerging as a critical complementary area, particularly in the context of real-world and clinical deployment. RQ5 underscores the growing role of AI-driven speech enhancement techniques in improving the intelligibility and perceptual quality of disordered or noisy speech. Enhancement methods such as multi-scale feature fusion networks (e.g., MFFR-Net), spiking neural networks (SpikingFullSubNet), lightweight recurrent units (SRU), and GANbased whispered-to-voiced conversion models not only contribute to improved user experience but also enable more accurate downstream classification in systems designed for disorder detection and monitoring. However, one key observation is that many enhancement models are trained predominantly on clean or artificially corrupted corpora, with limited validation on pathological or clinically diverse datasets. This discrepancy highlights the need for enhancement models to be adapted or retrained for real-world pathological speech conditions to ensure robust clinical application. From a clinical translation perspective, integrating enhancement models as a preprocessing step in speech disorder diagnostic pipelines offers tangible benefits, such as reduced background noise, improved clarity for ASR engines, and enhanced patient–clinician interaction, particularly in telemedicine and assistive contexts. Despite promising advances, speech enhancement remains underrepresented in current literature when compared to classification. As AI-enabled speech interfaces increasingly enter clinical and home-based settings, enhancement will be critical for generalizability, usability, and accessibility, especially for individuals with severe impairments or speech affected by environmental factors. Furthermore, embedding enhancement architectures in real-time, low-latency systems, such as mobile health platforms or wearable devices, aligns well with trends toward continuous monitoring and edge computing. Lightweight models such as Simple Recurrent Unit (SRU) or transformer-based speech enhancement architectures, when optimized for energy efficiency and response time, can support a broader ecosystem of AI-enabled assistive technologies. In the future, combining enhancement and classification in a unified multimodal framework will provide an end-to-end, robust solution for diagnosing and managing speech and language disorders. In summary, the discussion of RQ5 highlights that while classification remains the cornerstone of current AI research, speech enhancement plays a critical role in improving diagnostic performance, communication quality, and user engagement—thus serving as both a complementary and enabling technology in the broader AI-driven speech disorder landscape. To support deployable pipelines, enhancement should be co-optimized with classification (shared loss or curriculum training) so that clinically salient cues (e.g., formant structure, jitter/shimmer) are preserved while intelligibility improves. 177152 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE AND POLICY The following can be used to help build AI systems that are more adaptive, inclusive, and ethical, addressing the needs of patients, clinicians, and researchers: 1) DYNAMIC AI MODELS FOR EVOLVING NEEDS AI systems designed for neurodegenerative disorders must be capable of adapting to the progressive nature of these conditions. Techniques such as lifelong learning and adaptive modeling help models remain effective as patients’ symptoms evolve, while incorporating explainability ensures that clinicians can trust and understand AI decisions, particularly in monitoring disease progression. 2) LIMITED DATASETS A significant obstacle in tackling illnesses such as MS and LBD is the scarcity of publicly accessible and longitudinal datasets. In contrast to PD, which has advantages over well-organized datasets such as PC-GITA and the UCI repository, MS and LBD encounter difficulties in dataset development due to episodic symptoms and overlapping speech impairments, emphasizing the necessity for teamwork to create multimodal datasets that accurately reflect complicated illness development. Moreover, AI models for illnesses such as myasthenia gravis must consider symptom variability affected by treatment responses, introducing an additional layer of complexity. 3) LONGITUDINAL DATASETS Documenting temporal alterations in speech resulting from neurodegeneration necessitates varied and longitudinal datasets. These datasets must include consistent recordings of natural speech and task-specific prompts from the same participants for longitudinal progress analysis. Moreover, to enhance generalizability, datasets should encompass varied linguistic and cultural contexts to facilitate cross-cultural and multilingual applications. 4) PERSONALIZATION FOR PATIENT-SPECIFIC CARE The advancement of neurodegenerative diseases differs markedly among individuals, requiring customized AI systems. Multimodal methodologies that integrate acoustic and linguistic characteristics are inadequately employed in certain illnesses, such as specific language impairment (SLI) and stuttering, which could benefit from tailored instruments for improved results. These systems must incorporate carer and physician feedback to customize interventions, whereas mobile and telehealth platforms are employed for real-time progress monitoring and adaptive treatment modification. 5) MANAGING ETHICAL CHALLENGES WITH PUBLIC DATASETS Publicly available datasets are vital for advancing AI research in neurodegenerative disorders but raise significant privacy and security concerns. Ensuring privacy and minimizing bias in speech data remain significant challenges owing to the scarcity of publicly accessible, well-annotated datasets. Anonymization techniques such as differential privacy or synthetic data, tiered access models, and dynamic consent systems can safeguard patient identities and empower them to control their data, ensuring ethical and effective research. 6) EXPLAINABLE AND ETHICAL AI IN PRACTICE Models used for integrating AI into clinical workflows need to be both explainable and ethical. Transparent systems build trust with clinicians and facilitate sensible decisions. Enforcing ethics committees can ensure that datasets and models are developed based on high standards of privacy and inclusivity. We recommend integrating post-hoc explanations (e.g., SHAP/LIME/Grad-CAM) into model-selection criteria to support clinical auditability and stakeholder trust. B. FUTURE WORK To address the challenges and gaps identified in this review, the following areas represent future directions for advancing AI in speech and language disorder classification. 1) CREATING COMPREHENSIVE DATASETS Future research needs longitudinal, multimodal datasets capturing the temporal progression of speech impairment across diverse demographics and languages. The lack of multimodal datasets represents a significant research gap and an opportunity for interdisciplinary collaboration. Future work should prioritize collecting and curating such datasets while ensuring ethical data handling, anonymization, and accessibility. Cross-cultural datasets enhance AI generalizability, ensuring inclusive diagnostics, whereas variations in speaking styles and noise conditions improve adaptability to real-world scenarios. 2) DEVELOPMENT OF ADAPTIVE AI SYSTEMS speech and language disorders, particularly neurodegenerative disorders, show variability and progression; therefore, adaptive AI models are needed. Techniques such as lifelong learning and transfer learning can be pursued to allow AI systems to adapt dynamically to individual patient trajectories, enhancing clinical relevance and personalization. Moreover, reinforcement learning can be used to train interactive AI models that refine their predictions based on clinician feedback, thus creating a dynamic loop between the AI system and medical experts. 3) INTEGRATION OF MULTIMODAL DATA Future research should use wearable sensors that encompass acoustic, linguistic, and physiological data alongside real-time speech processing. The multimodal framework facilitates a comprehensive understanding of speech and language impairments, enhancing diagnosis and therapeutic strategies. Advanced multimodal fusion techniques, such as attention-based transformers or joint embedding spaces, VOLUME 13, 2025 177153 M. S. Remya et al.: AI for Speech Classification and Enhancement of Speech and Language Disorders should be explored to enhance heterogeneous data type integration. 4) EXPLAINABLE AND ETHICAL AI Explainability is critical for integrating AI into clinical workflows. Future studies should focus on developing transparent models that clinicians can interpret and trust. Several explainable AI techniques have been developed to address these concerns, including: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) which provides feature-level explanations based on cooperative game theory, indicating the contribution of each input feature to a model’s output. It is particularly useful for understanding acoustic or articulatory features that influence classification decisions. LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) perturbs the input space locally to approximate the behavior of Less Interpretable Models, making it suitable for model-agnostic interpretability in speech-based classification tasks. Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) helps visualize the spatial importance of spectrogram features in classification tasks related to voice disorders. In addition, ethical considerations such as privacy, informed consent, and equitable dataset usage should be the guiding principles in advancing AI to ensure responsible deployment. 5) EXPANDING RESEARCH ON UNDERREPRESENTED CONDITIONS high incidence but underrepresented disorders such as multiple sclerosis, Lewy body dementia, and myasthenia gravis, and therefore, research must be focused. The development of condition-specific datasets and AI models will help to fill the gap in the current literature and provide tools for diagnosing and managing those conditions. Using unsupervised pretraining methods under data-scarce conditions improves model performance with a decrease in dependence on large, annotated datasets. 6) VALIDATION ACROSS LANGUAGES AND CULTURES Validation across languages and cultures: AI systems need to be rigorously cross linguistically and culturally validated to ensure their effectiveness in diverse populations. This approach will enhance the global applicability of speech and language diagnostic tools, addressing disparities in healthcare access. Transfer learning and federated learning can be particularly effective for adapting models to low-resource languages without requiring extensive local datasets. 7) ADVANCING CLINICAL APPLICATIONS the integration of AI systems into clinical practice should focus on telemonitoring, assistive technologies, and rehabilitation tools. This will ensure that practical and scalable solutions for managing speech and language disorders are developed through collaborative partnerships between researchers, clinicians, and industry stakeholders. Real-time speech monitoring tools using edge computing can reduce latency and make AI systems function effectively in resourceconstrained environments. 8) AI TECHNIQUES Transformer architectures and large pretrained models incorporate knowledge learned from massive datasets, which can be fine-tuned to detect subtle anomalies in disordered speech. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Whisper are increasingly being applied to extract higher-level semantic and syntactic patterns from speech. For instance, LLMs can be leveraged to generate dynamic speech transcripts for clinical documentation or interact with patients as real-time dialogue agents for preliminary screening. These systems can also support symptom progression monitoring by correlating temporal linguistic features with disease trajectories. 9) DEVELOPMENT OF PATHOLOGY-SPECIFIC ENHANCEMENT MODELS Current enhancement techniques are predominantly trained on general-purpose or synthetic noise datasets. Future research should prioritize training and validating enhancement models on pathological speech corpora to ensure performance generalization across diverse disorder types such as dysarthria, stuttering, or aphasia. These models must be sensitive not only to background noise but also to the unique spectral distortions introduced by vocal pathologies. 10) FUSION OF ENHANCEMENT WITH CLASSIFICATION FRAMEWORKS Instead of treating enhancement and classification as independent modules, future systems should adopt end-to-end architectures that jointly optimize enhancement and classification. This co-training can ensure that the enhancement process preserves clinically relevant features while improving clarity and intelligibility, particularly for ASR-based diagnostic systems. 11) LOW-RESOURCE AND REAL-TIME ENHANCEMENT SYSTEMS There is a critical need for lightweight and energy-efficient enhancement models suitable for deployment on mobile or embedded devices. Architectures such as Spiking Neural Networks, efficient transformers, and quantized RNNs show potential for use in low latency telemonitoring and wearable platforms, enabling real-time feedback in remote care scenarios. 12) MULTIMODAL ENHANCEMENT STRATEGIES Future work should explore multimodal enhancement, where visual cues (e.g., lip movement, facial expressions) complement degraded audio signals to improve restoration accuracy. This is particularly valuable for disorders with articulatory disruptions, such as apraxia or severe dysarthria. Innovative approaches such as graph neural networks and federated learning provide effective solutions for handling intricate, distributed information while maintaining privacy and security. Moreover, self-supervised learning and generative models, including diffusion models, can improve performance by utilizing unlabeled speech data and generating synthetic data to address the insufficiency of databases for uncommon illnesses. VII. CONCLUSION The synthesized research on AI applications for speech and language disorder classification addressed key research questions, highlighting gaps and advancements in the field. For RQ1, a disproportionate focus on specific conditions, such as Parkinson’s disease, is driven largely by the availability of datasets tailored to these disorders. In contrast, high incidence yet underrepresented conditions, including multiple sclerosis and Lewy body dementia, remain insufficiently studied, highlighting a misalignment between research focus and clinical need. Addressing this imbalance is essential for advancing equitable AI applications in speech pathology. For RQ2, dataset limitations emerged as a critical barrier. Current datasets often lack longitudinal, multimodal, and crosslinguistic diversity, constraining the generalizability of AI models. The review emphasized that future advancements in dataset creation must focus on capturing the temporal progression of speech impairments across diverse populations and environments. Inclusive datasets from diverse languages, such as speech and language disorders, will help generalize applications to various populations. For RQ3, the identification and classification of speech and language disorders constitute a highly dynamic domain of research. However, there is notable reliance on CNN and DNN models, along with traditional features such as MFCCs. Few studies have used multimodal and advanced deep learning approaches. Neurodegenerative disorders pose unique challenges due to their progressive nature. Future research requires dynamic AI models such as self-supervised learning capable of tracking temporal changes in speech patterns and adapting to individual progression. For RQ4, the applications of AI in speech and language disorders are promising, particularly in diagnostics, telemonitoring, and rehabilitation. However, challenges in clinical adoption remain, including the limited interpretability of models and the need for real-world validation. Addressing these issues requires the integration of explainable AI techniques, such as SHAP values and counterfactual explanations, alongside ethical frameworks to ensure privacy, transparency, and equitable deployment. For RQ5, speech enhancement has emerged as a crucial yet underrepresented area in the domain of AI-based speech disorder systems. Enhancement techniques, particularly those employing deep learning architecture such as CNNs, BiLSTM, and transformer-based models, have shown potential in improving speech clarity and intelligibility in pathological speech. These methods are especially valuable when used as preprocessing modules to improve classification accuracy or are integrated into real-time assistive technologies. However, few studies address the pathology-specific nuances required for effective enhancement, signaling the need for disorder-adapted enhancement models and better evaluation metrics tailored to impaired speech. Future systems should prioritize the co-optimization of enhancement and classification tasks in a unified pipeline to better reflect real-world deployment scenarios. AI has transformative potential in diagnosing, monitoring, and managing neurodegenerative speech and language disorders. Leveraging advanced AI techniques and multidisciplinary collaboration can yield highly accurate, personalized, accessible diagnostic and assistive technologies, thereby substantially improving quality of life. Addressing the key challenges of data availability, model interpretability, and privacy concerns is crucial for fully realizing the benefits of AI in clinical practice. The findings highlight the need for a shift in AI research for speech and language disorders, prioritizing the creation of comprehensive datasets, the development of adaptive and multimodal models, and the application of novel AI techniques to underrepresented conditions and the integration of speech enhancement as a foundational step in building reliable speech technology for impaired populations. ## Abstract
Abstract Background: Dietary supplements (DSs) are widely used to improve health and nutrition, but challenges related to misinformation, safety, and efficacy persist due to less stringent regulations compared with pharmaceuticals. Accurate and reliable DS information is critical for both consumers and health care providers to make informed decisions. Objective: This study aimed to enhance DS-related question answering by integrating an advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system with the integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase 2.0 (iDISK2.0), a dietary supplement knowledge base, to improve accuracy and reliability.

## Introduction
Introduction Dietary supplements (DSs) are products intended to add nutritional value to the diet, often containing vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, or other substances [1,2]. In recent years, the role of DSs has become increasingly recognized, with a significant portion of the population acknowledging their importance. According to surveys, 9 out of 10 DS users believe in the necessity of these products, reflecting their widespread acceptance and use [3]. DSs may aid in preventing chronic conditions and offer the potential for reducing health care costs by minimizing the occurrence or severity of preventable diseases [4]. Unlike prescription and over-the-counter drugs, which are subject to stringent regulations, DSs are classified as food products and are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration under more lenient guidelines. Many individuals use DSs spontaneously, without clinician oversight, which introduces unique challenges related to efficacy, safety, and regulation [5]. A significant concern arises from the fact that around 23,000 doctor visits per year are linked to DS-related adverse effects [6]. This underscores the need for both consumers and health care providers to have access to accurate and comprehensive resources for DS-related information. In response to the increasing demand for reliable DS information, biomedical knowledge graphs (BKGs) have been developed over the past decade to manage large-scale, heterogeneous biomedical data [7-9]. In 2020, the integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase (iDISK) was established to meet the growing need for standardized DS information [10]. iDISK aggregates data from 4 major resources: the Natural Medicines Comprehensive Database (NMCD) [11], the “About Herbs” page on the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) website [12], the Dietary Supplement Label Database (DSLD) [13], and the Licensed Natural Health Products Database (LNHPD) [14]. iDISK includes over 4200 ingredient concepts connected to drugs, diseases, symptoms, therapeutic classes, organ systems, and products, providing an extensive repository of DS knowledge. However, as DS information continually evolves—such as updates to product labels and the discovery of new ingredient-drug interactions—some aspects of the original iDISK have become outdated. For instance, since the launch of DSLD in 2013, the number of recorded labels has increased from 16,712 to 183,012 by January 2024. To maintain accuracy, it is crucial to update iDISK using the latest database versions and optimize the integration process to minimize data noise. Large language models (LLMs) have also gained popularity for answering DS-related inquiries, yet these models are prone to generating “hallucinations” or inaccurate information [15-18]. To counter this, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines the retrieval power of knowledge bases with the generative capabilities of LLMs to produce more accurate responses [19]. An RAG system operates in two phases: first, it retrieves relevant data from a structured knowledge base, ensuring accuracy, and then it uses an LLM to generate responses [20,21]. By integrating iDISK with an RAG system, we mitigate the hallucination problem inherent in standalone LLMs [22,23]. In this paper, we (1) present a major update from iDISK to iDISK2.0, incorporating the latest database versions while minimizing data noise; (2) integrate an RAG system with LLMs to significantly improve the accuracy of DS question answering, the first of its kind for DS queries; and (3) develop the integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase—retrieval-augmented generation (iDISK2.0-RAG) web portal, which offers consumers and health care providers a reliable and user-friendly interface for DS information. Our work not only addresses the limitations of LLMs but also establishes a new standard for DS question answering. Although this work focuses on DSs, our successful integration and platform can provide new opportunities for other domains. Methods Overview Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow of this study. We first constructed iDISK2.0 by integrating the latest versions of data from 4 DS resource databases that were originally integrated into iDISK, including LNHPD, DSLD, MSKCC, and NMCD (Figure 1A). We further developed an RAG-based LLM on iDISK2.0 (Figure 1B). In addition, we developed a user-friendly intelligent user interface with iDISK2.0-RAG as the backend to answer DS-related questions (Figure 1C). An illustration of the study pipeline. DSLD: Dietary Supplement Label Database; NHP: Natural Health Products; iDISK2.0: integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase; LLM: large language model; iDISK2.0-RAG: integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase—retrieval-augmented generation. Data Collection and Preprocessing A total of 4 datasets were collected and preprocessed for the iDISK 2.0. Data from DSLD were downloaded directly from the data release, and the DSLD application programming interface (API) was used to enrich the dietary supplement-related information. Data from MSKCC were obtained after approval, using a web crawler to extract relevant information. LNHPD data were downloaded directly from the data release. After acquiring information from all sources, we converted them into a unified, structured format. The data of the NMCD used in the iDISK 2.0 were derived from information that already exists within iDISK. During the information extraction process, we used LLM (GPT-4) with the prompt (see Multimedia Appendix 1 for specific prompts) to assist in extracting and optimizing information. For example, relationships between DSs and diseases recorded in MSKCC were expressed in text format; we used the LLM to extract disease and drug entities from these sentences and organize them into a structured format for integration and processing. The source data contained inconsistencies and noise, such as variations in how company addresses were recorded in the DSLD product data (eg, “U.S.A.,” “United States of America,” and “United States”) and nonsensical ingredient names like “8” or “%.” We addressed these issues by using an LLM to identify and unify the differing expressions. In addition, we developed filtering patterns specifically designed to remove nonsensical ingredient names, such as those with fewer than two characters or those consisting solely of numbers or punctuation. This approach ensured a more consistent and accurate dataset by standardizing key information and eliminating irrelevant entries. Specifically, we extracted the dietary supplement product (DSP) name, purpose, safety information, and company address information from LNHPD, along with the dietary supplement ingredient (DSI) name, source material information, and relationships between DSP and DSI. From DSLD, we extracted the DSP name, company address information, DSI name, and the relationship between DSP and DSI. In DSLD, names of DSIs appeared as duplicate records due to synonyms (eg, “Fiber gum acacia,” “Acacia gum extract,” and “Acacia”). We used the DSLD API to collate these synonyms and eliminated duplicates by grouping the synonyms of DSIs representing the same entity using the “Ingredient Group” classification in DSLD. From MSKCC, we extracted the DSI name, common name, background information, mechanism of action, disease name, drug name, symptom name, and the relationships between DSI and disease, DSI and symptom, and DSI and drug. After completing the information extraction and optimization, we used QuickUMLS (Georgetown IR Lab) [24] to map DSI entities, symptom entities, disease entities, and drug entities from the source resources to the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) [25] Concept Unique Identifier (CUI). To ensure mapping accuracy, we restricted each entity type based on UMLS semantic types (see Multimedia Appendix 1). The results of the QuickUMLS mapping included the matched UMLS CUI, term name, similarity, and whether the term was J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 3 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX preferred. When QuickUMLS returned multiple results, we used a prioritization strategy: first, results with a similarity of 1, marked as preferred; next, results with a similarity of 1, even if not marked as preferred; and finally, those marked as preferred with the highest similarity. If none of these conditions were met, a UMLS CUI was not assigned to the entity to ensure mapping accuracy. Data Integration for IDISK2.0 We used a greedy strategy to standardize entity terminology and integrate data from different sources. For each specific entity type, we initially selected a single database to initialize the entity vocabulary. Each specific entity was linked with a unique identifier to integrate entities from all databases, progressively refining the entity vocabulary. Specifically, for DSP, we started with data from LNHPD, integrating DSP entities from both LNHPD and DSLD. We consolidated DSP with the same product name and company name into a single unique entity. We unified entities with the same UMLS CUI or identical term names for DSI. Similarly, we consolidated entities with the same UMLS CUI or identical term names for disease, symptom, and drug entities. Each integrated entity was assigned a unique iDISK ID as its identifier in iDISK. Following this normalization procedure, we obtained a CSV file for each entity type, storing all standardized entity terms and their associated attributes. This allowed us to integrate the extracted knowledge from different databases to build iDISK2.0. In the knowledge graph (KG), the basic knowledge unit is a triplet, typically defined as “<head entity, relation, tail entity>,” indicating a relationship from the head entity to the tail entity in the KG. We mapped the head and tail nodes of the knowledge from the source databases to iDISK IDs, establishing triples composed of iDISK IDs and their relations. We then deduplicated all these triples to reduce noise in iDISK while ensuring quality. Finally, multiple rounds of manual quality checks were conducted. iDISK2.0 Deployment with Neo4j We deployed the iDISK2.0 using Neo4j [26], a well-designed graph database platform that allows for structured queries within graphs. Specifically, we stored the generated entities and relationships of iDISK in corresponding CSV files, which Neo4j used as input to create a KG instance automatically. This setup enables iDISK2.0 to be efficiently and flexibly interacted with and updated. iDISK2.0-Based RAG System Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of iDISK2.0-RAG. We began by preprocessing all entities within the iDISK2.0 database, creating embedding vectors for each entity name using OpenAI’s embedding model, text-embedding-3-small (Figure 2A). This step allowed us to construct the iDISK2.0 entity vector database, which serves as a foundation for efficient and accurate entity matching. When a user inputs a query, we first extract relevant entities from the question by using an LLM (GPT-4.0; Figure 2B), using tailored prompts (see Multimedia Appendix 1 for specific prompts). The entities identified through this process are then transformed into corresponding vectors using the same OpenAI embeddings model. In the current implementation, relationships between entities are not embedded directly. Instead, we leverage the fixed and well-defined set of 6 relationship types in iDISK2.0 (eg, is_effective_for and interacts_with) to assign relationships based on the queried entity pairs. For instance, DSI-disease pairs are always associated with the is_effective_for relationship. This approach ensures computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy in retrieving relationship-based queries. Figure 2. The overall design of the iDISK2.0-RAG (integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase—retrieval-augmented generation). LLM: large language model. J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 4 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX To match these identified entities with those in the iDISK2.0 database, we calculate the cosine similarity between the vectors of the identified entities and the vectors in the preprocessed iDISK2.0 entity vector database. Cosine similarity, a measure of similarity between two vectors in an inner product space, is calculated based on the cosine of the angle between them (detailed information on cosine similarity is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1). We then select the entity with the highest similarity score, provided that the score is 0.75 or higher, to ensure a reliable match between the identified entity and a corresponding entity in iDISK2.0. Once a match is identified, the corresponding nodes are converted into Cypher queries, allowing for interaction with iDISK2.0, which is deployed on the Neo4j graph database platform. This process retrieves the relevant graph context (Figure 2C), which is returned as structured data in the form of triples (Figure 2D). Finally, an LLM is used to integrate the user’s original question with the retrieved structured data (triples) and generate a comprehensive and contextually enhanced response (Figure 2E; see Multimedia Appendix 1 for specific prompts). Evaluation We extracted two types of questions from information on the MSKCC website: true-or-false questions and multiple-choice questions (MCQs). Specifically, we extracted information regarding the effectiveness of DSs and diseases and the interactions between DSs and drugs. This information was formatted into true-or-false questions and MCQs (473 true-or-false questions and 329 MCQs). To evaluate the performance of iDISK2.0-RAG and two LLMs (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0), we randomly selected 100 questions from each type (true-or-false questions and MCQs). These questions were answered by iDISK2.0-RAG, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4.0, and their accuracy was calculated based on the correct answers. This process was repeated 10 times using bootstrapping, resulting in each system answering 1000 true-or-false questions and 1000 MCQs. Accuracy metrics for each sampling iteration were then computed to derive the performance distribution. To ensure a fair evaluation, all knowledge from MSKCC was excluded from the retrieval stage in the RAG framework, preventing any influence of MSKCC-integrated knowledge on the test results. The rose plot was drawn using ChiPlot [27]. RAG-Enhanced Intelligent Visual Interfaces We developed a web-based graphical portal that allows users to access knowledge from iDISK2.0 intuitively and flexibly. Specifically, we built the backend (server-side) using Django (Django Software Foundation) [28], an advanced web framework based on Python (Python Software Foundation). The backend also hosts our iDISK2.0-RAG framework to provide users with more accurate retrieval information. The front end (web application side) is constructed using HTML5 and CSS, with JavaScript used for data interaction. Specifically, when the backend receives a query from the front end, the system first uses an LLM, such as GPT-4.0, to extract relevant entities from the user’s question through tailored prompts. These extracted entities are then matched with pretrained embedding information from a comprehensive entity vocabulary stored in the backend. Once a match is identified, the RAG system generates corresponding Cypher queries based on the matched entities. These Cypher queries are subsequently used to interact with iDISK2.0, which is deployed on the Neo4j graph database platform, to retrieve the relevant contextual subgraphs. The retrieved subgraphs provide structured data that are essential for generating an accurate response. In the final step, the LLM, guided by specific prompts, is used once again to transform the structured data retrieved by the RAG system into natural language, which is then returned to the front end’s dialogue interface. In cases where the entities mentioned in the user’s question cannot be successfully matched within iDISK2.0, the LLM (GPT-4.0) relies on its internal knowledge base to generate a corresponding answer, which is also delivered to the front end’s dialogue interface. This approach ensures that users receive comprehensive and contextually relevant responses, whether through structured data retrieval or the LLM’s generative capabilities. Ethical Considerations This study exclusively used publicly available datasets from trusted sources, including NMCD, MSKCC, DSLD, and LNHPD, for the development and evaluation of iDISK2.0. The study did not involve human participants, and no personal, clinical, or proprietary data were accessed or used. Due to these reasons, this study did not require ethics board approval according to the University of British Columbia's Behavioral Research Ethics Board (BREB) guidelines [29]. The data collection and integration processes adhered to the terms and conditions of the respective data providers. For enhanced security, strict protocols were followed during data processing to prevent the inadvertent inclusion of sensitive information. The deployment and use of iDISK2.0 also comply with applicable ethical and legal standards to safeguard the privacy and integrity of the data. Results The Integrated Dietary Supplements Knowledge Base 2.0 Through systematic collection and coordination, we ultimately obtained 279 concepts of DSIs, 270 concepts of rugs, 231 concepts of diseases, and 425 concepts of symptoms from the latest version of the MSKCC website. From DSLD, we acquired 4318 concepts of DSIs and 92,651 concepts of DSPs. In addition, from the Natural Health Products database, we gathered 4690 concepts of DSIs and 71,364 concepts of DSPs. After conducting data management and data cleaning, we integrated data from the 3 sources through biomedical entity term normalization and knowledge integration. The iDISK 2.0 encompasses 174,317 entities across 7 types (Table 1), including 8091 DSI entities; 163,806 DSP entities; 786 disease entities; 625 drug entities; 425 symptom entities; 567 dietary therapeutic class (TC) entities; and 17 system organ class (SOC) entities. In addition, there are 6 types of relationships among the 7 entity types (Table 1), including DSP-DSI, DSI-disease, DSI-symptom, DSI-drug, DSI-TC, and DSI-SOC. The iDISK 2.0 also includes 471,063 attributes (Table 1), comprising 163,806 DSP company names; 163,806 DSP company addresses; 65,097 DSP purposes; 63,623 DSP risks; 1289 DSI backgrounds; 1179 DSI safety profiles; 277 DSI mechanisms of action; 4277 DSI source materials; 3086 DSI-drug interaction ratings; and 4623 DSI-disease effectiveness ratings. An iDISK2.0-Based RAG System To address the potential hallucination issue present in current LLMs and thereby improve the accuracy of user responses, we developed an iDISK2.0-based RAG system. This system integrates the strengths of KG and LLMs to efficiently retrieve relevant knowledge from iDISK and use the language model to generate feedback and facilitate user interaction. We collected data from the MSKCC website regarding the effectiveness of dietary supplements and diseases and the interactions between DSs and drugs. From these data, we generated a total of 473 true-or-false questions and 329 MCQs. Specifically, there are 164 true-or-false questions, 123 MCQs related to DSs and diseases, and 309 true-or-false questions and 206 MCQs related to DSs and drugs. For instance, in the MSKCC database, there is a record stating, “Vitamin C is used to prevent and treat the common cold.” We used this record to generate corresponding true-or-false questions and MCQs for evaluative purposes. The true-or-false question derived from J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 6 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX this statement is “Is it true that Vitamin C is effective for the common cold?” with the correct answer being “True.” In addition, we developed an MCQ to assess understanding: “Out of the given list, which disease is Vitamin C effective for?” The provided options are “Bladder stones, Common cold, Stroke, Bleeding hemorrhoids, and None of the above.” The correct answer is “Common cold.” Figure 3 illustrates the performance (accuracy) of two LLMs (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0) and the iDISK2.0-RAG system on true-or-false questions and MCQs related to DSs and diseases, as well as DSs and drugs. The results show that iDISK2.0-RAG achieves over 95% accuracy across all question types: 99% (990/1000) for true-or-false questions on DSs and diseases, 99% (993/100) for MCQs on DSs and diseases, 97% (974/1000) for true-or-false questions on DSs and drugs, and 95% (948/1000) for MCQs on DSs and drugs. In contrast, the performance of the two LLMs is notably lower, with GPT-4.0 outperforming GPT-3.5: GPT-4.0 achieved 93% (929/1000) accuracy on true-or-false questions related to DSs and diseases, compared with 85% (854/1000) for GPT-3.5; 73% (727/1000) accuracy on MCQs related to DSs and diseases, compared with 43% (426/1000) for GPT-3.5; 62% (618/1000) accuracy on true-or-false questions related to DSs and drugs, compared with 40% (400/1000) for GPT-3.5; and 52% (517/1000) accuracy on MCQs related to DSs and drugs, compared with 46% (457/1000) for GPT-3.5. Despite GPT-4.0’s superior performance over GPT-3.5, both models fall significantly short of the accuracy achieved by iDISK2.0-RAG in these specialized domains. Figure 3. A User-Friendly Intelligent User Interface for Knowledge Retrieval Knowledge retrieval is one of the most common application scenarios of BKG in biomedical research. In recent years, LLMs have shown outstanding performance in NLP tasks but suffer from the issue of “hallucinations,” especially within specific domains [15-17]. To facilitate the use of iDISK2.0 by biomedical and clinical researchers in DS studies, we developed a web portal based on iDISK2.0-RAG as the backend. This RAG-based user interface allows users to input free-form text queries, generating meaningful biomedical text responses based on the established knowledge within iDISK2.0 to answer users’ questions. Figure 4A illustrates an example of a user query using free-form text. When the user inputs a question such as “Which disease is Omega-3 Fatty Acids effective for?” the user interface retrieves relevant knowledge from the iDISK2.0-RAG backend and returns the corresponding answer: “Omega-3 Fatty Acids are effective for: - Cardiovascular disease - Lupus - Cancer - Depression - High cholesterol - Atherosclerosis.” In cases where the user’s query cannot be answered directly from the iDISK2.0 knowledge base, the RAG framework informs the user that the specific knowledge is not available within iDISK2.0. Subsequently, the LLM within the framework attempts to answer the question based on its own knowledge, as depicted in Figure 4B. Discussion Principal Findings iDISK integrates information from 4 well-designed DS databases, ensuring it contains the most comprehensive DS-related information available. iDISK2.0 inherits this feature, maintaining its status as the most thorough DS information repository. As source resources are updated, much DS-related information has been upgraded. For instance, when the DSLD was first launched in 2013, it contained nearly 17,000 label entries; now, it includes nearly 190,000, an increase of more than tenfold in just a decade. In addition, many DS details have been corrected; for example, the older version of iDISK included an ingredient from DSLD labeled “Araceae,” which was inaccurate. In the latest version of DSLD, this ingredient has been removed. The observed reduction in the number of entities, such as in the “signs/symptoms” category, further reflects the enhanced data integration and noise reduction strategies used in iDISK2.0. By consolidating duplicate entries, refining entity definitions, and filtering out ambiguous or irrelevant information, iDISK2.0 significantly improves the overall quality of the knowledge base. Upgrading iDISK to iDISK2.0 is crucial to maintaining the accuracy and relevance of DS information. Without regular updates, the knowledge base could become outdated, leading to potential misinformation and inefficiencies in DS-related research and health care decisions. The continuous integration of the latest data and refined processes in iDISK2.0 helps mitigate these risks, ensuring that users have reliable, current information to make informed decisions about dietary supplements. LLMs like GPT-4.0 have significantly advanced the field of natural language processing. However, they still exhibit notable limitations, particularly in domain-specific applications such as DS information retrieval. A key challenge is their propensity for generating “hallucinations”—plausible yet incorrect information—stemming from their reliance on extensive but often unverified data sources [18]. This issue is particularly problematic when precision is critical. For example, our evaluation highlighted a case involving the use of coenzyme Q10, also known as ubiquinone, which is documented for its effectiveness in preventing migraines according to the MSKCC database. To test our system’s accuracy, we posed an MCQ: “Which disease is Ubiquinone effective for?” with options including migraines, hypertension, menstrual disorders, cholestasis, and none of the above, despite the correct answer being “Migraines,” based on robust evidence. However, GPT-4.0 J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 8 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX returned “Cholestasis” as the answer, even though only limited studies have explored the relationship between coenzyme Q10 and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy [30,31], with no definitive conclusions indicating its efficacy in this context. In contrast, numerous studies have established the effectiveness of coenzyme Q10 in the prevention and treatment of migraines [32-34]. This error underscores a critical concern: while LLMs have vast knowledge bases, they can still falter by either misinterpreting context or lacking explicit, well-established information. To address these challenges, we developed iDISK2.0 and integrated it with an RAG system. This integration combines the expansive knowledge base of LLMs with the precise, validated data from iDISK2.0, significantly reducing the risk of hallucinations. In testing, the RAG system, drawing from verified knowledge within iDISK2.0, consistently provided accurate answers, such as correctly identifying coenzyme Q10’s efficacy for migraines. While the current evaluation focused on true-or-false questions and MCQs derived from the MSKCC database to ensure controlled and reproducible testing, we recognize that real-world, open-ended queries often require more nuanced and context-sensitive responses. Our evaluation results indicate that iDISK2.0-RAG achieves over 95% accuracy when retrieving structured knowledge, whereas stand-alone LLMs perform substantially worse, with GPT-4.0 achieving only 62% (618/1000) accuracy in true-or-false questions and 52% (517/1000) in MCQs on DS-drug interactions. This underscores the importance of structured knowledge retrieval in mitigating misinformation. However, instances where the system relies solely on the LLM’s generative capabilities without sufficient retrieval support may still be prone to inaccuracies. To address the limitations of structured retrieval and enhance real-world applicability, we plan to develop a more comprehensive BKG that integrates diverse data sources beyond iDISK2. This expanded BKG will include biomedical literature to summarize the evidence [35], social media data to capture public perceptions, electronic health records to extract evidence of efficacy and safety [36-38], and postmarket surveillance data to address safety concerns [39]. By leveraging this holistic BKG, we aim to enhance the system’s capability to interpret and respond to real-world, open-ended queries. Future evaluations will incorporate open-ended questions collected from diverse user groups and assess both quantitative metrics, such as accuracy, and qualitative metrics, such as user satisfaction. This integrated approach will provide deeper insights into the system’s robustness and applicability. Further enhancing this solution, we incorporated a user-friendly interface with the iDISK2.0-RAG backend, allowing users to access accurate DS information through simple conversational text inputs. This setup not only facilitates better-informed decisions but also improves the overall user experience by ensuring the dissemination of the most accurate and current DS information. The necessity of this innovation is emphasized by the potential risks of relying solely on LLMs, which can propagate misinformation and lead to inefficiencies in both research and health care decisions. Moving forward, future research should focus on refining the interaction between LLMs and RAG systems. A potential avenue could involve mechanisms that allow LLMs to defer to the more reliable RAG output in cases where the evidence is more compelling. This approach would significantly enhance the accuracy and trustworthiness of artificial intelligence–generated responses in biomedical applications. Despite adopting stricter mapping and integration schemes compared with the older version of iDISK, some errors and noise still exist in the final results. These inaccuracies partly stem from the imprecise expressions in the source databases. In addition, errors arise when attempting to map entities from the source databases to UMLS CUIs for subsequent entity integration. The entity extraction and mapping software QuickUMLS sometimes returns incorrect results. For instance, the MSKCC database records an interaction between “Andrographis” and “Blood pressure-lowering drugs”: “Andrographis interacts with Blood pressure-lowering drugs.” When extracting entities from this knowledge, we extracted the drug entity “Blood pressure-lowering drugs” from the text. However, QuickUMLS mapped “Blood pressure-lowering drugs” to “Drug (UMLS CUI: C0013227),” resulting in incorrect mapping and introduction of errors into the integration process. Given the current limitations of this study, we plan to implement different strategies in the future to further reduce errors. For instance, we can introduce entity extraction techniques based on LLMs to extract DS-related information stored in text. For example, we may employ various prompt strategies, including rule-based prompts (eg, HealthPrompt [40]), hard-prompt learning [41], and soft-prompt learning [42]. In addition, we can leverage LLMs to batch-check entity extraction and mapping results and perform quality control on the integration outcomes. Recent research has highlighted the beneficial applications of BKGs in the medical field [7,43]. Furthermore, the rise of LLMs has spurred discussions on how best to combine the strengths of these models and BKGs [44]. In the future, besides continuously maintaining iDISK to ensure it remains the most up-to-date and comprehensive DS information resource, we will also explore ways to better assist users in using iDISK. For example, we plan to introduce knowledge graph embedding technology. By using graph-structured reasoning, we aim to offer reasonable predictions for knowledge not yet included in existing databases, thereby helping users discover more information. This approach will not only enhance the precision of user queries but also expand the scope of knowledge available to them. To ensure the long-term reliability and accuracy of iDISK2.0, we plan to establish a pipeline for annual updates integrating new data from trusted sources, such as NMCD, MSKCC, DSLD, and LNHPD. This includes automated data extraction, preprocessing, and stringent quality control measures. In addition, we will continuously adapt the system’s embedding strategy and retrieval mechanisms to align with the evolution of commercial LLMs. The open-source nature of iDISK2.0 will enable contributions from the research community, fostering collaborative improvements. Regular evaluations with updated test sets will further ensure the sustained performance of the RAG system. The modular design of the iDISK2.0-RAG framework facilitates its adaptability to other areas of health care beyond dietary supplements. BKGs have shown significant promise in facilitating complex biomedical processes such as drug J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 9 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX discovery [45]. By integrating domain-specific knowledge bases, such as those focused on drug interactions or general medical advice, the framework could be extended to address broader biomedical applications. For example, incorporating drug interaction databases or broader biomedical ontologies could enable the system to handle queries related to drug-drug interactions, disease management, and care pathways. Future work will explore these possibilities, evaluating the system’s performance across diverse domains and refining its capabilities to support a wider range of health care–related tasks. Conclusion In this study, we developed iDISK2.0, an updated repository for DS information, integrating data from NMCD, MSKCC, DSLD, and LNHPD. To address the limitations of LLMs, we introduced an RAG system combining LLMs with a BKG for accurate DS queries. iDISK2.0-RAG outperformed stand-alone LLMs, achieving over 95% accuracy. While some challenges remain with source data and entity mapping, future efforts will focus on improving entity extraction and quality control, ensuring iDISK2.0 continues to support informed DS decision-making. In addition, the adaptable design of the iDISK2.0-RAG framework offers significant potential for expansion into broader health care domains, such as drug interactions and general medical advice.
