## Methodology
Methods: We developed iDISK2.0 by integrating updated data from authoritative sources, including the Natural Medicines Comprehensive Database, the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center database, Dietary Supplement Label Database, and Licensed Natural Health Products Database, and applied advanced data cleaning and standardization techniques to reduce noise. The RAG system combined the retrieval power of a biomedical knowledge graph with the generative capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to address limitations of stand-alone LLMs, such as hallucination. The system retrieves contextually relevant subgraphs from iDISK2.0 based on user queries, enabling accurate and evidence-based responses through a user-friendly interface. We evaluated the system using true-or-false and multiple-choice questions derived from the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center database and compared its performance with stand-alone LLMs.

## Results
Results: iDISK2.0 integrates 174,317 entities across 7 categories, including 8091 dietary supplement ingredients; 163,806 dietary supplement products; 786 diseases; and 625 drugs, along with 6 types of relationships. The RAG system achieved an accuracy of 99% (990/1000) for true-or-false questions on DS effectiveness and 95% (948/100) for multiple-choice questions on DS-drug interactions, substantially outperforming stand-alone LLMs like GPT-4o (OpenAI), which scored 62% (618/1000) and 52% (517/1000) on these respective tasks. The user interface enabled efficient interaction, supporting free-form text input and providing accurate responses. Integration strategies minimized data noise, ensuring access to up-to-date, DS-related information.

## Conclusion
Conclusions: By integrating a robust knowledge graph with RAG and LLM technologies, iDISK2.0 addresses the critical limitations of stand-alone LLMs in DS information retrieval. This study highlights the importance of combining structured data with advanced artificial intelligence methods to improve accuracy and reduce misinformation in health care applications. Future work includes extending the framework to broader biomedical domains and improving evaluation with real-world, open-ended queries. ## Figures_tables_captions
Figure 1. An illustration of the study pipeline. DSLD: Dietary Supplement Label Database; NHP: Natural Health Products; iDISK2.0: integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase; LLM: large language model; iDISK2.0-RAG: integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase—retrieval-augmented generation. Data Collection and Preprocessing A total of 4 datasets were collected and preprocessed for the iDISK 2.0. Data from DSLD were downloaded directly from the data release, and the DSLD application programming interface (API) was used to enrich the dietary supplement-related information. Data from MSKCC were obtained after approval, using a web crawler to extract relevant information. LNHPD data were downloaded directly from the data release. After acquiring information from all sources, we converted them into a unified, structured format. The data of the NMCD used in the iDISK 2.0 were derived from information that already exists within iDISK. During the information extraction process, we used LLM (GPT-4) with the prompt (see Multimedia Appendix 1 for specific prompts) to assist in extracting and optimizing information. For example, relationships between DSs and diseases recorded in MSKCC were expressed in text format; we used the LLM to extract disease and drug entities from these sentences and organize them into a structured format for integration and processing. The source data contained inconsistencies and noise, such as variations in how company addresses were recorded in the DSLD product data (eg, “U.S.A.,” “United States of America,” and “United States”) and nonsensical ingredient names like “8” or “%.” We addressed these issues by using an LLM to identify and unify the differing expressions. In addition, we developed filtering patterns specifically designed to remove nonsensical ingredient names, such as those with fewer than two characters or those consisting solely of numbers or punctuation. This approach ensured a more consistent and accurate dataset by standardizing key information and eliminating irrelevant entries. Specifically, we extracted the dietary supplement product (DSP) name, purpose, safety information, and company address information from LNHPD, along with the dietary supplement ingredient (DSI) name, source material information, and relationships between DSP and DSI. From DSLD, we extracted the DSP name, company address information, DSI name, and the relationship between DSP and DSI. In DSLD, names of DSIs appeared as duplicate records due to synonyms (eg, “Fiber gum acacia,” “Acacia gum extract,” and “Acacia”). We used the DSLD API to collate these synonyms and eliminated duplicates by grouping the synonyms of DSIs representing the same entity using the “Ingredient Group” classification in DSLD. From MSKCC, we extracted the DSI name, common name, background information, mechanism of action, disease name, drug name, symptom name, and the relationships between DSI and disease, DSI and symptom, and DSI and drug. After completing the information extraction and optimization, we used QuickUMLS (Georgetown IR Lab) [24] to map DSI entities, symptom entities, disease entities, and drug entities from the source resources to the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) [25] Concept Unique Identifier (CUI). To ensure mapping accuracy, we restricted each entity type based on UMLS semantic types (see Multimedia Appendix 1). The results of the QuickUMLS mapping included the matched UMLS CUI, term name, similarity, and whether the term was J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 3 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX preferred. When QuickUMLS returned multiple results, we used a prioritization strategy: first, results with a similarity of 1, marked as preferred; next, results with a similarity of 1, even if not marked as preferred; and finally, those marked as preferred with the highest similarity. If none of these conditions were met, a UMLS CUI was not assigned to the entity to ensure mapping accuracy. Data Integration for IDISK2.0 We used a greedy strategy to standardize entity terminology and integrate data from different sources. For each specific entity type, we initially selected a single database to initialize the entity vocabulary. Each specific entity was linked with a unique identifier to integrate entities from all databases, progressively refining the entity vocabulary. Specifically, for DSP, we started with data from LNHPD, integrating DSP entities from both LNHPD and DSLD. We consolidated DSP with the same product name and company name into a single unique entity. We unified entities with the same UMLS CUI or identical term names for DSI. Similarly, we consolidated entities with the same UMLS CUI or identical term names for disease, symptom, and drug entities. Each integrated entity was assigned a unique iDISK ID as its identifier in iDISK. Following this normalization procedure, we obtained a CSV file for each entity type, storing all standardized entity terms and their associated attributes. This allowed us to integrate the extracted knowledge from different databases to build iDISK2.0. In the knowledge graph (KG), the basic knowledge unit is a triplet, typically defined as “<head entity, relation, tail entity>,” indicating a relationship from the head entity to the tail entity in the KG. We mapped the head and tail nodes of the knowledge from the source databases to iDISK IDs, establishing triples composed of iDISK IDs and their relations. We then deduplicated all these triples to reduce noise in iDISK while ensuring quality. Finally, multiple rounds of manual quality checks were conducted. iDISK2.0 Deployment with Neo4j We deployed the iDISK2.0 using Neo4j [26], a well-designed graph database platform that allows for structured queries within graphs. Specifically, we stored the generated entities and relationships of iDISK in corresponding CSV files, which Neo4j used as input to create a KG instance automatically. This setup enables iDISK2.0 to be efficiently and flexibly interacted with and updated. iDISK2.0-Based RAG System Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework of iDISK2.0-RAG. We began by preprocessing all entities within the iDISK2.0 database, creating embedding vectors for each entity name using OpenAI’s embedding model, text-embedding-3-small (Figure 2A). This step allowed us to construct the iDISK2.0 entity vector database, which serves as a foundation for efficient and accurate entity matching. When a user inputs a query, we first extract relevant entities from the question by using an LLM (GPT-4.0; Figure 2B), using tailored prompts (see Multimedia Appendix 1 for specific prompts). The entities identified through this process are then transformed into corresponding vectors using the same OpenAI embeddings model. In the current implementation, relationships between entities are not embedded directly. Instead, we leverage the fixed and well-defined set of 6 relationship types in iDISK2.0 (eg, is_effective_for and interacts_with) to assign relationships based on the queried entity pairs. For instance, DSI-disease pairs are always associated with the is_effective_for relationship. This approach ensures computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy in retrieving relationship-based queries. Figure 2. The overall design of the iDISK2.0-RAG (integrated Dietary Supplement Knowledgebase—retrieval-augmented generation). LLM: large language model. J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 4 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX To match these identified entities with those in the iDISK2.0 database, we calculate the cosine similarity between the vectors of the identified entities and the vectors in the preprocessed iDISK2.0 entity vector database. Cosine similarity, a measure of similarity between two vectors in an inner product space, is calculated based on the cosine of the angle between them (detailed information on cosine similarity is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1). We then select the entity with the highest similarity score, provided that the score is 0.75 or higher, to ensure a reliable match between the identified entity and a corresponding entity in iDISK2.0. Once a match is identified, the corresponding nodes are converted into Cypher queries, allowing for interaction with iDISK2.0, which is deployed on the Neo4j graph database platform. This process retrieves the relevant graph context (Figure 2C), which is returned as structured data in the form of triples (Figure 2D). Finally, an LLM is used to integrate the user’s original question with the retrieved structured data (triples) and generate a comprehensive and contextually enhanced response (Figure 2E; see Multimedia Appendix 1 for specific prompts). Evaluation We extracted two types of questions from information on the MSKCC website: true-or-false questions and multiple-choice questions (MCQs). Specifically, we extracted information regarding the effectiveness of DSs and diseases and the interactions between DSs and drugs. This information was formatted into true-or-false questions and MCQs (473 true-or-false questions and 329 MCQs). To evaluate the performance of iDISK2.0-RAG and two LLMs (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0), we randomly selected 100 questions from each type (true-or-false questions and MCQs). These questions were answered by iDISK2.0-RAG, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4.0, and their accuracy was calculated based on the correct answers. This process was repeated 10 times using bootstrapping, resulting in each system answering 1000 true-or-false questions and 1000 MCQs. Accuracy metrics for each sampling iteration were then computed to derive the performance distribution. To ensure a fair evaluation, all knowledge from MSKCC was excluded from the retrieval stage in the RAG framework, preventing any influence of MSKCC-integrated knowledge on the test results. The rose plot was drawn using ChiPlot [27]. RAG-Enhanced Intelligent Visual Interfaces We developed a web-based graphical portal that allows users to access knowledge from iDISK2.0 intuitively and flexibly. Specifically, we built the backend (server-side) using Django (Django Software Foundation) [28], an advanced web framework based on Python (Python Software Foundation). The backend also hosts our iDISK2.0-RAG framework to provide users with more accurate retrieval information. The front end (web application side) is constructed using HTML5 and CSS, with JavaScript used for data interaction. Specifically, when the backend receives a query from the front end, the system first uses an LLM, such as GPT-4.0, to extract relevant entities from the user’s question through tailored prompts. These extracted entities are then matched with pretrained embedding information from a comprehensive entity vocabulary stored in the backend. Once a match is identified, the RAG system generates corresponding Cypher queries based on the matched entities. These Cypher queries are subsequently used to interact with iDISK2.0, which is deployed on the Neo4j graph database platform, to retrieve the relevant contextual subgraphs. The retrieved subgraphs provide structured data that are essential for generating an accurate response. In the final step, the LLM, guided by specific prompts, is used once again to transform the structured data retrieved by the RAG system into natural language, which is then returned to the front end’s dialogue interface. In cases where the entities mentioned in the user’s question cannot be successfully matched within iDISK2.0, the LLM (GPT-4.0) relies on its internal knowledge base to generate a corresponding answer, which is also delivered to the front end’s dialogue interface. This approach ensures that users receive comprehensive and contextually relevant responses, whether through structured data retrieval or the LLM’s generative capabilities. Ethical Considerations This study exclusively used publicly available datasets from trusted sources, including NMCD, MSKCC, DSLD, and LNHPD, for the development and evaluation of iDISK2.0. The study did not involve human participants, and no personal, clinical, or proprietary data were accessed or used. Due to these reasons, this study did not require ethics board approval according to the University of British Columbia's Behavioral Research Ethics Board (BREB) guidelines [29]. The data collection and integration processes adhered to the terms and conditions of the respective data providers. For enhanced security, strict protocols were followed during data processing to prevent the inadvertent inclusion of sensitive information. The deployment and use of iDISK2.0 also comply with applicable ethical and legal standards to safeguard the privacy and integrity of the data. Results The Integrated Dietary Supplements Knowledge Base 2.0 Through systematic collection and coordination, we ultimately obtained 279 concepts of DSIs, 270 concepts of rugs, 231 concepts of diseases, and 425 concepts of symptoms from the latest version of the MSKCC website. From DSLD, we acquired 4318 concepts of DSIs and 92,651 concepts of DSPs. In addition, from the Natural Health Products database, we gathered 4690 concepts of DSIs and 71,364 concepts of DSPs. After conducting data management and data cleaning, we integrated data from the 3 sources through biomedical entity term normalization and knowledge integration. The iDISK 2.0 encompasses 174,317 entities across 7 types (Table 1), including 8091 DSI entities; 163,806 DSP entities; 786 disease entities; 625 drug entities; 425 symptom entities; 567 dietary therapeutic class (TC) entities; and 17 system organ class (SOC) entities. In addition, there are 6 types of relationships among the 7 entity types (Table 1), including DSP-DSI, DSI-disease, DSI-symptom, DSI-drug, DSI-TC, and DSI-SOC. An iDISK2.0-Based RAG System To address the potential hallucination issue present in current LLMs and thereby improve the accuracy of user responses, we developed an iDISK2.0-based RAG system. This system integrates the strengths of KG and LLMs to efficiently retrieve relevant knowledge from iDISK and use the language model to generate feedback and facilitate user interaction. We collected data from the MSKCC website regarding the effectiveness of dietary supplements and diseases and the interactions between DSs and drugs. From these data, we generated a total of 473 true-or-false questions and 329 MCQs. Specifically, there are 164 true-or-false questions, 123 MCQs related to DSs and diseases, and 309 true-or-false questions and 206 MCQs related to DSs and drugs. For instance, in the MSKCC database, there is a record stating, “Vitamin C is used to prevent and treat the common cold.” We used this record to generate corresponding true-or-false questions and MCQs for evaluative purposes. The true-or-false question derived from J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 6 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX this statement is “Is it true that Vitamin C is effective for the common cold?” with the correct answer being “True.” In addition, we developed an MCQ to assess understanding: “Out of the given list, which disease is Vitamin C effective for?” The provided options are “Bladder stones, Common cold, Stroke, Bleeding hemorrhoids, and None of the above.” The correct answer is “Common cold.” Figure 3 illustrates the performance (accuracy) of two LLMs (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0) and the iDISK2.0-RAG system on true-or-false questions and MCQs related to DSs and diseases, as well as DSs and drugs. The results show that iDISK2.0-RAG achieves over 95% accuracy across all question types: 99% (990/1000) for true-or-false questions on DSs and diseases, 99% (993/100) for MCQs on DSs and diseases, 97% (974/1000) for true-or-false questions on DSs and drugs, and 95% (948/1000) for MCQs on DSs and drugs. In contrast, the performance of the two LLMs is notably lower, with GPT-4.0 outperforming GPT-3.5: GPT-4.0 achieved 93% (929/1000) accuracy on true-or-false questions related to DSs and diseases, compared with 85% (854/1000) for GPT-3.5; 73% (727/1000) accuracy on MCQs related to DSs and diseases, compared with 43% (426/1000) for GPT-3.5; 62% (618/1000) accuracy on true-or-false questions related to DSs and drugs, compared with 40% (400/1000) for GPT-3.5; and 52% (517/1000) accuracy on MCQs related to DSs and drugs, compared with 46% (457/1000) for GPT-3.5. Despite GPT-4.0’s superior performance over GPT-3.5, both models fall significantly short of the accuracy achieved by iDISK2.0-RAG in these specialized domains. Figure 3. A User-Friendly Intelligent User Interface for Knowledge Retrieval Knowledge retrieval is one of the most common application scenarios of BKG in biomedical research. In recent years, LLMs have shown outstanding performance in NLP tasks but suffer from the issue of “hallucinations,” especially within specific domains [15-17]. To facilitate the use of iDISK2.0 by biomedical and clinical researchers in DS studies, we developed a web portal based on iDISK2.0-RAG as the backend. This RAG-based user interface allows users to input free-form text queries, generating meaningful biomedical text responses based on the established knowledge within iDISK2.0 to answer users’ questions. Figure 4A illustrates an example of a user query using free-form text. When the user inputs a question such as “Which disease is Omega-3 Fatty Acids effective for?” the user interface retrieves relevant knowledge from the iDISK2.0-RAG backend and returns the corresponding answer: “Omega-3 Fatty Acids are effective for: - Cardiovascular disease - Lupus - Cancer - Depression - High cholesterol - Atherosclerosis.” In cases where the user’s query cannot be answered directly from the iDISK2.0 knowledge base, the RAG framework informs the user that the specific knowledge is not available within iDISK2.0. Subsequently, the LLM within the framework attempts to answer the question based on its own knowledge, as depicted in Figure 4B. Discussion Principal Findings iDISK integrates information from 4 well-designed DS databases, ensuring it contains the most comprehensive DS-related information available. iDISK2.0 inherits this feature, maintaining its status as the most thorough DS information repository. As source resources are updated, much DS-related information has been upgraded. For instance, when the DSLD was first launched in 2013, it contained nearly 17,000 label entries; now, it includes nearly 190,000, an increase of more than tenfold in just a decade. In addition, many DS details have been corrected; for example, the older version of iDISK included an ingredient from DSLD labeled “Araceae,” which was inaccurate. In the latest version of DSLD, this ingredient has been removed. The observed reduction in the number of entities, such as in the “signs/symptoms” category, further reflects the enhanced data integration and noise reduction strategies used in iDISK2.0. By consolidating duplicate entries, refining entity definitions, and filtering out ambiguous or irrelevant information, iDISK2.0 significantly improves the overall quality of the knowledge base. Upgrading iDISK to iDISK2.0 is crucial to maintaining the accuracy and relevance of DS information. Without regular updates, the knowledge base could become outdated, leading to potential misinformation and inefficiencies in DS-related research and health care decisions. The continuous integration of the latest data and refined processes in iDISK2.0 helps mitigate these risks, ensuring that users have reliable, current information to make informed decisions about dietary supplements. LLMs like GPT-4.0 have significantly advanced the field of natural language processing. However, they still exhibit notable limitations, particularly in domain-specific applications such as DS information retrieval. A key challenge is their propensity for generating “hallucinations”—plausible yet incorrect information—stemming from their reliance on extensive but often unverified data sources [18]. This issue is particularly problematic when precision is critical. For example, our evaluation highlighted a case involving the use of coenzyme Q10, also known as ubiquinone, which is documented for its effectiveness in preventing migraines according to the MSKCC database. To test our system’s accuracy, we posed an MCQ: “Which disease is Ubiquinone effective for?” with options including migraines, hypertension, menstrual disorders, cholestasis, and none of the above, despite the correct answer being “Migraines,” based on robust evidence. However, GPT-4.0 J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 8 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX returned “Cholestasis” as the answer, even though only limited studies have explored the relationship between coenzyme Q10 and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy [30,31], with no definitive conclusions indicating its efficacy in this context. In contrast, numerous studies have established the effectiveness of coenzyme Q10 in the prevention and treatment of migraines [32-34]. This error underscores a critical concern: while LLMs have vast knowledge bases, they can still falter by either misinterpreting context or lacking explicit, well-established information. To address these challenges, we developed iDISK2.0 and integrated it with an RAG system. This integration combines the expansive knowledge base of LLMs with the precise, validated data from iDISK2.0, significantly reducing the risk of hallucinations. In testing, the RAG system, drawing from verified knowledge within iDISK2.0, consistently provided accurate answers, such as correctly identifying coenzyme Q10’s efficacy for migraines. While the current evaluation focused on true-or-false questions and MCQs derived from the MSKCC database to ensure controlled and reproducible testing, we recognize that real-world, open-ended queries often require more nuanced and context-sensitive responses. Our evaluation results indicate that iDISK2.0-RAG achieves over 95% accuracy when retrieving structured knowledge, whereas stand-alone LLMs perform substantially worse, with GPT-4.0 achieving only 62% (618/1000) accuracy in true-or-false questions and 52% (517/1000) in MCQs on DS-drug interactions. This underscores the importance of structured knowledge retrieval in mitigating misinformation. However, instances where the system relies solely on the LLM’s generative capabilities without sufficient retrieval support may still be prone to inaccuracies. To address the limitations of structured retrieval and enhance real-world applicability, we plan to develop a more comprehensive BKG that integrates diverse data sources beyond iDISK2. This expanded BKG will include biomedical literature to summarize the evidence [35], social media data to capture public perceptions, electronic health records to extract evidence of efficacy and safety [36-38], and postmarket surveillance data to address safety concerns [39]. By leveraging this holistic BKG, we aim to enhance the system’s capability to interpret and respond to real-world, open-ended queries. Future evaluations will incorporate open-ended questions collected from diverse user groups and assess both quantitative metrics, such as accuracy, and qualitative metrics, such as user satisfaction. This integrated approach will provide deeper insights into the system’s robustness and applicability. Further enhancing this solution, we incorporated a user-friendly interface with the iDISK2.0-RAG backend, allowing users to access accurate DS information through simple conversational text inputs. This setup not only facilitates better-informed decisions but also improves the overall user experience by ensuring the dissemination of the most accurate and current DS information. The necessity of this innovation is emphasized by the potential risks of relying solely on LLMs, which can propagate misinformation and lead to inefficiencies in both research and health care decisions. Moving forward, future research should focus on refining the interaction between LLMs and RAG systems. A potential avenue could involve mechanisms that allow LLMs to defer to the more reliable RAG output in cases where the evidence is more compelling. This approach would significantly enhance the accuracy and trustworthiness of artificial intelligence–generated responses in biomedical applications. Despite adopting stricter mapping and integration schemes compared with the older version of iDISK, some errors and noise still exist in the final results. These inaccuracies partly stem from the imprecise expressions in the source databases. In addition, errors arise when attempting to map entities from the source databases to UMLS CUIs for subsequent entity integration. The entity extraction and mapping software QuickUMLS sometimes returns incorrect results. For instance, the MSKCC database records an interaction between “Andrographis” and “Blood pressure-lowering drugs”: “Andrographis interacts with Blood pressure-lowering drugs.” When extracting entities from this knowledge, we extracted the drug entity “Blood pressure-lowering drugs” from the text. However, QuickUMLS mapped “Blood pressure-lowering drugs” to “Drug (UMLS CUI: C0013227),” resulting in incorrect mapping and introduction of errors into the integration process. Given the current limitations of this study, we plan to implement different strategies in the future to further reduce errors. For instance, we can introduce entity extraction techniques based on LLMs to extract DS-related information stored in text. For example, we may employ various prompt strategies, including rule-based prompts (eg, HealthPrompt [40]), hard-prompt learning [41], and soft-prompt learning [42]. In addition, we can leverage LLMs to batch-check entity extraction and mapping results and perform quality control on the integration outcomes. Recent research has highlighted the beneficial applications of BKGs in the medical field [7,43]. Furthermore, the rise of LLMs has spurred discussions on how best to combine the strengths of these models and BKGs [44]. In the future, besides continuously maintaining iDISK to ensure it remains the most up-to-date and comprehensive DS information resource, we will also explore ways to better assist users in using iDISK. For example, we plan to introduce knowledge graph embedding technology. By using graph-structured reasoning, we aim to offer reasonable predictions for knowledge not yet included in existing databases, thereby helping users discover more information. This approach will not only enhance the precision of user queries but also expand the scope of knowledge available to them. To ensure the long-term reliability and accuracy of iDISK2.0, we plan to establish a pipeline for annual updates integrating new data from trusted sources, such as NMCD, MSKCC, DSLD, and LNHPD. This includes automated data extraction, preprocessing, and stringent quality control measures. In addition, we will continuously adapt the system’s embedding strategy and retrieval mechanisms to align with the evolution of commercial LLMs. The open-source nature of iDISK2.0 will enable contributions from the research community, fostering collaborative improvements. Regular evaluations with updated test sets will further ensure the sustained performance of the RAG system. The modular design of the iDISK2.0-RAG framework facilitates its adaptability to other areas of health care beyond dietary supplements. BKGs have shown significant promise in facilitating complex biomedical processes such as drug J Med Internet Res 2025 | vol. 27 | e67677 | p. 9 (page number not for citation purposes) Hou et al JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH XSL•FO RenderX discovery [45]. By integrating domain-specific knowledge bases, such as those focused on drug interactions or general medical advice, the framework could be extended to address broader biomedical applications. For example, incorporating drug interaction databases or broader biomedical ontologies could enable the system to handle queries related to drug-drug interactions, disease management, and care pathways. Future work will explore these possibilities, evaluating the system’s performance across diverse domains and refining its capabilities to support a wider range of health care–related tasks. Conclusion In this study, we developed iDISK2.0, an updated repository for DS information, integrating data from NMCD, MSKCC, DSLD, and LNHPD. To address the limitations of LLMs, we introduced an RAG system combining LLMs with a BKG for accurate DS queries. iDISK2.0-RAG outperformed stand-alone LLMs, achieving over 95% accuracy. While some challenges remain with source data and entity mapping, future efforts will focus on improving entity extraction and quality control, ensuring iDISK2.0 continues to support informed DS decision-making. In addition, the adaptable design of the iDISK2.0-RAG framework offers significant potential for expansion into broader health care domains, such as drug interactions and general medical advice. ## Introduction
Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are profoundly transforming the medical domain by leveraging their strong generalization capabilities and ability to model complex data patterns. In medical text processing and clinical decision support, models such as ClinicalBERT (Huang et al., 2019b) and BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020) have demonstrated signiﬁcant advantages in analyzing electronic health records (EHRs), mining medical literature, and supporting automated clinical consultation systems. In medical visual question answering, multimodal systems built upon visual transformers integrate medical images with natural language descriptions to assist clinicians in diagnostic decision-making. More broadly, multimodal models have been explored to jointly integrate EHRs, genetic data, medical images, and medical time-series data, providing technical foundations for precision medicine. Concurrently, the collection and analysis of medical time-series data, such as physiological signals like electrocardiograms (ECG) and elec- ∗Corresponding author. E-mail address: (H. Xiao). troencephalograms (EEG), are playing an increasingly vital role in clinical diagnosis, disease prediction, and health management. These tasks are diverse, encompassing classiﬁcation (Lin et al., 2019), prediction (Piccialli et al., 2021), anomaly detection (Pereira & Silveira, 2019), and semantic segmentation (Woodbridge et al., 2011). Traditionally, these tasks were often addressed using Classical Signal Processing Techniques. For instance, Huang et al. (2019a) proposed integrating the ARIMA model with the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to decompose and forecast ECG signals, signiﬁcantly enhancing shortterm prediction accuracy. Zhang et al. (2003) utilized the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) for the multi-scale decomposition of disease outbreak time series, achieving early warning by detecting local energy anomalies. However, these classic statistical models rely on a strong stationarity assumption, making it challenging to handle the pervasive non-stationarity, noise ﬂuctuations, and abrupt events found in medical signals (Acharya et al., 2017). ## Conclusion
Conclusion This survey systematically examines the research progress and development trajectory of multimodal medical temporal LLMs, providing a comprehensive overview of their theoretical foundations, technical methodologies, and clinical applications. In the theoretical foundation section, we ﬁrst survey the core architectures and pre-training strategies of general-purpose temporal large models, highlighting the evolution of key techniques such as temporal extensions of Transformers and self-supervised learning paradigms. These theories serve as the basis for domain-speciﬁc adaptations and innovations in the medical ﬁeld. Addressing the inherently multimodal nature of medical data, we integrate major medical time-series datasets including MIMIC-IV, VitalDB, and PhysioNet, and propose a dual classiﬁcation framework based on task type and signal modality. By analyzing diﬀerences in sampling frequency, signal type, annotation quality, and other dataset features, we construct a comprehensive data-task mapping system that provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating model training performance. At the methodological level, we investigate four core aspects. First, regarding backbone network selection and optimization, we analyze the adaptability and limitations of diﬀerent base models for medical time-series processing. Second, in architecture design, we highlight innovations for enabling semantic interaction between signals and text, including advanced attention mechanisms and optimized feature projection strategies. Third, for alignment mechanisms, we summarize the application of contrastive learning, prompt engineering, and related approaches, while exploring their intrinsic contributions to enhancing model reasoning. Finally, in loss function design, we examine balancing strategies in multi-task learning and the role of joint optimization in improving downstream performance in diagnostic prediction and report generation. This survey also addresses key challenges in clinical deployment. At the data level, challenges include standardizing heterogeneous sources, mitigating class imbalance, and safeguarding data privacy. At the model level, issues involve computational eﬃciency, interpretability, and generalization on out-of-distribution data. Clinically, reliability validation and integration with healthcare systems remain major obstacles. We Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 18 X. Given that medical time-series analysis is still in an exploratory stage, its diversity, complexity, and real-time nature present unprecedented opportunities and challenges for clinical diagnosis, disease prediction, and precision medicine. In response to these challenges, the main contributions of this survey are as follows: 1. We systematically reviewed methods for processing medical time series data using large language models for the ﬁrst time. By incorporating the latest research, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of their model architectures, feature encoding, cross-modal alignment, and task adaptation methods, thereby ﬁlling the gap left by existing reviews that predominantly focus on text-based tasks. 2. We innovatively categorized scattered research ﬁndings into two primary task types: text diagnosis tasks and signal processing tasks, which clearly illustrates the application logic and technical diﬀerFig. 1. The application of LLMs in various medical ﬁelds. ences of LLMs in various medical scenarios. Based on task type, data modality, and downstream application, this survey establishes a systematic classiﬁcation framework that not only distinguishes between clinical diagnosis/report generation tasks and time-series signal analysis tasks but also evaluates the performance, advantages, and limitations of diﬀerent backbone models and loss functions. 3. By conducting an in-depth analysis used by LLMs for medical timeseries tasks, we propose a forward-looking technical roadmap that offers valuable guidance for researchers and practitioners. This survey also highlights the importance of deeply integrating pretrained LLMs with medical time-series analysis techniques. This fusion promises to enable more eﬃcient and accurate real-time clinical warning systems in the future, leading to revolutionary advancements in clinical decision support, resource optimization, and personalized treatment strategies. 2. Medical time series data Medical time series data originate from diverse clinical and realworld sources, including intensive care unit (ICU) monitoring systems, EHRs, wearable devices, and temporally indexed measurements embedded in clinical reports. Compared with conventional time-series data, medical time series exhibit several distinctive characteristics that directly inﬂuence model design and evaluation. First, medical data often present heterogeneous temporal sampling patterns, ranging from regularly sampled physiological signals (e.g., ECG) to highly irregular measurements such as laboratory tests collected during hospitalization. Based on data acquisition settings, temporal characteristics, and downstream task requirements, medical time-series datasets can be broadly categorized into three groups: ICU and EHR data, wearable and remote monitoring data, and specialized task-oriented datasets (Fig. 2). This taxonomy clariﬁes the application scenarios and structural properties of diﬀerent data sources and establishes a coherent foundation for subsequent discussions on model selection and task adaptation. 2.1. ICU and EHR data Representative ICU and EHR datasets commonly used in large-scale multivariate time-series analysis are summarized in Table 2. MIMICIII (Johnson et al., 2016) and MIMIC-IV (Johnson et al., 2023) provide comprehensive clinical records, including vital signs, laboratory measurements, clinical notes, and diagnostic codes, covering approximately 50,000 and 60,000 patients, respectively. Their long temporal coverage and diverse variable sets have made them standard benchmarks for risk prediction tasks such as mortality, sepsis, and delirium, as well as for multi-task and representation learning studies. The eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) (Pollard et al., 2018) aggregates ICU data from over 300 hospitals, enabling systematic evaluation of crossinstitutional generalization, albeit at the cost of increased heterogeneity in data quality and annotation standards. In contrast, HiRID (Yèche et al., 2021) focuses on high-resolution ICU monitoring, providing dense waveform recordings and detailed event annotations across more than 34,000 admissions, thereby supporting ﬁne-grained anomaly detection and interpretable modeling. 2.2. Wearable devices and remote monitoring data Wearable and remote monitoring datasets (Table 3) enable continuous and unobtrusive physiological signal acquisition in naturalistic environments, supporting long-term monitoring for chronic disease Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 3 X. The OhioT1DM dataset (Marling & Bunescu, 2020) provides eight weeks of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data for 12 adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), accompanied by precise insulin administration records. Despite its limited cohort size, OhioT1DM has become a benchmark for glucose forecasting due to its high inter-subject variability, motivating research on personalized and adaptive control strategies. VitalDB (Lee et al., 2022), by contrast, oﬀers high-resolution perioperative waveforms spanning more than 70 physiological signals, making it suitable for intraoperative event detection and real-time alerting. However, its single-center origin and short monitoring duration limit its applicability for longitudinal outcome analysis and cross-site validation. Other datasets, such as WESAD (Schmidt et al., 2018), PPG-DaLiA (Reiss et al., 2019), and TROIKA (Zhang et al., 2014), provide valuable real-world multimodal signals for emotion recognition, heart-rate estimation, and activity analysis, despite relatively narrow application scopes. 2.3. Specialized task data Specialized task-oriented datasets provide high-quality annotations for domain-speciﬁc problems such as electrocardiography, sleep analysis, and neurophysiology, enabling the development and benchmarking of ﬁne-grained signal modeling approaches. As summarized in Table 4, the QT Database provides precise P/QRS/T wave annotations and serves as a stringent benchmark for ECG segmentation and localization tasks (Laguna et al., 1997). The MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database contains dual-lead ECG recordings with expert-labeled arrhythmia events and remains widely used for arrhythmia detection and classiﬁcation, despite inconsistencies in lead conﬁguration and annotation standards (Moody & Mark, 1992). For sleep-related studies, the Apnea-ECG and Sleep-EDF datasets provide annotated ECG and multimodal polysomnography signals, supporting sleep apnea detection and sleep stage classiﬁcation (Kemp et al., 2000). In neurophysiology, the CHB-MIT Epilepsy Database oﬀers precisely annotated multichannel EEG recordings of seizure events in pediatric patients, constituting a valuable resource for seizure prediction and abnormal event detection (Guttag, 2010). 3. Foundations of LLMs for time series analysis LLMs have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in natural language understanding, logical reasoning, and general representation learning. Motivated by these profound advances, researchers are actively exploring the potential for the transfer of LLMs’ powerful generalization ability to the domain of time series analysis. In this evolving landscape, current research primarily involves two distinct model paradigms: 1. Time Series Foundation Models: These models are typically constructed upon the Transformer architecture and leverage self-supervised learning for pre-training on large-scale heterogeneous time series data. This approach enables them to achieve robust generalization and multitask adaptability (Gao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b). The core principle underpinning TSFMs is the unsupervised pre-training on massive, multisource time series data to acquire universal temporal representations. 2. LLMs-based Time Series Methods: These methods directly utilize existing pre-trained Large Language Models by transforming the raw time series into textual or tokenized representations. To maintain terminological clarity and avoid ambiguity, this chapter will uniformly employ the term “LLMs” to denote general-purpose pre-trained language models, while “time series foundation models” will speciﬁcally refer to models explicitly designed for temporal data. This chapter is structured to introduce the theoretical foundations, architectural characteristics, and representative methods of both Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs-based Time Series Approaches. 3.1. Time series foundation models As illustrated in Fig. 3, large-scale time series foundation models predominantly adopt either Decoder-Only or Encoder-Decoder architectures. Decoder-Only models follow the autoregressive generation paradigm popularized by GPT, relying on a Transformer decoder with masked self-attention. They are well suited for sequential forecasting Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 4 X. Liu et al. In contrast, Encoder-Decoder architectures employ a two-stage design, where an encoder ﬁrst constructs a global representation of the input sequence and a decoder generates outputs conditioned on this representation. This paradigm is particularly eﬀective for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation, alignment, and reconstruction. Pure Encoder-Only architectures are relatively uncommon in large-scale time series modeling, as their lack of generative capability limits their applicability to feature extraction for downstream classiﬁcation or regression. Although both Decoder-Only and EncoderDecoder models are built upon the Transformer framework, they diﬀer fundamentally in attention masking, output interfaces, and task adaptation strategies. These architectural diﬀerences lead to distinct strengths and limitations across time series application scenarios, especially in medical contexts where both local dynamics and global dependencies are critical. 3.1.1. Decoder-only Decoder-Only models adopt a unidirectional attention mechanism and generate future values autoregressively by modeling chained conditional probabilities 𝑃(𝑥𝑡∣𝑥<𝑡 ). This design naturally aligns with forecasting tasks and enables eﬃcient next-step prediction. Representative Fig. 3. Liu et al. unifying prediction, imputation, and anomaly detection under a nexttime-step generation objective. Rasul et al. (2023) adopts the pure decoder-only architecture of LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023) and inherits its positional encoding design, adapting this framework to timeseries modeling. Speciﬁcally, Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE) embeds relative positional information through vector rotations in complex space, thereby facilitating the modeling of long-range dependencies. The primary advantage of Decoder-Only architectures lies in their strong autoregressive generalization. By framing diverse tasks as conditional sequence generation, these models often exhibit impressive zero-shot transfer across domains. TimeGPT, for example, demonstrates robust performance in ﬁnancial forecasting and power load prediction without task-speciﬁc retraining. However, this paradigm has notable limitations in medical signal processing. Physiological time series often contain high-frequency noise and abrupt anomalies, making autoregressive generation sensitive to early prediction errors that can propagate and amplify noise. Moreover, unidirectional attention restricts access to full-sequence context, limiting performance in diagnostic tasks that require holistic modeling of long-range pathological patterns. While Decoder-Only models are eﬃcient for real-time, single-step prediction, they are less suitable for tasks demanding robust integration of global and local dependencies. 3.1.2. Encoder-decoder As shown in Figure3, the decoder-only and encoder-decoder paradigms diﬀer fundamentally in how they process input history and global context, resulting in a distinct suitability for medical time series tasks. Decoder-Only models generate subsequent values autoregressively, relying exclusively on masked self-attention over previously generated outputs. This design makes them eﬃcient for continuous vital sign inference tasks, such as ECG waveform continuation or blood glucose trend prediction. In contrast, Encoder-Decoder architectures ﬁrst encode the entire input sequence using unmasked self-attention to construct a global representation. During decoding, cross-attention mechanisms integrate this global representation with the autoregressive generation process. This two-stage process is particularly eﬀective for sequence-to-sequence tasks, including ECG-to-ABP signal reconstruction, missing-value imputation, and multi-task learning across heterogeneous clinical settings. Several foundational models highlight the advantages of the Encoder-Decoder framework. For instance, TimesNet (Wu et al., 2023a) the encoder to capture trend and periodic components in physiological signals. MOMENT is pretrained on diverse medical signals, enabling its encoder to learn robust shared features for downstream ﬁne-tuning. UniTS (Gao et al., 2024) adapts ﬂexibly to prediction, imputation, and classiﬁcation by preﬁxing inputs with task identiﬁers (e.g. FORECAST, IMPUTE). Collectively, these models demonstrate the EncoderDecoder architecture’s ability to capture both short-term and long-term dependencies, align multimodal signals, and support parameter-eﬃcient multi-task learning. However, this paradigm also has limitations, including high computational and memory demands, susceptibility to error propagation in noisy data, and heavy reliance on high-quality annotated datasets. These factors constrain its broader application in low-resource annotation settings and real-time clinical scenarios. 3.2. LLMs-based time series methods Beyond architectures explicitly designed for time series modeling, a growing body of work explores an alternative direction: repurposing pre-trained LLMs for time series analysis (Cheng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2023b). Instead of training specialized temporal encoders from scratch, these approaches exploit the representation learning and reasoning capabilities of LLMs by converting time series into textual or symbolic forms and designing task-speciﬁc prompting strategies (Cao et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Representative models of this paradigm shift across domains (Ding et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024) as illustrated in 4, highlight a crucial distinction: these approaches no longer construct dedicated temporal encoders and decoders. Instead, they treat time series as a “new language,” thereby integrating time series analysis with recent advancements in natural language modeling (Kurisinkel et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024, 2023). For example, Time-LLM (Jin et al., 2024) introduces input reprogramming that maps time series segments into textual prototypes. Through a Prompt-as-Preﬁx mechanism, it feeds transformed sequence data alongside prompt tokens into a frozen LLM, guiding temporal reasoning without modifying the backbone architecture. This approach surpasses many specialized models across diverse prediction tasks, exhibiting particularly strong generalization in few-shot and zero-shot scenarios.Similarly, LLM4TS (Chang et al., 2025) adopts a two-stage ﬁnetuning framework: (1) distribution alignment pre-training, where the LLM is adapted to temporal data distributions to mitigate discrepancies with textual patterns, and (2) task-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning for downstream applications. Moreover, it employs a multi-scale aggregation mechanism to capture information across diﬀerent temporal granularities, thereby improving expressive capacity. Empirical results show that LLM4TS (Chang et al., 2025) not only outperforms models trained from scratch when data is abundant, but also achieves state-of-the-art performance under few-shot settings. By leveraging LLMs’ inherent strengths in representation learning and pattern induction, these methods substantially reduce reliance on large-scale labeled time series datasets. Nonetheless, challenges persist: the structural and multi-scale mismatches between time series and natural language limit direct transferability. Hence, eﬀective alignment strategies, such as input transformation, semantic guidance, or ﬁnetuning-remain essential. Overall, existing studies demonstrate that, with careful adaptation, pre-trained LLMs can yield signiﬁcant improvements in forecasting and analysis tasks (Kim et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025). 4. LLMs-based time series methods for medical time series LLMs have demonstrated remarkable representational capabilities and strong performance in general time series modeling, medical text analysis, and medical image interpretation.These advances naturally raise an important scientiﬁc question: whether the powerful generalpurpose representation abilities possessed by LLMs can be eﬀectively transferred to the ﬁeld of medical time series analysis, so as to provide more eﬃcient and accurate support for essential clinical tasks such as disease risk prediction, abnormal waveform detection, and diagnostic decision making?It is important to recognize that the general sequential modeling strategies described in Chapter 3 still face signiﬁcant limitations when dealing with the characteristic challenges of medical signals. Including high noise levels, long-term dependencies, and complex multimodal relationships. In this context, this chapter will conduct an in-depth examination of specialized technical approaches designed for medical time series.The discussion will focus on three major mechanisms: cross modal alignment between physiological signals and clinical text, prompt engineering frameworks guided by medical knowledge, and domain adaptive feature reconstruction strategies.The key methodological components include optimization of the backbone network of large language models, design of cross modal alignment strategies, construction of information fusion mechanisms, customization of loss functions, and selection of clinically relevant evaluation metrics. 4.1. Framework on medical time series LLMs Although the aforementioned general temporal models achieve strong performance in multi-task and cross-domain settings, they continue to face several critical challenges when applied to medical signals. First, signals such as ECG and ABP acquired from medical Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 6 X. Liu et al. Fig. 4. Representative methods for applying LLMs to time-series analysis. This study categorizes them into four main application domains: Industry & Infrastructure, Finance & Economics, General Method, and Healthcare.. monitoring devices are frequently contaminated by high-frequency motion artifacts, baseline drift, and instrument noise. General-purpose models typically lack specialized denoising mechanisms and robustness enhancements, rendering them prone to amplifying noise and compromising prediction stability. For example, Lahmiri’s comparative study highlights the advantages of wavelet methods in preserving ECG edges and details (Lahmiri, 2014). Without such preprocessing mechanisms, current Transformer-based models struggle to sustain high accuracy under noisy conditions.Second, many disease progression processes exhibit long-range dependencies ranging from seconds to hours, such as precursor signals of arrhythmia events or epileptic seizures. Decoder-Only architectures, constrained by their unidirectional autoregressive generation mechanism, suﬀer from exponential error accumulation during multi-step predictions. Although autoregressive models such as AR/ARIMA excel in short-term forecasting and linear correlation modeling, they fall short in capturing anomalous patterns spanning extended time intervals within physiological time-series tasks. This limitation stems from their inability to account for nonlinearity, nonstationarity, multivariate interactions, long-range physiological time series tasks, these traditional models struggle to capture anomalous patterns spanning extended time intervals due to factors like nonlinearity, non-stationarity, multivariate interactions, long-range dependencies, and abnormal disturbances. Limitations such as restricted lag orders, challenging parameter estimation, sensitivity to anomalies, and poor extrapolation capabilities may render them ineﬀective (Haderlein et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024). Furthermore, clinical decision-making frequently requires integrating multimodal information, including physiological signals, medical images, and electronic health record (EHR) texts. However, generalpurpose Transformers lack cross-modal alignment mechanisms informed by medical knowledge, limiting their ability to capture semantic relationships across modalities. As noted by Liu et al., specialized fusion strategies are necessary to prevent information loss when integrating structured and unstructured medical data (Stahlschmidt et al., 2022); applying general-purpose models directly often results in suboptimal diagnostic performance. Although the Encoder-Decoder architecture provides modeling advantages, it depends heavily on large volumes of high-quality annotated data, which are costly to obtain in real clinical environments. Moreover, such models suﬀer from limited interpretability, as their decision processes often lack transparency, making it diﬃcult to provide credible support for clinicians. Research by Tjoa and Guan on medical AI interpretability underscores that insuﬃcient model transparency severely restricts clinical adoption (Tjoa & Guan, 2020). Using MIMIC and eICU-CRD as examples, discrepancies in data quality and annotation consistency reduce model generalization across institutions. This issue constitutes not only a technical challenge but also a barrier to practical clinical deployment. Consequently, advanced domain adaptation and generalization techniques are required to enable LLMs to learn robust, source-independent representations or to explicitly model characteristics from diverse data sources during training, thereby enhancing applicability in real-world medical settings. To address these issues, researchers are exploring adaptive enhancements for LLMs in medical applications: on the one hand, leveraging inherent capabilities (e.g. instruction following and zero-shot reasoning) to reduce reliance on labeled data; on the other, employing domain adaptation techniques (e.g. medical knowledge infusion and signal-text alignment) to improve semantic understanding in medical contexts. The essence of medical temporal large models lies in achieving cross-modal semantic alignment. Their downstream applications can be broadly divided into two categories: clinical diagnosis and report generation (e.g., EHR interpretation, imaging report generation) and temporal signal analysis (e.g., pathology detection, physiological parameter prediction). Diﬀerent task objectives directly shape model architectures and evaluation frameworks, necessitating tailored adaptations to meet clinical needs. This section systematically reviews cutting-edge research, analyzing technical approaches and evaluation paradigms across both task categories. Fig. 5 presents the overall architecture and training methodology of medical time series large models, which improve task-speciﬁc performance through the joint training of text and time-series data. The core of the alignment method in Fig. 5 is the use of dedicated encoders and learnable projection layers to map medical time-series signals and their textual descriptions into a shared semantic space. This enables collaborative learning across modalities and eﬀective integration of cross-modal semantic information. Prompting mechanisms are further employed to enhance reasoning and prediction in downstream tasks. Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 7 X. Liu et al. Fig. 5. To achieve this, the alignment module undergoes specialized training, where joint optimization explicitly builds semantic associations between signal-text pairs, thus bridging the semantic gap across modalities. 4.2. Selection of pre-trained LLM backbones When LLMs are introduced as the core architecture for cross-modal semantic alignment in medical time series analysis, two complementary technical pathways have emerged. The ﬁrst focuses on exploiting the strong semantic representation and generation capabilities of LLMs for text-related tasks, including clinical diagnosis description, electronic health record (EHR) interpretation, and medical report generation. The second emphasizes encoding and aligning long-range semantics in timeseries signals to support pathological feature detection, clinical event prediction, and signal reconstruction. Although LLMs demonstrate remarkable performance in natural language understanding and generation, directly processing continuous, high-sampling-rate medical signals remains challenging because of modality diﬀerences. To bridge this semantic gap, explicit alignment mechanisms that incorporate conversion, alignment, and fusion strategies are required. Representative approaches adopt multi-stage ﬁne-tuning, prompt-based adaptation, or lightweight adapter modules to align physiological signals, structured records, and textual contexts within a uniﬁed representation space. For instance, recent studies on ECG analysis validate the feasibility of mapping ECG signals into token sequences interpretable by LLMs, thereby enabling natural language question answering and diagnostic report generation. In addition, models such as UniTS (Gao et al., 2024), TimeCMA (Liu et al., 2025), and the Structure-Guided Cross-Modal Alignment model (SGCMA) (Sun et al., 2025) highlight the importance of multi-scale representations and state-transition graphs for capturing long-range temporal dependencies. Taken together, these observations suggest that when selecting a model, particular attention should be paid to its usable context window length for long-range dependency modeling, its reasoning capability, and its compatibility with parameter-eﬃcient ﬁne-tuning approaches such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), Adapter (Pfeiﬀer et al., 2021), and PEFT (Mangrulkar et al., 2022). Based on these advances, selection criteria for backbone LLMs can be summarized as follows: (i) language understanding and generation capabilities for text-related tasks; (ii) context window size and long-sequence modeling capacity for time-series tasks; (iii) model accessibility and licensing to ensure compliance with medical data regulations and private deployment; and (iv) the availability of multimodal extensions or adapter ecosystems to reduce implementation costs. Accordingly, this paper categorizes candidate backbone models into several representative classes and systematically reviews their adaptability to the two task paradigms in Table 5, along with their typical application strategies, providing clear guidance for model selection under diverse research objectives and regulatory constraints. In longitudinal ICU trajectory modeling and complication prediction using time-stamped EHR, GPT-4 demonstrates strong medical reasoning and generates coherent, clinically aligned summaries that enhance temporal decision-making (Nori et al., 2023). Fine-tuning LLaMA models with LoRA achieves high predictive accuracy and computational eﬃciency in long-term ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-label cardiac diagnosis, showing that lightweight adaptation can retain strong temporal modeling capacity (Yu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024). In Chinese clinical contexts, Qwen and related medical variants exhibit strong multilingual understanding and cross-modal alignment when integrating clinical text with physiological time series, enabling consistent and interpretable diagnostic report generation (Cui et al., 2025). Mediumsized open models such as Falcon and Mistral provide a balance between inference speed, memory eﬃciency, and accuracy for vital-sign trend forecasting and early deterioration prediction using extended-context attention mechanisms (Chang et al., 2024). Lightweight distilled models are increasingly used in wearable health monitoring for real-time heartrate and PPG signal analysis due to low power consumption and deployment ﬂexibility, though their performance often depends on handcrafted features and task-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning (Xiao et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022b). In summary, diﬀerent backbone models exhibit distinct strengths. For research focused on clinical text generation or medical report synthesis, GPT-4 (as a reference benchmark) or open-source families such as LLaMA and Qwen are recommended as the backbone. These models can be further enhanced through supervised ﬁne-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to improve the safety, factual accuracy, and consistency of generated outputs. For studies emphasizing time-series signal analysis and cross-modal alignment, open-source models that support long-sequence tokenization, adapter-based integration, and extended context windows (e.g., LLaMA, Qwen, Falcon, Mistral) are preferable, in combination with structured alignment strategies to achieve multimodal semantic fusion and performance evaluation. The detailed discussion of these alignment methods will be presented in Sections 4.2 and 4.3. 4.3. Feature encoding and spatial mapping Feature encoding for medical temporal multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must tackle two core challenges: fusing heterogeneous modalities and embedding domain-speciﬁc knowledge. A pivotal step in this process is transforming continuous medical time-series data into discrete tokens that LLMs can process. This typically involves numerical tokenization, specialized encoding for structured or categorical data, and robust representation of temporal information. Fig. 6 illustrates the technical stack underpinning this transformation, highlighting how medical time series are “translated” into forms comprehensible to LLMs. As shown, data preprocessing is no longer a peripheral engineering task; it is a decisive factor in enabling LLMs to capture temporal patterns and clinical semantics, ultimately shaping both model performance and clinical applicability. Each layer builds on the previous one: Normalization provides the foundation, Data Representation transforms signals into tokens, Temporal Encoding adds order and dependencies, and LLM adaptation enables cross-modal reasoning and clinical task execution. 4.3.1. Tokenization and embedding of numeric time-series data LLMs were originally developed for text processing, and their vocabularies do not cover the full range of ﬂoating-point numbers. This limitation restricts their ability to represent numerical time series eﬀectively. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed several strategies. One straightforward method randomly maps time-series values to the tokenizer’s vocabulary, relying on the LLM’s in-context learning capability to produce meaningful outputs (Jin et al., 2024; Rasul et al., 2023). A more common strategy leverages patching techniques, where time series are divided into ﬁxed-length overlapping or non-overlapping segments that are then processed by the LLM. For example, PatchInstruct decomposes time series into trend and residual components, applies overlapping window patching, and even introduces a “recent-ﬁrst” reverse ordering to improve predictive accuracy (Bumb et al., 2025). Another line of work focuses on mapping continuous values into a discrete token space. Tokenization-Optimized Normalization (TOKON) is one such approach, scaling time-series values into the integer range of a tokenizer’s dictionary. This ensures each numerical value corresponds to a single token, reducing sequence length by half to two-thirds and simplifying the LLM’s prediction task. Within this discretization paradigm, researchers have also explored symbolic conversion. For instance, Adaptive Brownian Bridge Symbol Aggregation (ABBA) transforms numerical signals into symbolic sequences, enabling LLMs to recognize time-series patterns in a manner similar to natural language (Elsworth & Güttel, 2020). Such techniques capture amplitude and periodicity while maintaining compatibility with existing tokenization schemes. Similarly, the Chronos model discretizes continuous time series via scaling and quantization (binning), allowing oﬀ-the-shelf Transformer architectures to perform zero-shot prediction (Ansari et al., 2024). Tokenizing numerical time series is not simply a matter of format conversion; it is a critical process for both information compression and semantic alignment. Diﬀerent tokenization strategies represent distinct conceptualizations of the “language” of time series, and they directly inﬂuence an LLM’s ability to capture dependencies across multiple temporal scales. Patching preserves local structural information but may sacriﬁce global context. TOKON reduces token counts and improves eﬃciency, although it may compromise numerical precision. Symbolization abstracts temporal patterns into higher-level units, improving linguistic interpretability but potentially losing ﬁne-grained details. Collectively, these approaches aim to translate the syntax of time series, including trends, cycles, and recurring patterns, into token sequences that can fully leverage the sequence modeling capabilities of LLMs. Eﬀective encoding should enable LLMs to identify and generalize intrinsic temporal patterns rather than merely memorizing raw numerical values. This perspective underscores the importance of treating time series as a structured “language” in LLM-based modeling. Future research may extend this direction by designing adaptive tokenization strategies that dynamically adjust granularity according to signal characteristics such as frequency, variability, and noise, or by integrating multi-scale representations to achieve a more balanced trade-oﬀ between compression eﬃciency and information retention. Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 9 X. Liu et al. 4.3.2. Processing structured and categorized data EHRs contain extensive structured and categorized data, including diagnostic codes (ICD), drug codes (RxNorm), and laboratory test results. While this information is not inherently continuous time-series data, its timestamped attributes and sequential nature make it highly relevant to medical time-series analysis. Conventional tokenizers typically treat medical codes as isolated textual symbols, which often results in vocabulary inﬂation and fragmentation of rare codes. To address this limitation, MedTok introduces a multimodal tokenization framework for medical codes. This approach integrates textual descriptions of codes with ontological hierarchies and contextual relationships (e.g., disease co-occurrence, drug therapy associations). Textual information is processed through a language model encoder, while relational structures are captured by a graph encoder, producing richer and more structured embedding representations (Su et al., 2025). Another promising strategy serializes patient records into structured Markdown text. In this method, demographic data, LOINC concepts (such as the most recent three values of vital signs and laboratory results along with their units and classiﬁcations), and detailed visit records (including diagnoses, medications, and procedure codes) are converted into natural language descriptions before being fed into LLMs for encoding (Hegselmann et al., 2025). To mitigate the sparsity of laboratory data and enhance contextual reasoning, some studies translate numerical test results into textual form. For example, blood test values, temporal variations, and objective measurements from nursing records (e.g., vital signs) can be encoded as text, tokenized, and subsequently used for LLM pre-training (Zhu et al., 2024). Beyond textualization, integrating knowledge graphs (KGs) further enhances diagnostic reasoning. This is achieved by retrieving knowledge paths aligned with patient-speciﬁc information to improve EHR-based predictive performance (Park et al., 2025). The KG4Diagnosis framework exempliﬁes this approach, enabling diagnosis of 362 common diseases by automatically constructing knowledge graphs and employing multi-agent systems (Zuo et al., 2025). Transforming structured medical data such as diagnostic codes and laboratory results into textual or graph-based representations is an essential step for enabling LLMs to interpret complex clinical contexts. These strategies not only mitigate LLMs’ inherent limitations in processing coded data but also enhance clinical reasoning by embedding structured semantics. Converting discrete codes into semantic representations, for example as text or embedding vectors, allows LLMs to contextualize symbolic information within broader clinical narratives. Similarly, expressing numerical laboratory values in textual form provides semantic discretization of continuous signals, which facilitates contextual reasoning. In addition, the integration of knowledge graphs supplements structured and interpretable domain knowledge, thereby addressing LLMs’ limitations in factual recall and logical reasoning. Collectively, these transformation and integration approaches elevate LLMs from passive language processors to intelligent agents capable of medical knowledge reasoning. This shift lays the groundwork for their deployment in clinical decision support systems, where LLMs can synthesize patient physiological data, medical history, and structured knowledge to deliver more comprehensive and reliable analyses. 4.3.3. Position and time encoding of temporal information The Transformer architecture excels at capturing long-range dependencies, yet its self-attention mechanism inherently lacks temporal order information, making positional encoding essential for distinguishing time steps. Traditional approaches typically employ ﬁxed positional encodings, such as sinusoidal encoding, which assign unique absolute position identiﬁers to each time step (Vaswani et al., 2017). However, medical time series often feature irregular sampling and repeated timestamps, limiting the applicability of ﬁxed encodings. To address this issue, researchers have proposed more ﬂexible strategies. One approach constructs non-unique absolute indices based on record timestamps, allowing variables recorded simultaneously to share position identiﬁers, while relative positional encoding is introduced to capture dependencies among local tokens within the sequence (Çav¸si Zaim & Yolacan, 2025; Dai et al., 2019). Such reﬁnements are particularly crucial when processing long medical sequences. Beyond positional encoding, temporal encoding methods explicitly capture dynamic temporal patterns. For example, Time2Vec maps temporal intervals into learnable vector representations, enhancing the model’s ability to generalize across variable time gaps (Kazemi et al., 2019). Building on this idea, the MIRA model introduces Continuous Time Rotated Position Encoding (CT-RoPE), which discretizes continuous timestamps into rotation angles and incorporates an adjustable frequency mechanism. This design enables precise modeling of irregular time intervals and more eﬀective representation of relative temporal relationships (Li et al., 2025a). In multivariate clinical time series, such as vital signs and laboratory measurements, variables often exhibit heterogeneous scales, ranges, and temporal dynamics. Traditional uniﬁed encoders struggle to fully capture these complexities, motivating the use of independent encoders for each variable to preserve their unique characteristics while also modeling inter-variable dependencies (Li et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2025). Irregular sampling, heterogeneous intervals, and temporal redundancy pose persistent challenges in medical time-series analysis. Position-based encodings alone are insuﬃcient, as understanding temporal intervals between events is as critical as their sequence order. For instance, a one-hour versus a one-day gap between blood glucose measurements carries markedly diﬀerent implications for predicting complications in diabetes (Association, 2018). Reﬁned temporal encoding strategies, such as CT-RoPE, not only accommodate inconsistent sampling but also capture the nonlinear importance of temporal distance between events, thereby enhancing the ability of LLMs to model disease progression. By enriching temporal representations, LLMs can more eﬀectively extract long-range dependencies and dynamic patterns from clinical sequences. This capability is particularly signiﬁcant in chronic disease management and risk prediction, where multi-year datasets must be integrated to provide reliable and comprehensive insights. 4.4. Multimodal fusion strategy of medical time-series LLM 4.4.1. Multimodal fusion strategy Table 6 summarizes the primary applications of multimodal fusion strategies in medical LLMs, including strategy types, fusion mechanisms, integrated modalities, and representative application scenarios. In multimodal medical data analysis, the integration of time-series signals with textual information such as clinical notes, patient demographics, and medical histories provides LLMs with richer contextual knowledge and improves their ability to recognize physiological patterns. The most direct approach is to concatenate time-series embeddings, for example those obtained through patch processing, with text embeddings before feeding them into the LLM. MedTsLLM (Chan et al., 2024) illustrates this method by introducing a patch reprogramming layer that aligns timeseries patch embeddings with the embedding space of a pre-trained LLM. This enables the model to jointly process raw time-series data and textual context while preserving patient-speciﬁc information. Beyond concatenation, cross-modal attention mechanisms have emerged as a more sophisticated fusion approach. The ProMedTS framework (Niu et al., 2025), for instance, employs multi-head cross-attention to transform raw laboratory test time-series data into prompt embeddings, which are subsequently fused with textual information such as medical notes and anomaly descriptions. This mechanism not only preserves ﬁne-grained temporal dynamics but also extracts complementary semantic knowledge across modalities. In addition, some approaches bridge the gap between numerical sequences and textual semantics by embedding descriptive statistical features of time series into text prompts.
