Overall, fusion strategies for time-series and textual data have evolved from simple concatenation to cross-modal attention and semantic alignment, reﬂecting the shift of LLMs from basic text comprehension toward deep multimodal integration. This progression enables LLMs to perform more context-aware reasoning by jointly analyzing static patient histories (text) and dynamic physiological changes (time series). While early methods such as direct concatenation risked information redundancy or modal imbalance, and converting time series entirely into text often sacriﬁced temporal granularity, more advanced techniquessuch as patch reprogramming in MedTsLLM (Chan et al., 2024), crossmodal attention in ProMedTS (Niu et al., 2025), and statistically enhanced prompts-achieve deeper embedding alignment and semantic fusion. By constructing uniﬁed patient representations, these approaches allow LLMs to cross-reference textual descriptions (e.g. diagnoses and medication histories) with temporal signals (e.g. vital sign ﬂuctuations), thereby delivering more clinically meaningful and interpretable analyses. 4.4.2. Selection of multimodal fusion strategies To clarify the relationship between multimodal fusion strategies and downstream clinical tasks, it is essential to emphasize that no single fusion paradigm is universally optimal. Instead, the choice of fusion strategy should be guided by the primary task objective and the role of medical time series within the modeling pipeline. Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 11 X. Liu et al. For text-oriented clinical tasks, such as risk proﬁling, clinical summarization, and laboratory report interpretation, input-level fusion strategies are generally preferred. Methods including feature concatenation and numerical tokenization convert medical time series into auxiliary contextual information that supports language reasoning, while preserving the LLM’s strength in text generation and semantic inference. In these scenarios, time series serve primarily as structured evidence rather than the direct prediction target. In contrast, time-series-centric tasks, including forecasting, waveform reconstruction, and irregular time-series interpolation, beneﬁt more from intermediateor deep-level fusion strategies. Temporal reprogramming, gated fusion, and mixture-of-experts architectures allow medical time series to remain the dominant modality, while textual or knowledge-based inputs provide constraints, priors, or high-level guidance. These strategies explicitly preserve temporal continuity and multiscale dynamics, which are critical for accurate physiological signal modeling. For reasoning-intensive clinical decision support tasks, such as state monitoring, alert generation, and diagnostic assistance, intermediatelevel fusion via cross-modal attention or knowledge augmentation offers a balanced trade-oﬀ. By enabling bidirectional interactions between medical time series and text, these approaches allow models to jointly reason over temporal patterns and clinical semantics, aligning physiological evidence with medical knowledge and interpretive logic. Overall, Table 6 provides a task-oriented mapping between fusion levels and clinical objectives, highlighting that eﬀective multimodal fusion in medical time-series modeling should be driven by task demands rather than architectural complexity. 4.5. Loss function design When introducing LLMs as cross-modal semantic alignment backbones in medical time series analysis, the choice of loss function plays a decisive role in shaping model performance across diverse tasks. As summarized in Table 7, clinical diagnosis and report generation tasks primarily emphasize text generation quality and alignment losses, whereas time series analysis prioritizes numerical prediction accuracy and reconstruction losses. In text-oriented tasks, cross-entropy loss remains the fundamental training objective, ensuring consistency between model-generated diagnostic reports and reference medical texts. For example, the ECG-LM framework applies cross-entropy loss for ECG classiﬁcation and report generation (Yang et al., 2025). However, cross-entropy alone is insufﬁcient for achieving cross-modal semantic alignment. To address this, contrastive loss (Ketabi & Ramachandram, 2025) is frequently incorporated to minimize the distance between signal embeddings and text embeddings in the shared representation space. Matching loss further evaluates the correctness of signal-text pairing relationships (Wan et al., 2025a). For medical report generation, generative losses (Zhang et al., 2024a) are also employed, leveraging metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE to quantify discrepancies between generated and reference texts. Building on this, reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) (Hartsock & Rasool, 2024) introduces reward-based loss (Zhou et al., 2024), which enhances the clinical plausibility and utility of generated narratives. In time series tasks, the emphasis shifts toward numerical ﬁdelity and preservation of temporal structure. Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) remain standard objectives for predicting and reconstructing physiological signals such as blood pressure, ECG, and blood glucose (von Bachmann et al., 2024; Harvey et al., 2025). For tasks requiring sequential forecasting, autoregressive loss is employed to capture the dynamic evolution of signals. Simultaneously, contrastive losses are used in temporal tasks to align time series data with clinical text within the semantic space. For instance, an EHR-based study proposed a Global Contrastive Loss that improved postoperative complication prediction by aligning patient temporal representations with discharge summary texts (Ma et al., 2024). With the growing adoption of multi-task learning frameworks, models such as ProMedTS (Niu et al., 2025) and MedTsLLM (Chan et al., 2024) integrate multi-task joint losses. This strategy dynamically balances and coordinates multiple objectives including generation, contrastive learning, and reconstruction, thereby optimizing both semantic generation and temporal prediction. Overall, loss function design diverges across task categories: textbased applications prioritize language generation quality and semantic consistency, while temporal tasks emphasize numerical accuracy and long-range dependency modeling. Looking ahead, incorporating causally consistent or clinically constrained loss functions informed by medical knowledge graphs may further improve model interpretability and clinical utility. 4.6. Evaluation metrics and validation methods At the level of model application, evaluating performance solely based on oﬄine metrics is insuﬃcient. A comprehensive evaluation and validation framework is required to assess model eﬀectiveness, generalization capability, and clinical applicability. Traditional performance metrics, such as classiﬁcation and regression scores, primarily quantify numerical agreement between model outputs and ground-truth labels. However, these metrics do not fully capture model behavior under distribution shifts, across heterogeneous clinical environments, or within real-world clinical decision-making workﬂows. Therefore, evaluation and validation methods at diﬀerent levels should be jointly employed, as illustrated in Fig. 7, to comprehensively assess model practicality and reliability. 4.6.1. General-purpose evaluation metrics General-purpose evaluation metrics quantify the basic consistency between model outputs and ground-truth labels. They are mainly used for oﬄine performance comparison and benchmarking. In medical binary classiﬁcation or event prediction tasks, commonly used metrics include the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). These metrics reﬂect a model’s overall discriminative ability across diﬀerent decision thresholds. Which have been widely adopted in clinical data modeling tasks, including cardiovascular risk prediction and ICU early warning systems. For example, Bashiri et al. reported AUROC and AUPRC as primary evaluation metrics in external validation experiments for multicenter time-series prediction tasks (Bashiri et al., 2024). For medical natural language processing tasks with text generation as the primary output, commonly used general-purpose metrics include BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), BERTScore (Zhang* et al., 2020) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004). BLEU and ROUGE mainly measure lexical or ngram overlap between generated text and reference text. In contrast, BERTScore evaluates semantic similarity based on contextualized representations derived from pretrained language models. These metrics have been extensively used in biomedical NLP studies, including clinical report generation and medical text summarization. For physiological signal prediction and reconstruction tasks, such as ABP waveform reconstruction, ECG modeling, or PPG signal generation, general-purpose evaluation metrics are also widely used. Commonly used metrics include MSE, MAE, and dynamic time warping (DTW). MSE and MAE characterize point-wise numerical prediction errors. DTW, on the other hand, alleviates temporal misalignment to some extent by evaluating similarity at the waveform level. These metrics are widely adopted in physiological signal modeling and time-series prediction studies to evaluate reconstruction quality and predictive accuracy. Despite their importance for performance comparison, these generalpurpose metrics are fundamentally oﬄine numerical evaluations that reﬂect the degree of ﬁt between model outputs and annotated datasets. However, given the strong clinical semantics and context dependence inherent in medical time-series tasks, relying solely on them is insuﬃcient to fully assess a model’s reliability and practical utility in real clinical Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 12 X. Yellow boxes indicate metrics for text-based tasks (e.g., diagnosis and report generation), red boxes denote metrics for time-series tasks (e.g., waveform reconstruction), and mixed red-yellow boxes represent metrics and validation methods applicable to both tasks, including generalization and clinical eﬀectiveness assessment. environments. Therefore, in practice, they are typically combined with generalization assessment and clinical validation. This integrated strategy enables a more comprehensive evaluation of a model’s potential for clinical application. 4.6.2. Generalization capability validation During development, clinical AI models are typically evaluated on training or internal validation datasets. Such internal validation, however, often fails to reﬂect model performance under novel data distributions or in unseen clinical environments. Consequently, external validation is regarded as the standard method for assessing model generalization. This approach involves evaluating models on datasets collected from diﬀerent hospitals, populations, or data acquisition protocols, thereby examining the stability and reliability of performance metrics (e.g., AUROC and calibration) under new data conditions. This methodological principle has been widely emphasized and adopted in clinical prediction modeling (Snell et al., 2021). Furthermore, cross-dataset evaluation and cross-population generalization have emerged as key strategies for assessing generalization in medical AI research. For instance, performance assessment across datasets from disparate clinical centers or countries can reveal a model’s robustness to distributional shifts. In the context of time-series tasks, this approach helps identify sensitivity to distribution changes and potential performance degradation. The insights gained from such analyses, in turn, underscore the necessity for additional validation and adaptation prior to real-world clinical deployment. 4.6.3. Clinical eﬃcacy validation Even when a model demonstrates strong performance in multicentre or cross-population generalisation tests, performance metrics alone are insuﬃcient to guarantee clinical eﬀectiveness. Thus, clinical validation constitutes a critical step in translating models from research into clinical practice. Typically conducted with real patient data, clinical validation assesses whether model predictions oﬀer actionable support for clinical decision-making. In retrospective studies, historical clinical data are used to evaluate model performance and analyse its correlation with clinical outcomes. Multiple studies have conﬁrmed that metrics derived solely from development datasets do not reliably predict performance in real clinical settings (Collins et al., 2015), underscoring the need for rigorous clinical validation study designs to ensure reliability and safety. Prospective evaluation represents another key approach to establishing model trustworthiness and utility. It examines the impact of model outputs on clinical decision-making within real-time workﬂows, often incorporating human-AI collaboration (Sendak et al., 2020). For instance, through expert review of AI-generated diagnoses or alerts. Human-in-the-loop frameworks further integrate clinicians into the evaluation and decision process, allowing them to adjust or override model predictions. Such frameworks enable simultaneous assessment of a model’s accuracy, clinical plausibility, interpretability, and safety. Together, these validation strategies allow for a more comprehensive evaluation of model reliability and clinical usability under real-world conditions. They move beyond superﬁcial metric performance to better address the demands of actual clinical deployment. 5. Applications of LLMs in medical time series In real-world clinical settings, LLMs can fulﬁll multiple roles across heterogeneous data modalities and task formulations. Beyond conventional text-centric applications such as clinical documentation, diagnostic reporting, and question answering, recent advances increasingly position LLMs as core components for modeling, generating, and reconstructing medical time-series signals. Within multimodal frameworks that integrate natural language understanding and temporal signal modeling, LLMs are no longer limited to producing textual outputs, but can also mediate bidirectional mappings between physiological signals and clinical semantics. Accordingly, following the categorization framework established in Section IV, this survey similarly organizes existing applications into two complementary directions: (i) semantic decisionmaking tasks centered on textual outputs, and (ii) generation and reconstruction tasks centered on medical time series outputs. The following sections systematically review representative methods and clinical applications within each category, as summarized in Fig. 8. Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 13 X. Liu et al. Fig. 8. Applications of LLMs in Medical Time Series. 5.1. Semantic decision via textual outputs 5.1.1. Medical QA with medical time series LLM-based clinical question-answering systems are designed to interpret natural language queries posed by clinicians or patients, and to synthesize patient-speciﬁc physiological time-series data (e.g., continuous heart rate or blood pressure trends) together with EHR texts to generate clinically meaningful responses. Such systems are inherently well suited to clinical scenarios that rely heavily on dynamic physiological information, including intensive care monitoring, chronic disease management, and postoperative recovery assessment. Recent studies have begun to explore the direct coupling of continuous physiological signals with LLMs for clinically oriented semantic question-answering tasks. ECG-LM integrates ECG signals with LLMs to support questionanswering tasks, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization performance across diverse queries (Yang et al., 2025). The model is capable of generating responses aligned with clinical language conventions by reasoning over the temporal characteristics of ECG waveforms, providing preliminary evidence of LLMs’ capacity for semantic understanding of physiological signals. Similarly, ECG-Chat (Zhao et al., 2025) introduces a contrastive learning strategy to align cardiology knowledge with ECG representations, enabling multimodal conversational capabilities tailored to ECG-centered clinical scenarios. The common contribution of these studies lies not in the question-answering format itself, but in elevating continuous vital signs from purely numerical inputs to semantic modalities that can actively participate in clinical reasoning. 5.1.2. Diagnostic report generation for ECG As one of the most widely used continuous physiological signals in clinical practice, and the generation and interpretation of ECG reports are of substantial clinical importance. Traditional ECG report generation is time-consuming and subject to signiﬁcant inter-physician variability in narrative style, which can undermine the consistency and reusability of clinical information. Consequently, the use of LLMs to assist ECG report generation carries clear clinical relevance. At its core, automated ECG report generation focuses on identifying the temporal structures and pathological patterns embedded in ECG waveforms. These signal characteristics are then translated into structured or semi-structured textual descriptions that conform to established medical language standards. This process requires not only accurate signal feature recognition, but also a deep understanding of domain-speciﬁc diagnostic semantics and expression conventions. Recent approaches have gradually shifted from template-based descriptions toward semantically driven generation, enabling reports to reﬂect logical relationships among waveform features rather than mere concatenations of predeﬁned terms. MEIT (Wan et al., 2025b) employs instruction tuning to combine ECG data with the language generation capabilities of LLMs, enabling automated report generation at scale Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 14 X. Liu et al. across large ECG datasets. Furthermore, ESI (Yu et al., 2024) incorporates ECG semantic descriptions and clinical knowledge bases, improving the professional accuracy and consistency of the generated reports. These studies illustrate a clear trend toward leveraging LLMs to bridge low-level ECG signal representations and high-level diagnostic language, thereby enhancing both the eﬃciency and reliability of automated ECG reporting. 5.1.3. Personalized intelligent health guidance systems In home-based health monitoring and telemedicine settings, patients and caregivers are often less concerned with raw physiological measurements than with their underlying implications and their relationships to lifestyle and medication behaviors. Questions such as “Whether an elevated nocturnal heart rate is abnormal? ” or “Whether a recent decline in sleep quality may be related to reduced physical activity? ”, exemplify individualized physiological state interpretation tasks. Compared with traditional threshold-based alert systems, LLMs oﬀer a distinct advantage in generating explanations that are semantically coherent and tailored to individual contexts. Emerging studies have explored feeding long-term physiological signals and personal attributes jointly into LLMs to enable interactive, personalized health assessments. PhysioLLM (Fang et al., 2024) integrates wearable-derived physiological signals with user proﬁles (e.g., age, sex, and health goals), leveraging long-term data to generate actionable lifestyle suggestions. Such as “Incorporating more physical activity into your daily routine could potentially improve the quality of your deep sleep”. From both clinical and practical perspectives, the primary value of this direction lies not in advice generation per se, but in lowering the cognitive barrier to interpreting physiological signals through natural language interaction, thereby enhancing patient adherence and the eﬀectiveness of long-term monitoring. 5.2. Reconstruction and generation of medical time series outputs 5.2.1. Cuﬄess blood pressure measurement Blood pressure (BP) is one of the most critical vital signs reﬂecting the functional state of the cardiovascular system, and long-term abnormalities are closely associated with hypertension, heart failure, stroke, and renal impairment. In clinical practice, continuous and accurate blood pressure monitoring plays a vital role in chronic disease management and early risk stratiﬁcation. Cuﬄess blood pressure measurement aims to estimate blood pressure levels from continuous physiological signals without relying on external inﬂation-based devices. The central challenge lies in stably modeling the latent physiological mechanisms associated with BP from complex time-series signals that exhibit substantial inter-individual variability. Liu et al. (2024c) extract physiological features from ECG and PPG signals and integrate blood pressure domain knowledge with individual attributes to construct context-enhanced prompts that guide LLMs to explicitly leverage physiological priors and user-speciﬁc background information during inference. Through this formulation, cuﬄess blood pressure measurement is reframed from a conventional signal regression problem into a semantic reasoning task that jointly incorporates temporal features, medical knowledge, and personalized context. This paradigm oﬀers a more interpretable and scalable modeling pathway for the continuous estimation of complex physiological indicators. 5.2.2. Long-term ECG monitoring In practical wearable-device scenarios, periodic or non-periodic body movements during daily activities such as running or exercise introduce motion artifacts whose amplitudes often exceed those of the underlying ECG signals. These artifacts can severely distort ECG waveforms or even result in the loss of clinically relevant information. Such noise often overlaps with cardiac rhythms in the temporal domain. This overlap poses a fundamental challenge for separating genuine cardiac activity from motion-induced interference. Traditional ﬁltering methods based on ﬁxed frequency bands or linear assumptions are often insufﬁcient for eﬀective signal separation. As a result, ECG denoising and reconstruction tailored to wearable settings have become fundamental challenges in continuous cardiac monitoring, with their performance directly aﬀecting the reliability of downstream rhythm analysis, anomaly detection, and clinical decision-making. Recent studies have begun to introduce large language models into ECG reconstruction tasks, using language-based prompting mechanisms to impose explicit medical semantic constraints on temporal modeling processes. TELL-ME (Shi et al., 2025) adopts a forward-alignment strategy to enable joint modeling of ECG signals and textual information. This is achieved through cross-attention mechanisms that facilitate effective interaction between the ECG and language modalities. In addition, handcrafted features such as RR intervals and waveform morphology are explicitly embedded into language prompts, guiding the model to focus on clinically meaningful temporal structures. By explicitly encoding medical priors through language prompts, such approaches encourage greater consistency in waveform reconstruction and improved preservation of diagnostically relevant information. Consequently, under complex and dynamic monitoring conditions, large language models can serve as an eﬀective bridge between continuous physiological signals and medical semantics, oﬀering new modeling strategies to enhance signal quality and clinical usability in wearable ECG monitoring. 6. Challenges and solutions for LLMs in medical time series Despite demonstrating potential in medical time-series data analysis, LLMs still face numerous challenges in their application. This section focuses on identifying key technical challenges in applying LLMs to medical time-series analysis, and reviews representative solutions that have been proposed in current literature. For each challenge, we further discuss potential directions for improvement that remain within the scope of existing methodological paradigms. Broader and more visionary research directions are discussed separately in Section 7, as shown in Fig. 9. 6.1. Data complexity Challenge: Medical time series are often high-dimensional and multi-channel, with irregular sampling, frequent missing values, and substantial noise. Moreover, heterogeneous data collection protocols across devices and clinical departments lead to pronounced distribution shifts, even for the same type of physiological signal. Inter-individual physiological variability further limits the transferability of models across centers and departments (Li & Marlin, 2020; Zhang et al., 2022a). In electronic health records, follow-up measurements are typically collected at discrete time points, resulting in missing variables in the crosssectional dimension and sparse, inconsistent observations along the temporal dimension. For example, during general anesthesia, blood pressure and heart rate are nominally recorded every ﬁve minutes, but the actual intervals often vary due to clinical procedures (Kazijevs & Samad, 2023). Under irregular sampling, signals from diﬀerent sensors are diﬃcult to align, and the time gaps between consecutive observations vary with sensor type and system conﬁguration (Zhang, 2016). Current Solutions: To mitigate these issues, one common strategy is to integrate adaptive interpolation and denoising modules into end-toend preprocessing pipelines, allowing both operations to be optimized as diﬀerentiable components. For instance, variational autoencoder (VAE)- based denoising approaches learn robust representations of clean signals from large-scale cardiac datasets and have been shown to outperform traditional ﬁltering methods (Campillo et al., 2024). Another line of work focuses on multi-scale feature extraction to disentangle short-term transient ﬂuctuations from long-term trend patterns. Typical implementations combine wavelet transforms or empirical mode decomposition with attention-based fusion mechanisms to adaptively integrate information across temporal scales. More recently, graph-based approaches Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 15 X. Liu et al. have been proposed to model multivariate irregular time series by converting them into structured graph representations. In models such as RAINDROP, sensors are treated as nodes, and graph neural networks are applied to capture cross-modal temporal dependencies, achieving better performance than ﬁxed discretization strategies (Zhang et al., 2022a). Through message-passing mechanisms, these models exploit neighboring observations to impute missing values and better represent complex, irregular, and multi-source medical time series. Improvement Directions: Although graph-based representations have shown promise for modeling multivariate irregular medical time series, how to construct clinically meaningful and transferable graph structures remains an open problem. Existing approaches, such as sensor-level graph modeling, often rely on predeﬁned or task-speciﬁc graph topologies, which may limit generalization across clinical settings. Future improvements within existing paradigms may therefore focus on adaptive graph construction strategies that integrate physiological knowledge with data-driven priors. In addition, incorporating domain constraints, such as clinically meaningful temporal patterns, may further improve robustness and generalization across patient populations. 6.2. Bottlenecks in multimodal fusion Challenge: Clinical data are inherently multimodal, encompassing physiological time series, medical images, unstructured clinical notes, and structured tabular records. MLLMs aim to integrate these heterogeneous sources into a uniﬁed analytical framework that approximates clinical decision-making. However, multimodal fusion remains challenging due to substantial diﬀerences in temporal resolution, acquisition protocols, and noise characteristics across modalities. In real-world clinical settings, one or more modalities are frequently missing, further complicating model design. Current Solutions: A widely adopted solution is dual-stream contrastive learning, where each modality is encoded independently and aligned within a shared latent space using cross-modal contrastive objectives. This paradigm is inspired by vision-language pretraining frameworks such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and has been extended to medical applications. Representative examples include MedCLIP, which aligns chest X-ray images with corresponding radiology reports (Wang et al., 2022), as well as methods that associate physiological time series with diagnostic or clinical codes (Baldenweg et al., 2024). In addition, attention-based fusion mechanisms are commonly employed to dynamically reweight diﬀerent modalities during inference. By emphasizing informative modalities and down-weighting noisy or unreliable inputs, these approaches partially mitigate the impact of modality heterogeneity and missing data, thereby improving robustness across diverse clinical tasks. Improvement Directions: Despite these advances, multimodal fusion in clinical settings remains far from resolved. Existing methods often rely on ﬁxed fusion strategies that are not explicitly optimized for varying clinical contexts, disease states, or data availability patterns. Within current modeling paradigms, future improvements may focus on developing more adaptive fusion mechanisms that can ﬂexibly adjust integration strategies according to task requirements and input reliability. In addition, improving computational eﬃciency while preserving multimodal representational capacity remains an important direction for enabling scalable and deployable MLLM systems in real-world healthcare environments. 6.3. Computational intensity and resource constraints Challenge: Self-attention-based pre-trained models, such as Transformers, contain massive parameter scales and incur high computational costs (Bhosekar et al., 2025). Their deployment on portable or edge devices is constrained by intensive memory and resource demands during both training and inference. Since many healthcare applications require real-time monitoring and decision support, achieving an optimal balance between model capability and computational eﬃciency remains a critical challenge (Bhosekar et al., 2025). Current Solutions: Several strategies have been proposed to mitigate computational and resource constraints. Model compression and knowledge distillation techniques, aim to reduce model size while preserving performance by transferring knowledge from large models to lightweight counterparts. Empirical studies indicate that pruning, binarization, and distillation can substantially reduce Transformer parameter counts and accelerate inference (Jyoti Bajpai & Hanawal, 2025). Hierarchical inference architectures provide another solution, where lightweight edge models conduct preliminary screening and oﬄoad high-risk or complex cases to cloud servers or specialized hardware, thereby conserving bandwidth and improving response time. Furthermore, dynamic early-exit mechanisms introduce multiple output gates in intermediate layers, enabling simple cases to terminate inference early based on conﬁdence scores, while reserving deeper computation for complex inputs. This adaptive strategy has been shown to signiﬁcantly reduce average inference latency and improve eﬃciency (Jyoti Bajpai & Hanawal, 2025). Improvement Directions: Despite these advances, existing eﬃciency-oriented techniques are often designed in isolation and may not fully account for the unique characteristics of medical time-series data and clinical workﬂows. Within current modeling paradigms, future improvements may focus on jointly optimizing model eﬃciency and task performance under realistic deployment constraints. In particular, designing adaptive inference strategies that explicitly consider clinical risk levels, latency requirements, and resource availability could further enhance the practicality of LLM-based systems in healthcare settings. Improving the alignment between computational eﬃciency and clinical reliability remains an important direction for translating large models into real-world medical applications. 6.4. Lack of explainability Challenge: Although LLMs have demonstrated strong performance in medical diagnosis and prediction tasks, their lack of reliable explainability remains a major barrier to clinical adoption. Common post-hoc interpretability tools, such as LIME and SHAP, are often ineﬃcient or ineﬀective when applied to long temporal sequences and multimodal medical data, limiting their practical usability (Keles et al., 2023). In the absence of trustworthy explanations, clinicians face diﬃculties in validating model outputs and assessing their clinical plausibility, which substantially undermines conﬁdence in AI-assisted decision-making. This issue is particularly critical in high-stakes healthcare scenarios, where opaque predictions may pose ethical and safety concerns. Current Solutions: Existing studies primarily rely on post-hoc explainability techniques to provide insights into model behavior. Saliency-based methods, for instance, visualize regions of high importance in images or time series and are favored for their intuitive presentation. However, growing evidence suggests that such methods suﬀer from low robustness and sensitivity, and may fail to faithfully reﬂect the true decision logic of deep models (Keles et al., 2023). Recent evaluations further reveal that saliency maps produced by commercial AI systems can be weakly correlated with model predictions or even misleading, raising concerns about their clinical reliability (Zhang et al., 2023). While causal-inspired approaches have been explored to improve interpretability by modeling relationships among physiological variables, their integration with large-scale LLM-based systems remains limited and methodologically immature (Han et al., 2024). Improvement Directions: Future research should move beyond purely post-hoc explanations toward intrinsically interpretable or causally grounded modeling paradigms. Integrating causal inference frameworks into LLM-based medical time-series models may enable explicit reasoning over physiological mechanisms and pathological processes, supporting counterfactual analysis and more clinically Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 16 X. Liu et al. Fig. 9. Challenges and Future Prospects of LLMs in Medical Time Series Research. meaningful explanations. In addition, developing multi-level interpretability frameworks that link model decisions to speciﬁc time windows, signal patterns, or multimodal evidence could enhance transparency across diﬀerent abstraction levels. Finally, standardized and veriﬁable interpretability evaluation metrics are needed, such as clinically aligned consistency measures between model-highlighted features and physician annotations. Establishing human-AI collaborative evaluation protocols may provide objective benchmarks for assessing whether explanations genuinely support clinical reasoning and decision-making. 6.5. Data privacy breach Challenge: In healthcare applications, patient data are inherently privacy-sensitive, as they contain personal health conditions, longitudinal medical records, and even genetic information. Consequently, such data are strictly regulated by legal frameworks including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which impose rigorous constraints on data storage, access control, and cross-institutional sharing (Akinsiku, 2025). Traditional centralized training paradigms require aggregating raw data from multiple institutions into a single repository, which substantially increases the risk of data leakage during transmission and storage. These risks are further exacerbated by security threats such as inference attacks, where sensitive attributes can be reconstructed from trained models (Gosselin et al., 2022). Moreover, LLMs may exhibit memorization eﬀects during training, inadvertently reproducing sensitive patient information during inference, thereby intensifying privacy protection challenges. Beyond privacy risks, regulatory and technical constraints jointly contribute to severe data siloing in healthcare systems. Clinical data remain fragmented across individual hospitals, regional platforms, and national databases, limiting largescale validation and hindering the generalization of models in multicenter settings. Heterogeneity in data formats, annotation standards, and clinical workﬂows further restrict model portability, causing models trained on local datasets to perform poorly when deployed in external environments. Current Solutions: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to enable collaborative model training across institutions without requiring direct data sharing. In this framework, raw patient data remain stored locally within each institution, while only model parameters or gradient updates are exchanged and aggregated, thereby reducing the risk of sensitive data exposure. To further strengthen privacy guarantees, diﬀerential privacy techniques are often incorporated into the federated aggregation process. These methods inject controlled noise into local updates. As a result, the risk of inferring individual-level information from the global model is eﬀectively reduced. In scenarios that require stronger security guarantees, cryptographic techniques have been explored. Representative examples include homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation. These methods enable training and inference on encrypted data, ensuring that sensitive information remains protected throughout the learning pipeline (Adnan et al., 2022). Improvement Directions: Despite these advantages, existing privacy-preserving learning frameworks face notable limitations when applied to large-scale medical MLLMs. Federated learning systems may suﬀer from communication overhead, statistical heterogeneity across institutions, and performance degradation when privacy constraints are overly restrictive. Future research should therefore focus on developing scalable and communication-eﬃcient federated architectures tailored for multimodal and long-horizon medical time series. In addition, tighter integration between privacy-preserving mechanisms and model architectures is required to balance privacy guarantees with predictive performance. Establishing standardized evaluation protocols for privacyutility trade-oﬀs in clinical settings will also be essential for assessing real-world applicability and fostering broader clinical adoption. 7. Future directions for LLMs in medical time series 7.1. Multimodal data and RAG fusion Despite their strong general reasoning capabilities, current LLMs trained primarily on large-scale text corpora lack explicit and structured medical knowledge, which limits their reliability and interpretability Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 17 X. Liu et al. in clinical reasoning. To address this gap, future research may integrate medical knowledge graphs with LLMs by incorporating ontologybased constraints and rule-guided reasoning mechanisms, thereby enhancing both logical rigor and clinical credibility. Recent studies have demonstrated the eﬀectiveness of such integration in diagnostic scenarios. For instance, Zuo et al. proposed the KG4Diagnosis framework, which automatically constructs medical knowledge graphs and combines them with LLMs through a multi-layer agent architecture, resulting in improved diagnostic accuracy and interpretability (Zuo et al., 2025). Extending this paradigm to medical time series analysis represents a promising research direction. By constructing graph structures that encode disease mechanisms, physiological pathways, or treatment processes, LLMs can be guided to interpret temporal signal variations in a clinically meaningful manner rather than treating them as purely statistical patterns. Given the inherently multimodal nature of medical data, which includes physiological time series, medical imaging (e.g., CT and MRI), and unstructured clinical text, future LLM-based systems must move beyond single-modality processing. Clinical decision-making relies on the joint interpretation of dynamic signals, imaging evidence, and narrative descriptions. Accordingly, deep multimodal fusion combined with retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) is expected to play a central role in next-generation medical time series models. For example, integrating pharmacological knowledge graphs may help elucidate drug-induced changes in physiological signals, while anatomical structure representations can support the localization and interpretation of sensor-derived data. As a cross-disciplinary research direction at the intersection of artiﬁcial intelligence and biomedicine, this line of work oﬀers a principled pathway toward improving the precision, interpretability, and trustworthiness of LLM-assisted clinical decision-making. 7.2. From invasive to non-invasive signal monitoring Medical time series acquisition is undergoing a gradual transition from invasive monitoring toward non-invasive and contact-free sensing, which has emerged as a key direction for future healthcare technologies. Arterial blood pressure monitoring provides a representative example. Although invasive continuous blood pressure measurement remains the clinical gold standard due to its accuracy in assessing cardiac function, vascular resistance, and organ perfusion, its invasive nature introduces risks such as infection, thrombosis, and hemorrhage, limiting its applicability outside critical care settings. With advances in wearable and optical sensing technologies, devices such as smartwatches, Holter ECG monitors, and electronic blood pressure meters have enabled continuous, non-invasive physiological signal acquisition in both clinical and daily-life environments. Among these techniques, remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) estimates physiological parameters including heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation by analyzing subtle skin color changes from video signals, oﬀering a fully contact-free monitoring solution (Li et al., 2025b). This approach is particularly suitable for patients with skin damage or those unable to tolerate conventional sensors. Future research may explore the integration of LLMs with multimodal non-invasive signals such as rPPG, ECG, and PPG, leveraging their capacity for temporal modeling and semantic abstraction to improve robustness under noise, motion artifacts, and individual variability. Through cross-domain learning across ICU, home, and mobile scenarios, LLMs can adapt to heterogeneous signal distributions and complex real-world conditions. Moreover, the natural language generation capabilities of LLMs enable the translation of raw temporal signals into clinically interpretable reports, supporting explainable and user-friendly monitoring systems. The shift from invasive to non-invasive monitoring thus represents not only a technological trend but also a critical opportunity for coupling large models with intelligent sensing to advance personalized healthcare and telemedicine. 7.3. Create personalized virtual patients LLMs have recently been explored in clinical education to construct interactive virtual patients capable of natural language dialogue, simulating realistic clinical scenarios for training diagnostic reasoning and decision-making skills (Luo et al., 2025). As computational resources and modeling techniques continue to advance, LLM-based virtual patient systems are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Looking forward, this concept may be extended from generic simulations to personalized digital representations of real patients. By training LLMs on individual electronic health records and multisource medical time series data, future systems could model patientspeciﬁc physiological dynamics, disease trajectories, and treatment responses. Such personalized virtual patients hold promise for applications including disease progression forecasting, treatment optimization, and remote clinical training. From a scientiﬁc perspective, this direction requires the eﬀective integration of continuous temporal signals with structured medical knowledge, as well as the development of rigorous evaluation frameworks to assess the clinical validity of simulated outcomes. Despite substantial technical and ethical challenges, enabling LLMs to represent and simulate patient state evolution would mark a signiﬁcant step toward personalized medicine. In chronic disease management, for example, virtual patients could be used to simulate intervention eﬀects and compare alternative treatment strategies. At a broader scale, they may support population-level analysis and public health policy evaluation, highlighting their potential for multi-scenario deployment and interdisciplinary impact. 8. Conclusion This survey systematically examines the research progress and development trajectory of multimodal medical temporal LLMs, providing a comprehensive overview of their theoretical foundations, technical methodologies, and clinical applications. In the theoretical foundation section, we ﬁrst survey the core architectures and pre-training strategies of general-purpose temporal large models, highlighting the evolution of key techniques such as temporal extensions of Transformers and self-supervised learning paradigms. These theories serve as the basis for domain-speciﬁc adaptations and innovations in the medical ﬁeld. Addressing the inherently multimodal nature of medical data, we integrate major medical time-series datasets including MIMIC-IV, VitalDB, and PhysioNet, and propose a dual classiﬁcation framework based on task type and signal modality. By analyzing diﬀerences in sampling frequency, signal type, annotation quality, and other dataset features, we construct a comprehensive data-task mapping system that provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating model training performance. At the methodological level, we investigate four core aspects. First, regarding backbone network selection and optimization, we analyze the adaptability and limitations of diﬀerent base models for medical time-series processing. Second, in architecture design, we highlight innovations for enabling semantic interaction between signals and text, including advanced attention mechanisms and optimized feature projection strategies. Third, for alignment mechanisms, we summarize the application of contrastive learning, prompt engineering, and related approaches, while exploring their intrinsic contributions to enhancing model reasoning. Finally, in loss function design, we examine balancing strategies in multi-task learning and the role of joint optimization in improving downstream performance in diagnostic prediction and report generation. This survey also addresses key challenges in clinical deployment. At the data level, challenges include standardizing heterogeneous sources, mitigating class imbalance, and safeguarding data privacy. At the model level, issues involve computational eﬃciency, interpretability, and generalization on out-of-distribution data. Clinically, reliability validation and integration with healthcare systems remain major obstacles. We Expert Systems With Applications 311 (2026) 131364 18 X. Liu et al. propose corresponding solutions such as privacy-preserving training based on federated learning and eﬃciency optimization through knowledge graph-enhanced inference, providing important references for future studies. Looking ahead, several promising research directions are identiﬁed. From a technological perspective, further eﬀorts are required to develop more eﬃcient architectures, robust modality alignment methods, and novel paradigms that incorporate medical prior knowledge. From an application perspective, the growing adoption of wearable devices and non-invasive monitoring highlights the potential of temporal LLMs in telemedicine and health management. Moreover, establishing comprehensive evaluation systems, including standards for clinical interpretability and robustness testing, will be essential for translating research advances into practice. As an emerging interdisciplinary ﬁeld, multimodal medical temporal LLMs are moving from technical exploration toward clinical application. With continued algorithmic innovation and the expansion of medical data resources, these models are expected to play a central role in clinical decision support and personalized medicine. Ultimately, they will provide foundational support for building intelligent, precise, and reliable next-generation healthcare systems. ## Abstract
ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) can retrieve, reason over, and make inferences about a wide range of information. In health, most LLM efforts to date have focused on clinical tasks. However, mobile and wearable devices, which are rarely integrated into clinical tasks, provide a rich, continuous, and longitudinal source of data relevant for personal health monitoring. Here we present a new model, Personal Health Large Language Model (PH-LLM), a version of Gemini fine-tuned for text understanding and reasoning over numerical time-series personal health data for applications in sleep and fitness. To systematically evaluate PH-LLM, we created and curated three novel benchmark datasets that test 1) production of personalized insights and recommendations from measured sleep patterns, physical activity, and physiological responses, 2) expert domain knowledge, and 3) prediction of self-reported sleep quality outcomes. For the insights and recommendations tasks we created 857 case studies in sleep and fitness. These case studies, designed in collaboration with domain experts, represent real-world scenarios and highlight the model’s capabilities in understanding and coaching. Through comprehensive human and automatic

## Introduction
Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are versatile tools for generating language and have shown strong performance across a range of diverse domains. LLMs have achieved passing grades on the US legal bar exam [28] and second year medical school exams [43,48,53]. In medicine in particular, natural language as an interface has shown potential to influence clinical practice [37], education, and research [39]. When enriched with healthcare-specific data, LLMs attain impressive performance in medical question-answering [48,53], nuanced analysis of electronic health records [61], differential arXiv:2406.06474v1 [cs.AI] 10 Jun 2024 A PREPRINT - JUNE 11, 2024 diagnosis from medical images [56], assessment of psychiatric functioning based on standardized assessments [20], and the delivery of psychological interventions [33,50,51]. High levels of performance on these tasks shows that LLMs have been able to effectively capture signal from “clinical data”, collected within a clinical setting. Due to their sporadic nature, conventional clinical visits often fail to capture key aspects of human health and well-being that are measurable with wearable devices including sleep, physical activity, stress, and cardiometabolic health measured through physiological response and behavior. These continuous, longitudinal measures have significant advantages for health monitoring in that they are passively and continuously acquired, and provide direct physiological and behavioral signals. However, they have neither been deeply integrated into clinical practice nor incorporated into standard datasets used for medical question-answering [23,27], despite statistics on adverse health outcomes, morbidity, and DisabilityAdjusted Life Years that underscore the profound impact these factors have on overall health [3,9,18,44,58]. This limited adoption is likely because these data are typically captured without context, are computationally demanding to store and analyze, and can be difficult to interpret. As a result, general foundation LLMs or even medically-tuned LLMs may lack the ability to use these data effectively to reason about and recommend interventions based on personalized individual health behaviors. Mobile devices, including smart wearables and smartphones, have become instrumental tools for monitoring personal health metrics and gathering longitudinal data that cannot be obtained in traditional clinical settings [54]. Unlike structured clinical data, personal health data is heterogeneous across data types, sources, and timescales [36], ranging from continuous streams of biometric data from wearables, such as sleep patterns or heart rate, to sporadic and qualitative inputs like exercise logs, dietary logs, mood journals, and even social media activity. In this paper, we introduce Personal Health Large Language Model (PH-LLM), a version of Gemini fine-tuned to generate both insights about and recommendations to improve personal health behaviors related to sleep and fitness patterns. We evaluate the performance of PH-LLM across three tasks: coaching recommendations, multiple choice exams assessing expert knowledge, and prediction of subjective patient-reported outcomes (PROs). The coaching recommendations tasks are tailored to two verticals of high personal health interest: sleep and fitness. The sleep tasks leverage individual’s sleep metrics to derive insights, possible etiological factors, and provide personalized recommendations to improve sleep quality. The fitness tasks integrate information from training load, sleep, health metrics, and subjective feedback to provide personalized recommendations for the intensity of a physical activity that day. For the coaching recommendations tasks, we create the first personal health case study dataset to benchmark LLM performance on reasoning and understanding of personal health behaviors. This dataset consists of long-form questions grounded in summarized personal health behavior data, vertical-specific evaluation rubrics, and expert human responses for 857 case studies across sleep and fitness. Through rigorous human and automatic evaluation, we demonstrate that Gemini Ultra 1.0 approaches expert performance in fitness while fine-tuning PH-LLM enables it reduce the gap with experts in sleep coaching experiences, explore the breadth of personal health knowledge encoded within Gemini models, and apply multimodal capabilities to prediction of PROs in sleep (Figure 1). Our key contributions are summarized as follows: • PH-LLM: We introduce a new model fine-tuned from Gemini for applications in personal health, capable of performing interpretation of time-series sensor data from wearables (i.e., Fitbit and Pixel Watch) for analysis and recommendations in sleep and fitness. • Long-form case studies from domain experts: We create the first dataset of detailed personal health case studies in sleep and fitness curated by multiple experts in the associated domains. The dataset contains individual wearable sensor data and corresponding long-form insights and recommendations. We present rubrics for evaluation of long-form responses that span domain knowledge, use of user data, personalization, and potential for harm, and provide insights on training experts for accurate evaluation. • Benchmark and contextualize personal health question-answering: We curate a set of validated domain-specific multiple choice examination questions on sleep and fitness, establish strong benchmarks based on continuing medical education requirements, and provide context for the scores through a set of human experts who completed a representative set of exam questions. • Multimodal sensor interpretation of self-reported outcomes: We successfully integrate longitudinal time-series sensor features to interpret a user’s subjective experience. To do so, we evaluate the capabilities of PH-LLM in predicting sleep disturbance and impairment PROs (acquired through validated survey instruments) from passive sensor readouts and show that accurate model performance requires native multimodal data integration. 2 A PREPRINT - JUNE 11, 2024 Recommendation & Insights Quality 1 2 3 4 5 (A) Coaching Recommendations Professional Examinations Patient-Reported Outcomes Sleep Area Under ROC Curve 0% 20% 40% 60% Naive Performance Accuracy 20% 40% 60% 80% 100% 0% Human Experts Personal Health LLM (PH-LLM) Professional Examinations Sleep Fitness (B) Make sure your bedroom is cool and dark.
