Sentence Prime PO The barista brewed [a(n excellent) coffee]𝑁𝑃1 [for the speaker]𝑁𝑃2 DO The barista brewed [the speaker]𝑁𝑃1 [a(n excellent) coffee]𝑁𝑃2 Target PO The thief wrote [the coded message]𝑁𝑃1 [for the accomplice]𝑁𝑃2 DO The thief wrote [the accomplice]𝑁𝑃1 [the coded message]𝑁𝑃2 or Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, Ouyang et al., 2022) in order to generate more human-preference-aligned responses. We include alignment-tuned models in our analysis to investigate whether models that are better at downstream tasks are better at capturing human signals, but also whether the alignment tuning itself makes LMs more or less successful models of human language processing (although recent work has shown no improvement over base models; Kuribayashi, Oseki et al., 2024). We hope that examining structural priming and its similarity to human priming behaviours in a range of LMs will further inform the protocols of model selection in this emerging research field. Magnitude of priming effects We expected exposure to prime sentences to influence predictions made for structurally similar targets by both humans and LMs, increasing target structure predictability and decreasing processing costs. In the human data, we expected the priming effect to be (a) weakly, if at all, reflected in gaze durations (given the lack of lexical overlap across prime-target sentences in our design; Tooley, 2023) and (b) more strongly reflected in changes of the EEG signal magnitude across conditions (Van Boxtel & Lawyer, 2023). In the LMs, we expected to see decreased surprisal values (calculated as negative log probabilities) for target sentences given a structurally similar vs. dissimilar prime sentence (Sinclair et al., 2022). There are reasons to expect that LM structural priming would be weaker than in humans. First, surprisal has been shown to underestimate human reading times for less expected words (Van Schijndel & Linzen, 2021; Wilcox et al., 2021). LM-derived structural measures are also affected by the semantic content of both prime and target sentences (Huang et al., 2024). We further hypothesised that priming effects will be present in target sentences in both human data and in LMs irrespective of the presence of the modifier in the primes, i.e., regardless of exact word order overlap between structurally similar primes and targets. Robustness of priming effects across prime-target pairs with and without modifiers would suggest that the syntactic predictions generated by humans and LMs are, to a large extent, abstract in nature. In contrast, modulation of priming effects by a linear word order match between primes and targets (such as observing enhanced priming across sentences with an exact sequential match) would imply that word order sequence matching facilitates syntactic processing. Finally, we expected potential differences in the magnitude of the priming effects for PO and DO targets in both the human and LM data. Dative PO syntax is generally preferred over DO syntax by human participants, and this was the case for our materials as well (see norming data below). According to the implicit learning account, which predicts an inverse frequency effect for priming (Chang et al., 2006; Fine & Florian Jaeger, 2013; Fraundorf & Jaeger, 2016), we would expect weaker priming effects for target sentences with the more frequent and predictable PO structure compared to the dispreferred DO structure. In LMs, it is not clear if greater exposure to a specific structure in the learning corpus will produce human-like inverse frequency effects in priming. Locus of priming effects Previous behavioural and EEG studies reported the peaks of structural priming effects on the first or second post-verbal NPs. In PO and DO sentences, the first post-verbal NP (NP1) is the first location where prime-based structural predictions are tested. Structural interpretations of this NP can be largely driven by noun animacy (and thus semantic predictions): animate nouns suggest a DO structure and inanimate nouns suggest a PO structure, although this relationship is not deterministic. The syntactic structure of the target sentence is then fully disambiguated at the second post-verbal NP (NP2): NP2 in sentences with PO syntax starts with a preposition (e.g., ‘to/for’; an overt marker for the PO structure) while NP2 in sentences with DO syntax does not (instead, in our materials, NP2 started with the determiner ‘the/a’). We expect that, if human participants generate strong and immediate syntactic predictions on the basis of prime sentences, we should see clear effects of structural priming at NP1 in target sentences. Effects emerging only at NP2 are more consistent with the presence of weak or late syntactic predictions generated (a) on the basis of primespecific structural information and (b) on the basis of already available structural information in the target sentence (i.e., integration of NP1 into the parse of the target sentence). For both NP1 and NP2, we expect EEG signal differences between structurally primed and unprimed targets to peak in the P600 time window (from 400 to 700 ms) following reading of the first word within the noun phrase (NP1 or NP2; Ledoux et al., 2007; Tooley & Traxler, 2010). In the case of LM priming effects, we expect the largest priming effects to occur at the onset of NP2 (i.e., peaking at the first word in NP2), where the model is forced to make a prediction about the sentence structure (Jumelet et al., 2024b). Similarity between human and LM priming behaviour LM per-word surprisal has been successfully and widely used to predict cortical responses to words in context, providing confirmatory evidence that predictive processing fundamentally shapes comprehension in the human brain (Schrimpf et al., 2021). It is an open question whether the Priming Effect measure (Sinclair et al., 2022), which we will use as the main index of structural priming in LMs, will be equally predictive of the human-derived indices of structural priming. If it is (for example, if human and LM priming effects are both found to be consistently larger or smaller for specific stimuli), this would provide initial evidence that the priming behaviours produced by the LMs and the human participants are similar. However, to conclude that syntactic priming effects (and therefore aspects of syntactic processing) are similar in LMs and humans, we have to exclude other non-syntactic factors that may be driving such similarities. Syntactic priming in both LMs and humans is known to be sensitive to lexico-semantic links between the prime and target sentences (Tooley, 2023) and grammatical preferences of target verbs (Scheepers & Crocker, 2004). Hence, the similarity in priming behaviours can also be driven by such factors. To isolate the contribution of syntactic and non-syntactic properties of the context to any priming effects in LM and human responses, we derived several measures of relevant nonsyntactic sentence properties (see below) and asked if LM priming Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 6 A. Sinclair et al. responses can predict human priming responses over and above these non-syntactic measures. First, we used the human-derived measure of 𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑒𝑝𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 computed from a norming study that was conducted with a separate group of participants (see Section ‘‘Methodology’’). These norming ratings provide an overall assessment of sentence acceptability and processing difficulty for our stimuli: absolute differences across sentences indicate whether each sentence sounds ‘‘natural’’ or not, and relative differences between the same sentence with PO and DO syntax provide an item-specific measure of structural preference and parsing difficulty. Second, we use a Target Verb structural preference measure (𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀) capturing the preference of each verb for PO or DO syntax in each sentence (see Section ‘‘Prime-Target Verb Similarity - 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝐿𝑀’’). Finally, we add a measure of Prime-Target Lexico-semantic dependence (𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁, Section ‘‘WordNet verb similarity - 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁’’), which is a graph-based measure of semantic similarity between prime and target verbs. If LM structural priming explains variance in the human responses over and above these measures (𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑒𝑝𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦, 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀, 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁), we can be more confident that similarity between human and LM priming behaviours is driven by abstract syntactic processing and not solely by predictions based on the preceding lexico-semantic context (whether within the prime or within the target) or on target sentence acceptability. Methodology Participants 27 native speakers of English took part in the EEG reading experiment. All were undergraduate or postgraduate students at the University of Aberdeen, with ages ranging between 18 and 40 years (19 female, 6 male, 2 non-binary). Materials 64 dative verbs allowing both DO and PO syntax were selected for the experiment. Four sentences with DO and PO syntax were written with each verb (e.g., DO: The thief wrote the accomplice the coded message; PO: The thief wrote the coded message for the accomplice), for a total of 256 sentences (see Table 1 and Appendix A for the full list). These sentences were grouped into four blocks of 64 sentences each, such that each block included one sentence with each of the 64 verbs. In each block, sentences were paired to created 32 prime-target pairs. One sentence was randomly designated to serve as the prime and one as the target. Across the four blocks, all prime-target verb combinations were unique (i.e., a prime/target sentence with one verb was paired with another target/prime sentence with a different verb in each block). The 256 prime and target sentences had a total of 768 nouns (sentence-initial subjects and two post-verbal NPs), of which 698 were unique nouns and 35 were repeated once. Each pairing of primes and targets included a unique set of nouns. Direct object NPs were primarily inanimate nouns (250 inanimate, 6 animate nouns), while indirect object NPs were primarily animate (240 animate, 16 inanimate nouns). The prime and target sentences also included a modifier for the direct object (250 modifiers were unique, 3 were repeated once). When constructing our stimuli, the primary aim was to obtain sentences that sounded as natural as possible. As a result, our stimuli contain a degree of minimal overlap in function words (determiners and prepositions). In target sentences, the post-verbal NPs (NP1 and NP2) started with a definite determiner (the). Prime sentences included both definite and indefinite determiners (the, a) in these positions, ensuring no complete overlap in determiners in prime-target sentence pairs. In the PO-primed condition (where both primes and targets had PO syntax), 62% of the prime-target sentence pairs items did not have prepositional overlap. Prime and target sentences were embedded in a list of 396 filler sentences. The filler sentences used a range of syntactic structures (excluding dative syntax) and ranged in length from 4 to 14 words. Repetition in sentence meaning was avoided. Three fillers were presented before each prime-target sentence pair, and there was no lexical repetition between content words in each quintuplet made up of 3 filler and 2 prime/target sentences. Design The EEG reading experiment used a 2 (Prime Structure: PO vs. DO) x 2 (Target Structure: PO vs. DO) x 2 (Modifier Presence in the primes: with modifier vs. without modifier) design. Thus, eight lists of stimuli were created to counterbalance all conditions within-participants and within-items. Each participant received four blocks of stimuli, and to control for practice and fatigue effects, the four blocks were rotated to create a total of 32 lists of stimuli. Procedure Participants were tested individually. The experiment was programmed in ExperimentBuilder and conducted with an SR Research EyeLink1000 (monocular tracking). A Cambridge Research Systems 32’’ Display++ LCD monitor set to 1920 𝑥 1080 pixels resolution and a 120 Hz refresh rate was used for stimulus presentation. Participants’ head position was secured with a chin rest approximately 60 cm away from the screen. The display was hardware linearised. The experiment was conducted in a darkened room, where the only source of light was the monitor. Participants were informed that their task was to read sentences silently for comprehension as they would naturally. The experimental session consisted of 4 blocks of approximately 160 sentences each (the first block began with 4 practice trials and each subsequent block with 2 practice trials). A 9-point calibration procedure was performed before each block and was repeated when required during each block. Each trial then started with a fixation point at the top of the screen: participants were instructed to fixate this point and press the space bar when they were ready to begin. A second fixation point was then presented in the location of the first word of the sentence and, with a fixation-contingent display change function, was replaced by a sentence once the participant fixated on this point. Each sentence was presented in.30 font for 3.5 s. Concurrent EEG data were recorded using an ActiveTwo amplifier system (Biosemi) from 64 Ag/AgCl electrodes at a sampling rate of 500 Hz using the default 10–20 electrode layout. Eye movements and blinks were collected by electro-oculographic recordings from supraorbital and infraorbital right eye electrodes (vertical vEOG) and outer canthi of both eyes (horizontal hEOG). During acquisition, the reference electrodes were positioned at the centres of right and left earlobes, and offline EEG data was re-referenced to the average virtual electrode. EEG data pre-processing EEG data were processed using the MNEPython toolbox (Gramfort et al., 2013) as well as custom Python and R-routines. Data was rereferenced (averaged) and bandpass filtered between 0.2 and 40 Hz with a zero-phase fourth-order finite impulse response filter. Continuous data was then visually inspected for bad channels. Bad channels were interpolated using weighted average of the neighbouring channels (interpolate_bads). Ocular artefacts (blinks and horizontal eye movements) were detected and removed using the independent component analysis (ICA) function. Components with the highest correlation to the vEOG and hEOG channels were visually inspected and removed from the data. Data was then epoched and re-aligned to critical events of interest within target sentences using the time stamps from gaze meaJournal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 7 A. Sinclair et al. surements (the first fixation to a given interest area). We deliberately chose to align EEG data to the first fixations within the areas of interest (i.e., NP1 and NP2) and not to specific words (i.e., prepositions, articles, or nouns). This was done for two reasons. First, the first fixation in the area of interest represents the time point when participants can unambiguously confirm or dis-confirm their expectations about the syntactic structures they are processing (DO or PO). We expect that effects of syntactic priming will peak at this time point. Second, choosing to align our analysis to specific lexical items (i.e. the prepositions or articles as the first word of NP2) results in data loss, since during naturalistic reading participants often skip individual words during first-pass reading. In our sample, participants fixated on the first word of NP2 (’to’ for POs and ‘the’ for DOs) on average only 51 and 49 percent of the time respectively. Finally, during epoching, a withinsentence baseline was used, corresponding to the period form −0.4 s to −0.2 s before the onset of the critical event (see below). Epochs exceeding the 130𝑒−6𝜇𝑉 threshold were removed. For further analysis, we generated three separate epochs, centred around the three critical sentence locations: the verb, the first postverbal NP (NP1, i.e., the direct object in PO sentences, the indirect object in DO sentences) and the second post-verbal NP (NP2, i.e., the indirect object in PO sentences, the direct object in DO sentences). For each of these locations, we wanted to check whether effects of priming began before or after the first fixation in that location. We therefore took the baseline from −0.4 to −0.2 s (200 ms of baseline) and left 0.1 s before the onset of the first fixation to these sentence locations (verb, NP1, NP2). This baseline will allow us to see if the effects of priming began before the onset of the key event and would justify an analysis of earlier epochs within the sentence. With this approach, we would be able to confirm or dis-confirm the presence of structural priming effects as far back as the main verb — the first linguistic event that can give readers information whether the target sentence will have PO or DO syntax in the case of verbs with strong preferences for one structure over another. Human-generated measures Sentence norming — 𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑒𝑝𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 The prime and target sentences were normed in a separate online study, programmed in Testable, and conducted with 60 new participants (all native speakers of English). The norming study used the design of the main experiment. The stimuli were counterbalanced over 8 lists (crossing the variables Prime Structure, Target Structure, and Modifier presence) and were divided into 4 blocks of 32 prime-target pairs each. To reduce fatigue, however, each participant received only one block of sentences to rate. The 32 prime-target pairs in each block were embedded in a sequence of 96 fillers, with two fillers occurring between any two prime-target pairs and one filler between the prime and target sentences of each pair. The same fillers were used in each list. The fillers included 81 sentences that were presented in the main experiment as well as 15 trials that served as attention checks (10 sentences with grammatical errors and 5 sentences with scrambled word order). Thus, in total, each participant rated 160 sentences. The instructions asked participants to indicate how natural each sentence sounded to them on a 1-6 Likert scale. The results confirmed participants’ preference for PO syntax over DO syntax: PO primes received reliably higher ratings (M = 4.56, SD =.71) than DO primes (M = 4.07, SD = 1.01), and similarly PO targets received reliably higher ratings (M = 4.42, SD =.69) than DO targets (M = 3.83, SD =.92). Comparing ratings given to target sentences across conditions in a linear mixed-effects model analysis showed a reliable difference between PO and DO targets (𝑡= 6.07) but no influence of the primes on target ratings (𝑡< 1.4 for the main effect of Prime Structure and interaction with Target Structure). The presence of the modifier in prime sentences also did not influence target ratings (𝑡< 1.65 for the main effect and interaction with Target Structure). These ratings were used as predictors in the analyses we report below to test whether priming effects varied systematically with readers’ item-specific preferences for PO and DO syntax. Ratings for prime sentences were not included as they did not generate stable effects. WordNet verb similarity — 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 Wordnet (Miller, 1995) is a large electronic lexical database which contains human-curated semantic relationships between words as a hierarchy of concepts. We make use of this resource, and NLTK (Bird & Loper, 2004), to calculate verb similarity as the shortest path that connects two verbs via their semantic relations. While the experimental sentences were deliberately combined into prime-target pairs to avoid semantic similarity, adding this measure to our analyses captures any within-item sources of similarity. Language model methodology We selected Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) language models, evaluating a suite of contemporary auto-regressive pretrained models. Auto-regressive language models – also known as causal or left-to-right LMs – are trained to predict the next word in a sequence and learn to do this based on the difference between the model’s prediction and the actual word in the training data.3 Language models This incremental processing and error-based learning is arguably similar to human language processing. All models are loaded from the transformers library (Wolf et al., 2019), and model predictions are extracted using the diagnnose library (Jumelet, 2020). We select a range of model sizes which can provide more robust evidence of any priming effects observed. We considered the following language models: GPT2 We select the GPT2-large and GPT2-xl models (Radford et al., 2019), as their estimates are shown to be more predictive of comprehension behaviour than larger LM variants (Oh & Schuler, 2023; Schrimpf et al., 2021; Shain et al., 2022). These OpenAI model, with respectively 774M and 1.5B parameters, were the main focus of analysis in Sinclair et al. (2022). OPT The OPT models (Zhang et al., 2022) form a publicly available suite of models ranging up to 175B parameters. OPT models have demonstrated competitive performance across a range of benchmarks (Beeching et al., 2023; Paperno et al., 2016). To investigate a range of sizes we use OPT-125m, 350m, 1.4b, 2.7b, and 6.7b. Llama The Llama models (Touvron et al., 2023) have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks (Hendrycks et al., 2021). We consider both the Llama-2-7b and Llama-3-8b models, as well as their instruction-tuned variants. Instructiontuning is a procedure in which a pre-trained model is aligned with human preferences, and an important procedure for creating models that can generate fluent responses in dialogue (Ouyang et al., 2022). 3 We make use of auto-regressive models, since these are more cognitively plausible with respect to the linear manner that humans process sentences, unlike, bi-directional models such as e.g. BERT (Devlin et al., 2018). These models do not account for potential parafoveal effects that are know to affect humans in naturalistic reading – whereby some information from the following word is available to a reader as they read, partially visible in peripheral vision – which could limit explanatory power. Heilbron et al. (2023), however, have found that models of reading times are better explained by non-contextual observer parafoveal entropy, in other words, that including LM-derived signal for the following word does not increase the explanatory power. Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 8 A. Sinclair et al. Gemma The Gemma models (Team et al., 2024) are part of a suite of open models based on Google’s (closed-source) Gemini models. We use the 2b and 7b variants of Gemma. They have been shown to be comparable to or outperform Llama and Mistral models on a range of benchmarks. Measuring priming in language models We make use of the log probabilities of the language models (LMs) for a word given a preceding context. The inverse of this log probability is our main measure of surprisal. From these probability estimates, we compute surprisal over the target, and thus can extract the conditional surprisal of a target given a structurally similar or dissimilar prime. This is a similar signal to that obtained in the EEG data with human participants, but with an important advantage. In the LMs, there is no updating of the model from trial to trial (i.e., unlike in human participants, the model’s performance on a given target sentence is influenced by the preceding prime but not by any other sentences presented in the same task). Hence, we can also obtain independent measures performance for all stimuli (i.e., each prime-target pairing in the 2×2×2 design) which is not possible in the human experiment as each participant saw each prime-target pairing in only one condition from the 2×2×2 design. We can thus compute a Priming Effect (PE) from the differences in conditional surprisal in the primed and unprimed conditions for each prime-target pairing. We propose that the PE measure presented by Sinclair et al. (2022), adapted to measure only the regions of interest (noun phrases) and making use of the per-word 𝑃𝐸 introduced by Jumelet et al. (2024b), will provide a highly-controlled measure for making predictions of priming strength in humans, allowing direct comparison of whether priming in LMs predicts human priming in the same stimuli. We describe these measures in more detail below. Target surprisal Conditional surprisal. We explore the effect of the context (i.e., of exposure to a prime sentence) on target surprisal by calculating perword surprisal in each target after a structurally similar and dissimilar prime. The surprisal of a word 𝑤𝑖 is the negative logarithm of the word probability given words encountered in the target sentence so far (t∶𝑤𝑖) and given the preceding prime sentence p: 𝑆(𝑤𝑖∣p, t∶𝑤𝑖) = −ln 𝑃(𝑤𝑖∣p, t∶𝑤𝑖) (1) To compute the surprisal 𝑆 of a specific noun phrase (np), we average its per-word surprisal values. Taking the sum, instead of the average, would heavily conflate phrase surprisal with phrase length: a modified phrase would in most cases have a larger surprisal than an unmodified phrase. As such, phrase surprisal in our linear models would be heavily confounded with the binary variable of the modification of the noun phrase. By taking the average, we thus mitigate this problem and we express the surprisal of each word in the noun phrase on average. We compute this for NP1 and NP2 in the target sentences. 𝑆(np ∣p, t∶np) = 1 |np| ∑ 𝑤𝑖∈np 𝑆(𝑤𝑖∣p, t∶np, np∶𝑖) (2) Unconditional surprisal. We also calculate per-word surprisal for each target in the same manner outlined in the previous section, but with no preceding prime context (i.e., without exposure to a prime sentence). We use this ‘unconditional’ surprisal measure to capture surprisal driven by collocational frequencies of the words within the target sentence alone. Surprisal has been shown to predict N400 amplitude (Goldstein et al., 2022) so we expect it to capture some of the variance in our data as well. We therefore use this measure as a factor in our trial-level LM analysis to assess the extent to which we observe a priming effect over and above per-word surprisal. We expect this factor to serve as a partial equivalent to the norming data we collected. Priming effects To obtain a controlled measure that isolates the effects of prime structure on the model surprisal for target, we calculated priming effects as the difference in log probabilities of a target sentence of structure x (PO or DO) given a structurally similar vs. a dissimilar prime sentence4 (px vs. py) (Sinclair et al., 2022): 𝑠-𝑃𝐸(tx) = ln 𝑃(tx ∣px) −ln 𝑃(tx ∣py) (3) This 𝑠-𝑃𝐸 metric expresses the priming effect on the sentence (i.e., item) level. Through examining per-word priming effects – as in Jumelet et al. (2024b) – we are able to investigate which words within the target were most responsible for such an effect, and thus locate the onset of priming within each target sentence. For this, we make use of the word-level priming effect metric (𝑤-𝑃𝐸) (Jumelet et al., 2024b), which expresses priming effects for each individual target word 𝑇x 𝑖: 𝑤-𝑃𝐸(tx, 𝑖) = ln 𝑃(tx 𝑖|px, tx <𝑖) −ln 𝑃(tx 𝑖|py, tx <𝑖) (4) As with Conditional Surprisal, we compute the 𝑤-𝑃𝐸 scores for NP1 and NP2 by averaging the word-level PE scores. As an example, consider the following prime and target sentence, taken from our evaluation data: ppo ∶𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑤𝑎𝑖𝑡𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑓𝑖𝑥𝑒𝑑𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑔𝑒𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑙𝑒𝑠𝑜𝑢𝑝𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑒𝑟. pdo ∶𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑤𝑎𝑖𝑡𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑓𝑖𝑥𝑒𝑑𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑝𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑒𝑟𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑣𝑒𝑔𝑒𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑙𝑒𝑠𝑜𝑢𝑝. tpo ∶𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑝𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑙𝑔𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑑𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑥𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑜𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑝𝑢𝑝𝑖𝑙. tdo ∶𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑝𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑙𝑔𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑑𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑝𝑢𝑝𝑖𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑥𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛. If we want to compute the 𝑤-𝑃𝐸 score for NP1 (an extension) in PO structure, we had express this as follows: 𝑤-𝑃𝐸(tpo, 𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑥𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛) = ln 𝑃(𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑥𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛∣ppo, 𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑝𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑙𝑔𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑑) −ln 𝑃(𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑥𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛∣pdo, 𝑇ℎ𝑒𝑝𝑎𝑛𝑒𝑙𝑔𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑑) This word-level priming effect measure allows us to compare at a more fine-grained level the extent to which priming effects in LMs differ from humans at certain key points over the processing of a sentence. A sentence-level measure would restrict us to comparing only an aggregate of the detailed temporal information that we obtain from human measures: word-level priming effects, on the other hand, allow us to examine the extent to which human processing signal is predictable via LM-derived metrics at different positions in a sentence. Priming effect factors Verb structural preference — 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 Complementary to the sentence norming study, we also calculated the structural preferences of our stimuli verbs in each LM. We express the structural preference of a verb as the average difference in log probabilities of the verb occurring in a PO structure vs. a DO structure (Hawkins et al., 2020; Jumelet et al., 2024b; Veenboer & Bloem, 2023). A similar methodology has been deployed in corpusbased studies of structural preferences (Bresnan et al., 2007; Gries & Stefanowitsch, 2004). po−𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓(𝑣) = 1 || ∑ 𝑠∈ log 𝑃(𝑠po) −log 𝑃(𝑠do) (5) where  is the set of sentences containing verb 𝑣. This score expresses a verb’s preference towards a particular structure on a scale from DO to PO: smaller values on this scale indicate a preference for DO syntax, and larger values indicate a preference for PO syntax. We computed these scores for all our target sentences. 4 American versions of the spellings of the original stimuli presented to the participants were used with the LMs, since LMs are likely they have a bias towards American English. See Appendix A for more details. Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 9 A. Sinclair et al. Prime-target verb similarity — 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝐿𝑀 We extracted LM measures of semantic similarity between prime (𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒) and target (𝑉𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡) verbs in our materials making use of modelspecific embedding of the root form of the verbs. We calculate similarity as the Cosine Similarity between these embeddings. 𝑉𝑆𝑖𝑚𝐿𝑀= 𝐶𝑜𝑠𝑖𝑛𝑒(𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒, 𝑉𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡) (6) We include this LM-derived measure of verb similarity, rather than the human-derived measure described in Section ‘‘WordNet verb similarity — 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁’’, because our aim is to understand the extent to which the structural interaction plays a role over and above the semantic signal present in the LM’s predictions.5 Analysis plan To address our key questions, we conducted three sets of analyses. Priming in humans. In the first set of analyses, we explored the presence of syntactic priming effects in the gaze and EEG data (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in eye movements’’ and Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in EEG’’). For gaze data, we calculated first-pass fixation durations for NP1 and NP2 (i.e., all fixations to words in the direct object and indirect object phrases) in target sentences, as well as total gaze durations and regressions to these regions. Analyses were limited to first-pass gaze durations on NP1 and tested for the presence of a structural priming effect (a reduction in gaze durations in structurally primed sentences) with linear mixed-effects models. The analysis of EEG data used two approaches. Our first goal was to confirm the presence of structural priming, i.e., changes in response amplitudes for post-verbal NPs following structurally similar than dissimilar primes (with primed conditions showing reduced response amplitude compared to unprimed ones). For this initial analysis, event-related potentials (ERPs) were generated for all primed and unprimed target sentences for each participant for NP1 and NP2. To test for significant differences within these ERPs at the participantgroup level, we conducted spatio-temporal cluster-based permutation t-tests CBPT (as implemented in the permutation_cluster_1samp_test MNE function). CBPT allows for estimating the presence of statistical differences between conditions in a high-dimensional space of the EEG signal (sensors x time), as it accounts for the spatial adjacency between the electrodes and time points of the data (Maris & Oostenveld, 2007). To test whether priming was stronger for one of the two dative structures (DO vs. PO) or dependent on the presence of the adjectival modifier in the primes, we also ran an interaction analysis. A second analysis was then conducted on trial-level responses with linear mixed-effect models. The mixed-effects analyses for gaze and EEG data consisted of a series of models, conducted with the Pymer4 package of Jolly (2018) which relies on an underlying R implementation from lmer. The first model (the ‘‘base’’ model; MLM1) included the three-way interaction between the three categorical predictors built into the 2×2×2 design (Prime Structure, Target Structure, Modifier Presence), and thus tested for the presence of a structural priming effect in target sentences that followed primes with and without modifiers. This model was then built up sequentially to test whether a priming effect is still present after the inclusion of two item-level variables capturing lexico-semantic 5 Recent work has shown that semantic similarity in LM representations can be heavily skewed by a small set of rogue dimensions (this is called anisotropy) (Mimno & Thompson, 2017; Timkey & van Schijndel, 2021). However, this effect is mainly prevalent in the contextual representations of the higher LM layers, and less in the static word embeddings that serve as input to the LM. Since we compute verb similarity based on these static embeddings, we do not incorporate the proposed correction of Timkey and van Schijndel (2021) in our setup. We leave an exploration of the impact of anisotropy on semantic similarity and priming open for future work. properties of the stimuli. In the first step, we added human-derived Semantic Similarity ratings 𝑉𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 (MLM2) and Target Acceptability ratings 𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐 (MLM3) to test whether similarity between primes and targets as well as overall target sentence acceptability explained additional variance. In the second step, both continuous predictors were included in the same model (MLM4). In all cases, categorical variables were coded with deviation contrasts (-.5 and.5 for the two levels of each variable) and continuous variables were standardised. Models with the maximal random effects structure failed to converge; thus, individual random slopes were removed iteratively, starting with the effect accounting for the smallest amount of variance, until convergence was reached. We specify the random effects structure of each model we report below. Improvements in model fit with the addition of new variables were tested via a series of model comparisons. 𝑀𝐿𝑀1 𝐷𝑒𝑝∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡 (Base) 𝑀𝐿𝑀2 𝐷𝑒𝑝∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡∗𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 (Base + Semantic Similarity) 𝑀𝐿𝑀3 𝐷𝑒𝑝∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡∗𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐 (Base + Target Acceptability) 𝑀𝐿𝑀4 𝐷𝑒𝑝∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡∗𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐∗𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 (Full) Priming in language models. In the second set of analyses (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in Language Models’’), we focused only on the LM data and aimed to replicate previously reported syntactic priming effects (Sinclair et al., 2022). We calculated a priming effect 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 from the conditional surprisal signal, as defined in Section ‘‘Priming Effects’’, and investigated patterns at the word and NP level. In parallel to the human data analysis (MLM1–MLM4), we conducted a series of linear mixed-effects analyses (one for each LM) predicting conditional surprisal from the variables in the 2×2×2 design (Prime Structure x Target Structure x Modifier Presence) as well as three additional itemspecific predictors. We replaced (a) the verb similarity measure from WordNet with an LM-specific measure of semantic similarity (𝑉𝑆𝑖𝑚𝐿𝑀, Section ‘‘Prime-Target Verb Similarity — 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝐿𝑀’’). We also replaced (b) the Target Acceptability variable, which captures aspects of target processing difficulty, with LM estimates of Target Surprisal ̄𝑆𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡 and Verb Preference, 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀. Consistent with prior work examining structural priming in LMs, we then also computed PEs (i.e., priming effects; see below) for each LM and tested whether a significant PE was observed for NP1 and NP2. Comparing humanvs. LM-derived measures of priming. The third set of analyses directly compared human and LM-derived measures of structural priming (Section ‘‘Do LMs predict human priming?’’). As discussed, priming in LMs is best expressed as a 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀, i.e., the difference in surprisal between the primed and unprimed conditions for each item (see the LM measures section below). To facilitate comparisons with EEG priming effects, we computed an equivalent Priming Effect, i.e., the difference between by-item averaged voltage amplitudes in the primed and unprimed conditions. Since participants never read the same targets twice, this measure aggregates across participants to compute by-item effects. To ensure that our effects are not skewed by absolute differences in the voltage amplitude across participants (e.g., due to physiological differences in head shape and recording quality), voltage amplitudes were first standardised within participants. Thus priming effects represent the difference between standardised voltage amplitudes in the primed and unprimed conditions. We produced this group-level EEG PE measure (𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺) for four theoretically motivated analysis windows for both the NP1 and NP2 epochs. These analyses windows, aligned to the onset of each NP, were: 0–100 ms Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 10 A. Sinclair et al. Fig. 1. (a) First-pass gaze durations, (b) total gaze durations, and (c) number of times each sentence location (NP1, NP2) was inspected. Error bars show 95% CIs in all plots. (Window 1), 150–300 ms (Window 2), 300–450 (Window 3), and 450–700 ms (Window 4). In reading experiments, the earlier time windows (Window 1 and 2) are typically linked to early perceptuallygrounded processes of visual analysis of written words and onset of lexical processing (Grainger & Holcomb, 2009; Hauk et al., 2012), while the later time windows (Window 3 and 4) are linked to semantic and syntactic information processing and integration of words into the sentence context (Pylkkänen & Marantz, 2003). We then used OLS regressions to explore whether LM-derived PEs, 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀, predicted EEG PEs, 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺. We expected that, if there is a relationship between PEs in LM and EEG responses, any such effects should peak in later windows, particularly in Window 4 which includes the P600 effect time-window linked to syntactic processing. Additionally, we wanted to know if LM-derived PEs predicted EEG PEs after controlling for other non-syntactic prime and target properties. We ran an additional set of OLS regressions where EEG PE was predicted by Target Acceptability scores, prime-target verb similarity 𝑉𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑊𝑁, and LM-derived target verb preference 𝑉𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 (see Section ‘‘Results’’ for a description and justification of each OLS regression). Jointly, these sets of analyses provide an assessment of the extent to which the similarity between LM and human priming behaviours is driven by syntactic processes, or alternatively, by other non-syntactic properties of the prime and target sentences that both systems are sensitive to. Results Results are reported in four sections. First, we report individual priming effects across eye movements (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in eye movements’’), EEG (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in EEG’’), and LMs (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in Language Models’’). Following our analysis plan (Section ‘‘Analysis Plan’’), we investigate the presence of priming as a predictor of processing effort (Dep) in terms of first pass gaze duration, EEG voltage, and LM conditional surprisal. Finally, in Section ‘‘Do LMs predict human priming?’’, we report the analysis testing the extent to which priming effects observed in LMs can predict priming effects in human-derived measures. Structural priming effects in eye movements Fig. 1 shows first-pass gaze durations, as well as total gaze durations and the number of entries (first-pass views and regressions) for NP1 and NP2. On average, both First Pass and Total Gaze Durations were longer for NP2 compared to NP1 (See Fig. 1). This was expected as, during whole sentence reading, readers spend more time looking at sentence-final words (wrap-up effects). These effects are explained in the literature as a consequence of multiple cognitive processes, some of which are relevant and linguistic (e.g., integration of context into a coherent sentential representation; Just & Carpenter, 1980) and other non-linguistic in nature (e.g., oculomotor response to punctuation; Warren et al., 2009; or implicit end-of-sentence prosody; Hirotani et al., 2006). The presence of these effects makes an analysis of NP2 gaze patterns, and its comparisons with NP1 data, problematic. We therefore excluded this data from further analysis. Analyses were conducted on first-pass gaze durations on NP1, testing for all interactions between Prime Structure, Target Structure, Modifier Presence (the Base model; 𝑀𝐿𝑀1) and then effects of Semantic Similarity and Target Acceptability ratings (𝑀𝐿𝑀2, 𝑀𝐿𝑀3, 𝑀𝐿𝑀4). All models included by-participant and by-item random intercepts and a by-item Target Structure slope. The Base model (𝑀𝐿𝑀1) showed two reliable effects (see Appendix B.1, Table B.7). First, as expected, gaze durations on NP1 were longer in PO targets than in DO targets due to the presence of a modifier in PO sentences. Second, the analysis showed no interactions between Prime and Target Structure, indicating the absence of an effect consistent with structural priming. In the next step, Semantic Similarity and Target Acceptability ratings were added to the Base model. There was no significant improvement in model fit when these variables were added individually (𝑀𝐿𝑀2, 𝑀𝐿𝑀3) or together (𝑀𝐿𝑀4) (all 𝑋2 < 14.3, 𝑝> 0.2). Structural priming effects in EEG ERP analyses (condition-averaged responses) Group-level ERP responses in the primed and unprimed conditions (see Methods section) were compared in two separate epochs (NP1 and NP2), and are plotted in Fig. 2. For transparency, we also plot the EEG signal from the fronto-central electrode cluster for primed and unprimed targets in each of the four conditions separately: PO and DO targets read after modified primes and PO and DO targets read after unmodified primes (see Figs. C.14 and C.15 in the Appendix). The difference between the primed and unprimed conditions reached significance only in the NP2 analysis (cluster p value = 0.003; Fig. 2). Consistent with previous findings (Ledoux et al., 2007; Van Boxtel & Lawyer, 2023), a structural priming effect emerged in the frontal and central electrodes, with the unprimed condition showing more negative response amplitudes than the primed condition. To test whether the effect of priming was different across DO and PO targets and in targets following modified versus unmodified primes, a further interaction analysis was performed where the difference waveforms (Unprimed minus Primed) we derived for each pair of conditions (PO, DO; Modified, Unmodified) and a set of secondary subtractions were performed (PO minus DO and Modified minus Unmodified) and subjected to the cluster permutation analysis. Priming effects did not differ across the two Prime Structures and across targets preceded by modified and unmodified primes. Interestingly, differences between the primed and unprimed conditions were present in a large time-window (from 100 ms to 659 ms post the onset of NP2), implying that structural priming effects could have started earlier at NP1 and were therefore observable as early as 100 ms into the analysis window for NP2. For the NP1 epoch itself, however, no priming effects were observed when grouping all conditions together, nor were there differences in priming magnitude for the two target structures (PO vs. DO) or modifier conditions (Modified vs. Unmodified) when considered separately. To illustrate this in Fig. 2, we show the results of the cluster permutation analysis on NP1, where, in the absence of any significant effects, we plot the average EEG voltage for primed and unprimed target sentences from the frontal and central electrodes that showed significant effects in NP2. ## Results
experiments reliably show the presence of priming effects across prime and target sentences with no semantic or lexical overlap, as well as enhanced priming across sentences with repetition of meaning and lexical items. Evidence of priming is similarly robust in comprehension (e.g. Tooley & Bock, 2014). In eye-tracking studies examining reading performance in individual sentences, priming is evidenced by shorter gaze durations in structurally relevant sentence regions (see Tooley, 2023; Traxler & Tooley, 2008, for reviews). The first studies in this area compared reading of sentences with temporary ambiguities and showed priming primarily across sentences sharing lexical content but not across sentences with no lexical overlap (Traxler & Tooley, 2008). Similar effects were observed in visual-world eye-tracking studies examining anticipatory gaze shifts to parts of visual displays containing structurally-relevant characters (Arai et al., 2007; Carminati et al., 2008). Importantly, later studies also showed evidence of lexically-unsupported priming (e.g., Kim et al., 2014; Thothathiri & Snedeker, 2008; Tooley, 2020; Tooley & Bock, 2014; Ziegler & Snedeker, 2019. As in production, persistence of structure in comprehension suggests the existence of and reliance on abstract syntactic structures during processing. The magnitude of the lexical boost in comprehension compared to the weakness of abstract priming was initially taken to suggest that comprehension relied strongly on lexically-bound syntactic information, with direct implications for language acquisition (see Tomasello, 2000 vs Fisher, 2002, and see Rowland et al., 2012 for updates on this debate). Newer evidence of abstract priming in comprehension, however, is more consistent with theories proposing that speakers and listeners rely on similar – and similarly abstract – structural information (Tooley & Bock, 2014). Mechanistic accounts of structural priming generally converge on the proposal that the persistence of lexically-unsupported priming reflects implicit learning of structure-building procedures (Bock & Griffin, 2000; Hartsuiker et al., 2008). This learning process can be modelled with an error-based network architecture where the producer or the comprehender generates predictions about upcoming words and then fine-tunes these predictions based on feedback generated upon exposure to those words (Chang et al., 2006, 2012; Dell & Chang, 2014; Fine & Florian Jaeger, 2013; Fine et al., 2013; Fraundorf & Jaeger, 2016; Jaeger & Snider, 2013; Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016). Specifically, in comprehension, facilitation of processing in structurally primed sentences is driven by the fact that exposure to one sentence with a given structure supports the generation of syntacticallysensitive predictions or expectations that influence processing of new, upcoming linguistic material. When the input is consistent with the comprehender’s predictions, processing of the new material is facilitated. When the input does not match the comprehender’s predictions, an error signal is generated that leads to adaptation in structurallyrelevant computations to enable generation of potentially more accurate predictions in the future. The degree to which these predictions are supported by abstract structural processes is still debated, with some accounts postulating a clear separation between an abstract sequencing pathway and a meaning-encoding pathway (e.g., Chang et al.’s 2006 dual-path model) and accounts assuming stronger involvement of lexical semantics (such as the emergence of verb bias; e.g., Kaschak & Borreggine, 2008). Importantly, in both cases, the processes involved in generating these types of predictions are argued to support longterm statistical learning of syntactic structures (Bock & Griffin, 2000; Chang et al., 2012; Dell & Chang, 2014; Kidd, 2012; Messenger et al., 2022), rather than reflecting transient residual activation of individual structural nodes. Compared to the behavioural literature, neuro-imaging research on structural priming in comprehension is relatively limited and has shown mixed results. Converging with the behavioural and eye-tracking evidence, stronger priming is observed for sentences with than without lexical overlap. In one of the first EEG studies on this topic, Ledoux et al. (2007) showed smaller (i.e., less positive) response amplitudes in the P600 time window for key nouns in target sentences with reduced relative clauses (e.g. ‘‘The speaker proposed by the group would work perfectly for the program’’) which are considered difficult to parse, Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 2 A. Sinclair et al. when these targets were preceded by prime sentences with matching (relative clause) than mismatching (main clause) syntax. The authors explained the reduction in the P600 component amplitude (which is linked to syntactic processing difficulty; Fitz & Chang, 2019) as being driven by easier syntactic parsing of the reduced relative clause after a structurally similar prime with a repeated verb. Critically, this study only investigated lexically-boosted structural priming, making it difficult to conclude that the observed effects stemmed from abstract syntactic processes. In a follow-up study, Tooley et al. (2009) expanded the relative clause paradigm to compare priming effects in primetarget pairs where verbs were repeated to prime-target pairs that had lexically different but semantically similar verbs. Structural priming was observed in target sentences with repeated verbs, evidenced by a reduced P600 amplitude, but no such effect was present in the semantically related prime-target pairs. Comparing the two conditions directly, targets with repeated verbs showed a smaller (less positive) P600 magnitude than targets with semantically related verbs. These effects appear to be robust and have been observed across languages, with several other studies showing that structural priming combined with lexical overlap reduces the P600 amplitude and thus presumably processing effort for normatively syntactically difficult or ambiguous sentences (Boudewyn et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013; Tooley et al., 2014). Recently, Van Boxtel and Lawyer (2023) showed abstract structural priming in sentences without lexical overlap. The authors used a similar paradigm as Ledoux et al. (2007) to test whether cortical processing of relative clauses was modulated by a prime with the same syntactic structure and no lexical or semantic similarity to the target. The authors also included a lexical overlap condition (verb repetition) for comparison with previous literature. Unlike previous research, they showed evidence of abstract structural priming through two effects at different points within the target sentence. First, the processing of the main verb was modulated both in the abstract prime condition and lexical overlap condition — showing a reduced P600 effect over the frontal electrodes, when contrasted with the unprimed targets. Second, at the preposition that signalled the start of the relative clause, syntactically primed targets showed an overall signal amplitude reduction (i.e., more negativity) compared to unprimed targets over both N400 and P600 time windows, with a similar trajectory continuing over the following noun phrase. The magnitude of the N400 component in the wider literature has been linked to semantic processing difficulty of a given word given the preceding context. More negative responses are typically reported to less semantically predictable or plausible words (Fitz & Chang, 2019; Hodapp & Rabovsky, 2021). The P600 effects reported in this paper, however, go in the opposite direction to previous findings: the P600 is smaller (rather than larger) for syntactically unprimed sentences and larger for syntactically primed sentences. One plausible explanation for this difference is that the authors reported these effects in frontal electrodes, while previous literature has reported effects in central and posterior electrodes. Critically, this recent work highlights the importance of examining structural priming effects in multiple time windows and topographical locations. In summary, the EEG literature is largely consistent with behavioural and eye-tracking studies in that abstract structural priming in comprehension is weaker than lexically-boosted structural priming. Nonetheless, there is emerging evidence of structural priming that is not mediated by lexico-semantic overlap, and critically, this more abstract syntactic priming may have a more temporally extended and complex cortical signature than previously assumed. Finally, there are several noteworthy methodological differences across the studies cited above. Many reading studies present sentences one word or one phrase at a time, and participants are asked to press a button to proceed from one word to the next. This way of testing has methodological advantages: it is easy to assess per-word reading times and to accurately time-lock brain activity to reading of specific words. The key disadvantage of this method, however, is that it is highly unnatural when compared to everyday reading. For instance, in natural reading, when readers are presented with full sentences, they often skip words and can begin processing new words parafoveally before launching saccades to those words. This means that, in natural reading, sentences are typically processed faster and information about still-tobe-fixated words (i.e, words to the right of a currently-fixated word in a language with a left-to-right writing system) is integrated earlier compared to word-by-word self-paced reading paradigms. To circumvent limitations imposed by word-by-word reading paradigms, the current study assessed structural priming during naturalistic reading. Previous work has established that processing of syntactically anomalous or unpredictable words does produce the expected P600 responses in naturalist reading paradigms (Osterhout et al., 2002), albeit with earlier component onsets. We therefore expect that effects of syntactic priming would likewise peak at the previously reported P600 time window but may start earlier due to faster reading speed (compared to word-byword presentation) and parafoveal effects, i.e., the ability to partially process upcoming words while fixating earlier words (Antúnez et al., 2022). Learning of structure and structural priming in language models Large language models show interesting human-like linguistic behaviour in some domains (see Chang & Bergen, 2024 for a review). Human readers normally find sentences with high-frequency words and simple structures (e.g., I love going to the beach) easier to process than sentences with less frequent words and more complex syntax (One has been known to enjoy partaking in seaside activities). The same words and structures can also be easier to process in predictable contexts. Similarly, models show lower prediction error for predictable input. Prediction error is quantified as surprisal and corresponds to the negative log of the conditional probability that a LM assigns to a given word within a sentence, given its preceding context. Thus, LM surprisal can be used as a measure of how unexpected a given word, phrase, or sentence is, depending on the level of analysis. In the computational linguistics literature (reviewed below), surprisal has been shown to capture both structural syntactic and lexico-semantic expectations, although these LM-derived measures tend to underestimate human indices of processing effort (e.g. Arehalli et al., 2022; Oh & Schuler, 2023). It is therefore critical to evaluate the relative contributions of the structural syntactic content to the predictions of LMs, before contrasting them to measures of human syntactic processing. Syntactic ability. Interdisciplinary research on the linguistic abilities of LLMs has been essential to broaden our understanding of their capabilities. In particular, analyses of their syntactic proficiency have significantly improved evaluation benchmarks and deepened our understanding of syntactic behaviour in LMs (e.g. Gauthier et al., 2020; Goldberg, 2019; McCoy et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2021; Warstadt et al., 2020). These investigations contribute to larger, multi-faceted benchmarks of general LM capabilities, which are essential for moving the field forward (e.g., GenBench (Hupkes et al., 2023) provides a benchmark for evaluating generalisation in LMs). It has been shown that increasing the number of parameters of a language model and the size of the training corpora not only improves their performance on next-word prediction, but also leads to an improvement on other downstream tasks they are applied to, such as question answering, summarisation, or sentiment analysis (Chowdhery et al., 2023; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Kaplan et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022). Furthermore, LMs have been shown to acquire properties of linguistic structure by encoding dependency trees and phrasestructure rules in their high-dimensional representations (Jumelet & Zuidema, 2023; Manning et al., 2020; Murty et al., 2023), by building up abstract classes such as part-of-speech (Tenney et al., 2019), and by demonstrating a deeper understanding of grammaticality judgements (Hu et al., 2020; Patil et al., 2024; Warstadt et al., 2020). Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 3 A. Sinclair et al. These findings have inspired research that proposes to use language models as a tool for studying statistical properties of human language (Beinborn & Hollenstein, 2023; Futrell & Levy, 2019; Jumelet et al., 2024a; Linzen & Baroni, 2021), as well as models of language acquisition (Chang & Bergen, 2022; Constantinescu et al., 2025; Kallini et al., 2024). An open question that remains, however, is whether the recent improvements in LM performance imply a corresponding improvement in the human-likeness of their predictions, and thus, their potential as psycholinguistic models of cognition. There is conflicting evidence in this regard. On the one hand, neuro-linguistic work has shown that brain decoding performance is proportional to next-word prediction performance (Caucheteux & King, 2022; Schrimpf et al., 2021). Likewise, the degree to which LMs encode dependency tree structure in their representations has been shown to be predictive of brain decoding performance (Fresen et al., 2024). On the other hand, recent studies have shown that better language modelling performance follows a ‘Ushaped’ trajectory in reading time prediction (Kuribayashi, Oseki et al., 2024; Oh & Schuler, 2023; Shain et al., 2022): training models on corpora up to 2 billion words improves their predictive performance of reading times, but gets worse after that point (Oh et al., 2024). Measures of surprisal from language models have also been shown to predict but underestimate human processing difficulty arising from syntactic ambiguities (Arehalli et al., 2022), and more recently, Huang et al. (2024) demonstrate that, at an item level, the word-by-word predictions of LMs are insufficient to explain human processing difficulty in syntactically complex sentences. This suggests that while surprisal is an important component of a cognitive model of such processes, more careful targeted evaluation is needed to isolate the syntactic signal of surprisal from other linguistic contributors of surprisal (such as lexical, semantic and discourse coherence). Priming in language models. Two main approaches have been used to test hypotheses about the contribution of abstract syntax to the predictions generated by LMs. The first is an adaptation-based

## Conclusion
conclusions about the plausibility of LMs as models of human language processing. They further stress the need to go beyond surface-level similarities in the linguistic behaviours of humans and LMs and compare responses generated by the two systems on an item-by-item basis.

In reading experiments, the earlier time windows (Window 1 and 2) are typically linked to early perceptuallygrounded processes of visual analysis of written words and onset of lexical processing (Grainger & Holcomb, 2009; Hauk et al., 2012), while the later time windows (Window 3 and 4) are linked to semantic and syntactic information processing and integration of words into the sentence context (Pylkkänen & Marantz, 2003). We then used OLS regressions to explore whether LM-derived PEs, 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀, predicted EEG PEs, 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺. We expected that, if there is a relationship between PEs in LM and EEG responses, any such effects should peak in later windows, particularly in Window 4 which includes the P600 effect time-window linked to syntactic processing. Additionally, we wanted to know if LM-derived PEs predicted EEG PEs after controlling for other non-syntactic prime and target properties. We ran an additional set of OLS regressions where EEG PE was predicted by Target Acceptability scores, prime-target verb similarity 𝑉𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑊𝑁, and LM-derived target verb preference 𝑉𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 (see Section ‘‘Results’’ for a description and justification of each OLS regression). Jointly, these sets of analyses provide an assessment of the extent to which the similarity between LM and human priming behaviours is driven by syntactic processes, or alternatively, by other non-syntactic properties of the prime and target sentences that both systems are sensitive to. Results Results are reported in four sections. First, we report individual priming effects across eye movements (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in eye movements’’), EEG (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in EEG’’), and LMs (Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in Language Models’’). Following our analysis plan (Section ‘‘Analysis Plan’’), we investigate the presence of priming as a predictor of processing effort (Dep) in terms of first pass gaze duration, EEG voltage, and LM conditional surprisal. Finally, in Section ‘‘Do LMs predict human priming?’’, we report the analysis testing the extent to which priming effects observed in LMs can predict priming effects in human-derived measures. Adding Target Acceptability in 𝑀𝐿𝑀3 showed a similar pattern. The models with Target Acceptability did not have a significantly better fit relative to the Base models, all 𝑋2 < 29.64, 𝑝𝑠> 0.06, for NP1 and NP2, with the exception of window 4. These analyses showed two effects of interest: first, the analysis of Window 4 for NP2 showed a significant interaction between Prime Structure, Target Structure, and Target Acceptability: importantly, stronger priming effects were observed for target sentences with low acceptability ratings. Second, an interaction between Prime Structure, Modifier Presence and Target Norming was observed in Windows 2, 3 and 4 in NP1, and Window 3 for NP2: this indicates that the relationship between the normative difficulty of items and the presence of a modifier. Finally, adding both continuous predictors in the analysis of NP1 and NP2 voltage amplitudes in 𝑀𝐿𝑀4 and testing for five-way interactions did not yield significant improvements in model fit over the Base model (all 𝑋2 < 29.64, 𝑝𝑠> 0.2), indicating that the continuous predictors explained relatively low additional amounts of variance. We include an expanded analysis of these interactions in Appendix B.3. Structural priming effects in Language Models We investigate the presence of priming in LMs via two approaches. Section ‘‘Language Model effects’’ conducts a similar analysis to those in the preceding sections, whereby we conduct an lmer analysis to predict Conditional Surprisal in order to evaluate the presence of a priming effect over and above other non-structural factors. In Section ‘‘Magnitude and onset of priming effects’’, we examine priming effects via our 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 measure, allowing us to examine the magnitude and onset of these effects within a target sentence. Language model effects Following the analysis performed on the EEG data, we repeated these analyses, as outlined in Section ‘‘Analysis Plan’’, for each of the 13 LMs, with Conditional Surprisal (𝑆) for NP1 and NP2 as the dependent variable, in several steps. As outlined in the Method section, this measure averaged across the surprisal values of all words within NPs. Due to the large number of analyses, we only report the significant effects in Table 3 and the full set of results in Appendix B.4. Presence of priming. The first set of analyses tested for a three-way interaction between Prime Structure, Target Structure and Modifier Presence (Base models; 𝑀𝐿𝑀1) for each LM. Importantly, the interaction between Prime Structure and Target Structure was significant in all models for both NP1 and NP2, showing a robust priming effect. This is consistent with the EEG results for NP2, but shows an earlier emergence of structural priming in LMs in NP1 than in human data. The consistent presence of an interaction between Prime Structure and Target Structure in all analyses suggests that LMs generated abstract, structural predictions that were sensitive to the order of verb arguments (the post-verbal order of direct objects and indirect objects in dative sentences) rather than to the length of individual NPs. Additionally, there was a significant main effect of Target Structure in all 13 models for NP1 and NP2 (See Table B.9), indicating higher overall conditional surprisal in DO than PO sentences, in line with similar findings with different dative stimuli (Jumelet et al., 2024b). Finally, a main effect of Modifier Presence was present in 9 of the 13 LMs for NP1 and in 10 of the 13 LMs for NP2. Interactions between Target Structure and Modifier Presence were present in 8 out of 13 of the models for NP1, and in all models (13 out of 13) for NP2. Most importantly, however, none of the analyses showed a significant interaction between Prime Structure, Target Structure and Modifier Presence, indicating that LMs do not rely on linearly matching sequences to exhibit structural priming. Non-syntactic predictors. In a second step, we added LM-specific continuous predictors to the analyses (Section ‘‘Priming Effect Factors’’): Unconditional Target Surprisal (𝑆(t)), Verb Preference 𝑉𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 and Verb Similarity 𝑉𝑆𝑖𝑚𝐿𝑀. These measures were extracted from each LM itself and are therefore a direct representation of the processing difficulty and similarity of prime-target verb pairs estimated for each model. Each variable was added to the Base model (𝑀𝐿𝑀1) individually first, testing for all interactions between predictors. In all cases, we checked whether adding each new variable changed the interaction between Prime Structure and Target Structure observed in the Base model (i.e., whether it modulated the priming effect), whether it produced new interactions, and whether the overall fit of the model improved significantly with a sequence of likelihood ratio comparisons. We find that the addition of the continuous predictors, both separately and jointly, did not eliminate the interaction between Prime Structure and Target Structure: this interaction was significant in all analyses (all 𝑝𝑠< 0.02) for both NP1 and NP2, demonstrating a robust priming effect. Magnitude and onset of priming effects In order to investigate the magnitude and onset of the priming effects, we turn to the priming effect 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 measure. Fig. 4 shows perword priming effects observed in the 13 LMs in PO and DO targets. Overall, a larger priming effect was observed in DO than PO sentences. Before discussing priming effects at the level of NPs in the next section, we note that a per-word comparison of the magnitude of priming effects within each NP shows a theoretically interesting pattern. Priming effects were largest at the onset of the second NP (i.e., the determiner in DO sentences and the preposition in PO sentences). This shows that it is specifically at the position in the sentence where an LM is forced to make a decision about the upcoming sentence structure that a priming effect is most robustly observed. The location of this effect in LMs adds validity to our chosen alignment point for the EEG epochs — the first fixation within the second NP, where human participants for the first time are able to unambiguously confirm or dis-confirm syntactic preferences about the sentence structure (DO vs PO). For clarity, all subsequent analyses were carried out with a 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 measure that averaged across the surprisal values of all words within each NP (see Fig. 5). Average LM Priming Effects (𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀) for (a) NP1 and (b) NP2 in DO and PO target sentences across all 13 LMs. Colours represent LM families; colour intensity represents model size within family. Priming effects were larger in DO than PO targets, with minimal differences in targets following modified and unmodified primes. Fig. 6. In-keeping with results observed in Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in EEG’’, we observe highest and most consistent 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 in later windows for PO in NP2. Do LMs predict human priming? Finally, we test to what extent the priming effects observed in LMs can predict human results. To simplify these analyses, we use the Priming Effect measure calculated from EEG and LM responses, allowing us to directly compare the magnitude of the human and LM priming effects in the same sentence locations. For both the EEG and LM data, item-specific priming effects for PO and DO sentences were computed as the difference between the structurally unprimed and primed conditions. Given that average voltage amplitudes are more negative in the unprimed conditions, priming effects in the EEG signal are represented by negative values: larger negative differences represent larger priming effects. In LMs, average surprisal is higher (i.e., more positive) in the unprimed conditions, so larger priming effects are represented by larger negative differences. To facilitate comparisons of EEG and LM priming, we changed the sign of all priming effects, such that larger magnitudes always represent larger priming effects in both EEG and LMs. The priming effects observed in LM surprisal (Fig. 5), and EEG voltage amplitudes (Fig. 6) are markedly different, most so for DO targets: while priming is the strongest in NP1 in DO targets for LMs, the inverse is true of the human data. Priming in LMs was also stronger in DO than in PO sentences, for both NP1 and NP2. However, priming effects for PO targets appeared to be more similar, particularly for NP2, with little difference between Modified and Unmodified conditions for both human and LM priming responses. Likewise, priming effects were somewhat stronger in NP2 than in NP1. Given these surface-level differences and similarities, we next tested how well 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predicts 𝑃𝐸𝐻 in PO and DO target sentences separately. Predicting human priming 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 from LM priming effects 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 We fit OLS regression models predicting item-specific human priming effects (i.e., 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺) separately for PO and DO target sentences from a combination of variables. To provide a fair and comprehensive comparison of human and LM priming, we considered a number of regression models. The first model (𝑂𝐿𝑆1) tested for an effect of Modifier Presence on the magnitude of the priming effect. Given that we compared performance for PO and DO targets separately (the Target Structure variable) and that priming effects represent the difference between the primed and unprimed conditions (the Prime Structure variable), this leaves only Modifier Presence as a manipulated variable for the first analysis. The second set of regression models (the 𝑂𝐿𝑆2 family) included both the Modifier variable and 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 (separately for each LM). The third set of regression models (the 𝑂𝐿𝑆3 family) tested whether priming effects could be predicted from Modifier Presence and three continuous variables (Human-derived Target Acceptability ratings and Semantic Similarity, and LM-derived Verb Preference ratings). Finally, the fourth set of regression models (the 𝑂𝐿𝑆4 family) included all the variables mentioned above in the most complex analysis (Modifier, Target Acceptability ratings, Semantic Similarity, LM-specific Verb Preference, and 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀). Thus the sequence of models was: 𝑂𝐿𝑆1 𝑃𝐸𝐻∼𝑀𝑜𝑑 𝑂𝐿𝑆2 𝑃𝐸𝐻∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 𝑂𝐿𝑆3 𝑃𝐸𝐻∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐∗𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁∗𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 𝑂𝐿𝑆4 𝑃𝐸𝐻∼𝑀𝑜𝑑∗𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝐴𝑐𝑐∗𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁∗𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀∗𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 The full results of these models are reported in Appendix F. We then performed four series of likelihood ratio comparisons to address specific questions, outlined below, about the extent to which 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 could explain variance in 𝑃𝐸𝐻 on its own as well as in models that already included additional predictors for completeness. For clarity, the tables below list only statistically significant comparisons for specific NPs (NP1, NP2), target structures (PO, DO), EEG windows (W1–W4), and LMs. Is priming modulated by modifier presence? First, we compared model 𝑂𝐿𝑆1 against model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆2 to test whether LM-derived indices of priming predict human effects over and above any variance already explained by the manipulated Modifier variable, in a very simple model (see Table F.11). For NP1, 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predicts 𝑃𝐸𝐻 only for PO targets, and only in 2 out of 13 LMs (OPT6.7𝑏, Llama2.7𝑏). This suggests that, although observable priming effects are weaker in NP1 for humans, they are predictable via 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 and only for a limited set of models. When considering only NP2 in PO targets (where priming effects are strongest in humans; Fig. 6), LMs generally show increasing predictive power for 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 in later windows. For NP2, only 2 out of 13 LMs (OPT125𝑚; LlamaChat2.7𝑏) were found to significantly predict 𝑃𝐸𝐻 in PO targets and only 2 in DO targets (OPT125𝑚, Meta llama). Is priming modulated by non-priming predictors? Second, we compared model 𝑂𝐿𝑆1 against model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆3 to test whether human priming effects were modulated by the continuous predictors. We used the same predictors as in Section ‘‘Structural priming effects in EEG’’ for the full model in the EEG analysis, with the addition of 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀, to provide additional LM-specific measures of verb preference. The results are reported in Table F.12. For NP1, there was a significant boost in model fit with the addition of these predictors across 9 out of 13 LMs (excluding the GPT models and Lama 3 8b models). However, these improvements are highly variable across target structures (POs and DOs), likely due to differences in verb preferences obtained in the different LMs, and to the variation in how predictable the Target Acceptability ratings are to each model (see Appendix D to see the variation between 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀). For NP2, only 1 out of 13 LMs (OPT 350m) significantly predicted human priming. These results thus show that the continuous variables are better predictors of human priming in NP1 than NP2. Does 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predict 𝑃𝐸𝐻 above other factors? To assess the degree to which 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predicted human priming relative to other variables, we took a complementary approach. In the third set, we compared model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆2 against model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆4 to test whether continuous variables have any explanatory value over and above 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀. In the complementary fourth set (which represents the strictest test), we compared model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆3 against model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆4 to test whether 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 had any explanatory value over and above the other variables. The results are reported in Tables F.13 and F.14 respectively. The third set of comparisons (𝑂𝐿𝑆2 vs. 𝑂𝐿𝑆4) showed an improvement in model fit in 4 out of 13 LMs for DOs and in 8 out of 13 LMs for POs for NP1. For NP2, an improvement in model fit was observed in 4 out of 13 LMs only for POs. Overall, these results suggest that continuous predictors explain substantial variance over and above variance explained by 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀. Finally, the fourth set of comparisons (𝑂𝐿𝑆3 vs. 𝑂𝐿𝑆4) showed that, when comparing models that differed only in the inclusion of 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 as a predictor, improvements in model fit driven by 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 were observed inconsistently. Specifically, for NP1, improvements were observed in 5 out of 13 LMs for DOs and in 6 out of 13 LMs for POs. For NP2, improvements in model fit were observed in only 3 out of 13 LMs and only for POs. Thus, in the final and strictest set of comparisons, the contribution of 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 to explaining 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 was found to be relatively limited, indeed only robustly present for Llama-3 8b (base and instruct) in Window 3 for NP1 and NP2. Main effects of non-syntactic variables and interactions with modifier presence To understand whether and how individual non-syntactic variables affected human priming effects 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺, we investigate those which are significant in model family 𝑂𝐿𝑆4, i.e., in the analyses with all continuous predictors (Semantic Similarity 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁, Target Acceptability, LM Verb Preference). Fig. 8 shows the interactions we consider. Target Acceptability significantly predicted 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 for both DO and PO targets (in windows 3 and 4 respectively) but only in NP1. This was true for a number of models (see Fig. 9). Fig. 9 shows that priming effects were larger for less acceptable targets. Model-specific 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓 only had a modest effect on 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 in NP1 in both PO and DO targets (this was true only for 2 models in DO windows 1–3 and 1 model in PO, window 1), whereby targets with verbs that preferred PO structures showing greater priming effects. 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 did not show a significant main effect on the 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺. Next, examining the 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predictor and its interaction with Modifier Presence in both the most simple (𝑂𝐿𝑆1) and the most complex (𝑂𝐿𝑆4) of the models, we observe that, although predictive, 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 does not have a consistently positive relationship with 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 across LMs and this is in part driven by the modifier. Firstly, Fig. 8, shows that when 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predicts 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 for PO targets in both NP1 and NP2, this relationship is positive for PO targets preceded by modified primes and negative when they are preceded by non-modified primes (with the exception of one model where the directionality is always negative (see Fig. 10a). For DOs, the situation is different, with only 1 gemma-family model’s 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 positively predicting 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 in NP1 with no effect of the modifier (Fig. 10c). Outlook Taken together, our results suggest that, for these stimuli and participant sample, LM priming effects can provide significant predictive effects over and above other non-syntactic factors for human priming. This picture, however is limited to specific models – notably although one of the only models to significantly predict priming is amongst the larger models, it is not the largest, and others of comparable size do not exhibit the same behaviour, as demonstrated in Fig. 10 – and specific subsets of stimuli. We also observe that the priming effects of one LM do not reliably predict the effects of each other for the same stimuli, even though these models are in the same model family (see Appendix E, Fig. E.19), highlighting the risk of reporting only results from a single LM to confirm a hypothesis. Overall, this suggests that while at a higher, behavioural level, the two systems – both humans and LMs – display priming behaviour, there are clear differences in what drives this behaviour at the item level. Discussion The goal of this study was to compare structural priming effects in human reading comprehension to LM responses elicited for the same Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 16 A.
