Relationship between Target Acceptability ratings and 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 for (a) NP1 and (b) NP2, and between Word Net Similarity and 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 for (c) NP1 and (d) NP2 in DO and PO targets. materials, and, in doing so, inform theoretical accounts of syntacticallydriven predictions in LMs and humans. We asked (a) whether robust abstract syntactic priming is detectable independently in human cortical and gaze responses and in the transformer architecture auto-regressive LMs, (b) whether the magnitude and loci of priming effects are similar in human and LM responses, and critically (c) whether the LM-derived measure of structural priming (PE) is predictive of human priming. Below, we address each set of questions in turn and discuss their implications. Magnitude and loci of syntactic priming in human and LM responses Human effects Given our materials, analyses of gaze durations were limited to NP1, where there was little evidence of structural priming. There was also little evidence of priming in NP1 in the EEG data. More interestingly, the condition-level cluster-permutation ERP analysis contrasting conditionaverage evoked EEG responses for structurally primed and unprimed target sentences confirmed the presence of robust priming in NP2. While early EEG work reported structural priming only between primes and targets with lexical overlap (Ledoux et al., 2007; Tooley et al., 2014; Tooley & Traxler, 2010), more recent work showed evidence of abstract syntactic priming in EEG (Van Boxtel & Lawyer, 2023) and other behavioural markers of sentence processing (see Tooley, 2023). Importantly, the priming effect in NP2 began early in our data — from 100 ms after participants first fixated on the NP2 and when their predictions about the grammatical structure (PO vs. DO) were unambiguously confirmed or dis-confirmed. Effects lasted up to 650 ms into the epoch. Previous research showed structural priming effects much later in the epochs aligned to the onset of the critical NPs, mainly in the P600 component time window (Ledoux et al., 2007; Tooley et al., 2014; Van Boxtel & Lawyer, 2023) thought to reflect more efficient grammatical integration of the given word into the sentence context given a prime-induced syntactic expectation (i.e., in structurally primed target sentences). The early start of these effects in our data can be largely explained by our choice of (a) the ERP analysis baseline and (b) the naturalistic reading paradigm. We deliberately did not chose a more traditional baseline that minimises the effects observed before the onset of the linguistic structure of interest (i.e., NP2) and instead opted for a baseline (−0.4 s to −0.2 s) before the onset of NP2 that did not mask any potential early and pre-epoch effects. Our rationale was that the priming effects could already be present at NP1 and therefore will spill Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 17 A. Sinclair et al. Fig. 10. Coloured lines show models where 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predicted 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 over and above other factors from the largest model family (Table F.14), and that show significant main effects of 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 or a significant interaction 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀∶𝑀𝑜𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑖𝑒𝑟𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒 in Fig. 8. Focussing on (d) NP2: PO, prediction quality is affected by sequential similarity between prime and target: 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 only predicts 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 where both prime and target are modified, sharing the same linear sequence of parts of speech. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.) over or naturally continue into NP2. Another reason for both early and temporally smoothed priming effects that span the NP2 epoch is the choice of the natural reading paradigm. Previous work overwhelmingly used the rapid serial presentation paradigm where participants read one word at a time on the screen and pressed a button to progress from one word to the next. Such paradigms typically generate much better defined peaks of the typically post-word ERP components. Such components are also present during naturalistic reading, but are much less sharp and delineated (Osterhout et al., 2002). In this paradigm, the choice of the pre-epoch baseline (typically form −100 to 0 ms before critical word onset) is justified since such a baseline is designed to have no visual signal being presented. In contrast, in naturalistic reading, there are large effects of parafoveal processing: when the eye lands on a word, its near neighbours are processed simultaneously (Antúnez et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2021). Therefore, we do expect that, before the eye landed on the critical and structure-informative article or preposition at the beginning of each NP, those words had already been partially processed and integrated into the sentence context during preceding fixations (Pan et al., 2022), explaining the early onset of the observed effects. Nonetheless, this paper being the first, to our knowledge, to report EEG signatures of abstract structural priming in naturalistic reading, it is critical to replicate these findings in future research. Both the topographical distribution and the polarity of the effects we observed is similar to those reported by Van Boxtel and Lawyer (2023). Here we show structural priming effects over NP2 with unprimed targets having more a negative deviation of the EEG signal amplitude compared to primed targets. This is consistent with recent findings by Van Boxtel and Lawyer (2023) where the authors explored priming for reduced relative English sentences and similarly showed that abstract syntactic priming resulted in a more negative deviation of the EEG signal for unprimed targets at the onset of the preposition that confirmed or disconfirmed the prime-induced syntactic prediction (e.g., the word ‘by’ confirms the start of a reduced relative clause in ‘‘The worker praised by the leader resigned’’). The topography of this effect similarly showed a fronto-central distribution, unlike other studies that reported central and posterior electrodes contributing most to the priming effects (Ledoux et al., 2007). The authors interpreted their findings as linked to memory and syntactic pattern recognition since the frontal distribution has been linked to re-activation of previously encountered information (Guillem et al., 1995). In the broader sentence processing literature outside of the syntactic priming paradigm, positive ERP components that emerge over the frontal electrodes 500+ milliseconds after contextually less plausible words have been referred to as a Late Frontal Positivity (LFP) and are often equated to the P600 component. The directionality of the priming effects that we observe (greater positivity for primed targets) and their frontal distribution is also consistent with the LFP component. LFPs have been shown as a greater positivity for more contextually predictable words, which is modulated by both contextual semantic (Brothers et al., 2015; DeLong et al., 2014) and syntactic (Friederici et al., 2002) plausibility of a given word in the current sentence context. LFPs have been proposed to reflect integration of new linguistic information into the broader situation narrative (Brothers et al., 2020; Kuperberg et al., 2020). In the literature on sentential constraints and predictions, more anterior distributions of the P600 (also referred to as post-N400 positivities, or PNPs) have been reported for sentences that are contextually less predictable but not anomalous. This led multiple researchers to suggest that the anterior distribution of the P600/aPNP effects is linked to suppression/inhibition of highly expected lexical items (Meltzer & Braun, 2013; Ness & Meltzer-Asscher, 2018). While the anterior topographical distribution of our effects is consistent with some of the mentioned literature, we cannot make any arguments about the suppression of lexical items in our stimuli since we did not explicitly manipulate their lexico-semantic predictability. Furthermore, one key difference between our analysis and previous work is that we deliberately did not align our EEG data to specific lexical items in NP1 and NP2 (see Methods section). While this prevented data loss and improved informational content alignment between the EEG and LM data, this approach has limitations. Specifically, we are limited in our ability to say whether the observed effects of syntactic priming are maximal at or indeed triggered initially by specific lexical items within the NP2 (i.e., the determiner in DO sentences and the preposition in PO sentences). Having acknowledged this limitation, in the following section, we contribute to this debate by examining whether the observed cortical signatures of structural priming can be predicted by LM-derived Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 18 A. Sinclair et al. measures of structural priming and by non-syntactic properties of our stimuli. To complement these analyses, the trial-level mixed-effects models confirmed the presence of a priming effect (evidenced by an interaction between Prime Structure and Target Structure) in all analysis windows for NP2 but not for NP1. Testing for interactions with two continuous predictors – Target Acceptability ratings and 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 – showed little sensitivity to 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁. The priming effect was modulated by Target Acceptability only in window 4 in the NP2 analysis. In summary, the EEG data shows robust abstract priming effects across our stimuli that peak at the second post-verbal noun phrase (NP2) but are also sensitive to how difficult our target sentences are to process for the participants. LM effects In parallel to the EEG results, our LM analyses showed robust abstract structural priming across the suite of 13 models tested. Consistent with Jumelet et al. (2024b), we found that priming effects in DO dative sentences peaked at the onset of the sentence-final phrase (NP2), even in the presence of a modifier in prime sentences. This is a replication of previous findings in a new set of sentences which contain relatively less frequent vocabulary than in earlier studies. While our prime and target sentences share overlap only in the function and not content words,8 which have been shown to both boost and predict structural priming effects in LMs (Jumelet et al., 2024b; Sinclair et al., 2022), words in our sentences were not deliberately chosen to be of high frequency. It is therefore not surprising to observe priming effects that are slightly larger than those shown in previous work (e.g. comparing Llama-27b, used in both works: our mean peak for 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 in NP2 is DO:0.6, and PO:0.25, whereas Jumelet et al. found peaks closer to DO:0.5 and PO:0.1). An interesting future line of work is to investigate the extent to which this rarer vocabulary may be driving our relatively larger and more balanced priming effects. One surprising finding given prior work is the minimal effect of the presence of a modifier in prime sentences on priming in the targets. Prior work showed a reduction in priming when primes and targets did not have a linear word order match, suggesting that priming could be explained in terms of simple sequence matching rather than providing evidence of more abstract structure. The current result could be due to the fact we only included a single pre-nominal adjective, rather than multi-word modifications as in Sinclair et al. (2022), but it implies the presence of a more abstract level of syntactic priming in the LMs we used. Trial-level mixed-effects models confirmed the presence of a priming effect (evidenced by an interaction between Prime Structure and Target Structure) in all LMs in both NP1 and NP2. This effect was present even in more complex models (i.e., with the addition of Semantic Similarity, Target Norming ratings, and LM-specific Verb Preference), indicating a robust influence of the abstract structural properties of prime sentences on processing of subsequent targets. Interim summary In summary, both LM and EEG data independently showed (a) abstract syntactic priming for both PO and DO sentences (b) irrespective of exact word order match (i.e., priming effects were not driven by exact word order overlap between prime and target sentences). Furthermore, for both LM and human data, the peaks of structural priming were on the second post-verbal noun phrase (NP2). This implies that prime-induced syntactic expectations shape target sentence processing relatively late, only when sufficient information about the target sentence structure has been accumulated. There are, however, notable differences between the LM and human-based responses. Specifically, LMs show significantly stronger structural priming for DO sentences, while no such preference is apparent in human responses. We discuss these differences in more detail in the following sections. 8 Our stimuli contain items where a small proportion contain the same determiners/prepositions in the same position within the sentence (See Appendix A). Does syntactic priming in LMs predict human responses? We examined similarities in syntactic priming behaviours in humans and LMs using the PE measures, testing the extent to which structural priming effects in cortical responses can be explained by the LM effects. To conclude that the priming effect of a given LM (𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀) successfully predicts human priming (i.e., 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺), the PE of that LM needed to be predictive of 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 over and above the effects of any non-syntactic variables that can plausible drive some of the observed priming effects in humans. First, contrary to our expectations, we did not observe an across-the-board similarity between LM-based and human-based structural priming effects: the syntactic priming behaviours of the majority of the LMs we considered are not predictive of human priming effects. Fig. 7 shows clearly that 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 significantly predicted 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 only in a subset of LMs (5 out of 13 LMS) and only in a limited set of our stimuli. No single LM showed consistent predictive capacity for human priming effects, and different LMs were predictive of human priming effects only for different subsets of the stimuli. Moreover, the directionality of the priming effects in these LMs and in the human data did not always align. In some cases, LMs significantly but negatively predicted human priming effects, meaning that sentences showing more priming in humans consistently showed less priming in the models; in other cases, the effects reversed. Other LMs either did not predict human priming effects or showed complex interactions with non-syntactic variables (discussed in Section ‘‘Is Syntactic priming modulated by non-syntactic factors?’’). Notably, most of these models predict human structural priming in EEG responses for PO sentences but not DO sentences (only one model, gemma-7b, predicted human priming in DO sentences). This was not surprising, since human and LM responses, when considered separately, showed different patterns, with LMs showing greater priming for DO sentences and the human data showing no difference in susceptibility to priming in PO and DO sentences. We believe that the mismatch in human-LM syntactic priming for DO structures may be due to inherent differences in how LMs and the human language system use frequency information about individual syntactic structures when making syntactic predictions. We elaborate on this in the next section (Section ‘‘LM vs. human similarities in syntactic priming’’). Another key observation is that, out of the five models that do predict human priming responses, only four would be considered relatively ‘‘large’’ by the current industrial standard and were trained on several billions of words. This is in line with the notion that larger models (i.e., models that capture statistical regularities of the language to a larger extent than smaller models) show better explanatory power for human cortical responses (Caucheteux & King, 2022). However, the lack of consistency in LMs in their ability to predict human syntactic priming has important implications for future research, highlighting the need to test multiple LMs with different training corpora and with different frequencies of syntactic structures. Our results suggest that the base frequency of syntactic structures for LMs may influence priming (e.g., LM training corpora likely include more DO than PO sentences, given their higher prevalence in American English corpora (Bock & Griffin, 2000; Grimm & Bresnan, 2009)), and it is important to verify the relationship between structure frequency in the input and the magnitude of priming for other syntactic structures. We discuss this in more detail in Section ‘‘Language models as cognitive models of syntactic prediction and priming’’. LM vs. human similarities in syntactic priming While different LMs show different patterns in their ability to predict human priming, there are several notable consistencies across them. Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 19 A. Sinclair et al. Syntactic variation. First, of the five models where 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 predicts human priming, only one model Gemma-7-b predicts priming for DO sentences. All other LMs (OPT and Llama) only successfully predict human priming for PO sentences. Our norming data shows that participants generally prefer PO syntax over DO syntax in our stimuli. We also observe the same effect in the LMs, which showed significantly higher likelihood estimates in POs (e.g., the smallest difference between PO and DO is for model: OPT-2.7b with 𝑡−𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡= 2.97, 𝑝< 0.05). While it is not feasible to precisely quantify the proportion of examples present in these models’ training data, we expect that, given evidence from corpus studies (e.g. Grimm & Bresnan, 2009), the models will have encountered more examples of DO sentences if the training data reflects American English language use. Given this input, higher syntactic priming for DO sentences in LMs plausibly reflects one the two different priming-related strategies. On one hand, since DOs may be more prevalent in the training data, LMs could have an inherent bias in their syntactically-informed predictions towards the DO structures and are therefore surprised (i.e., generate greater surprisal) when DOs are not encountered after they have been primed, and this greater surprisal directly translates into a larger 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀. On the other hand, we know that for the current set of stimuli, LMs show preference for PO structures (i.e., we saw higher likelihood estimates for POs), suggesting that encountering DO sentences can be more surprising overall, irrespective of the prime. It is not possible to distinguish between these two interpretations in the context of the current experiment (and indeed without a better understanding of the properties of the training data). However, the absence of differences in syntactic priming in DO and PO structures in the human data suggests that, unlike LMs, human participants are less driven by the base frequency of DO and PO structures when making syntactic predictions. This links to previous research showing human participants to be less sensitive to global/corpus-based frequency patterns, and more sensitive to the ‘local’ frequency of linguistic items within the experimental context. Modifier presence. The second noteworthy observation is that LM and human priming behaviours show different directionality when the adjectival modifier is absent in the target sentences. In such cases, there is no exact word order overlap between structurally similar prime and target sentences. As shown in Fig. 10, models that do predict 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 for the PO structures in both NP1 and NP2 do so in the inverse direction for unmodified targets, i.e., models show less priming for stimuli that elicit more priming in humans. LMs that do not significantly predict human priming show a similar trend. This means that structural predictions in humans and LMs diverge in the absence of complete word order overlap between primes and targets. In the presence of this overlap, LMs can rely on relative positional features more than hierarchical features for the facilitated prediction of primed targets. However, in the absence of overlap, models cannot rely on relative positional cues for their boost in prediction, and thus may be more likely to rely on higher-level structural information about the prime. When such overlap is present, large LMs of the Llama family show a similar trajectory of syntactic priming (more priming in humans corresponding to more priming in those LMs) while the OPT family models show inverse predictive effects in both conditions. We view this as an indication that, when unable to rely on relative positional features, LMs are less predictive of human behaviour. These effects support our conclusion that LM and human participants may be using different types of information when generating syntactic predictions and further highlights the need to use more naturalistic and diverse stimuli (with no exact word match) when investigating syntactic priming in LMs as well as broader comparisons between the LM and cortical responses to complex sentences (Frank et al., 2015). Related recent work has found that when analysing the network of LMs trained on the language modelling objective, LMs can contain sub-networks with different generalisation behaviour — some that correspond to linear order, and some that correspond to hierarchical generalisation behaviour (Ahuja et al., 2025). The existence of both types of networks suggests that, when there is a linear order relationship between our prime and target pairs (e.g., our modified condition), it may be that the linear order subnetwork takes precedence. However, in the absence of this cue (unmodified condition), the model should rely more on the hierarchical subnetwork for its predictions, and it is in this case that LM priming effects should most predict the human ones. This could be an exciting future direction for the analysis of our data to make use of LMs where the linear order subnetwork is suppressed, and the model can only rely on the hierarchical one for its predictions, in line with what we expect humans to rely on. Lexical facilitation effects. Finally, we inspected differences in structural priming in the subsets of our stimuli split by whether they contain overlapping prepositions — e.g., to/for in both primes and targets with PO syntax. We observed that the significant prediction of the human signal is likely led by the absence of prepositional overlap, since the positive relationship is far stronger in the subset of prime-target pairs that contained no prepositional overlap (see Fig. F.26 in Appendix F). This, taken with results finding higher priming effects in lexically overlapping items (Sinclair et al., 2022) – see Fig. F.25 in Appendix F) – suggests that the presence of lexical overlap artificially boosts priming in LMs over and above the extent to which it affects humans. This is in line with results showing that overlap in meaning is a stronger predictor of semantic activation in GPT3 than in humans (Digutsch & Kosinski, 2023), suggesting that, in the presence of lexico-semantic constraints, LMs are likely to rely on lexico-semantic signal more strongly than humans do. Our results pattern suggests that increased expectations based on lexico-semantic factors can hinder LMs’ predictive utility as an estimate of processing effort and priming in humans (e.g. Krieger et al., 2024). Future work should experimentally explore the extent to which LMs overestimate the importance of lexical material and how this affects their predictive power for human data, as well as begin to develop new metrics more specific than surprisal and that zoom in on the structural, isolating the influence of lexical overlap on syntactic prediction. Is syntactic priming modulated by non-syntactic factors? In our study, we used PE measures for both LM and human data in order to isolate – as much as possible – the contributions of primedriven syntactic predictions on target processing from other nonsyntactic factors that can affect processing of target sentences. However, from computational linguistics research, it is clear that LMderived syntactic priming (𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀) is still influenced by lexico-semantic properties of the prime and target sentences (Jumelet et al., 2024b). In parallel, the cognitive literature has consistently shown that syntactic priming in comprehension is boosted by the lexico-semantic similarity of primes and targets (Traxler, 2015; Traxler et al., 2014), and is further affected by lexico-semantic and grammatical properties like word order (Scheepers & Crocker, 2004). It was therefore important to test explicitly whether LM PE measures remain significant predictors of human priming after accounting for these non-syntactic factors. Following previous research (Tooley et al., 2009), we asked if syntactic priming was affected by the semantic similarity of the prime and the target verbs, which was captured by the WordNet Similarity measure (𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁). Differences in any properties of the PO and DO targets sentences themselves that contributed to readers’ perception of naturalness (i.e., combinations of lexico-semantic and structural properties of individual target sentences) were captured in the Acceptability ratings collected from a separate group of participants. An LM-derived structural preference measure for each target verb quantified its preference for DO vs. PO structure (𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀). The OLS regressions (Tables F.11–F.14) show that these features modulate priming effects in human EEG data, as models with these predictors had a better fit than the simplest Base model can explain variance in the human priming over and above 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀. The main contributor to this effect is Target Acceptability measured through norming: during NP1 processing (for both Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 20 A. Sinclair et al. DOs and POs), more acceptable targets showed smaller priming effects as captured by 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 (see Fig. 9). This finding could be linked to previously reported effects where syntactic priming in comprehension seem to be prominent for sentences that are complex, semantically more ambiguous (Pickering et al., 2013) and arguably more difficult to parse, thus requiring a more active role of structure-supported parsing mechanisms (Ziegler & Snedeker, 2019). Verb structural preference (𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀) was a small contributor to these effects, and primarily for NP1 in DO sentences where we observed significant effects of 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 on 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 only in two LMs (one model from Llama family and one from the opt family, both large 1b+ models). In these cases, DO target sentences showed stronger priming in NP1 when their verbs preferred PO structures. This is in line with prior findings in humans (Gries, 2005; Gries et al., 2005) and LMs (Jumelet et al., 2024b), providing evidence for the inverse frequency effect (i.e., stronger priming for less frequent prime structures). 𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑊𝑁 was not a significant predictor of the 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺 for any of the models, so we will not discuss this factor further. Overall, specific linguistic features (notably, target acceptability and to lesser extent verb structural preferences) modulate syntactic priming early – at the first post-verbal NP – and most strongly in Windows 3 and 4 (350–700 ms post NP1 onset). This suggests that the effects of nonsyntactic features on priming peak in the human data at NP1 and fade by the time that NP2 is processed. On the one hand, these findings contrast with previous literature (Tooley et al., 2009) that failed to find modulation of syntactic priming by semantic links between primes and targets in English. On the other hand, our results show parallels with the broader cross-linguistic literature that reports modulation of syntactic priming in comprehension by frequency-derived measures of syntactic structure preference or prevalence directly comparable to our LM-derived 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 measure. For instance, in German, structural priming can be modulated by the base frequency of the syntactic structure that was being primed (Scheepers & Crocker, 2004), while in Chinese, structural priming is contingent on the likelihood the verb frequency of occurrence in a given syntactic structure, with priming being modulated only by the frequency of the dispreferred structures (Wei et al., 2016). The 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 effects that we discussed above are broadly consistent with these findings: we see that, for less preferred DO sentences, the priming effect is stronger if the target verbs preferred another (PO) structure (Garnsey et al., 1997). This set of findings contributes to the recent literature contrasting lexico-semantic and syntactic information analysis in the human brain and in LMs. While previous studies used neuro-imaging technology (primarily fMRI) and paradigms that differ from the one used in this study, there is an emerging consensus on several points. First, semantic contextual dependencies captured within the LMs can explain brain responses during sentence processing better that syntactic information captured within the LM embeddings (Kauf et al., 2023; Alex et al., 2022) as tested by training data manipulation. This has been linked to the possibility that brains, similarly to LMs, encode meanings of words and semantic dependencies between them by exploiting the principles of predictive processing and statistical learning from word co-occurrence statistics (Caucheteux et al., 2021; Caucheteux & King, 2022; Goldstein et al., 2022; Schrimpf et al., 2021). Second, it is noteworthy that LM-derived measures of semantic and syntactic information processing jointly explain greater variance in cortical signals than when considered separately (Caucheteux et al., 2021; Alex et al., 2022). Despite the paradigm differences, here we show a similar trend: adding human-derived Target Acceptability and LM-derived measures of target verb preference 𝑉𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑓𝐿𝑀 (for some LMs) boosts our ability to explain variance in the cortical signatures of syntactic priming. Within the broader literature, our findings are consistent with the view that the cortical P600 component, typically linked to syntactic structure analysis, can be modelled with NLP measures that capture both semantic and structural dependencies within sentences (Frank, 2024; Li & Futrell, 2023) It is, however, critical to note that only a subset of LMs generated measures of either lexico-semantic or syntactic processing that were able to predict cortical responses. This is a key consideration for reproducibility in this field: using a slightly different version of the same model architecture may yield different findings, which calls into question the possibility of drawing strong conclusions from any single LM. We therefore stress that, when drawing conclusions about similarities and differences of linguistic analysis in the cortex and in LMs, it is critical to consider multiple LMs of diverging sizes and training corpus characteristics. We discuss these considerations in the next section. Limitations Our experimental results raise several questions that extend beyond the scope of the present study. First, we note that we compare the outputs of two systems that are fundamentally different. While our results highlight interesting similarities, an important future step will be to extend such analyses to more human-like LMs — either those exposed to additional input modalities such as vision-language models with an arguably more grounded understanding of language (see, e.g. Bavaresco & Fernández, 2025) or models trained in more humanlike interactive language learning paradigms (e.g. Ma et al., 2025). Second, while using a naturalistic reading paradigm enables us to gather ecologically valid human data, it presents limitations in terms of isolating potential parafoveal effects. At the same time, it remains an open question to what extent LMs predict upcoming tokens in a manner comparable to human parafoveal processing, and whether they can serve as accurate predictors of such effects on reading times (Heilbron et al., 2023). Finally, a critical difference between the data collected from humans and from LMs in our study concerns trial-to-trial learning. Human responses are unavoidably influenced by prior experimental context and manipulations, whereas the surprisal values obtained for targets from LMs only reflect modulation by a one-sentence context (one prime sentence). Future work will investigate how priming effects in humans and LMs may be shaped by coherent narrative contexts, potentially improving comparability with human processing, and leading to better understanding of in-context-learning in LMs. Language models as cognitive models of syntactic prediction and priming We set out to explore where syntactic priming in a suite of LMs can predict human syntactic priming. We concluded that the syntactic priming effects in the two systems, while present in both, are not well aligned and not strongly predictive of each other. Of the models that do explain variance in the human-derived priming measure 𝑃𝐸ℎ𝑢𝑚𝑎𝑛 over and above other non-syntactic factors (Table F.14), GPT2 models are not present, but they do significantly predict 𝑃𝐸ℎ𝑢𝑚𝑎𝑛 when non-syntactic factors are not explicitly modelled. This implies that GPT2’s ability to mirror human priming effects is relatively weak and contingent on the lexico-semantic properties of the stimuli. Of the models that are significantly predictive of 𝑃𝐸ℎ𝑢𝑚𝑎𝑛 over and above other variables, only Llama3−8𝑏 – both the base version and the instruction-tuned version – produced effects in both analyses (i.e., analyses that did and did not include non-syntactic variables). The auto-regressive LMs tested in this study have a distinct property different to humans: model predictions are optimised for the next word, and are not trained to make longer-window predictions about upcoming semantic and syntactic content. More concretely, given a certain position in the sentence, e.g. starting from ‘the’ in the sentence The man gave the... the next prediction only considers possible alternatives from this point that are likely with respect to the context. A human reader, however, may have already generated alternative hypotheses about future continuations of this sentence as soon as the first content word ‘man’ was processed, and this could further influence their processing Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 21 A. Sinclair et al. of the next word. While recent work investigates the presence of future prediction behaviour in LMs despite their training objectives (see, e.g. Pal et al., 2023, or Wu et al., 2024), it remains an open question the extent to which this future prediction is akin to that we make as humans. This mechanism of LM learning may in fact constrain them for use as plausible cognitive models of syntactic processing in humans, since surprisal measures capture processing of the next word given a context, not the likelihood of possible alternative continuations that reach multiple words/syntactic structures into the future — such as alternative measures of utterance level predictability (see e.g. Giulianelli et al., 2023, Information value). While it is reassuring that our results show some similarity between LM and human abstract syntactic priming behaviours, the fact that these similarities are limited to a subset of LMs and to subsets of our stimuli (e.g., we observed clear differences between LM and human priming pattern for POs and DOs) suggests important differences in the nature of their syntactic predictions. As such, our results highlight the importance of distinguishing human-to-model comparisons on a macroand a micro-level: on the macro-level, we observe structural priming effects in both humans and LMs, but on a micro-level we find fundamental differences in the distribution of these effects, demonstrated by the weak fit between human behaviour and LM predictions when accounting for non-syntactic factors. Implications for future work Earlier psycholinguistic models (e.g. Chang et al., 2006) explicitly explained adaptation to syntactic structures in the input via errordriven learning and by means of an architecture that explicitly separates syntactic and semantic processing. The LMs we used in this study do not make such distinctions; rather, they rely on a more complex architecture without built-in assumptions about the time-course or the separation of syntactic and semantic information. In this regard, they resemble recent neurocognitive models without in-built syntax, where syntactic representations and operations emerge from general mechanisms like statistical learning and predictive processing (Bock & Griffin, 2000; Jaeger & Snider, 2008; Reitter et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2021). However, the main drawback of LMs as cognitively plausible models of syntactic prediction and priming, from a classic psycholinguistic perspective, is the difficulty in ‘‘tracing back’’ the activity inside the model that gives rise to specific model outputs. In this sense, the models behave like a ‘‘black box’’ (see the title of the special issue). The processes of ‘‘tracing back’’ cognitive processes to any observed surface level linguistic behaviours (such as syntactic priming) is complicated, yet it is still essential for testing specific hypotheses about the nature of the mechanisms supporting priming-like behaviour in LMs or the nature of the training required for LMs to show priming-like behaviour (Futrell & Mahowald, 2025). In the current study, we chose the approach to directly compare the LM and human-derived indices of structural priming in a tightly controlled set of stimuli. While this did not allow us to open the ‘black box’, our efforts to isolate the structural signal present within their predictions take significant steps in that direction. When accounting for the influence of non-syntactic factors, we find that many of our LMs cease to significantly predict human-derived syntactic priming responses. Our results suggest that, whatever contextuallyinformed syntactic predictions are generated by these LMs, they do not consistently simulate human-like processes — in our case, item-level structural priming. Moreover, our approach highlights human signal in certain sub-conditions as more predictable with the LM-derived signal than in others. Importantly, this approach can allow us to reason further about their divergent behaviours, in particular the influence of function word overlap as a marker of structure. For computational linguistics research, this highlights the need to inspect characteristics of the corpora used to train LMs and how those affect LM behaviours (Patil et al., 2024). It also highlights the importance of interpretability research, which seeks to investigate and develop methods for assessing how LM processing of a given input is associated with specific outputs. New methods that allow us to trace back any learned statistical dependencies to the LM outputs are required to find and quantify parallels between human and LM mechanisms for language processing. In this direction, Attribution techniques (e.g., Madsen et al., 2022) which inspect where within the input context an LM places importance when making its predictions, can be a useful technique to examine mechanisms that lead to priming behaviour, since they can capture interesting nuances of recency behaviour in construction repetition (e.g., Molnar et al., 2023). For cognitive theories of structural priming, this suggests that viewing LMs as a potential implementation of priming via statistical and error-based learning captures only a fragment of the underlying cognitive machinery. Thus, an important future direction is to consider how different LM architectures and processes through which the LMs make predictions about upcoming content affect the degree of syntactic knowledge they accumulate, and the human-likeness of their behaviour. Having acknowledged this, in the current work, we have only examined the behaviour of auto-regressive LMs. Alternative implementations like bi-directional (e.g. BERT, Devlin et al., 2018) models that have access to not only the context preceding a given word, but also access to the text following it to inform its prediction estimations, may provide estimates of word likelihood which can also test interesting alternative hypotheses about the nature of human sentence prediction. We also tested models without any updating of their weights. Extracting predictions from an adaptive language model (e.g. Giulianelli et al., 2022; van Schijndel & Linzen, 2018; Yee et al., 2024), – one where the LM learns from the context it has been exposed to via backpropagation on the cross-entropy next-word prediction error as a continual learning mechanism – may provide one interesting direction through which to explore a different kind of priming behaviour in LMs. Finally, our findings invite the exploration of other measures of predictability beyond surprisal. Specifically, we can capture the likelihood of word sequences rather than individual words, i.e., Information Value, Giulianelli et al. (2023) to compute 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 and test whether this leads to estimates that better capture human properties of priming. Summary and conclusions To our knowledge, we present the first controlled item-level comparison between human and LM syntactic predictions in a structural priming experiment. Overall, our findings show several high-level similarities and clear low-level similarities in structural prediction behaviour in humans and language models, which is an important step towards understanding mechanisms underlying priming in human language processing and LMs as computational language models. In terms of the high-level similarities, we observe significant syntactic priming effects in both humans and LMs. In terms of magnitude, we find that LMs display priming effects in both PO and DO targets with stronger effects in DO targets, while human participants showed priming for both dative alternatives (PO and DO targets). In terms of the locus of these effects, priming effects were present at NP1 and peaked at the onset of NP2 in LMs (consistent with Jumelet et al., 2024b) and were strongest in the second NP in human data (consistent with Ledoux et al., 2007). We also find that priming effects in both LM and human data were robust after controlling for non-syntactic variables. On the lower level, however, LM priming effects did not consistently and strongly predict human EEG priming effects, showing that, at an item level, there are substantial differences. We find that only a few LMs predict human priming effects over and above non-syntactic factors; indeed, there is a deal of variation between LMs in terms of their priming behaviour. We also find that the presence of a modifier in the prime can greatly influence whether LM priming effects positively or negatively predict human priming effects: no one LM positively predicts human Journal of Memory and Language 149 (2026) 104713 22 A. Sinclair et al. priming effects across all target structures, noun phrases and modifier conditions. Our measure of LM priming is dependent on per-word prediction, and thus is susceptible to the same weaknesses in predicting syntactic properties of language as reported by Huang et al. (2024) where LMderived measures of next-word predictability were unable to explain variation in the human reading times for syntactically complex sentences. This and other recent work (Caucheteux et al., 2021; Kauf et al., 2023) shows an emerging trend that auto-regressive models do not appear to encode syntactic information complex enough to be comparable to that encoded in the human behavioural or cortical responses. Our findings contribute to this by showing that while LM and human syntactic priming behaviours are similar at a macro level, there are many differences at the micro (item-specific) level which question the validity of LMs as cognitive models of human-like syntactic processing at the moment. In future work, it would be useful to test whether a 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 measure that is based on a different measure of LM prediction provides a more consistent pattern of results, explaining human priming more robustly. Finally, we hope that our work provides a starting point for future studies directly comparing human and model priming behaviour across a wider range of stimuli and conditions than were feasible in this study, and that our dataset can serve as a testbed for evaluating future computational models of human priming behaviour. EEG Voltage — linear mixed analysis The lmer formula for the Base model for EEG is: 𝐸𝐸𝐺𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒∼ 𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒∗𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑇𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡∗𝑀𝑜𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑖𝑒𝑟−𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒+ (1|𝑆𝑢𝑏𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡). B.3. EEG Voltage — interaction analysis In terms of interactions with Modifier Presence in the Base models, the only effect observed consistently for NP1 was a significant interaction between Prime Structure and Modifier Presence in windows 1–3 (Fig. B.11). This interaction occurred because voltage amplitudes were more positive in targets that followed PO primes without modifiers (e.g., ‘‘brewed a coffee for the speaker’’) compared to those with modifiers (‘‘brewed an excellent coffee for the speaker’’), suggesting that targets after unmodified primes may have been easier to process. The presence of a modifier in DO primes had a negligible effect on targets. Interestingly, there were no significant effects of Modifier Presence for NP2 in any time window. When adding non syntactic predictors, as mentioned in Section ‘‘Trial-level EEG analyses’’ we find some interaction effects of interest. First, the analysis of Window 4 for NP2 showed a significant interaction between Prime Structure, Target Structure, and Target Acceptability (see Fig. B.12). Voltage amplitudes for PO and DO targets varied with Prime Structure, and, importantly, stronger priming effects were observed for target sentences with low acceptability ratings. PO targets with the lowest acceptability ratings had the lowest voltage amplitudes (i.e., were more difficult to process) after structurally dissimilar DO primes, but showed the largest boost – or the largest increase in voltage amplitudes – after structurally similar PO primes. DO targets showed a similar pattern. Voltage amplitudes for DO targets were not sensitive to target acceptability in the unprimed condition (i.e., in sentences read after structurally dissimilar PO primes), but DO targets with the lowest acceptability ratings showed the largest boost, or the largest increase in voltage amplitudes, after structurally similar DO primes. Both effects indicate a reduction in processing effort driven by structural priming in target sentences that were normatively more difficult to process. Second, an interaction between Prime Structure, Modifier Presence and Target Norming was observed in Windows 2, 3 and 4 in NP1, and Window 3 for NP2. This effect is shown in Fig. B.13. In both NP1 and NP2, mean voltage amplitudes were relatively stable across target sentences with higher and lower ratings after PO and DO primes that included modifiers. This pattern was different in target sentences after primes that did not include modifiers. Voltage amplitudes for target sentences with low ratings were more positive after DO primes than PO primes (suggesting that these target sentences were easier to process). For the NP2 alignment we found that priming was stronger in the first chronological block 1 (see Fig. C.16, A) when contracted to block 2 (sig. cluster in the 20–272 ms window, p = 0.009) and 3 (sig. Cluster in the 0–198 ms window, p = 0.02) but not block 4 (only marginal effects at p = 0.1 level). Other comparisons (block 2 vs 3 and 4, and block 3 vs block 4) were not significant. Fig. C.16 shows these effects — with stronger differentiation between Primed and Unprimed conditions emerging in early time-windows of block 1. Such effects can be expected as participants become more tired and less attentive in later blocks, as well as potentially habituating to the paradigm. Appendix D. Appendix E. LM analysis: Variation in 𝑷𝑬𝑳𝑴 across LMs To better understand the variation between LMs in their ability to predict 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺, we investigate the extent to which 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 varies across different LMs, finding low between-LM correlations (See Fig. E.19). We investigated whether 𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 correlated across models, Fig. E.19 and found relatively low correlation between models, except between similarly sized families and instruction-tuned variants. Lowest correlations are between the smallest OPT models (125 and 350) with all other models, and highest correlations are found between models and their instruction-tuned variants, or those of similar size within the same family. Comparison of relationship of 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺∼𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 differences when stimuli contain an overlap in preposition (e.g. both prime and target contain for). We observe that the positive relationship we observe between 𝑃𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐺∼𝑃𝐸𝐿𝑀 in our results is driven by the cases with no prepositional overlap, in other words, in the absence of preposition overlap, LM priming effects are more predictive of human ones. ## Abstract
Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can capture rich representations of concepts that are useful for real-world tasks. However, language alone is limited. While existing LLMs excel at text-based inferences, health applications require that models be grounded in numerical data (e.g., vital signs, laboratory values in clinical domains; steps, movement in the wellness domain) that is not easily or readily expressed as text in existing training corpus. We demonstrate that with only few-shot tuning, a large language model is capable of grounding various physiological and behavioral time-series data and making meaningful inferences on numerous health tasks for both clinical and wellness contexts. Using data from wearable and medical sensor recordings, we evaluate these capabilities on the tasks of cardiac signal analysis, physical activity recognition, metabolic calculation (e.g., calories burned), and estimation of stress reports and mental health screeners. 1

## Introduction
Introduction The fundamental ability of large language models (LLMs) to capture knowledge and concepts has improved dramatically as neural architectures have been scaled. Exponentially greater numbers of parameters and training samples has led to models that can encode vast amounts of information [3,5, 19,24,25]. These models present opportunities in many domains including software engineering [4], information retrieval and data mining [10], content creation [6] and health [22]. However, in many cases text alone is not enough. Grounding in non-linguistic observations such as actions, experiences or perceptions is an essential part of deriving meaning from language [8] as words alone does not capture all the necessary information to complete a given task. Tuning, or grounding, of this kind is necessary to connect the knowledge contained within a language model to events or actions in the physical world [1]. For these reasons, models have been combined with data from other modalities, most commonly images [11,16,18], audio [27], video [23,30] or physical actions [1]. Despite the importance of physiology and behavior to human health, evaluating and grounding models with these data has been relatively unexplored. Medical-domain language models have shown remarkable capabilities to capture sophisticated knowledge [10, 22], performing well on multiple-choice examination questions (e.g., board exams). However, they have not been tested extensively on tasks that involve analysis of physiological (e.g., heart rate) and behavioral timeseries (e.g., daily steps), which are important for many consumer health tasks. Without data of this kind, derived from actual measurements of the human body, these models may be limited in their ability to provide specific health insights, particularly when the insight involves inference from physiological data. For example, an individual searching for a diagnosis for their ailment may have limited success if the model has no insight into physiology (e.g., elevated heart rate, fever) that could be underlying their symptoms. Conversely, models capable of incorporating user physiological data may be able to provide enhanced insight to queries within a medical domain. We hypothesize that LLMs have some capability to interpret and reason about health information, but that that ability will dramatically improve with grounding from even a small number of examples of numerical health data. arXiv:2305.15525v1 [cs.CL] 24 May 2023 Prompt: Classify the accelerometer data in meters per second squared as either walking or running. Physiological sensing and monitoring represents the quantitative measurement of physiological processes in the human body and is a cornerstone of clinical-based diagnosis and patient management. Such monitoring is now also commonplace using commodity consumer electronics such wearables, phones and other low-cost sensing platforms. Wearable devices and unobtrusive sensing have helped individuals realize meaningful changes in their health, such as helping to increase the amount of physical activity people engage in [7]. Moreover, when done thoughtfully and in an evidence-based manner, it is generally accepted that helping individuals derive insight from their data could increase the frequency of engaging in beneficial health behaviors. Traditionally, researchers have had to collect substantial amounts of individual health data for each task (e.g., to train an atrial fibrillation classifier [17]). This process is time-consuming and resource-intensive. Yet, there is evidence that LLMs have the potential to act as universal pretrained models and perform zeroor few-shot inferences (e.g., translation, question-answering) [21]. However, it is not clear to what extent this is true for tasks that involve physiological or behavioral data. For example, classifying atrial fibrillation from a series of interbeat-intervals not only requires understanding of how to process time-series data but also domain knowledge in cardiology. Can LLMs act as efficient few-shot learners of arrhythmia? In this paper, we compile a dataset of common consumer health tasks (e.g. activity recognition, heart rhythm classification) to explore whether LLMs can ground time-series health data and serve as universal few-shot learners. We systematically demonstrate that with few-shot prompt tuning LLMs can ground numerical time series data, derived from wearable and clinical-grade sensing devices, resulting in large improvements over zero-shot inferences and supervised baselines on tasks as varied as activity recognition, computing calories burned and atrial fibrillation classification. To summarize, our contributions are to: 1) curate a dataset of numerical consumer health tasks for evaluating LLM performance in grounding time-series data. 2) demonstrate the capability of a large language model as a universal few-shot learner for a range of wellness and clinical level health tasks. 3) expose the limitations of pretrained large language models on these tasks. 4) present an set of physiologically and behaviorally tuned models that perform efficiently with a small number of training examples. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper exploring grounding LLMs with time-series physiological and behavioral data and using LLMs as few-shot learners on health tasks. 2 Background Large Language Models. The ability for language models trained with vast corpora of text data to produce text that is indistinguishable from that written by humans [19] and to reach human performance on multiple benchmarks [26] is impressive. It is possible for these models to encode a large amount of knowledge from a range of domains. One of the most significant properties of LLMs is their capability to perform zero-shot or few-shot inferences, a product of the large amount of text from diverse domains that was used to train them [13,25]. These LLMs have so far obeyed scaling laws with consistent, smooth model improvement as the model, dataset and compute size used for training is a compelling argument for further improvements [13]. 2 Table 1: Consumer health tasks. ## Methodology
approach enables us to move beyond manual prompt design and facilitates learning of an optimal prefix for 1Reference removed because of anonymization. 5 Figure 2: Our dataset construction and training configurations. We use physiological data to construct question-answer pairs. We create training, validation and test splits and compare zero-shot prediction performance to models created via prompt engineering and prompt tuning. each task. In our particular case, the prompt layer encodes information that assists the language model in comprehending numerical and time-series data that is absent in the original frozen language model. Specifically, the size of the prompt embedding is 4096 × 1. The input for prompt tuning is similar to that used in the zero-shot setting, the only difference is that prompt tuning requires paired labels for each individual task. For instance, the input and the corresponding label for the activity recognition task would be: Input: "Classify the following accelerometer data in meters per second squared as either walking or running: 0.052,0.052,0.052,0.051,0.052,0.055,0.051,0.056,0.06,0.064" Label: "Running" To better understand how language can utilize inherent domain knowledge, we present two unique sets of prompts that are used during prompt tuning for cardiovascular and activity recognition tasks: 1) Context-Inclusive Prompts, and 2) Numerical-Only Prompts. The Numerical-Only prompt approach presents only the sequence of numbers to the model, devoid of any additional textual context. This strategy aims to test the language model’s ability to discern patterns and generate accurate predictions based purely on the input numerical data, without any supplementary information about the nature and source of the data. We elected not to use the Numerical-Only prompt for tasks associated with mental health and metabolic calorie expenditure. As these tasks do not involve sequential data, and it is difficult to imagine how context-free numerical data would yield any meaningful prediction. Furthermore, in these situations, the contextual cues are particularly vital for the model to comprehend the task and apply its domain knowledge. The Context-Inclusive prompts involve incorporating relevant contextual information into the prompt. For instance, in cardiovascular tasks, we unambiguously indicated that the input sequence signifies Inter-beat Intervals (IBIs). Similarly, in the activity recognition task, we clarify that the input data originates from accelerometer readings and provided the units of measurement. The inclusion of this additional context is based on the hypothesis that it could steer the language model towards utilizing its domain-specific knowledge, potentially improving its predictive accuracy. In summary, these two prompt tuning strategies enable us to investigate the influence of contextual information on the model’s performance. Significantly, they offer insights into the model’s capacity to harness its domain knowledge when provided with suitable hints, as well as its ability to identify patterns and execute tasks without explicit contextual information. We assess our prompt tuning method in 3-shot, 10-shot, and 25-shot scenarios. The language model, augmented with an additional tunable prompt layer, is trained over 5000 steps using a learning rate of 3.0. 6 Table 2: Results. Comparison of performance between prompt-tuned LLMs (w/ Context-Inclusive Prompts) and supervised neural network training across all consumer health tasks. Supervised Baseline LLM with Context Prompt Engineering. As with zero-shot learning, in this setting we leverage a pre-trained model to perform inference with frozen weights. However, we incorporate additional context within the input prompt as a series of examples before asking the test question. The examples guide the language model toward the structure of the task. As an example, in the calorie estimation task a prompt might be framed as follows: "Question: How many total calories will I burn after walking for 50 minutes? My weight is 156 lbs. Answer: 214. Question: How many total calories I bured after walking for 48 minutes? My weight is 221 lbs. Answer: " In this paper, we specifically focus on a 3-shot setting for prompt engineering, largely due to the nature of our data. Given that our data consisted of sequential and time-series information, the samples are typically lengthy. However, LLMs are subject to a limit on the number of tokens that can be inputted, which motivated our decision to concentrate on a 3-shot setting. It’s noteworthy that this prompt engineering approach did not involve any additional training of the model. Instead, it relied entirely on the out-of-the-box capabilities of the pre-trained model, testing its ability to perform tasks based on the provided prompts and its existing knowledge. This experiment provide valuable insights into the model’s few-shot performance capabilities and the effectiveness of carefully engineered prompts in guiding the model towards desired task performance compared against to prompt tuning. The results of prompt engineering are included in the supplementary materials. Supervised Baseline. Finally, we juxtapose all these grounding methods with a supervised learning baseline for comparison. In this paper, we intentionally maintain a small number of training samples in order to evaluate few-shot performance. Nevertheless, we find it valuable to establish a supervised baseline, as it helps discern whether large language models could offer additional benefits by leveraging the knowledge encapsulated within pre-trained weights, knowledge that the training samples themselves might not encapsulate. To this end, we utilize a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with 4096 × 1, training it on the same samples used for prompt tuning in our large language model. We use 32 TPU-v4 chips for all our experiments including training and evaluation. 5 Result & Discussion Are language models effective few-shot learners for health tasks? As illustrated in Table 2 and Figure 3, the LLM functions as a universal few-shot learner for various consumer health tasks. These tasks assume a number of operations: interpreting time-series/sequential data, executing arithmetic operations, understanding context with domain knowledge, and recognizing patterns. We noted large decreases in error and increases in accuracy when the model was prompt tuned using only a small number of examples (from 3-shot to 10-shot and to 25-shot). A substantial benefit is observed when comparing our few-shot prompt tuning results with few-shot supervised training. For example, for five cardiovascular tasks, the 25-shot prompt tuned LLM performance improvement is up to 130 % and the up to 75 % when compared to zero-shot performance and supervised 25-shot baseline performance. Furthermore, we saw a 29% increase in accuracy over zero-shot and a 33% accuracy improvement in activity recognition tasks; a 66% error reduction over zero-shot and a 46% error 7 Mean Absolute Error (calories) Calories G C H I IMU to Activity Fitbit to Stress Fitbit to PHQ Instantaneous HR to Average Hea Rate 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot 3-Shot 10-Shot 25-Shot Mean Absolute Error (beats/min) Accuracy Accuracy Accuracy Accuracy Accuracy Lower = Beer Higher = Beer Higher = Beer Figure 3: Results of 3, 10 and 25-shot experiments for nine health tasks..
