Oracle LLM: A strong foundation, powerful direction, excellent production presentation makes it easy to be transported away into the life of Jacob Jensen, who is not only a pianist, but is a good human being, too. signiﬁcant performance improvements, there are still issues that require further exploration in the future. First, our method uses EEG signals to guide LLMs in generating the desired text. It is curious whether this decoding process resembles brain activity during human thinking, and whether the LLM shares similarities with the human brain. We believe that with the continuous development of neuroscience, these questions can be answered more clearly, which will further guide us in designing better methods. Second, there is a signiﬁcant performance gap between our method and the Oracle LLM. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 9, although our method still outperforms translation-based baselines without the ﬁrstword prompt, the performance gain is reduced. These results indicate that our EEG representation model needs further improvement to break away from its reliance on the ﬁrst-word prompt. We believe better handling the low signal-to-noise ratio in EEG signals is key to improving model performance. Third, our method relies on eye-tracking ﬁxations to divide EEG signals into word-level segments, which limits its practical application. Furthermore, the word-level EEG segments divided by eye-tracking ﬁxations are not always strictly aligned with the text, presenting challenges for training EEG representation models and generating candidates with LLMs during decoding. Therefore, research on text decoding methods based on raw EEG signals is crucial. Finally, the decoding eﬃciency of our method needs further optimization. Beam search based on a large beam size is very timeconsuming. In the future, we will explore better ways to generate candidate words, such as sampling-based methods to improve inference speed. 6. Conclusion This paper proposes a novel framework for the open vocabulary EEGto-Text task. During training, we focus on EEG signal representation and introduce a dual contrastive learning method to eﬀectively align EEG representations with corresponding word semantics, eliminating the language bias of the teacher-forcing strategy used in previous translation methods. In the decoding stage, we leverage LLMs’ powerful text generation capabilities and guide them to generate accurate text by re-ranking candidate words based on semantic similarity. Experimental results on the ZuCo benchmark demonstrate the eﬀectiveness of our method, which not only achieves signiﬁcantly better performance than previous methods in both multi-subject and single-subject settings but also shows strong generalization capabilities in cross-subject scenarios. ## Abstract
Abstract—Immersive technologies such as virtual reality and haptic systems create complex multisensory experiences that challenge traditional user experience (UX)

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION The rapid evolution of interactive technologies, particularly in virtual reality (VR), augmented reality, and haptic-enabled systems, has fundamentally transformed how users engage with digital environments [1, 2]. These immersive technologies create rich, multisensory experiences that engage users' cognitive, emotional, and physiological systems in ways that traditional desktop or mobile interfaces cannot match [3]. However, this technological advancement has exposed a critical gap in user experience (UX) evaluation methodologies [4, 5]: conventional assessment tools, designed for simpler interaction paradigms, struggle to capture the complexity and individual variability of responses in these sophisticated digital environments. Traditional UX evaluation methods rely heavily on standardized questionnaires and post-interaction surveys that assume uniform user responses and static assessment needs [6, 7]. These approaches face several fundamental limitations when applied to modern interactive systems. First, they fail to account for the significant individual differences in how users process, respond to, and remember complex interactive experiences [8]. Second, static questionnaires cannot adapt to the dynamic nature of user states during prolonged or varied interactions [9]. Third, self-report measures are susceptible to recall bias, social desirability effects, and users' limited introspective awareness of their own cognitive and emotional states during immersive experiences [10]. Electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising solution for objective, real-time monitoring of user states during human-computer interaction. EEG can capture neural correlates of attention, cognitive load, emotional engagement, and frustration with millisecond precision, providing insights into user experience that are often inaccessible through traditional self-report methods [11, 12]. However, the complexity of EEG signal interpretation and the challenge of translating neurophysiological patterns into actionable UX insights have limited its practical application in routine evaluation practices [13]. The expertise required to analyze EEG data and generate meaningful UX assessments has remained a significant barrier to widespread adoption. Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) and multi-agent artificial intelligence systems offer unprecedented opportunities to bridge the gap between objective neurophysiological data and practical UX evaluation [14]. Multi-agent LLM frameworks can leverage vast knowledge bases and sophisticated reasoning capabilities to interpret complex physiological signals, understand their implications for user experience, and generate contextually appropriate assessment instruments. These systems can potentially automate the process of translating EEG patterns into personalized, adaptive questionnaires that target specific aspects of user experience revealed by individual neural responses [15, 16]. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for EEGinformed adaptive UX questionnaire generation using multiagent LLMs (EUEQ-mLLM). Our methodology employs a sophisticated four-stage multi-agent workflow where specialized LLMs collaborate to analyze EEG patterns, interpret their experiential significance, and dynamically create targeted questions that adapt to individual brain functional states during interaction. Designed for practical deployment with relatively small-scale language models, our approach addresses the fundamental limitations of static assessment tools by generating contextually relevant, datadriven questionnaires that respond to actual neurophysiological patterns rather than predetermined assumptions. By integrating objective physiological evidence with intelligent question generation, our framework represents a paradigm shift toward more precise, adaptive, and comprehensive UX evaluation methodologies that can evolve with the complexity of modern interactive experiences. 2025 IEEE/IEIE International Conference on Consumer Electronics-Asia (ICCE-Asia) | 979-8-3315-7402-4/25/$31.00

## Methodology
methods. Conventional static questionnaires fail to capture individual variability and dynamic nature of user responses. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers an objective means to monitor attention, cognitive load, and emotional engagement; however, the complexity of interpreting EEG signals has hindered its practical adoption. To address this, we propose EUEQ-mLLM, a framework that integrates EEG data with multi-agent large language models (LLMs) to generate adaptive UX questionnaire. The framework employs a fourstage workflow in which specialized LLMs collaborate to analyze EEG patterns, extract experiential significance, and dynamically create personalized assessment instruments tailored to individual brain functional states during interaction. EUEQ-mLLM generates contextually relevant questionnaires responding to actual neurophysiological patterns rather than static assumptions. Evaluation using G-Eval demonstrated EUEQ-mLLM achieved 80.96, representing 45.32% improvement over single-stage baselines. Designed for smallscale language models, our approach demonstrates the potential of EEG-informed multi-agent architectures for precise, adaptive UX evaluation methodologies that evolve with modern interactive experience complexity. Keywords—Large Language Models, Multi-Agent, User Experience Questionnaire, EEG I.

## Results
evaluation

## Conclusion
CONCLUSIONS This study introduced EUEQ-mLLM, a novel framework designed to generate adaptive UX questionnaires by integrating EEG signals with multi-agent LLMs. Our approach employed a four-stage collaborative workflow that effectively transforms neurophysiological data into personalized and contextually relevant assessment tools, which adapt dynamically to individual user responses during interactions. A comprehensive evaluation using the G-Eval framework demonstrated that EUEQ-mLLM consistently produces high-quality questionnaires that capture nuanced aspects of UX often overlooked by traditional static assessment tools. This work represents a significant advancement toward intelligent, data-driven UX evaluation methodologies enabling tools that can evolve with emerging interactive technologies. Ultimately, EUEQ-mLLM lays the groundwork for next-generation assessment instruments that promise a more precise understanding of human-computer interactions across diverse technological contexts, including virtual reality and haptic systems. ## Figures_tables_captions
Fig. 1. Process for generating EEG-informed adaptive UX questionnaire generation with multi-agent LLMs. II. METHODS A. Multi-Agent User Experience Questionnaire Generation Our proposed EUEQ-mLLM extends the four-stage LLM-based UX questionnaire generation framework introduced in our previous study [17] by incorporating EEG signals, thereby enabling the creation of UX questionnaires that capture both experimental conditions and individual user states. At each stage, specialized LLMs act as agents, and their outputs are systematically integrated to form the final UX questionnaire (Fig. 1). 1) User-adaptive question generation (LLM-1): LLM1 generates user-specific questions based on individual experimental conditions, user information, and EEG signals. EEG activity is typically categorized into five frequency bands, each associated with distinct cognitive and physiological states. To leverage these properties, prior knowledge of EEG frequency bands is provided to the model as a prompt (Section II.B). This allows the model to capture EEG-relevant features and formulate deeper, more meaningful questions. For consistency and interpretation, the generated questions adopt a 1–7 Likert scale format. 2) Experiment-tailored question generation (LLM-2): LLM-2 produces a comprehensive questionnaire aligned with the UX Honeycomb model, a widely used UX evaluation framework [18]. Drawing on individual experimental conditions, it generates detailed items across the seven facets of the UX Honeycomb: useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible, and valuable. This ensures that the questionnaire reflects both general experimental contexts and individual characteristics. As in LLM-1, the questions are structured for responses on a 1–7 Likert scale. 3) Questionnaire harmonization (LLM-3): Since the personalized questions from LLM-1 do not inherently follow the UX Honeycomb structure. LLM-3 aligns and integrates them into the Honeycomb-based framework. This step ensures structural coherence between personalized and standardized components. 4) Questionnaire refinement (LLM-4): Finally, LLM4 reviews the integrated questionnaire for logical flow, structural clarity, and readability, refining the wording to ensure consistency and usability. B. Prompt Engineering To enhance the generative performance of the LLMs, we employed robust prompt engineering strategies based on the UEQ-mLLM framework. Each LLM was assigned the role of a domain expert, provided with the overall task objective, and guided by stage-specific procedural instructions. The UX questionnaire format, along with few-shot examples, was also supplied to standardize outputs. In particular, to ensure that generated questions accurately reflect EEG characteristics, we incorporated the properties of each frequency band into the prompts. Specifically, Delta waves (0.5–4 Hz) are linked to reduced consciousness and are prominent during deep sleep, anesthesia, and coma [19]; Theta waves (4–8 Hz) are associated with drowsiness, relaxation, and working memory [20, 21]; Alpha waves (8–12 Hz) emerge during relaxed states with eyes closed but are suppressed during cognitive activity, primarily in the occipital lobe [22]; Beta waves (12– 30 Hz) correspond to active cognitive processing, attention, arousal, and motor activity, and also increase under emotional states such as anxiety and stress [23, 24]; and Gamma waves (30–55 Hz) are implicated in sensory integration and higher-order cognition, with alterations observed in disorders such as depression and schizophrenia [25]. These neurophysiological properties were explicitly embedded in the prompts to guide question generation, enabling the system to capture both cognitive and physiological dimensions of user states. III. EXPERIMENTS A. EEG Acquisition and Processing The experiment was conducted using a DSI-24 EEG headset, a Meta Quest 3 HMD, and a bHaptics TactGlove. Participants performed a musical task in which they pressed the same string of a gayageum with the left hand while plucking it with the right hand. The study was designed with four distinct visuo-haptic conditions: (i) real visual with a real gayageum prop; (ii) virtual visual with a real gayageum prop; (iii) virtual visual with hand tracking; (iv) virtual visual with the bHaptics glove. In this study, EEG data were collected using 21 electrodes positioned according to the international 10–20 system (Fp1, Fp2, Fz, F3, F4, F7, F8, Cz, C3, C4, T7, T8, Pz, P3, P4, P7, P8, O1, O2, A1, A2). After excluding the reference electrodes (A1, A2), 19 channels were analyzed. Preprocessing was performed in MATLAB R2024a using the EEGLAB toolbox and included line-noise removal, bandpass filtering, bad-channel rejection, and independent component analysis. Data from six participants across the four visuo-haptic conditions (24 trials total) were then decomposed into five canonical frequency bands (delta– gamma). Finally, the 24 trials within each condition were Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 08,2026 at 20:15:41 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. Fig. 2. Example of a user experience questionnaire generated by the EUEQ-mLLM model. averaged to obtain representative EEG features for subsequent analysis. B. LLM Implementation Details For the four-stage LLM-based UX questionnaire generation process, we employed Meta’s open-source, MetaLlama-3.1-8B-Instruct [26]. To validate the model’s capability to generate customized questions based on user data, the output of LLM-2 was held constant while LLM-1 produced responses under identical experimental conditions. All experiments were conducted on a computing system equipped with four NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs (24GB memory each). C. Baseline Model To evaluate the effectiveness of the four-stage LLMbased UX questionnaire generation process, we implemented a single-stage baseline, EUEQ-sLLM. Unlike EUEQ-mLLM, which incrementally refines the questionnaire across four stages, EUEQ-sLLM generates the complete questionnaire in a single step. Its prompt was constructed by compressively integrating the information provided to each stage of EUEQmLLM, while applying the same prompt engineering strategies to maintain consistency. This design enables a direct comparison between single-stage and multi-stage approaches, thereby isolating the contribution of staged generation to overall questionnaire quality. D. Evaluation Methodology To evaluate user-adaptive UX questionnaires tailored to individual contexts, we employed G-Eval, an LLM-based evaluation framework [27]. G-Eval leverages the reasoning capabilities of LLMs to provide reliable text assessments, making it particularly suitable for UX questionnaires that can yield multiple valid responses [17]. Using this framework, we quantitatively evaluated the generated questionnaires and compared the performance of the proposed EUEQ-mLLM against the single-stage baseline, EUEQ-sLLM. Statistical significance was assessed using t-tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. 1) Evaluation criteria: To assess the extent to which the UX questionnaire captures specific experimental conditions and user data, we defined four evaluation criteria suitable for UX assessment: consistency, personalization, fluency, and relevance. The detailed criteria were adapted from the G-Eval prompt and modified to align with our model. Consistency evaluates whether the generated questionnaires conform to the structure of the seven facets of the UX Honeycomb. Personalization evaluates the extent to which the questionnaire incorporates questions derived from the user’s information and physiological signals. Fluency evaluates grammatical accuracy and readability. Relevance evaluates whether the generated questions are effective and meaningful in supporting the interpretation of experimental outcomes. By adopting this multifaceted evaluation framework, we aimed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed UX questionnaire generation approach. All evaluation criteria were rated on a 1-to-5 scale. The four criteria were then aggregated and converted into a single 100-point score to provide an overall assessment of the generated questionnaires. 2) G-Eval implementation: We employed OpenAI’s GPT-5 for G-Eval, which has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in recent LLM benchmarks. Notably, GPT-5 has achieved high performance in benchmarks designed to test instruction-following capabilities, while also possessing advanced reasoning abilities. These features make the model especially suitable for evaluating the generated questionnaires according to the carefully designed evaluation prompts. To reduce potential bias from a single evaluation and to capture diverse perspectives in the assessment, we conducted 5 repeated evaluations with parameters set as temperature = 1, top_p = 1, and reasoning effort specified as "medium". The results were then averaged across the four evaluation criteria. IV. RESULTS Fig. 2 shows an example of a user-adaptive UX questionnaire generated by EUEQ-mLLM. Underlined sections indicate the experimental conditions, while highlighted questions are specifically designed to link EEG signals with UX. Overall, EUEQ-mLLM achieved a score of 80.96, representing a 45.32% improvement over EUEQ-sLLM. These results demonstrate that a multi-LLM approach is effective for generating high-quality, user-adaptive UX questionnaires. V. CONCLUSIONS This study introduced EUEQ-mLLM, a novel framework designed to generate adaptive UX questionnaires by integrating EEG signals with multi-agent LLMs. Our approach employed a four-stage collaborative workflow that effectively transforms neurophysiological data into personalized and contextually relevant assessment tools, which adapt dynamically to individual user responses during interactions. A comprehensive evaluation using the G-Eval framework demonstrated that EUEQ-mLLM consistently produces high-quality questionnaires that capture nuanced aspects of UX often overlooked by traditional static assessment tools. This work represents a significant advancement toward intelligent, data-driven UX evaluation methodologies enabling tools that can evolve with emerging interactive technologies. Ultimately, EUEQ-mLLM lays the groundwork for next-generation assessment instruments that promise a more precise understanding of human-computer interactions across diverse technological contexts, including virtual reality and haptic systems. ## Abstract
Abstract—With the recent proliferation of large language models (LLMs), such as Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT), there has been a significant shift in exploring human and machine comprehension of semantic language meaning. This shift calls for interdisciplinary research that bridges cognitive science and natural language processing (NLP). This pilot study aims to provide insights into individuals’ neural states during a semantic relation reading-comprehension task. We propose jointly analyzing LLMs, eye-gaze, and electroencephalographic (EEG) data to study how the brain processes words with varying degrees of relevance to a keyword during reading. We also use a feature engineering

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION R ECENT advancements in LLMs and generative AI have significantly impacted various aspects of human society and industry. Notable examples include GPT-X models developed by OpenAI and Midjourney, among others [1]–[4]. As artificial agents improve their proficiency, it becomes increasingly crucial to deepen our understanding of machine learning, decision-making processes, and human cognitive functions [5]. For instance, both humans and machines employ strategies for semantic inference. Humans extract crucial information from texts via specific gaze patterns during reading [6]– [8], whereas language models predict subsequent words using contextual cues [9]. Therefore, this pilot study raises the question: Can we differentiate individuals’ mental states when their gaze fixates on words of varying significance within a sentence, particularly at a word level, during tasks involving semantic inference and reading comprehension? The successfulness of the prediction tasks could have significant implications for current machine learning applications and both science and technology, such as Human-in-the-loop Machine Learning [10], BrainComputer Interfaces (BCI) for text communications [11], and personalized Learning and Accessibility Tools in real-time [12]. Previous studies demonstrate biomarkers that affirm patterns in subjects during reading comprehension tasks. For example, several neurobiological markers linked to reading comprehension, including P300 and N400, were first identified in the 1980s [13]. As the groundbreaking research in reading comprehension, the study revealed arXiv:2309.15714v2 [cs.CL] 17 Oct 2023 2 that there are distinct patterns in N400 for “semantic moderate” and “semantic strong” words [14]. Furthermore, numerous classical theories within the cognitive science community aim to elucidate and delineate the processes through which humans comprehend text and make inferences. Kintsch [15] introduced the Construction-Integration (CI) model, which posits text comprehension as a two-stage process: initially constructing a textbase (comprehending the text at the surface and propositional level) and subsequently integrating it with prior knowledge to form a situation model (a mental representation of the text’s content). Evans [16] suggests that cognition comprises two types of processes - automatic (Type 1) and deliberative (Type 2). The automatic process operates swiftly and relies on heuristics, whereas the deliberative process is slower, conscious, and grounded in logical reasoning. Rumelhart [17] suggests that all knowledge is organized into units called schemas, representing generic concepts stored in our memory. According to this theory, reading comprehension is activating appropriate schema matching the text’s information [18]. Similar orthodox theories for text comprehension are Mental Models [19], Landscape Model [19], etc. While these theories in cognitive science offer valuable insights into text comprehension and inference, they often oversimplify cognitive processes and do not fully account for individual differences and context variability [20]. For instance, [21] attempted to analyze how both brain hemispheres comprehend expository versus narrative texts, which are reportedly more complex. However, their approach was limited to time-domain analysis of EEG signals, and the statistical evidence they provided was not robust enough to substantiate their

This study represents the first attempt to classify brain states at a word level using LLM knowledge. ## Results

This study represents the first attempt to integrate the GPT model with EEG signal analysis to explain potential patterns in human comprehension and inference-making, specifically concerning words with substantial meaning. The remainder of this study is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the dataset used in our study, including subject information, experiment paradigms, and the data collection process and equipment. Section 3 explains our data processing pipeline methods involving the EEG feature extraction pipeline and classification algorithms. Section 4 exhibits our LLM comparison, eyefixation statistics, fixation-related potential, classification results for 12 subjects across eight-word relations, and the corresponding analysis. Lastly, in Section 5, we juxtapose our findings with existing literature, deliberate on the limitations of our study, and propose potential avenues for future research. II. DATASET The ZuCo dataset includes high-density 128-channel EEG and eye-tracking data from 12 native English 3 Fig. 1. Task 3: Experiment Paradigm and Sample LLM Outputs. (a) Experimental setup: In Task 3 of the ZuCo study, participants read 407 sentences featuring nine relationships (keywords ) on a computer screen. Simultaneously, we recorded both eye-gaze tracking data and EEG signals. Subsequently, participants were tasked with determining if the sentence contained the relation mentioned in a subsequent question. (b) Sample Language Model Output: A sample output from the language model is presented here. The top row displays a sentence with the “AWARD” relation. The language model identifies highand low-relevance words to the keyword and highlights them in red and blue font colors in the following two rows. speakers, covering 21,629 words, 1,107 sentences, and 154,173 fixations over 4-6 hours of natural text reading. The ZuCo dataset offers preprocessed EEG segments corresponding to each word, corresponded by eye fixations on word boundaries. These segments exhibit variable time steps, averaging around 150ms in duration. This study focused on Task 3 of the ZuCo dataset. This task, which achieved the highest mean accuracy score of 93.16% among the participants, involves reading sentences from the Wikipedia corpus that emphasize specific word relations. Eight of the nine-word relations in Task 3 were selected for analysis, excluding the “VISITED” relation due to its ambiguous interpretability. In this subset, 356 out of 407 sentences were used. Subjectspecific omissions were also noted: ZGW missed “JOB,” ZKB missed “WIFE,” and ZPH missed “POLITICAL AFFILIATION” and “WIFE.” Figure 1 is a visual representation of Task 3. This study analyzed many eye-fixation and EEG data features, specifically examining five features on both HRW and LRW. These features are gaze duration (GD), total reading time (TRT), first fixation duration (FFD), single fixation duration (SFD), and go-past time (GPT). For eye-fixation features, we used the data directly from ZuCo; for EEG data, we extracted our features based on its preprocessed data. The original data were collected in a controlled environment. EEG data were recorded using a 128-channel EEG Geodesic Hydrocel system with a sampling rate of 500 Hz and a bandpass of 0.1 to 100 Hz. The original recording reference was at Cz, we re-reference channels to the average of mastoids. Eye position and pupil size were captured using an EyeLink 1000 Plus eye tracker, also with a sampling rate of 500 Hz. For additional details on the data collection methodology and protocols, readers are referred to the original ZuCo study [30]. 4 III. METHOD A. LLM and word extraction Algorithm 1 Grouping words and Extracting EEG epochs using LLMs Require: SentenceTable, WdEEGSegment Ensure: WdsGps, Mistakes, EEGGps 1: Initialize: Mistakes, TempWds, WdsGps, EEGGps 2: Models ←[’GPT-3.5 Turbo’, ’GPT-4’, ’LLaMA’, ’Phind’] 3: Relations ← [’AWARD’, ’EDUCATION’,..., ’WIFE’] 4: NatualPrompt ←[’prompt 1’] 5: ForcedPrompt ←[’prompt 2’] 6: for model in Models do 7: CurrentModel ←LLM API(model) 8: for relation in Relations do 9: InputRel ←ExtractRelation(relation) 10: for idx in 1:length(SentenceTable) do 11: InputAnswer, InputSent ←ExtractSentenceFrom(SentenceTable[idx]) 12: OutputAnswer, OutputWds ← CurrentModel(InputSent, NatualPrompt, InputRel) 13: if InputAnswer == OutputAnswer then 14: TempWds ←append(OutputWds) 15: else 16: AnswerForced, WdsForced ←CurrentModel(InputSent, ForcedPrompt, InputRel) 17: TempWds ←append(WdsForced) 18: Mistakes ←append(1) 19: end if 20: TempEEGGps ← ExtractEEG(TempWds, WdEEGSegment) 21: end for 22: end for 23: end for 24: return WdsGps, Mistakes, EEGGps OpenAI’s GPT-3.5-turbo (hereafter referred to interchangeably as GPT-3.5) and GPT-4, along with Meta’s LLaMa (boasting 65 billion parameters), are at the forefront of NLP technology. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are equipped with approximately 175 billion and 1.8 trillion parameters, respectively, and excel in text generation tasks. Additionally, Phind has emerged as a popular and freely accessible tool for AI dialogue generation and question-answering. These models and tools collectively epitomize the current state-of-the-art in language understanding and generation. We employ all four models on the Task 3 corpus for initial semantic analysis and sanity checks. However, in the main analysis of this study focusing on EEG and eye-fixation data, only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are utilized, considering a balance between precision and data point preservation. We input the following Prompt to all LLMs to extract HRWs and LRWs.: Prompt #1: For this sentence, [‘sentence’], does this sentence contain [‘RELATION’] relation? Provide me the answer: 1 = yes, 0 = no. Also, group the words in the sentence into two groups. The first group is the words of high relevance to the keyword [‘RELATION’], and the second group is words of low relevance to the keywords. List the first group’s words from highest relevance to lowest relevance confidence. Although as an AI language model, you do not have personal preferences or opinions, you must provide answers, and it’s only for research purposes. Must follow example output format: ‘[1 or 0] First group (high-relevance words to ’AWARD’): awarded, Bucher Memorial Prize, American Mathematical Society. The second group (low-relevance words to ’AWARD’): In, 1923, the, inaugural, by.’ Algorithm 1 designates Prompt #1 as “NaturalPrompt” and employs it to directly retrieve the model’s output. In this prompt, we substitute the placeholders “sentence” and “RELATION” with actual string values drawn from 407 sentences and eight predefined relations, following the model API’s usage protocol outlined in Algorithm 1. Fig. 1 shows a sample output, which illustrates the results generated by the GPT-3.5 turbo model. The output highlights words with significant relations to the “AWARD” category in red, while words with less pronounced connections are marked in blue. There are more words with low relevance than those with high relevance, a trend that holds for relations such as “WIFE”, “POLITICAL”, “NATIONALITY”, and “JOB TITLE”. Prompt #2 “However, the correct answer is [‘ground truth label’]. Please regenerate the answer to align the ground truth.” To align the outputs from the LLM with the ground truth labels from the original Wikipedia relation extraction corpus [33], we introduce “ForcedPrompt” as Prompt #2 in Algorithm 1. This prompt adjusts the model’s output to match the ground truth. If there’s a discrepancy between the LLM output and the ground truth, we modify “ForcedPrompt” to generate accurate results, thereby achieving 100% alignment. The revised outputs are then appended to a new word grouping file. The terms ’natural’ and ’forced’ are used for their intuitive meanings and have no relation to their usage in electrical circuit theory. While a forced response prompt can achieve 100% accuracy in condition checks, the unsupervised generation of HRW and LRW groups may introduce bias. To mitigate this, our study employs a dual-model approach using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, rather than relying on a single Language Model. We enhance the signal-to-noise ratio 5 Fig. 2. Binary classification pipeline. This diagram depicts a comprehensive pipeline for analyzing EEG signals from study participants. Initially, two language models evaluate sentences and classify words as either ’High’ or ’Low’ relevance. Subsequently, a joint selection process identifies a shared set of HRWs. Leveraging eye-gaze data from the subjects, we extract corresponding EEG signals. We use four distinct feature-extraction techniques to condense information from these signals, reducing their complexity. Finally, these refined features are fed into three separate classifiers, following a standard procedure in brain-computer interface pipelines, to perform binary HRW/LRW classification. within the HRW-LRW dataset through a joint selection process across all generated datasets, i.e., we select words that belong to both groups. B. Physiological data processing 1) Pipeline overview: Fig. 2 depicts the overview of neural and physiological data processing pipelines. After the joint selection of the HRW and LRW word groups, we extract the eye fixations and fixation-locked EEG data for binary classification tasks. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), we employed three feature extraction methods across domains of time-frequency analysis, information theory, connectivity network, and their combined features; these will be elaborated in subsequent sections. An embedded classifier architecture was utilized, incorporating established classifiers such as Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Discriminant Analysis. For Fixation-Related Potential (FRP) analysis, EEG signal extraction was restricted to a predefined time window for each word, ranging from 100ms pre-fixation to 400ms post-fixation. 2) FRP Analysis: In contrast to one-dimensional ERP averages, which can obscure dynamic information and inter-trial variability [34], we employed ERPimage for a two-dimensional representation that allows for trialby-trial analysis. Utilizing the ERPimage.m function in the eeglab toolbox (MATLAB 2022b, EEGlab 2020), we generated FRPs for both HRWs and LRWs across 12 subjects. A smoothing parameter of 10 was applied to enhance the clarity of the FRPimage, which span a temporal window from 100ms pre-fixation to 400ms post-fixation, resulting in a comprehensive ERP signal duration of 500ms. 3) EEG feature extraction: Band power: We calculated the power in five EEG frequency bands: delta (0.5-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (30-64 Hz). We employed MATLAB’s “bandpower” function from the Signal Processing Toolbox. The band power (BP) Pa,b is computed as follows: Pa,b = Z b a P(ω)dω = Z b a |F(ω)|2dω (1) Where Pa,b represents the power in the frequency band [a, b], P(ω) denotes the power spectral density, |F(ω)|2 is the squared magnitude of the Fourier transforms, with a and b being the lower and upper bounds of the frequency band, respectively. The EEG data comprised 105 channels, resulting in 525 feature variables per trial. To address the challenge posed by this extensive variable set, many of which exhibited redundancy, we used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of the data to 30 variables. Conditional entropy: This study used conditional entropy (CondEn) to extract features of the EEG trail. It serves as a metric quantifying the level of mutual information between the two random variables. The mutual information between two discrete random variables is 6 defined as follows: I(X; Y ) = X y∈Y X x∈X p(x, y) log  p(x, y) p(x)p(y)  (2) Where p(x) is the approximate density function. By employing this approach, the mutual information I(X; Y ) is computed, establishing its connection with the CondEn I(X; Y ). H(X|Y ) = − X y∈Y p(y) X x∈X p(x|y) log2 p(x|y) (3) Where H(X|Y ) is the CondEn of X given Y, p(y) is the probability of occurrence of a value y from Y, p(x|y) is the conditional probability of x given y, the sums are performed over all possible values of x in X and y in Y. For 105 EEG channels, we generate a 105by-105 CondEn matrix. This matrix is asymmetric because mutual information and CondEn measure different aspects of the relationship between X and Y. Flattening this matrix results in over 10,000 feature variables. To manage this high dimensionality, we focus on one half of the matrix and apply PCA to reduce the feature space to 30 principal components. Connectivity network: The human brain is an expansive and intricate network of electrical activity akin to a vast ocean of electric currents [35]. Understanding the intricate connections within the brain and quantifying its connectivity has garnered increasing interest [36]–[38]. This study employed the Phase Locking Value (PLV) to construct a weighted undirected brain connectivity network [33]. Each channel is represented as a node in the graph, and we depict the correlation strength between channels as the edges connecting them. After constructing the weighted brain network, a range of graph theory measurements can be used as features for analyzing EEG signals. These measurements capture various aspects of the network’s structure and organization, including degree, similarity, assortativity, and core structures [39], [40]. We use the clustering coefficient to reduce the dimension to 30 variables. C(v) = 2e(N(v)) |N(v)|(|N(v)| −1) (4) In this equation, 2e(N(v)) counts the total number of edges in the neighborhood of v, and |N(v)|(|N(v)|−1) is the total number of possible edges in the neighborhood of v. The coefficient 2 in the numerator accounts for each edge connecting two vertices and is counted twice. The clustering coefficient provides insights into the tendency of nodes in a graph to form clusters or communities, with higher values indicating a greater density of interconnected nodes [40]. Combine all three features: Inspired by [41], combining features from different domains might improve the quality of features and classification performance. We concatenate the three features we introduced above, resulting in 90 variables. 4) Machine learning classifiers and feature selection: Initially, the features—BP, CondEn, and PLVconnectivity network—have high dimensions with original dimensions of 525 (105 × 5), 5565, and 5565  (11025−105) 2 + 105 , respectively. We reduced the input variables for subsequent classifier training to 30 for each feature by applying PCA and the clustering coefficient for feature selection. Generally, Discriminant Analysis and SVMs are frequently used as non-neural network classifiers in BCI [42]. We incorporated features extracted from EEG signals to train 11 classifiers simultaneously: LDA, QDA, Logistic Regression, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Kernel Naive Bayes, Linear SVM, Quadratic SVM, Cubic SVM, Fine Gaussian SVM, Medium Gaussian SVM, and Coarse Gaussian SVM. The highest classification accuracy is selected as the final result. To ensure the validity of our outcomes, particularly for smaller sample groups, we report 5-fold cross-validation accuracy. Given the significant class imbalance—LRW EEG data points outnumbering HRW by over 3:1—we applied non-repetitive random downsampling to the LRW class. This ensures equal representation of HRW and LRW data points in the training set. Consequently, the chance label of validation accuracy is 50%. While deep learning approaches like EEGnet have shown promise in EEG classification [43], [44], their core feature extraction layers are primarily designed for image data [45]. The applicability of such methods to time-series EEG data remains a subject of ongoing discussion. We refrained from using deep neural network techniques in this study to maintain model explainability. IV. RESULTS This section presents the results of our pipeline. We first present the results concerning the LLM comparisons, providing statistical insights into the distinctions between GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Then, we delve into the specifics of each relation class, aiming to gain a more profound understanding. Then, we demonstrate eye fixation statistics for HRWs and LRWs. Next, we highlight the ERP analysis of the Fixation-locked EEG signal. Finally, we present the results of our binary classification. A. ## Conclusion
conclusions [22]. With the advancement of machine learning (ML) algorithms, BCI technologies [23], and NLP techniques [24], conducting studies on reading comprehension in natural settings has become increasingly feasible. BCI systems establish a direct link between the human brain and the external environment, using the user’s brain activity signals as a communication medium and translating them into usable data. Various signal modalities are employed in cognitive studies to investigate subjects’ mental states, including Electroencephalography (EEG) [25], Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) [26], Magnetoencephalography (MEG) [27], Positron Emission Tomography (PET) [28], and Eye-tracking methods [29]. For our study, because of its high temporal and spatial resolution and non-invasive properties, we specifically employ high-density EEG. Particularly, Hollenstein [30] have recorded simultaneous EEG and Eyetracking data while subjects engage in sentence reading tasks, suggesting integrating these technologies with NLP tools holds significant potential. This integration enables us to delve deeply into the natural reading process, potentially paving the way for developing realtime reading monitors and converting everyday reading materials into computationally analyzable formats [31], [32]. This study uses the Zurich Cognitive Language Processing Corpus (ZuCo) dataset [30] to explore potential patterns distinguishing two specific mental states—those triggered when subjects fixate on semantically salient words (High-Relevance Words or HRW) and less significant words (Low-Relevance Words or LRW) during ZuCo’s Task 3, which is centered on semantic inference. The main contribution of this study lies in the unique integration of NLP, EEG, and eye-tracking biomarker analysis across multiple disciplines. Prior work by [24] used seven NLP methods to build a comprehensive model for extracting keywords from sentences, employing deep neural networks for binary classification. However, the inflexibility of the embedded NLP model and the extreme data imbalance between the two classes resulted in significant over-fitting during the training of the classification model. As an improvement, this study uses advanced LLMs, such as GPT-4, to generate robust ground truths for HRWs and LRWs to the keyword. These ground truths are the foundation for extracting EEG time series data at the word level for 12 subjects. Given the exploratory nature of this research as a pilot study and the overall classification

(a) Experimental setup: In Task 3 of the ZuCo study, participants read 407 sentences featuring nine relationships (keywords ) on a computer screen. Subsequently, participants were tasked with determining if the sentence contained the relation mentioned in a subsequent question. The ZuCo dataset offers preprocessed EEG segments corresponding to each word, corresponded by eye fixations on word boundaries. These segments exhibit variable time steps, averaging around 150ms in duration. This study focused on Task 3 of the ZuCo dataset. This task, which achieved the highest mean accuracy score of 93.16% among the participants, involves reading sentences from the Wikipedia corpus that emphasize specific word relations. Eight of the nine-word relations in Task 3 were selected for analysis, excluding the “VISITED” relation due to its ambiguous interpretability. In this subset, 356 out of 407 sentences were used. Subjectspecific omissions were also noted: ZGW missed “JOB,” ZKB missed “WIFE,” and ZPH missed “POLITICAL AFFILIATION” and “WIFE.” Figure 1 is a visual representation of Task 3. This study analyzed many eye-fixation and EEG data features, specifically examining five features on both HRW and LRW. These features are gaze duration (GD), total reading time (TRT), first fixation duration (FFD), single fixation duration (SFD), and go-past time (GPT). For eye-fixation features, we used the data directly from ZuCo; for EEG data, we extracted our features based on its preprocessed data. The original data were collected in a controlled environment. EEG data were recorded using a 128-channel EEG Geodesic Hydrocel system with a sampling rate of 500 Hz and a bandpass of 0.1 to 100 Hz. The original recording reference was at Cz, we re-reference channels to the average of mastoids. Eye position and pupil size were captured using an EyeLink 1000 Plus eye tracker, also with a sampling rate of 500 Hz. For additional details on the data collection methodology and protocols, readers are referred to the original ZuCo study [30]. 4 III. METHOD A. LLM and word extraction Algorithm 1 Grouping words and Extracting EEG epochs using LLMs Require: SentenceTable, WdEEGSegment Ensure: WdsGps, Mistakes, EEGGps 1: Initialize: Mistakes, TempWds, WdsGps, EEGGps 2: Models ←[’GPT-3.5 Turbo’, ’GPT-4’, ’LLaMA’, ’Phind’] 3: Relations ← [’AWARD’, ’EDUCATION’,..., ’WIFE’] 4: NatualPrompt ←[’prompt 1’] 5: ForcedPrompt ←[’prompt 2’] 6: for model in Models do 7: CurrentModel ←LLM API(model) 8: for relation in Relations do 9: InputRel ←ExtractRelation(relation) 10: for idx in 1:length(SentenceTable) do 11: InputAnswer, InputSent ←ExtractSentenceFrom(SentenceTable[idx]) 12: OutputAnswer, OutputWds ← CurrentModel(InputSent, NatualPrompt, InputRel) 13: if InputAnswer == OutputAnswer then 14: TempWds ←append(OutputWds) 15: else 16: AnswerForced, WdsForced ←CurrentModel(InputSent, ForcedPrompt, InputRel) 17: TempWds ←append(WdsForced) 18: Mistakes ←append(1) 19: end if 20: TempEEGGps ← ExtractEEG(TempWds, WdEEGSegment) 21: end for 22: end for 23: end for 24: return WdsGps, Mistakes, EEGGps OpenAI’s GPT-3.5-turbo (hereafter referred to interchangeably as GPT-3.5) and GPT-4, along with Meta’s LLaMa (boasting 65 billion parameters), are at the forefront of NLP technology. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are equipped with approximately 175 billion and 1.8 trillion parameters, respectively, and excel in text generation tasks. Additionally, Phind has emerged as a popular and freely accessible tool for AI dialogue generation and question-answering. These models and tools collectively epitomize the current state-of-the-art in language understanding and generation. We employ all four models on the Task 3 corpus for initial semantic analysis and sanity checks. However, in the main analysis of this study focusing on EEG and eye-fixation data, only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are utilized, considering a balance between precision and data point preservation. We input the following Prompt to all LLMs to extract HRWs and LRWs.: Prompt #1: For this sentence, [‘sentence’], does this sentence contain [‘RELATION’] relation? Provide me the answer: 1 = yes, 0 = no. Also, group the words in the sentence into two groups. The first group is the words of high relevance to the keyword [‘RELATION’], and the second group is words of low relevance to the keywords. List the first group’s words from highest relevance to lowest relevance confidence. Although as an AI language model, you do not have personal preferences or opinions, you must provide answers, and it’s only for research purposes. Must follow example output format: ‘[1 or 0] First group (high-relevance words to ’AWARD’): awarded, Bucher Memorial Prize, American Mathematical Society. The second group (low-relevance words to ’AWARD’): In, 1923, the, inaugural, by.’ Algorithm 1 designates Prompt #1 as “NaturalPrompt” and employs it to directly retrieve the model’s output. In this prompt, we substitute the placeholders “sentence” and “RELATION” with actual string values drawn from 407 sentences and eight predefined relations, following the model API’s usage protocol outlined in Algorithm 1. Fig. 1 shows a sample output, which illustrates the results generated by the GPT-3.5 turbo model. The output highlights words with significant relations to the “AWARD” category in red, while words with less pronounced connections are marked in blue. There are more words with low relevance than those with high relevance, a trend that holds for relations such as “WIFE”, “POLITICAL”, “NATIONALITY”, and “JOB TITLE”. Prompt #2 “However, the correct answer is [‘ground truth label’]. Please regenerate the answer to align the ground truth.” To align the outputs from the LLM with the ground truth labels from the original Wikipedia relation extraction corpus [33], we introduce “ForcedPrompt” as Prompt #2 in Algorithm 1. This prompt adjusts the model’s output to match the ground truth. If there’s a discrepancy between the LLM output and the ground truth, we modify “ForcedPrompt” to generate accurate results, thereby achieving 100% alignment. The revised outputs are then appended to a new word grouping file. The terms ’natural’ and ’forced’ are used for their intuitive meanings and have no relation to their usage in electrical circuit theory. While a forced response prompt can achieve 100% accuracy in condition checks, the unsupervised generation of HRW and LRW groups may introduce bias. To mitigate this, our study employs a dual-model approach using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, rather than relying on a single Language Model. We enhance the signal-to-noise ratio 5 Fig. 2. Binary classification pipeline. This diagram depicts a comprehensive pipeline for analyzing EEG signals from study participants. Initially, two language models evaluate sentences and classify words as either ’High’ or ’Low’ relevance. Subsequently, a joint selection process identifies a shared set of HRWs. Leveraging eye-gaze data from the subjects, we extract corresponding EEG signals. We use four distinct feature-extraction techniques to condense information from these signals, reducing their complexity. Finally, these refined features are fed into three separate classifiers, following a standard procedure in brain-computer interface pipelines, to perform binary HRW/LRW classification. within the HRW-LRW dataset through a joint selection process across all generated datasets, i.e., we select words that belong to both groups. B. Physiological data processing 1) Pipeline overview: Fig. 2 depicts the overview of neural and physiological data processing pipelines. After the joint selection of the HRW and LRW word groups, we extract the eye fixations and fixation-locked EEG data for binary classification tasks. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), we employed three feature extraction methods across domains of time-frequency analysis, information theory, connectivity network, and their combined features; these will be elaborated in subsequent sections. An embedded classifier architecture was utilized, incorporating established classifiers such as Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Discriminant Analysis. For Fixation-Related Potential (FRP) analysis, EEG signal extraction was restricted to a predefined time window for each word, ranging from 100ms pre-fixation to 400ms post-fixation. 2) FRP Analysis: In contrast to one-dimensional ERP averages, which can obscure dynamic information and inter-trial variability [34], we employed ERPimage for a two-dimensional representation that allows for trialby-trial analysis. Utilizing the ERPimage.m function in the eeglab toolbox (MATLAB 2022b, EEGlab 2020), we generated FRPs for both HRWs and LRWs across 12 subjects. A smoothing parameter of 10 was applied to enhance the clarity of the FRPimage, which span a temporal window from 100ms pre-fixation to 400ms post-fixation, resulting in a comprehensive ERP signal duration of 500ms. 3) EEG feature extraction: Band power: We calculated the power in five EEG frequency bands: delta (0.5-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (30-64 Hz). We employed MATLAB’s “bandpower” function from the Signal Processing Toolbox. The band power (BP) Pa,b is computed as follows: Pa,b = Z b a P(ω)dω = Z b a |F(ω)|2dω (1) Where Pa,b represents the power in the frequency band [a, b], P(ω) denotes the power spectral density, |F(ω)|2 is the squared magnitude of the Fourier transforms, with a and b being the lower and upper bounds of the frequency band, respectively. The EEG data comprised 105 channels, resulting in 525 feature variables per trial. To address the challenge posed by this extensive variable set, many of which exhibited redundancy, we used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of the data to 30 variables. Conditional entropy: This study used conditional entropy (CondEn) to extract features of the EEG trail. It serves as a metric quantifying the level of mutual information between the two random variables. The mutual information between two discrete random variables is 6 defined as follows: I(X; Y ) = X y∈Y X x∈X p(x, y) log  p(x, y) p(x)p(y)  (2) Where p(x) is the approximate density function. By employing this approach, the mutual information I(X; Y ) is computed, establishing its connection with the CondEn I(X; Y ). H(X|Y ) = − X y∈Y p(y) X x∈X p(x|y) log2 p(x|y) (3) Where H(X|Y ) is the CondEn of X given Y, p(y) is the probability of occurrence of a value y from Y, p(x|y) is the conditional probability of x given y, the sums are performed over all possible values of x in X and y in Y. For 105 EEG channels, we generate a 105by-105 CondEn matrix. This matrix is asymmetric because mutual information and CondEn measure different aspects of the relationship between X and Y. Flattening this matrix results in over 10,000 feature variables. To manage this high dimensionality, we focus on one half of the matrix and apply PCA to reduce the feature space to 30 principal components. Connectivity network: The human brain is an expansive and intricate network of electrical activity akin to a vast ocean of electric currents [35]. Understanding the intricate connections within the brain and quantifying its connectivity has garnered increasing interest [36]–[38]. This study employed the Phase Locking Value (PLV) to construct a weighted undirected brain connectivity network [33]. Each channel is represented as a node in the graph, and we depict the correlation strength between channels as the edges connecting them. After constructing the weighted brain network, a range of graph theory measurements can be used as features for analyzing EEG signals. These measurements capture various aspects of the network’s structure and organization, including degree, similarity, assortativity, and core structures [39], [40]. We use the clustering coefficient to reduce the dimension to 30 variables. C(v) = 2e(N(v)) |N(v)|(|N(v)| −1) (4) In this equation, 2e(N(v)) counts the total number of edges in the neighborhood of v, and |N(v)|(|N(v)|−1) is the total number of possible edges in the neighborhood of v. The coefficient 2 in the numerator accounts for each edge connecting two vertices and is counted twice. The clustering coefficient provides insights into the tendency of nodes in a graph to form clusters or communities, with higher values indicating a greater density of interconnected nodes [40]. Combine all three features: Inspired by [41], combining features from different domains might improve the quality of features and classification performance. We concatenate the three features we introduced above, resulting in 90 variables. 4) Machine learning classifiers and feature selection: Initially, the features—BP, CondEn, and PLVconnectivity network—have high dimensions with original dimensions of 525 (105 × 5), 5565, and 5565  (11025−105) 2 + 105 , respectively. We reduced the input variables for subsequent classifier training to 30 for each feature by applying PCA and the clustering coefficient for feature selection. Generally, Discriminant Analysis and SVMs are frequently used as non-neural network classifiers in BCI [42]. We incorporated features extracted from EEG signals to train 11 classifiers simultaneously: LDA, QDA, Logistic Regression, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Kernel Naive Bayes, Linear SVM, Quadratic SVM, Cubic SVM, Fine Gaussian SVM, Medium Gaussian SVM, and Coarse Gaussian SVM. The highest classification accuracy is selected as the final result. To ensure the validity of our outcomes, particularly for smaller sample groups, we report 5-fold cross-validation accuracy. Given the significant class imbalance—LRW EEG data points outnumbering HRW by over 3:1—we applied non-repetitive random downsampling to the LRW class. This ensures equal representation of HRW and LRW data points in the training set. Consequently, the chance label of validation accuracy is 50%. While deep learning approaches like EEGnet have shown promise in EEG classification [43], [44], their core feature extraction layers are primarily designed for image data [45]. The applicability of such methods to time-series EEG data remains a subject of ongoing discussion. We refrained from using deep neural network techniques in this study to maintain model explainability. IV. RESULTS This section presents the results of our pipeline. This is one of the first efforts to use GPT capability for this specialized intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Eye gaze is a prominent biomarker, holding crucial information for comprehending cognitive processes in individuals involved in task-specific reading activities [49]. In this study, we conducted average fixation analyses across three distinct dimensions: on a subject-bysubject basis, concerning specific semantic relations, and at the level of individual words. We performed these analyses on data collected from 12 participants and encompassing eight different semantic relations. Our results unequivocally show that participants allocate significantly more time to words that exhibit high semantic relevance to specific relations (i.e., keywords) during inference tasks. Appendices A and B provide additional support for this observation. These findings provide valuable insights into how participants comprehend the reading corpus. Despite these advances, the study has several limitations. This study faces challenges because of the ’black box’ nature of LLMs, particularly in the context of the non-deterministic relation, such as ‘AWARD,’ where certain outputted words appear incongruous. This limitation might affect our findings’ generalizability and underscore the need for a quantitative assessment to ensure the accuracy and validity of keyword identification. Additionally, contextual complexities often influence semantic classifications. For example, “gold” acquire distinct semantic relevance when juxtaposed with terms like “medal.” The sentences incorporating specific target terms, such as “NATIONALITY” or “WIFE,” exhibit a significant disparity in the distribution between HRW and LRW, making them more deterministic. These discrepancies add complexity to the classification of EEG data and introduce the possibility of contamination within the dataset, especially when the meaning of words is most effectively comprehended within the context of phrases rather than in isolation. This study underscores the potential for more expansive research on elucidating reading-related cognitive behaviors. The promise of integrating LLMs into BCIs also points towards future advancements in reading assistance technologies. While acknowledging its limitations and complexities, our work is an early yet significant contribution, paving the way for more integrated studies to foster a deeper understanding of the multifaceted interplay between neuroscience and computational linguistics

## Abstract
Abstract Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings play a vital role in sleep medicine, offering critical insights into brain activity for diagnosing and predicting disorders like insomnia and sleep apnea. Traditionally, sleep disorder analysis relied on manual

## Introduction
Introduction Sleep is essential for rest and restoration. Around 48% of Australian adults experience at least two sleep disorders, such as Insomnia and Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), which raise risks of obesity, cardiovascular diseases, and diabetes. Sleep has distinct stages: three Non-REM stages and REM sleep, characterized by brain wave patterns [1]. During sleep, the brain cycles through 4 stages: wake, N-REM (N1, N2, N3), and REM. Classifying these stages helps assess sleep quality and diagnose disorders. N1 is a transition from wakefulness to sleep, with alpha and theta waves. N2 is marked by deep relaxation and sleep spindles. N3, or deep sleep, is characterized by delta waves and a slowed heart rate. REM, stage 4, involves rapid eye movement and dreaming, with saw-tooth waves [2]. EEG monitors brain activity, aiding in diagnosing disorders and analyzing sleep stages, as the brain activity changes across stages, with REM increasing as the night progresses [3]. Manual sleep disorder diagnostics is tedious, error-prone, and time-consuming. Machine learning offers faster, more accurate, automated solutions, reducing reliance on manual diagnosis. However, data scarcity limits its effectiveness as hospitals restrict access due to privacy concerns. Large Language Models (LLMs) can process diverse datasets, identifying sleep patterns, but remain underutilised in this field. By leveraging LLMs to process manual annotations of sleep stages in textual form, we can streamline and standardise data interpretation across studies. This approach enhances generalisation across datasets, as it decouples analysis from the variability inherent in raw sleep study signals. LLMs are advanced machine learning models designed to process and generate human language. They are pretrained on massive datasets using transformer architectures, which rely on neural networks with trillions of parameters to capture intricate patterns in language. When input data is fed into an LLM, it generates text output and represents this information in numeric form, allowing the model to recognise, predict, translate, and produce text. Due to their capabilities, LLMs are widely used in various applications such as content generation, language translation, customer service chatbots, and even medical research [4]. Their efficiency as fast learners and ability to support multiple languages make them versatile tools. Given their recent development, LLMs are continually evolving and improving. Notable examples of LLMs include GPT-4, PaLLM, and LLaMA. These models are primarily recognized for their ability to generate content, write code, and engage in conversational dialogue, showcasing their proficiency in understanding natural language and performing complex tasks in daily life [5]. 1.1. Related Work The past methods for automated sleep disorder detection, particularly insomnia include approaches that utilize raw EEG signals or RGB images derived from EEG spectrograms. For example, Cheng et al. (2023) [6] implemented a system based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Meanwhile, Dimitriadis et al. (2021) [7] employed a random forest (RF) model combined with majority voting to predict sleep disorders. There has been limited previous research focused on finetuning LLMs to classify sleep health based on input sleep stage sequences from real patient data. The closest work in terms of analysing health disorders was a study in 2023 by Yu et al. [8] explored the use of large language models (LLMs) in diagnosing arrhythmia and sleep apnea from ECG data. The process involved extracting features such as heart rate and spectral power for annotating key segments (PR, ST, QT). Prompts, created from ECG knowledge and sleep apnea detection information, were crucial for guiding LLMs to generate accurate diagnoses. The study utilized zero-shot generation, where LLMs, such as LLaMA2 and GPT-3.5, predicted ECG conditions without prior training. GPT-3.5 outperformed LLaMA2 in accuracy, precision, and F1-score, indicating that the approach could be effective for arrhythmia 979-8-3315-8618-8/25/$31.00

## Methodology
methods showed accuracy on small datasets, they struggled with scalability for larger ones. This paper explores the use of Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically BERT and Longformer, to classify EEG-derived sleep stages as healthy or unhealthy. Fine-tuning is performed on curated datasets containing full-night sequences, two-hour segments, and mid-sleep windows. Results demonstrate a promising performance in classifying sleep stages with accuracies between 70-80%, showcasing their adaptability for sleep medicine. Index Terms: sleep disorders, large language model, classification, fine-tuning 1.

## Results

## Conclusion
Conclusion and Future Work This project demonstrated the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) in sleep medicine for analysing disorders. Fine-tuning BERT and Longformer models on diverse datasets achieved accuracies and F1 scores of 70–90%, with BERT performing better on shorter sequences and Longformer on longer ones. However, overfitting due to dataset imbalance and limited public data hindered generalizability, and the models couldn’t classify specific disorders like insomnia or apnea. Advancing this field requires better data availability, trust in data sharing, and robust privacy protections. Future work could involve finetuning LLMs to classify sleep stages from raw EEG data, potentially outperforming traditional classifiers. Katana Katana is a High Performance Computing System from the University of New South Wales that provides the GPU memory required to set up the necessary environment for fine-tuning the LLMs. It contains over 6000 CPU cores, 8 GPU compute nodes, and up to 6Pb of disk storage [22]. Katana can be connected through Terminal on the local machine and running jobs can be initiated using qsub to request memory and training duration. 3.2. Hugging Face also has a datasets library which allows users to easily access numerous shared public datasets and most importantly being able to load custom datasets for training and evaluating LLMs [24]. 3.3. Training Hyperparameters Tuning hyperparameters is crucial for optimizing LLM performance. The hyperparameters used are detailed in Table 2. Training is conducted over 10 epochs, with the learning rate determining weight updates and the batch size set to 2 due to GPU memory constraints on Katana. To address this limitation, gradient accumulation steps are set to 64, yielding an effective batch size of 128 [25]. This ensures efficient GPU utilization while maintaining the benefits of a larger batch size. The validation loss (eval loss) is used to save the best checkpoint, mitigating overfitting risks from the duplicated healthy dataset described in section 2.1.5, which could hinder generalization to unseen data. 3.4. Tokenization To reduce the size of the input provided to LLMs, large text strings are segmented into smaller tokens using a tokenizer module. We used a tokenizer module as shown in Figure 2 that inserted human-labelled sleep stages W, N1, N2, N3 and R as special tokens. This ensured that the stages are never split and allows the LLMs to learn patterns in the sleep sequences and their LLM’s predictive accuracy with unseen data. 3.5. Classification The training process uses the Hugging Face Trainer API, with the trainer.train() method managing training, evaluation, and logging [26]. After training, the best-performing model is reloaded to generate predictions in the test set, which are compared to true labels and logged alongside the recording IDs.Each sleep stage sequence is classified as ’0’ (healthy) or ’1’ (unhealthy). The fine-tuned LLM, loaded from its saved checkpoint, predicts class probabilities on the test split using trainer.predict(). The final label is determined by np.argmax(), selecting the class with the highest probability for comparison with the true labels [27] 4. Results 4.1. ## Abstract
Abstract—The use of vision large language models (VLLMs) for the analysis and diagnosis of respiratory patterns is affected by limited specialist training data and the lack of integrated medical expertise. This article introduces a method that uses a multimodal VLLM to analyze electrocardiogram (ECG) data transformed to Gramian angular fields (GAFs) 2-D image to determine respiratory patterns. Using advanced Shimmer3 sensing, five VLLMs are fine-tuned using four different ECG datasets for training, each containing 5000 samples, to improve the interpretation of ECG signals. VLLMs are then evaluated against an independent set of data to determine normal, rapid, and difficult breathing patterns. The low-rank adaptation method is used to optimize VLLMs for the analysis of ECG signals obtained from the shimmer sensing platform.

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION T HE applications of large language models (LLMs) aim to transform multiple aspects of modern medicine [1], [2]. LLMs have paved the way for more sophisticated medical data analysis in various domains. Although they excel at processing and interpreting textual medical information, their capabilities can be extended to analyze complex biomedical signals [3], [4]. This convergence of LLM with specialized medical data analysis is particularly evident in the field of electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, while artificial intelligence (AI) driven approaches are revolutionizing diagnostic

## Methodology
methods [5]. However, handling vast medical ECG data can be a challenge due to time restrictions, privacy, and security concerns, especially with limited labeled data, affecting the training of LLM or AI models in general [6], [7]. Moreover, several articles mentioned the difficulty of breathing associated with heart problems [8]. Radaelli et al. [9] discussed both breathing patterns and heart-related breathing problems. The latter explores how different breathing patterns, such as fast-paced and slow-paced breathing, affect baroreflex 1558-1748

## Results
Results show that Idefics outperforms other fine-tuned VLLMs with a BLEU score of 0.572 for 2-D ECG signals and 0.549 for 1-D ECG signals, which demonstrates that the 2-D image representation of the GAF improves the visualization of ECG respiratory patterns. Index Terms— Breathing pattern, electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis, Gramian angular fields (GAFs), Shimmer3 sensing, vision large language models (VLLMs). ## Conclusion
CONCLUSION This article proposes a framework that integrates Shimmer3 ECG signals and VLLMs for the classification of breathing patterns. The framework employs 2-D GAF representation to transform ECG signals into images, improving visualization of respiratory patterns demonstrating the transformative potential of sensing platform and AI in the field of respiratory health monitoring. By matching ECG-derived respiratory patterns to clinical symptoms, this technology translates ambulatory data into actionable insights, allowing early detection of exacerbations. This framework employs the LoRA approach to fine-tune the capabilities of pretrained VLLMs, optimizing the extraction and synthesis of both visual and textual data. However, the method has limitations, including potential bias due to the diversity of the dataset and the reliance on ECG signals, which may not fully capture respiratory patterns. In addition, the computational cost of fine-tuning VLLMs remains a challenge for real-time applications. The results derived from comparative analysis across diverse datasets emphasize not only the robustness but also the clinical applicability of our method. Future efforts will optimize LoRA fine-tuning for edge devices, using federated learning across distributed sensor networks to improve computational efficiency and data privacy. In addition, to mitigate dataset bias by integrating more diverse data sources, additional methods, such as direct respiratory signals, have been proposed to increase accuracy and develop fine-tuning techniques to allow real-time applications. These efforts will further improve the performance of the model, advance the early detection and treatment of respiratory diseases, and improve real-time analysis of breathing, early intervention strategies, and individualized treatment of asthma. Data Preprocessing (Stage 2) The transformation process for ECG data and signal processing begins with retrieving ECG DAT files and converting them to 2-D GAF representations [18] for improved visual pattern recognition, while preserving data integrity through error management and reporting. In the GAF transformation process, the ECG time series data are first converted to polar coordinates using the arctangent function φ = arccos(x) and then mapped to both Gramian angular summation field (GASF) and Gramian angular difference field (GADF) matrices [19], where GASF matrices are computed as Gs i, j = cos(φi + φ j) to preserve temporal correlations through summation operations, while GADF matrices are calculated as Gd i, j = sin(φi −φ j) to capture temporal differences and phase variations. This dual GAF approach creates complementary 2-D image representations that capture both synchronized cardiac-respiratory coupling (via GASF) and breathing pattern transitions (via GADF), enabling temporal pattern analysis within the signal. The resulting combined GAF images are then converted to grayscale to simplify the data and highlight intensity variations, followed by normalization by scaling values between 0 and 1 and filtering with a Butterworth filter, fourth-order Butterworth bandpass filter with cutoff frequencies of 0.5–40 Hz to isolate clinically relevant ECG frequencies. The low-frequency cutoff (0.5 Hz) removes baseline drift and motion artifacts while preserving P-wave and STsegment information, while the high-frequency cutoff (40 Hz) eliminates muscle noise and power line interference while retaining QRS complexes and T-wave details essential for arrhythmia detection. The fourth-order configuration provides an optimal balance between sharp frequency response and minimal phase distortion, preserving temporal relationships critical for cardiac rhythm analysis. The contour detection then extracts the coordinates from these GAF representations. Experimental Setup The setup is created using an AWS P5 instance (p5.48∗ large instance) equipped with 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, with 80 GB of HBM3 memory integrated into each unit. The dataset is divided into an 80–20 split, whereby 80% is allocated for training and 20% is reserved for validation. C. Performance Metrics The performance of the model is evaluated using training loss, validation loss, perplexity, BLEU, and ROUGE scores to assess generated text and analysis of respiratory patterns. Training loss measures how the model learns from training data during fine-tuning, quantifying the difference between predicted and actual outputs on GAF-transformed ECG data, while validation loss quantifies generalization to unseen data and helps to optimize hyperparameters and determine stopping points. Perplexity measures the uncertainty of the language model when predicting the next token in respiratory pattern descriptions, with lower values indicating better performance. The BLEU score evaluates the quality of the generated text by comparing the overlap of n grams between the model output and the reference responses, ranging from 0 to 1, with scores indicating alignment with the groundtruth annotations. ROUGE metrics assess text overlap through approaches: ROUGE-1 measures unigram overlap for word matching, ROUGE-2 focuses on bigram overlap to capture word sequences and relationships, and ROUGE-L calculates the subsequence to measure fluency and coherence in respiratory pattern analysis outputs. These metrics provide an evaluation framework for assessing the quality and precision of VLLM performance in respiratory pattern analysis tasks. The proposed framework integrates Shimmer3 ECG sensing platforms and VLLMs to classify breathing patterns, demonstrating the transformative potential of wearable sensing and AI in respiratory health monitoring. By correlating TABLE IV FINE-TUNING PARAMETERS FOR THE LLMS ECG-derived respiratory patterns with clinical symptoms, this framework translates ambulatory data into actionable insights, allowing early detection of exacerbations. However, it sometimes experiences minor increases in validation loss, hinting at possible overfitting or sensitivity to shifts in the data distribution. In contrast, Idefics presents a more balanced performance between training and validation losses in WCTECGdb but encounters difficulties with datasets such as BUT QDB, where validation loss reaches 0.4521. Finally, Florence achieves a very low validation loss for PTB-XL (0.001) but a higher one for BUT QDB (1.4338), reflecting a dependency on the dataset. The Florence model demonstrates strong performance, as indicated by its moderate training and validation losses across every dataset. These findings reveal that no single model consistently outperforms others in all datasets. They highlight the need to align the model architectures with the characteristics of each dataset. In addition, this study shows the potential of using multimodal approaches, through LoRAs, to blend visual (ECG waveform images) and textual details to identify unique breathing patterns. The baseline results show consistent but modest degradation compared with the LoRA fine-tuned versions, with improvements ranging from marginal (Pixtral) to substantial (Idefics: +0.089 BLEU and p < 0.001; Florence-2: +0.124 BLEU in 1-D and p < 0.001), demonstrating the significant contribution of LoRA adaptation across different model architectures.
