Direct neural interface or EEG sensors are particularly advantageous due to their information rate, enabling effective control of the upper limbs [6]. This capability is crucial for individuals with neuromuscular dysfunction, as it supports their ability to perform activities of daily living (ADL) [7]. Recent advancements have proposed the use of EEG for intelligent control of daily activities [8], [9], efficient speech prostheses [10], and representation decoding [11], [12]. However, a significant drawback of direct neural interfaces is the requirement for invasive or semi-invasive surgical procedures. An alternative is noninvasive interface with the neuromuscular system using sEMG. sEMG is generated from the innervation of several 100 muscle fibers, recorded via electrodes placed on the skin surface. In contrast to EEG, sEMG exhibits a significantly higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), making it a less intrusive method for intelligent prosthetic control [14] and broader human–computer interaction applications [15], [16], [17], [18]. We employed a 224-pixel input size into the model, along with 128-token input text sequences. We fine-tuned the Paligemma model on the Flickr30k dataset [47], selected due to its inclusion of objects relevant to the evaluation of the Toronto Rehabilitation Institute Hand Function Test (TRI-HFT) and the Jebsen–Taylor Hand Function Test. No additional data were used to fine-tune the VLM model. To enhance the performance of both the vision encoder and the Gemma decoder within the Paligemma framework, we employed QLoRa [48] for fine-tuning. We developed a prompt designed to effectively detect user intentions related to grasping, releasing actions, or neutral states, which is illustrated in Fig. 2. The specifics of this prompt are detailed in Algorithm 1. In step 1, to infer user grasp intention, the prompts in Fig. 2 must return True in both questions. If questions 1 and 2 return False, the intention is classified as Neutral. In scenarios where question 1 is True and question 2 is also False, the user intention decoder determines that the action about to be performed is release. This step ensures the reliability of the decoding pipeline by avoiding involuntary action. B. EMG Decoder Previous studies have reported shallow neural networks with sufficient capacity can achieve optimal decoding performance [15] when trained with a large dataset comprising data from over 4000 participants. Building upon this foundational insight, our study employs an efficient Fourier analysis network (FAN) [49] for EMG-based gesture decoding. The architecture of the EMG-FAN follows the EMG-Net proposed in [20], with the primary modification being the replacement of fully connected (FC) layers with the FAN algorithm. The FAN layer represents a function using a Fourier series expansion by computing the sine and cosine components of the input, specifically sin(Wpx) and cos(Wpx). These components are then concatenated with the nonlinear activation of the affine transformation of the input, σ(Bq + Wqx), as defined in the following equation: ϕ(x) ≜[cos(Wpx), ||, sin(Wpx), ||, σ(Bq + Wqx)]. (1) The learnable weight parameters in this formulation are Wp ∈RCin×K for projecting the input, Wq ∈RCin×O for the linear transformation preceding activation, and Bq ∈RO for the bias term associated with Wq. Cin denotes the number of input channels. The dimensionalities K and O are defined as K = Cout × R and O = Cout −2K, where Cout is the number of output channels. R is a hyperparameter set to 0.25 in our study. To enhance the expressive power of FAN, the Gaussian error linear unit (GELU) activation function (σ) was employed for both the weight matrix Wq and the bias term Bq. The FAN algorithm, utilized as a nonlinearity layer, enables EMG-FAN to learn periodic structures effectively while capturing the frequency components of the input signal in a compact representation. In this study, we utilized the pretraining dataset [20] to conduct hyperparameter optimization on an EMG decoder model. The hyperparameters of both the EMG-FAN decoder and the training configuration were optimized to achieve the best accuracy on a test dataset derived from the first participant. In addition, all hyperparameter settings were kept consistent for comparative analysis of the EMG decoders. C. VLM for Pseudolabeling As detailed in Algorithm 1, the VLM takes input from a camera and utilizes predefined prompts in Fig. 2. The VLM generates outputs indicating True or False based on two critical questions: 1) is the hand strained or relaxed? and 2) is the hand sufficiently close to the object for successful grasping? The second criterion aligns with the methodology presented in [34]. If the hand is not visible in the image and the intention to grasp is indicated, the VLM will return False, even in the presence of involuntary muscle contractions and subsequent inferences from the EMG decoder. In instances where the hand is present in the image and the first condition returns True, the VLM is prompted with a follow-up question (Step 2), as depicted in Fig. 2. The VLM is tasked with identifying the object and determining the appropriate gesture from the EMG-based grasp gestures needed to complete the object grasp. A window size of 10 utilizing a majority voting mechanism was employed for EMG gesture prediction [50], [51]. The VLM’s inference latency averaged 60 ± 5 s on AMD Ryzen 9 7900 and improved to 25 ± 1 s using 4-bit quantized weight precision and 16-bit computation on GPU RTX 4090 to return pseudolabels. If the gesture decoded from the EMG aligns with the top two options provided by the pseudolabel, the grasp is grounded (Step 3), and the intent to grasp is used to control the upper limb exoskeleton. IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS A. EMG-Based Decoding Sussillo et al. [15] demonstrated that using a dataset comprising over 4000 participants can result in a model capable of generalizing effectively to new individuals. However, obtaining access to such a large dataset remains impractical for small-scale laboratories. To address this limitation, we utilized a publicly available EMG dataset from [20], selecting large diameter, medium diameter, three fingers, and prismatic pinch gestures. The choice of these gestures was also influenced by their ability to facilitate the TRI-HFT and Jebsen–Taylor Hand Function Tests. In addition, the sensor used for the EMG dataset acquisition in [20] is similar to the EMG sensor we employed for on-device inference evaluation, which informed our choice of dataset. Furthermore, the EMG dataset from [20] was only used for pretraining the EMG decoder. To validate the proposed decoding pipeline in Fig. 1, four new participants who provided informed consent prior to participation in the study were invited to participate in the inference stage. The study protocol was approved by the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology Institutional Review Board (20240215-HR-75-03-02). The participants had a mean age of 28 ± 3.8 years and were right-handed, with no previous clinically diagnosed neurological problems (that Fig. 3. Average accuracy of the EMG-FAN model across 33 participants used to pretrain the model. could affect upper limbs). Participants were novices to the BCI experiment, and no part of the participants was included in the pretraining dataset [20]. The participants were positioned in front of a screen running custom-developed supervised software [20], which randomly presented a series of four gestures. Each participant was shown one gesture at random, followed by asking them to replicate it. Each gesture was displayed for ten trials, with each trial followed by a brief rest period of 3 s. According to [15], a fine-tuned model with 20 min of data is equivalent to training on a model with 14 000 min of data. This assertion from the study highlights personalized approaches to fine-tuning as a potential solution when dealing with distribution shifts. We employed two fine-tuning approaches: Full-Train, which involves fine-tuning all the layers, and LastLayer, which involves fine-tuning only the last layer [52]. For each model, we utilized five trials from the inference stage for fine-tuning, with the remaining data reserved for evaluation. The offline and inference data were preprocessed using a notch filter at 60 Hz with a bandpass range between 5.0 and 99.0 Hz. Offline pretraining EMG data evaluation involved random splitting of the dataset, allocating 80% for training and 20% for evaluation. A window size of 200 ms with a 60% overlap was used consistently during the offline stage. This choice of window size was made to ensure an electromechanical delay of less than 300 ms, which aligns with findings from studies that have proposed similar window sizes [53], [54], [55] CLER =  1 −Number of correct predictions Total number of true events  × 100 (2) Classification Accuracy (CA) = 100 −CLER. One drawback of MVC is that it treats release as a voluntary contraction without distinct gesture classification. The results indicate the vision-based approach demonstrated high reliability by significantly reducing false positives. Furthermore, the result suggests that there were no performance variations across the different versions of the Paligemma VLM. In Table II, the VLM outperformed both VIDEONet and DEEPOSENet, which were previously proposed for participant intent decoding, while VIDEONet and DEEPOSENet relied on curated datasets for similar purposes. Our findings demonstrate that without incurring any data collection overhead, we achieved superior performance utilizing an offthe-shelf VLM. To further investigate the efficacy of the VLM, we conducted segmentation analyses to ensure consistency with the methodologies employed in previous studies [34], [59]. Fig. 6 qualitatively demonstrates that the VLM effectively captures and segments intrinsic parts of the hand, distinguishing them from other objects within both simple and complex environments. Moreover, when evaluating all objects included in the TRI-HFT and the Jebsen Hand Function Test, the VLM successfully recognized all objects without the need for finetuning. This capability is significant for the development of products that integrate vision and language functionalities in rehabilitation therapy for patients with SCI, stroke, and ALS. The ability to operate without the necessity for curated datasets for training or model fine-tuning enhances the practicality and accessibility. C. VLM for Pseudolabeling The degradation of model performance due to variations in participant characteristics and session conditions can be attributed to various factors [15], [19], [57]. In our study, a CLER of 30.84% was reported for new participants without undergoing fine-tuning. Furthermore, in real-time cases, implementing fine-tuning would require data and computational resources on the edge devices. To reduce the CLER without additional data acquisition and on-device fine-tuning, we propose pseudolabels generated by VLM. Based on these findings, we advocate for a decoding pipeline that incorporates vision capabilities to enhance active rehabilitation devices, thereby reducing classification errors and ultimately boosting confidence and acceptance among users. D. Discussion Active rehabilitation devices designed to assist individuals with ALS, SCI, and stroke in performing ADLs often face significant reliability issues, contributing to a high abandonment rate. The challenges posed by low SNR in EEG and the limited generalization capabilities of EMG decoders remain unresolved, hindering the acceptance of biosignal-controlled rehabilitation devices [25]. To address these challenges, we propose the fusion of vision data to enhance the reliability of the EMG decoder. While previous studies have explored vision-based approaches to mitigate these issues, our work introduces a novel gesture decoding pipeline that employs an off-the-shelf VLM without the need for pretraining or finetuning, as demonstrated in Table II. Recent studies utilizing vision approaches rely heavily on extensive data acquisition methods, which may not be feasible for smaller laboratories or industrial applications. Therefore, our proposed pipeline integrating a VLM aims to democratize the development of reliable biosignal-controlled active rehabilitation devices. Table III provides a comparative analysis of various intention detection studies, focusing on the types of sensors used, the number of gestures recognized, CA, and the decoding methods adopted. The studies utilize different sensor combinations, such as vision, EMG, EEG, and ultrasound, with gesture counts ranging from 4 to 21. CA varies, with some studies achieving over 90%, such as [24], which attains 94.14% accuracy with the multimodal multilevel converged attention network (MMCANet). Wang et al. [44] employed vision and strain sensors, while we adopted vision and EMG. Both studies resulted in 100% CA. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that has employed VLM for intention detection using vision and EMG data. In our study, we utilized the Paligemma model, which has a lightweight architecture comprising approximately three billion parameters. With the rapid advancements in edge computing hardware, this model is well-suited for deployment on edge devices, enabling real-time capabilities crucial for effective rehabilitation applications. Currently, we have only deployed the EMG decoder to the extreme edge; however, we envision deploying the VLM to the extreme edge in future iterations. This extreme edge deployment could Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 08,2026 at 19:49:39 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. 22684 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 25, NO. 12, 15 JUNE 2025 facilitate low-latency, data privacy without relying on visual data acquisition, thereby significantly improving the practicality and effectiveness of these devices in both clinical and home settings. Furthermore, we observed that both the VLM deployment hardware and the quantization approach influenced the latency. Inference on the CPU took longer than 60 s, which exceeded the acceptable electromechanical delay for real-time exoskeleton control. In addition, pruning model parameters, extreme low-bit quantization, operation parallelism, and deploying the model to application-specific integrated circuits are potential approaches we recommend to optimize latency in future studies. Moreover, the image data utilized in our study lack temporal information, which is essential for capturing the dynamics of rehabilitation exercises. Therefore, we recommend improving the inference latency of the VLM and the integration of a video language model with low-latency capabilities at the edge to enhance performance and ensure a more responsive, effective, and reliable exoskeleton control. V.

## Conclusion
CONCLUSION The use of biosignals to control active rehabilitation devices presents significant challenges, primarily due to distribution shifts. This contributes to the reduced reliability of active rehabilitation devices, frequently leading to their abandonment. In response, we propose the integration of an off-the-shelf VLM for intention detection, object recognition, and pseudolabeling. This approach aims to enhance the performance of EMG decoders without necessitating domain-specific data acquisition. We have demonstrated the advantages of incorporating a VLM within the decoding pipeline, significantly improving system reliability in contexts where accuracy is paramount. Our findings underscore the importance of innovative methodologies in advancing the effectiveness of active rehabilitation technologies

These disturbances arise from anatomical variations, electrode shifts, and body artifacts, which can lead to poor on-device model accuracy and task limitations. Furthermore, when using EMG for active control of upper limb exoskeletons, the system often fails to account for false positives as a result of involuntary muscle contraction [20]. To address these issues, multimodal sensory fusion has been proposed as a viable solution [21]. EMG and EEG fusion has been proposed to enhance the decoding performance [20], [22], [23]. Moreover, the integration of ultrasound imaging with EMG data has been shown to improve gesture detection tasks [24]. Recently, Gionfrida et al. [25] argued for the necessity of incorporating visual capabilities in-loop to foster a more naturalistic development of wearable upper limb exoskeletons aimed at assisting individuals with neuromuscular dysfunction during ADL. While this approach appears promising, the collection and annotation of data specifically tailored to these tasks remain significant constraints [25]. In addressing the challenges associated with system reliability and user intent decoding, we propose the integration of a vision language model (VLM) within the gesture decoding pipeline. This approach aims to enhance the generation of pseudolabels, thereby mitigating false positives that may arise from involuntary muscle contractions. The use of pseudolabeling has been established in computer vision tasks, demonstrating its efficacy on various benchmarks [26], [27]. Recent advances have illustrated the application of VLMs in verifying ground truth [28], as well as in the generation of multiple pseudolabels [29]. In our study, we introduce a novel application of VLMs for pseudolabel generation, as depicted in Fig. 1, specifically targeting model degradation resulting from distribution shifts. This integration not only improves the overall performance of the system but also enhances the accuracy of user intent interpretation. VLM integrates the foundational principles of natural language processing and computer vision, enabling comprehension and generation of content that encompasses both visual and textual elements [30]. This innovative approach equips models to analyze images and videos while interpreting the corresponding text, thereby facilitating richer interactions and yielding more nuanced outputs across a variety of tasks [31]. VLMs have shown considerable success in applications such as image classification [32], object detection [28], and semantic segmentation [33], leveraging off-the-shelf models to achieve these outcomes. There is a notable scarcity of vision data tailored for rehabilitation purposes, as highlighted by previous studies [25], [34]. In response to this challenge, we propose an alternative by generating pseudolabels for verifying EMG-generated gestures. Although a large language model has been developed to control the upper limb exoskeleton [35], to the best of our knowledge, the integration of VLMs into the EMG decoding pipeline has yet to be explored. Our proposed gesture decoding pipeline, as illustrated in Fig. 1, aims to integrate vision and language capabilities into the decision-making loop, specifically targeting the challenges associated with involuntary muscle contractions and distribution shifts that frequently lead to false positives and model degradation. The visual input serves to identify the user intention to grasp or release, while the EMG signals provide crucial information on how to execute the grasp in a naturalistic manner. In addition, the VLM generates pseudolabels to verify the EMG ground truth. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to incorporate off-the-shelf VLMs with EMG decoders for intelligent control applications, thereby advancing the field of assistive rehabilitation. II. RELATED WORKS In the subsequent sections, we categorize the literature into two primary dimensions. While vision has been extensively validated in domains such as robotic control, embodied imitation learning, and general dexterous grasping, our emphasis is on the application of vision specifically within the context of control of orthotic and prosthetic devices. In Section II-B, we present studies that have successfully integrated visual Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Vision-Driven Upper Limb Control Kim et al. [36] proposed a vision-based approach for decoding grasp and release intentions, as opposed to relying on biological signals for orthotic device control. They contended that in the absence of sufficient residual EMG signals and due to the stochastic characteristics of EEG, vision sensors can effectively perceive intention for a twoand four-class hand function task. Building upon their earlier work, the authors introduced DEEPOSE-Net [34], which facilitates vision-based control of exoskeletons to assist stroke patients in engaging in ADL. DEEPOSE-Net infers three grasp intentions (grasp, release, and neutral) and five posture intentions (lateral pinch, tripod, thumb-2-finger, power sphere, and medium wrap) utilizing depth and RGB cameras. The performance of DEEPOSE-Net surpassed that of single-modal EMG and EEG modalities, as well as the combined EMG + EEG multimodal approach. A vision-based approach was implemented in [37] for object type detection, grasp type determination, and prosthetic device control. This study generated a synthetic dataset to enhance the competitive performance of hand functions. The GraspGF framework proposed in [38] utilized an adaptive policy approach to ascertain how and when to grasp an object within a scene, employing camera inputs for real-time decision-making. In addition, [39] introduced a reinforcement learning framework aimed at optimizing hand grasp functionality. B. Visual and Biological Signals’ Fusion for Exoskeleton Control A brain–robot interaction system leveraging both vision and EEG signals, named NOIR, was introduced in [8] to facilitate household tasks such as setting a dinner table. The decoding pipeline proposed by the authors determines what object to interact with using steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) in conjunction with visual input, how to interact with the object through motor imagery (MI), and where to interact using MI. Traditionally, brain–machine interactions have relied on the flickering of light-emitting diodes (LEDs) as stimuli to evoke neural responses. To eliminate the necessity of physically attaching LEDs to each object, the authors employed an off-the-shelf foundation model [40] to generate a segmentation mask that overlays all interactable objects. This mask flickers at different frequencies, enabling the stimulation of SSVEP based on the user’s attentional focus. In addition, the authors utilized DINOv2 [41] for adaptive learning of robot parameters. A follow-up study, NOIR 2.0 [42], adopted a pretrained VLM (GPT-4O, DINOv2) with preset prompts for state understanding, mapping, inference, and task retrieval. A novel cross-modal integration framework specifically designed for upper limb prostheses, which effectively combines sEMG signals with computer vision data to enhance gesture recognition capabilities, was proposed in [43]. A type2 fuzzy logic system integrates sEMG and visual information, enabling precise identification of grasp postures. This integration significantly enhances the dexterity and cognitive functionality of prosthetic devices. Moreover, the incorporation of transfer learning techniques further refines the decoding process of human intent, thereby alleviating the training burdens and improving classification accuracy (CA) compared to single modal EMG. Wang et al. [44] proposed a solution that fuses vision and strain sensor data for high-performance gesture decoding. The datasets employed in [34], [36], [37], [38], [39], and [44] were specifically curated for the purpose of exoskeleton control. However, a limitation of these datasets is the need to specially curate the dataset for domain specification and, hence, restriction to the specific gesture types captured during the data collection process. This narrow focus may hinder the generalization of the findings and their applicability to a broader range of gestures that users may wish to perform. Furthermore, many of these datasets are not openly accessible, posing additional challenges for both research advancement and commercial development. This lack of availability can significantly impede the progress of new methodologies and applications in the field, thereby underscoring the necessity for alternative approaches. Our study addresses these limitations by incorporating off-the-shelf VLMs with EMG decoders, thereby expanding the potential for diverse gesture recognition and intelligent control applications. III. PROPOSED APPROACH Our objective is to leverage off-the-shelf VLMs and integrate them into an intuitive feedback loop for EMG-based intention recognition, pseudo-ground-truth generation, and effective control of upper limb rehabilitation devices. We conceptualize our study by inferring user intentions to grasp, release, or maintain the hand in a neutral position, as discussed in Section III-A. In Section III-B, we discuss the EMG decoder, while, in Section III-C, we detail the visual pseudolabel algorithm. The EMG inference was done on an Nvidia Jetson Nano, while the inference for the VLM was performed on a desktop equipped with an AMD Ryzen 9 7900 processor and an Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 graphics card. A. VLM for User Intent Decoding Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in VLMs [31], leading to the release of several lightweight models suitable for various applications. In this study, we utilize the Paligemma model [13] due to its lightweight architecture, making it ideal for deployment on edge devices such as the Nvidia Jetson Orin series. The captioning objective and stagewise pretraining strategy of Paligemma ensure minimal data requirements for domain-specific fine-tuning. In addition, the Paligemma model incorporates the sigmoid loss for language-image pretraining (SligLib), a vision encoder with 40 million parameters [45], alongside the Gemma model, which features two billion parameters [46]. The objective function proposed in SligLip ensures semantic understanding compared to other similar VLMs. In active rehabilitation Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Thus, we made the decision to adopt the Paligemma VLM for our study. We conducted experiments with pretrained, mixed, and fine-tuned versions of the Paligemma model to evaluate its performance in our context. We employed a 224-pixel input size into the model, along with 128-token input text sequences. We fine-tuned the Paligemma model on the Flickr30k dataset [47], selected due to its inclusion of objects relevant to the evaluation of the Toronto Rehabilitation Institute Hand Function Test (TRI-HFT) and the Jebsen–Taylor Hand Function Test. No additional data were used to fine-tune the VLM model. To enhance the performance of both the vision encoder and the Gemma decoder within the Paligemma framework, we employed QLoRa [48] for fine-tuning. We developed a prompt designed to effectively detect user intentions related to grasping, releasing actions, or neutral states, which is illustrated in Fig. 2. The specifics of this prompt are detailed in Algorithm 1. In step 1, to infer user grasp intention, the prompts in Fig. 2 must return True in both questions. If questions 1 and 2 return False, the intention is classified as Neutral. In scenarios where question 1 is True and question 2 is also False, the user intention decoder determines that the action about to be performed is release. This step ensures the reliability of the decoding pipeline by avoiding involuntary action. B. EMG Decoder Previous studies have reported shallow neural networks with sufficient capacity can achieve optimal decoding performance [15] when trained with a large dataset comprising data from over 4000 participants. Building upon this foundational insight, our study employs an efficient Fourier analysis network (FAN) [49] for EMG-based gesture decoding. The architecture of the EMG-FAN follows the EMG-Net proposed in [20], with the primary modification being the replacement of fully connected (FC) layers with the FAN algorithm. The FAN layer represents a function using a Fourier series expansion by computing the sine and cosine components of the input, specifically sin(Wpx) and cos(Wpx). These components are then concatenated with the nonlinear activation of the affine transformation of the input, σ(Bq + Wqx), as defined in the following equation: ϕ(x) ≜[cos(Wpx), ||, sin(Wpx), ||, σ(Bq + Wqx)]. (1) The learnable weight parameters in this formulation are Wp ∈RCin×K for projecting the input, Wq ∈RCin×O for the linear transformation preceding activation, and Bq ∈RO for the bias term associated with Wq. Cin denotes the number of input channels. The dimensionalities K and O are defined as K = Cout × R and O = Cout −2K, where Cout is the number of output channels. R is a hyperparameter set to 0.25 in our study. To enhance the expressive power of FAN, the Gaussian error linear unit (GELU) activation function (σ) was employed for both the weight matrix Wq and the bias term Bq. The FAN algorithm, utilized as a nonlinearity layer, enables EMG-FAN to learn periodic structures effectively while capturing the frequency components of the input signal in a compact representation. In this study, we utilized the pretraining dataset [20] to conduct hyperparameter optimization on an EMG decoder model. The hyperparameters of both the EMG-FAN decoder and the training configuration were optimized to achieve the best accuracy on a test dataset derived from the first participant. In addition, all hyperparameter settings were kept consistent for comparative analysis of the EMG decoders. C. VLM for Pseudolabeling As detailed in Algorithm 1, the VLM takes input from a camera and utilizes predefined prompts in Fig. 2. The VLM generates outputs indicating True or False based on two critical questions: 1) is the hand strained or relaxed? and 2) is the hand sufficiently close to the object for successful grasping? The second criterion aligns with the methodology presented in [34]. If the hand is not visible in the image and the intention to grasp is indicated, the VLM will return False, even in the presence of involuntary muscle contractions and subsequent inferences from the EMG decoder. In instances where the hand is present in the image and the first condition returns True, the VLM is prompted with a follow-up question (Step 2), as depicted in Fig. 2. The VLM is tasked with identifying the object and determining the appropriate gesture from the EMG-based grasp gestures needed to complete the object grasp. A window size of 10 utilizing a majority voting mechanism was employed for EMG gesture prediction [50], [51]. The VLM’s inference latency averaged 60 ± 5 s on AMD Ryzen 9 7900 and improved to 25 ± 1 s using 4-bit quantized weight precision and 16-bit computation on GPU RTX 4090 to return pseudolabels. If the gesture decoded from the EMG aligns with the top two options provided by the pseudolabel, the grasp is grounded (Step 3), and the intent to grasp is used to control the upper limb exoskeleton. IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS A. EMG-Based Decoding Sussillo et al. [15] demonstrated that using a dataset comprising over 4000 participants can result in a model capable of generalizing effectively to new individuals. However, obtaining access to such a large dataset remains impractical for small-scale laboratories. To address this limitation, we utilized a publicly available EMG dataset from [20], selecting large diameter, medium diameter, three fingers, and prismatic pinch gestures. The choice of these gestures was also influenced by their ability to facilitate the TRI-HFT and Jebsen–Taylor Hand Function Tests. In addition, the sensor used for the EMG dataset acquisition in [20] is similar to the EMG sensor we employed for on-device inference evaluation, which informed our choice of dataset. Furthermore, the EMG dataset from [20] was only used for pretraining the EMG decoder. To validate the proposed decoding pipeline in Fig. 1, four new participants who provided informed consent prior to participation in the study were invited to participate in the inference stage. The study protocol was approved by the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology Institutional Review Board (20240215-HR-75-03-02). The participants had a mean age of 28 ± 3.8 years and were right-handed, with no previous clinically diagnosed neurological problems (that Fig. 3. Average accuracy of the EMG-FAN model across 33 participants used to pretrain the model. could affect upper limbs). Participants were novices to the BCI experiment, and no part of the participants was included in the pretraining dataset [20]. The participants were positioned in front of a screen running custom-developed supervised software [20], which randomly presented a series of four gestures. Each participant was shown one gesture at random, followed by asking them to replicate it. Each gesture was displayed for ten trials, with each trial followed by a brief rest period of 3 s. According to [15], a fine-tuned model with 20 min of data is equivalent to training on a model with 14 000 min of data. This assertion from the study highlights personalized approaches to fine-tuning as a potential solution when dealing with distribution shifts. We employed two fine-tuning approaches: Full-Train, which involves fine-tuning all the layers, and LastLayer, which involves fine-tuning only the last layer [52]. For each model, we utilized five trials from the inference stage for fine-tuning, with the remaining data reserved for evaluation. The offline and inference data were preprocessed using a notch filter at 60 Hz with a bandpass range between 5.0 and 99.0 Hz. Offline pretraining EMG data evaluation involved random splitting of the dataset, allocating 80% for training and 20% for evaluation. A window size of 200 ms with a 60% overlap was used consistently during the offline stage. This choice of window size was made to ensure an electromechanical delay of less than 300 ms, which aligns with findings from studies that have proposed similar window sizes [53], [54], [55] CLER =  1 −Number of correct predictions Total number of true events  × 100 (2) Classification Accuracy (CA) = 100 −CLER. Discussion Active rehabilitation devices designed to assist individuals with ALS, SCI, and stroke in performing ADLs often face significant reliability issues, contributing to a high abandonment rate. The challenges posed by low SNR in EEG and the limited generalization capabilities of EMG decoders remain unresolved, hindering the acceptance of biosignal-controlled rehabilitation devices [25]. To address these challenges, we propose the fusion of vision data to enhance the reliability of the EMG decoder. While previous studies have explored vision-based approaches to mitigate these issues, our work introduces a novel gesture decoding pipeline that employs an off-the-shelf VLM without the need for pretraining or finetuning, as demonstrated in Table II. Recent studies utilizing vision approaches rely heavily on extensive data acquisition methods, which may not be feasible for smaller laboratories or industrial applications. Therefore, our proposed pipeline integrating a VLM aims to democratize the development of reliable biosignal-controlled active rehabilitation devices. CA varies, with some studies achieving over 90%, such as [24], which attains 94.14% accuracy with the multimodal multilevel converged attention network (MMCANet). Wang et al. [44] employed vision and strain sensors, while we adopted vision and EMG. Both studies resulted in 100% CA. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that has employed VLM for intention detection using vision and EMG data. In our study, we utilized the Paligemma model, which has a lightweight architecture comprising approximately three billion parameters. With the rapid advancements in edge computing hardware, this model is well-suited for deployment on edge devices, enabling real-time capabilities crucial for effective rehabilitation applications. Currently, we have only deployed the EMG decoder to the extreme edge; however, we envision deploying the VLM to the extreme edge in future iterations. This extreme edge deployment could Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 08,2026 at 19:49:39 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. 22684 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 25, NO. 12, 15 JUNE 2025 facilitate low-latency, data privacy without relying on visual data acquisition, thereby significantly improving the practicality and effectiveness of these devices in both clinical and home settings. Furthermore, we observed that both the VLM deployment hardware and the quantization approach influenced the latency. Inference on the CPU took longer than 60 s, which exceeded the acceptable electromechanical delay for real-time exoskeleton control. In addition, pruning model parameters, extreme low-bit quantization, operation parallelism, and deploying the model to application-specific integrated circuits are potential approaches we recommend to optimize latency in future studies. Moreover, the image data utilized in our study lack temporal information, which is essential for capturing the dynamics of rehabilitation exercises. Therefore, we recommend improving the inference latency of the VLM and the integration of a video language model with low-latency capabilities at the edge to enhance performance and ensure a more responsive, effective, and reliable exoskeleton control. V. CONCLUSION The use of biosignals to control active rehabilitation devices presents significant challenges, primarily due to distribution shifts. This contributes to the reduced reliability of active rehabilitation devices, frequently leading to their abandonment. In response, we propose the integration of an off-the-shelf VLM for intention detection, object recognition, and pseudolabeling. This approach aims to enhance the performance of EMG decoders without necessitating domain-specific data acquisition. We have demonstrated the advantages of incorporating a VLM within the decoding pipeline, significantly improving system reliability in contexts where accuracy is paramount. Our findings underscore the importance of innovative methodologies in advancing the effectiveness of active rehabilitation technologies

## Abstract
Abstract. This study explores the intersection of electroencephalography (EEG) microstates and Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance the assessment of cognitive load states. By utilizing EEG microstate features, the research aims to fine-tune LLMs for improved predictions of distinct cognitive states, specifically ’Rest’ and ’Load’. The experimental design is delineated in four comprehensive stages: dataset collection and preprocessing, microstate segmentation and EEG backfitting, feature extraction paired with prompt engineering, and meticulous LLM model selection and refinement. Employing a supervised learning paradigm, the LLM is trained to identify cognitive load states based on EEG microstate features integrated into prompts, producing accurate discrimination of cognitive load. A curated dataset, linking EEG features to specified cognitive load conditions, underpins the experimental framework. The results indicate a significant improvement in model performance following the proposed fine-tuning, showcasing the potential of EEG-informed LLMs in cognitive neuroscience and cognitive AI applications. This approach not only contributes to the understanding of brain dynamics but also paves the way for advancements in machine learning techniques applicable to cognitive load and cognitive AI research. Keywords: EEG Microstates · Cognitive Load · Large Language Models (LLMs) · Fine-tuning · Supervised Learning 1

## Introduction
Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP) by demonstrating remarkable capabilities across various tasks. These models, which are typically based on transformer architectures and trained on large amounts of data, have shown significant improvements in performance as their size increases. LLMs exhibit some cognitive abilities similar to humans, ⋆Supported by: School of Computer Science, Technological University Dublin arXiv:2508.07283v1 [cs.HC] 10 Aug 2025 2 B. Raufi. particularly in formal linguistic tasks and certain reasoning scenarios[30, 11, 15]. However, they fail in more complex cognitive tasks requiring deeper understanding and planning. While advanced LLM models like GPT-4 or Llama 3.2 show improvements, significant differences remain between LLMs and human cognitive systems[21, 5]. A promising avenue for enhancing the cognitive capabilities of AI systems lies in integrating biological data that reflect the underlying cognitive processes. Among the various neurophysiological measures, electroencephalography (EEG) microstates have emerged as significant markers of cognitive function. EEG microstates represent transient, patterned, quasi-stable states of EEG brain activity. These quasi-stable brain activities in a range of milliseconds are thought to reflect the temporal dynamics of neural processing involved in perception, attention, and information integration, thus often nicknamed the "atoms of thought" [7]. EEG microstates have been associated with specific cognitive processes. Changes in microstate parameters (duration, occurrence, and coverage) are influenced by cognitive tasks, indicating their role in cognitive processing [2, 14, 22]. EEG microstates correlate with resting-state networks identified by fMRI, suggesting that they reflect the activity of large-scale brain networks [13, 6, 10]. The temporal dynamics of EEG microstates are altered in various cognitive and mental states, including neurological and psychiatric conditions, indicating their significance in cognitive processes [13, 6, 26]. EEG microstates are influenced by mental workload and task types, with different tasks affecting the parameters and topographies of these microstates in varied ways. Specific microstates are sensitive to cognitive manipulations, such as attention tasks and visual input, further supporting their role in cognitive functions [22]. The microstates of the EEG change during altered states of consciousness, such as sleep, anaesthesia, and meditation, suggesting their involvement in the underlying characteristics of self-consciousness [1]. Alterations in EEG microstate dynamics are observed in conditions such as mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer’s disease, indicating their potential as biomarkers for cognitive impairment [10]. Differences in microstate parameters are also found in children and adolescents with autism spectrum development, reflecting the atypical activity of the resting state network [25]. In general, EEG microstates play a significant role in cognitive processes, reflecting the functional state of the brain and its large-scale network dynamics. They are influenced by cognitive tasks, mental workload, and altered states of consciousness and show potential as biomarkers of cognitive impairments and developmental conditions. The study of EEG microstates provides valuable information on the temporal dynamics of brain activity and their association with various cognitive functions. This paper provides a detailed experiment design on how a potential finetuning of LLMs with EEG microstates can be utilized to asses two distinct cognitive load states ("Rest" and "Load"). The experiment design offers sufficient details to allow valid reproducibility. Furthermore, the experiment opens Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length 3 an exciting path to LLM contextualization through fine-tuning with cognitive data reflecting the underlying brain cognitive activities. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: section 2 provides an overview of LLMs and their applications in cognitive tasks and discusses the research on EEG microstates and their relationship to cognitive processes as well as tackles the concept of fine-tuning LLMs and its potential benefits. Section 3 provides an experiment design of fine-tuning LLMs with EEG microstates. Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines the future work. 2 Related Work Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools in natural language processing, demonstrating capabilities that extend beyond their initial design of predicting the next word in a sequence. These models, such as GPT-4 and others, have shown remarkable performance in various cognitive tasks, often paralleling human-like reasoning and problem-solving abilities [21, 17, 19]. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown cognitive abilities that extend beyond their initial training objectives. These capabilities include complex reasoning, problem-solving, and decision-making tasks, which are typically associated with human cognition [17, 29]. For example, LLMs have been utilized to model human decision-making processes, such as risky and intertemporal choices, by employing computationally equivalent tasks [29]. Moreover, LLMs can perform zero-shot reasoning, meaning they can solve tasks without having received specific prior examples, indicating a broad cognitive capacity [8]. Increasingly, researchers in cognitive psychology are leveraging LLMs to investigate the mechanisms underlying intelligence and reasoning. They have been applied to various tasks, including arithmetic, symbolic reasoning, and logical reasoning, often achieving performance levels comparable to human benchmarks [21, 8]. Moreover, LLMs are used to study cognitive biases in decision-making, providing insights into human-like biases and offering frameworks to mitigate these biases in high-stakes scenarios [4]. Despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs face challenges in specific cognitive tasks. For example, they struggle with planning and understanding complex relational structures, known as cognitive maps, which are essential for goal-directed behaviour. These limitations highlight the need for systematic

## Methodology

Due to the limited number of subjects from which the microstate features were extracted (a total of 103), data synthesis is employed to augment the number of training samples. For this purpose, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) was utilised to enhance the training samples. To verify the quality of the synthesised training set, a synthetic quality score was employed to evaluate the goodness of the generated data. Adopting a weighted approach, the Synthetic Data Quality Score is determined by integrating individual quality metrics such as Field Distribution Stability, Field Correlation Stability, and Deep Structure Stability. This score serves as an estimate of the degree to which the synthetic data preserves the statistical properties of the original dataset [20]. Field Distribution Stability measures how closely the synthetic data distributions match the original data. It uses the Jensen-Shannon Distance to compare numeric or categorical fields. A lower average JS Distance score across fields indicates higher Field Distribution Stability quality. The Field Correlation Stability is calculated by first computing the correlation between each pair of fields in the training data, followed by the synthetic data. The absolute difference between these values is then computed and averaged across all fields. A lower average value indicates a higher quality score for Field Correlation Stability. The deep 6 B. Raufi. structure stability is a metric calculated by comparing the distributional distance between the principal components found in the original and synthetic datasets. Gretel AI is used to generate the synthetic training data 3. 3.2 EEG Microstate segmentation and backfitting A brain microstate is defined by a coordinate vector representing a point at a unit distance from the origin. Any point along the line extending from the origin to this microstate belongs to the same microstate, meaning all such points share a uniquely normalized scalp electric potential field (strictly unique only when an infinite number of electrodes is considered). Consequently, as long as a trajectory remains along this line, the brain remains in the same microstate. The distance from the origin to a point on this line corresponds to the neuronal generators’ intensity (or strength) associated with the microstate [18]. This distance is also directly proportional to the global field power (GFP’) given as: GFP(t) = v u u t 1 N n X i=1 (Vi(t) −V (t))2 (1) where, Vi(t) represents the electric potential of an electrode i at time t, V (t) is the mean potential across all N electrodes at time t, and N represents the number of electrodes. The equation 1 reflects the instantaneous standard deviation of scalp potential measurements. There is an ongoing debate in the research community whether the microstate identification should focus on GFPs or adopt a wider approach by omitting the GFP and capturing broader brain dynamics [23]. The experiment adopted here followed a well-established methodology outlined by Lehman [9] and is a two-step process. 1. In the first step, microstate identification is performed, whereby EEG data is partitioned into clusters using the modified K-means (mod K-means) clustering algorithm. This process involves identifying distinct topographies of electric potentials that remain stable for short periods [18]. These topographies, often termed archetypes, represent the topography of specific classes and are associated with various cognitive processes such as verbal, visual, and attention-related activities [14, 13]. 2. In the second step, the identified microstate archetypes are reinserted into the EEG dataset by substituting the EEG data at each time point with the microstate label that most closely aligns with the EEG topography at that moment[9]. This close alignment is quantified Global Explained Variance (GEV) given as: GEV = Pmax t=1 (GFPu(t) · Cu,Tt)2 · γu,k,t Pmax t=1 GFP 2u(t) (2) 3 Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length 7 where Cu,Tt is the spatial correlation between data of a certain condition U at time point t, and the respected microstate archetype and the GFPu(t) is the Global Field Power of EEG signal at the given time t. The mapping function γu,k,t represents the data that have been labelled (L) as belonging to the kth segment on EEG signal and is given as: γu,k,t = ( 1 if k = Lu,t 0 if k ̸= Lu,t 3.3 Feature Extraction and Prompt Engineering From the back-fitted EEG microstates, five features are extracted. These features are well-established in microstate research and specifically relate to modalities of thinking. – Global Explained Variance (gev): This feature represents the total explained variance expressed by a given state. It is computed as the sum of the global explained variance values of each time point assigned to a given state. Given as a percentage between 0.0 −1.0. – Mean correlation (mean_corr) corresponds to the mean correlation value of each time point assigned to a given state. Given as a percentage between 0.0 −1.0 – Time coverage (timecov) is the proportion of time during which a given state is active. Given in seconds (s, ms) – Mean durations (meandurs) relates to the mean temporal duration of segments assigned to a given state. Given in seconds or milliseconds. – Occurrence per seconds (occurence): indicates the mean number of segments assigned to a given state per second. This metric is expressed in segments per second and is given in Hertz (Hz). The subsequent step involves crafting the prompts for training the large language model (LLM). This prompt engineering adopts a prompt learning strategy, which utilizes unsupervised prompt learning for classification alongside blackbox LLMs. Here, prompts are represented as sequences of discrete tokens featuring learnable categorical distributions. This method takes advantage of the in-context learning abilities of LLMs and integrates pseudo-labeled data as incontext examples throughout the training process [28]. In our case, the learnable categorical distributions are the features embedded within the designed prompts. Finally, the target class represents two distinct prompts outlining the two cognitive load states, the "Rest" state and the "Load" state. 3.4 LLM Model Selection & Fine-Tuning This study utilizes a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuned on a dataset consisting of prompts of EEG microstates as mentioned in subsection 3.3. Model selection criteria focused on the following considerations: 8 B. Raufi. – Models free access, openness and usage. – LLMs that demonstrate strong performance in complex reasoning and sequential data processing, mirroring the structured nature of thought processes related to cognitive load on arithmetic task setting. – LLM models that excel in tasks like logical reasoning, given their conceptual alignment with arithmetic problem-solving. – Architectural compatibility with EEG data, publicly available checkpoints, and established fine-tuning procedures essential for reproducibility and comparability with future research. – Model’s pre-training data and size to ensure relevance and computational feasibility within the study’s scope. The selected LLM undergoes fine-tuning using a curated dataset linking EEG microstate features to corresponding classes of cognitive load states. This dataset encompasses diverse microstate classes across the cognitive state levels to promote generalizability and robustness. We employ a supervised learning approach, training the LLM to predict the cognitive load state based on prompts, including the EEG microstate feature, to produce a response outlining the cognitive load states. The fine-tuning process will optimize model parameters to minimize a suitable loss function, potentially combining cross-entropy loss for solution steps with a distance-based metric for EEG microstate features. Various fine-tuning strategies, including prompt engineering and parameter-efficient methods, will be explored to balance performance gains with computational resource constraints. 4 Results 4.1 Dataset Preprocessing The dataset comprises EEG recordings collected from 103 subjects across two sources, as detailed in Section 3.1. EEG microstates are brief, 60 to 120 milliseconds long time periods during which the brain’s electrical activity remains quasi-stable, reflecting the global functional state of the brain. These microstates are thought to represent the basic building blocks of spontaneous conscious mental processes and are associated with large-scale brain networks [13, 29]. Typically, four microstate classes (A, B, C, and D) are identified, each associated with different cognitive functions and brain networks [14, 22, 13]. Research has shown that EEG microstates are linked to various cognitive processes. For instance, microstate A is often associated with verbal and phonological processing, while microstate B is linked to visual pro4 B. Raufi. cessing [14, 3]. Microstate C is related to the default mode network and cognitive control systems, and microstate D is associated with attention reorientation and the dorsal attention network [22, 1, 27]. Studies seem to indicate that cognitive tasks can alter the spatial and temporal properties of EEG microstates. For example, during tasks requiring attention, such as serial subtraction, the duration and occurrence of microstate D increase, reflecting its association with the dorsal attention network [22]. Similarly, visual tasks can increase the occurrence and coverage of microstate B, highlighting its connection to the visual system [22, 3]. EEG microstates have also been used to study cognitive impairments, such as mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Alterations in microstate dynamics, such as increased duration and coverage of specific microstates, have been observed in these conditions, suggesting changes in brain network functionality [10, 12, 16]. For instance, microstate A, linked to the temporal lobes, shows increased occurrence in MCI and AD, which may reflect early pathological changes in these regions [16]. Fine-tuning plays an essential role in customizing large language models (LLMs) for specific tasks or domains by modifying the model’s parameters using a smaller, dedicated dataset. This method improves the model’s effectiveness on specific tasks without requiring the development of an entirely new model. The advantages of fine-tuning include enhanced task performance, increased data efficiency, better domain adaptation, optimized resource use, and greater generalization and versatility. Large Language Models (LLMs) represent a breakthrough in modelling cognitive tasks, offering insights into human-like reasoning and decision-making. While promising for various applications, ongoing research is essential to address their limitations in AI and cognitive science. EEG microstates provide insights into brain network dynamics linked to cognitive processes. This non-invasive method studies typical cognitive functions and atypical neurological conditions. More research is necessary to understand the relationship between microstates and cognition and their potential applications in AI. Fine-tuning LLMs is one direction and yields many benefits, including enhanced task performance, better data use, and tailored applications, improving their effectiveness across fields. Optimizing resource use and generalization abilities makes LLMs more flexible and efficient for diverse applications. 3 Experiment Design The proposed experiment design is outlined in four stages: dataset collection and preprocessing, microstate segmentation and EEG backfitting, feature extraction and prompt engineering and LLM model selection and fine-tuning. ## Conclusion
Conclusion and Future Work This paper has addressed the issue of LLM fine-tuning with brain thought processes such as EEG microstates during mental arithmetic tasks. The research contributes to the field of cognitive load studies by introducing the fine-tuning of LLM models with EEG microstate features for detecting cognitive load conditions, including ’Rest’ and ’Load’ states. It provides a comprehensive and reproducible experimental setup for LLM fine-tuning with EEG microstate data, creating a highly contextualised LLM model. The results demonstrate exceptionally high model performance compared to the same model prior to the proposed fine-tuning. The model’s capability to detect cognitive load states increases by approximately 24 times. The direct implications of the study indicate that EEG microstate data can be effectively employed to differentiate between cognitive load conditions. The indirect implications, which necessitate further intrinsic analysis of microstates, suggest that these findings could underpin advancements in our understanding of cognition within the context of AI as a whole and provide a solid foundation for future exploration in the realm of Cognitive AI. Future opportunities for further research that could advance the initial finding outlined in this research are: – Exploring and comparing the capabilities of other Large Language Models that excel in cognitive tasks, such as Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude, and OpenAI’s GPT. – Designing specialised LLM models that are contextualised for specific cognitive tasks can be implemented in various intelligent agents. For instance, inputting EEG microstate data from a user during particular decision-making tasks, where high alertness or vigilance is necessary (such as driving and operating heavy vehicles) into an LLM model for fine-tuning and assessing the model’s decision-making capabilities regarding these decisions. – Further experiments with different parameters or datasets could enhance the robustness of the findings. We are excited to see how subsequent studies can build upon and extend our work. Data & Code Statement: The data and the code used in this experiment are available at: upon request from the author. The prompt dataset used in the study is public and available on Huggingface ( promts)

Gretel AI is used to generate the synthetic training data 3. 3.2 EEG Microstate segmentation and backfitting A brain microstate is defined by a coordinate vector representing a point at a unit distance from the origin. Any point along the line extending from the origin to this microstate belongs to the same microstate, meaning all such points share a uniquely normalized scalp electric potential field (strictly unique only when an infinite number of electrodes is considered). Consequently, as long as a trajectory remains along this line, the brain remains in the same microstate. The distance from the origin to a point on this line corresponds to the neuronal generators’ intensity (or strength) associated with the microstate [18]. This distance is also directly proportional to the global field power (GFP’) given as: GFP(t) = v u u t 1 N n X i=1 (Vi(t) −V (t))2 (1) where, Vi(t) represents the electric potential of an electrode i at time t, V (t) is the mean potential across all N electrodes at time t, and N represents the number of electrodes. The equation 1 reflects the instantaneous standard deviation of scalp potential measurements. There is an ongoing debate in the research community whether the microstate identification should focus on GFPs or adopt a wider approach by omitting the GFP and capturing broader brain dynamics [23]. The experiment adopted here followed a well-established methodology outlined by Lehman [9] and is a two-step process. 1. In the first step, microstate identification is performed, whereby EEG data is partitioned into clusters using the modified K-means (mod K-means) clustering algorithm. This process involves identifying distinct topographies of electric potentials that remain stable for short periods [18]. These topographies, often termed archetypes, represent the topography of specific classes and are associated with various cognitive processes such as verbal, visual, and attention-related activities [14, 13]. 2. In the second step, the identified microstate archetypes are reinserted into the EEG dataset by substituting the EEG data at each time point with the microstate label that most closely aligns with the EEG topography at that moment[9]. This close alignment is quantified Global Explained Variance (GEV) given as: GEV = Pmax t=1 (GFPu(t) · Cu,Tt)2 · γu,k,t Pmax t=1 GFP 2u(t) (2) 3 Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length 7 where Cu,Tt is the spatial correlation between data of a certain condition U at time point t, and the respected microstate archetype and the GFPu(t) is the Global Field Power of EEG signal at the given time t. The mapping function γu,k,t represents the data that have been labelled (L) as belonging to the kth segment on EEG signal and is given as: γu,k,t = ( 1 if k = Lu,t 0 if k ̸= Lu,t 3.3 Feature Extraction and Prompt Engineering From the back-fitted EEG microstates, five features are extracted. These features are well-established in microstate research and specifically relate to modalities of thinking. – Global Explained Variance (gev): This feature represents the total explained variance expressed by a given state. It is computed as the sum of the global explained variance values of each time point assigned to a given state. Given as a percentage between 0.0 −1.0. – Mean correlation (mean_corr) corresponds to the mean correlation value of each time point assigned to a given state. Given as a percentage between 0.0 −1.0 – Time coverage (timecov) is the proportion of time during which a given state is active. Given in seconds (s, ms) – Mean durations (meandurs) relates to the mean temporal duration of segments assigned to a given state. Given in seconds or milliseconds. – Occurrence per seconds (occurence): indicates the mean number of segments assigned to a given state per second. This metric is expressed in segments per second and is given in Hertz (Hz). The subsequent step involves crafting the prompts for training the large language model (LLM). This prompt engineering adopts a prompt learning strategy, which utilizes unsupervised prompt learning for classification alongside blackbox LLMs. Here, prompts are represented as sequences of discrete tokens featuring learnable categorical distributions. This method takes advantage of the in-context learning abilities of LLMs and integrates pseudo-labeled data as incontext examples throughout the training process [28]. In our case, the learnable categorical distributions are the features embedded within the designed prompts. Finally, the target class represents two distinct prompts outlining the two cognitive load states, the "Rest" state and the "Load" state. 3.4 LLM Model Selection & Fine-Tuning This study utilizes a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuned on a dataset consisting of prompts of EEG microstates as mentioned in subsection 3.3. Model selection criteria focused on the following considerations: 8 B. Raufi. – Models free access, openness and usage. – LLMs that demonstrate strong performance in complex reasoning and sequential data processing, mirroring the structured nature of thought processes related to cognitive load on arithmetic task setting. – LLM models that excel in tasks like logical reasoning, given their conceptual alignment with arithmetic problem-solving. – Architectural compatibility with EEG data, publicly available checkpoints, and established fine-tuning procedures essential for reproducibility and comparability with future research. – Model’s pre-training data and size to ensure relevance and computational feasibility within the study’s scope. The selected LLM undergoes fine-tuning using a curated dataset linking EEG microstate features to corresponding classes of cognitive load states. This dataset encompasses diverse microstate classes across the cognitive state levels to promote generalizability and robustness. We employ a supervised learning approach, training the LLM to predict the cognitive load state based on prompts, including the EEG microstate feature, to produce a response outlining the cognitive load states. The fine-tuning process will optimize model parameters to minimize a suitable loss function, potentially combining cross-entropy loss for solution steps with a distance-based metric for EEG microstate features. Various fine-tuning strategies, including prompt engineering and parameter-efficient methods, will be explored to balance performance gains with computational resource constraints. 4 Results 4.1 Dataset Preprocessing The dataset comprises EEG recordings collected from 103 subjects across two sources, as detailed in Section 3.1. The first dataset (Dataset 1), provided by Zyma et al. [31], includes discrete EEG segments of 180 seconds for the resting state and 60 seconds for mental counting. The research contributes to the field of cognitive load studies by introducing the fine-tuning of LLM models with EEG microstate features for detecting cognitive load conditions, including ’Rest’ and ’Load’ states. It provides a comprehensive and reproducible experimental setup for LLM fine-tuning with EEG microstate data, creating a highly contextualised LLM model. The results demonstrate exceptionally high model performance compared to the same model prior to the proposed fine-tuning. The model’s capability to detect cognitive load states increases by approximately 24 times. The direct implications of the study indicate that EEG microstate data can be effectively employed to differentiate between cognitive load conditions. The indirect implications, which necessitate further intrinsic analysis of microstates, suggest that these findings could underpin advancements in our understanding of cognition within the context of AI as a whole and provide a solid foundation for future exploration in the realm of Cognitive AI. Future opportunities for further research that could advance the initial finding outlined in this research are: – Exploring and comparing the capabilities of other Large Language Models that excel in cognitive tasks, such as Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude, and OpenAI’s GPT. – Designing specialised LLM models that are contextualised for specific cognitive tasks can be implemented in various intelligent agents. For instance, inputting EEG microstate data from a user during particular decision-making tasks, where high alertness or vigilance is necessary (such as driving and operating heavy vehicles) into an LLM model for fine-tuning and assessing the model’s decision-making capabilities regarding these decisions. – Further experiments with different parameters or datasets could enhance the robustness of the findings. We are excited to see how subsequent studies can build upon and extend our work. Data & Code Statement: The data and the code used in this experiment are available at: upon request from the author. ## Abstract
Abstract—This article introduces dual-view foundation model (FM), a generative pretrained FM specifically designed for forecasting human inertial signals from body-worn sensors. Unlike traditional transformer-based approaches, dualview FM employs a novel architecture that mixes global and local signal properties in the time and feature domains to build a comprehensive understanding of inertial activity data. The global view identifies general trends in human inertial signals, while the local view addresses their spontaneous nature by individually analyzing short, sensor-specific signal frames. Our

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION H UMAN activity recognition (HAR) is the process of identifying human actions and behavior using data collected from a variety of sensors, including vision sensors (e.g., cameras), environmental sensors (e.g., pressure or particulate matter sensors), wearable inertial sensors (e.g., accelerometers or gyroscopes), and others [1]. Among these modalities, inertial sensors embedded in wearable devices such as smartphones and smartwatches have become particularly popular for HAR (cf. [2], [3], [4]), thanks to their unobtrusiveness, affordability, and effectiveness in continuous on-body monitoring under real-world conditions. Many publications have devoted lots of attention to activity classification (e.g., [5], [6], [7]), however, more and more current use cases afford forecasting features for human activities. For instance, forecast signals can act as proxies for actual inertial data in activity classification tasks (e.g., [8]) or facilitate the identification of anomalies within collected Received 12 June 2025; revised 30 July 2025; accepted 24 August 2025. Date of publication 3 September 2025; date of current version 2 October 2025. The associate editor coordinating the review of this article and approving it for publication was Dr. Yuchen Jiang. (Corresponding author: Christoph Wieland.) Christoph Wieland is with Bosch Sensortec GmbH, 72770 Reutlingen, Germany (e-mail: Victor Pankratius is with Robert Bosch GmbH, 70839 Stuttgart-Feuerbach, Germany (e-mail: Digital Object Identifier 10.1109/JSEN.2025.3603456 signals (e.g., [9]). Despite advances in model design and deployment, wearable-based HAR still faces challenges in generalizing across users, activities, and sensor placements. Moreover, collecting labeled training data is time-consuming, which motivates the exploration of alternative approaches that reduce data dependence. Foundation models (FMs) [10] are large neural networks that are pretrained on diverse, unlabeled datasets to perform various tasks across multiple domains. So far, however, there has been only little research on FMs for wearable HAR. Inspired by the great success of FMs in language processing (e.g., [11], [12]), this article introduces dual-view FM, a context-aware FM for the forecasting of multivariate human inertial signals. Dual-view FM combines local and global signal properties in time and feature space to gain a deep understanding of human inertial signals. This allows dual-view FM to accurately generate inertial sensor signals from various activities, users, and sensing setups. Dual-view FM learns this ability by analyzing a diverse corpus that consolidates inertial signals from eight publicly available datasets with the help of two self-supervised pretraining objectives. In contrast to recent FMs for time series forecasting [13], [14], [15] that consider time series from multiple domains, such as finance or weather, dual-view FM focuses on a domain-specific task: deriving general knowledge about human inertial signals from the numerous openly available datasets. This cross-dataset task is complex because different

## Methodology
approach offers greater flexibility than multilocation models, as it does not require a predefined arrangement of sensors and thus, simplifies the merging of signals from different sources. V. EVALUATION—SETUP To handle large, unlabeled datasets, FMs are usually pretrained in a self-supervised fashion. This section gives an overview of different pretraining objectives (Section V-A) and model configurations (Section V-B) for dual-view FM’s selfsupervised pretraining. Furthermore, it presents the training loss and evaluation metrics (Section V-C), and the training environment (Section V-D) for the subsequent evaluation of dual-view FM (Sections VI and VII). A. Pretraining Objectives We leverage masked signal modeling (MSM) and causal signal modeling (CSM) for the self-supervised pretraining of dual-view FM (Fig. 8). Both pretraining objectives partially mask input signals and learn to reconstruct the masked time steps but differ in their masking strategies. MSM [Fig. 8(a)] randomly nullifies sensor readings at nmask time steps and trains the model to reconstruct the unmasked 36848 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 25, NO. 19, 1 OCTOBER 2025 TABLE II MODEL PARAMETERS OF DUAL-VIEW FM FOR THE TWO PRETRAINING OBJECTIVES MSM AND CSM signals using the reconstruction head [cf. Fig. 6(a)]. During pretraining, each mini-batch generates a new random mask and applies it to all its samples. MSM learns embeddings that capture the general context of the signals. CSM [Fig. 8(b)] masks the last nmask time steps of an input sequence with zeros and trains the model to forecast the masked time steps using the forecasting head [cf. Fig. 6(b)]. CSM learns temporal dependencies from past signal features without knowing future time steps. MSM is similar to masked language modeling [12], where nmask input tokens are arbitrarily masked with placeholder tokens. CSM resembles causal language modeling [11], [41] that predicts the next token in a token sequence. B. Model Configuration We evaluate dual-view FM with the architectural parameters from Table II. These configurations result in similar-sized dual-view FMs for both pretraining objectives: the CSM models have 4 54 615 trainable weights with and about 7.86 MMACs (millions of multiply–accumulate operations); the MSM models have 4 51 673 weights and 8.16 MMACs. The number of dual-view blocks in the heads (Nobjective) differs between MSM and CSM. For MSM, we use only one dual-view block in the reconstruction head that returns the output shape (w, f ). For CSM, we use a forecasting head with three dual-view blocks where each one reduces its input length by half. This results in the CSM output shape (nmask, f ). nmask = 16 corresponds to 12.5 % of the input length w = 128. All dual-view blocks bi in the bases and heads follow the same rule for their latent dimension hi: hi = 2wi−1, where wi−1 is the output length of the previous block bi−1 and w0 = w. Thus, the blocks in the base and the reconstruction head have hi = 2w = 256, while each bi in the forecasting head reduces hi−1 by half. This configuration ensures that MSM and CSM models have similar number of trainable weights. Local time mixing splits signals in st = 4 equally sized temporal splits. This number ensures that even the last dual-view block in the forecasting head considers an adequate split size of nmask/st = 4 time steps. Local feature mixing learns sensor-specific features by splitting the feature dimension in three-axis acceleration and three-axis angular velocity (s f = 2). To improve dual-view FM’s generalizability and to avoid overfitting, we apply dropout (0.2), layer normalization [42] (ε = 0.001), and L2 regularization (l2 = 0.01) to all dual-view blocks in the base. We omit these regularization techniques in the heads to prevent them from deriving distorted signals. C. Loss Function and Evaluation Metrics We join the cosine distance CD and the mean absolute error (MAE) in the following loss function (lower values are better): MAE/CD-Loss y, ˆy  = 0.5 MAE y, ˆy  + 0.5 CD y, ˆy  (1) where y and ˆy are the actual and the predicted values. MAE ∈[0, ∞) measures the magnitude of the error between y and ˆy (lower values are better). CD ∈[0, 2] measures the similarity of y and ˆy based on their shape (lower values are better). MAE and CD are equally important for the forecasting or reconstruction of signals and are therefore equally weighted. We evaluate the models in terms of MAE and root-meansquare error RMSE ∈[0, ∞] (lower values are better). D. Training Environment We train all models on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. Furthermore, we set the PYTHONHASHSEED environment variable to 0 to obtain reproducible result [43]. VI. EVALUATION—PRETRAINING Self-supervised pretraining is an important concept of FMs. To evaluate the pretraining performance of Dual-View FM in a cross-dataset setup, we leverage the pretraining configuration and data splits from Sections VI-A and VI-B. Sections VI-C and VI-D evaluate dual-view FM’s generalizability when using CSM and MSM pretraining objectives with and without location awareness. Section VI-E analyzes the impact of pretraining sets with increasing data volumes on the model. A. Pretraining Setup We pretrain dual-view FM using the Adam optimizer [44] with learning rate 1e−3 for up to 500 epochs and early stopping with patience 10. The batch size is set to 256. To account for statistical fluctuations, we repeat each pretraining three times with varying random seeds ∈{1, 2, 3}. B. Pretraining Data Split We pretrain dual-view FM with a leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) approach that enables us to assess its cross-dataset generalizability (Fig. 9). We take seven datasets from Table I for pretraining and one for testing. Since each dataset was collected by a different research group, they leverage sensors from different manufacturers and collect signals from different activities, users, and locations. We randomly split the signals in the seven training sets into 80 % train and 20 % validation data. We ensure that both training and validation sets contain signals from all locations and activities so that dual-view FM learns from a broad context. TimeGPT-1’s authors claim the production-readiness of their pretrained FM across a variety of domains [45]. It therefore serves as a strong state-of-the-art benchmark for signal forecasting. Thus, it is easier to forecast smooth movements than signals that exhibit abrupt changes. In RMSE, the dual-view FMs outperform TimeGPT-1 on seven test sets. On average, the LU models show an improvement of 0.258 points (13.18 %) over TimeGPT-1.
