The comparison with the production-ready TimeGPT-1 FM confirms the first-class signal forecasting qualities of dual-view FM and emphasizes the importance of domain-specific FMs. D. Evaluation of MSM Table IV compares the average metrics of the pretrained MSM dual-view FMs on the test sets with and without LA. To account for statistical deviations between different masks, we have randomly masked each sample eight times. We do not compare the MSM models with TimeGPT-1 because MSM models reconstruct signals instead of forecasting future values. The small MAEs and RMSEs show that the reconstructed signals are very similar to the original signals. However, the reconstruction of signals with sudden peaks appears to be more difficult than the reconstruction of more consistent movements. Overall, the MSM models achieve better performance indicators than the CSM models, even with the same number of missing time steps. This behavior is expected, given that the MSM models learn to reconstruct complete signals from information about past and future values while the CSM models are limited to past values. The LU models and the location-aware models achieve similar performance scores. For MAE, the LU models perform slightly better than the location-aware models with average improvements of 0.003 points. For RMSE, the location-aware models surpass the LU models by 0.009 points. The impact of location information on the MSM models is therefore negligible. E. EVALUATION—FINE-TUNING To further evaluate the generative capabilities of dual-view FM, we fine-tune our pretrained models for signal forecasting on their pretrain test sets (Sections VII-A and VII-B) and compare them with state-of-the-art TSMixer and transformer models (Sections VII-C and VII-D). We omit TimeGPT-1 [13] from the fine-tuning evaluation as it is a closed-source model with fixed parameters. Since forecasting nonperiodic signals is much harder than predicting recurring movements, we also study the forecasting performance per activity (Section VII-E) and location (Section VII-F), and leverage the forecast signals for downstream classification (Section VII-G). A. Fine-Tuning Data Split For fine-tuning, we randomly split the holdout test datasets from pretraining (cf. Section VI-B) into 60 % train, 20 % validation, and 20 % test data (Fig. 11). We make sure that all activities and all locations appear in all splits. B. Fine-Tuning for Signal Forecasting Following the pretraining parameters of the CSM models (cf. Table II), the signal forecasting task involves predicting the next w′ = nmask = 16 time steps based on the previous w −w′ = 112 time steps. The model input retains the (w, f ) shape, with the final w′ time steps masked [cf. Fig. 8(b)]. As the primary objective of MSM is to reconstruct signals with missing time steps, we adapt the MSM models to the forecasting task by replacing their pretrained reconstruction heads [cf. Fig.6(a)] with freshly initialized forecasting heads [cf. Fig.6(b)]. The CSM models remain unchanged as they perform the forecasting task by design. Following [46], we fine-tune the models in two steps. 1) Freeze the pretrained base and RevIN weights. Retrain the head with a large learning rate (1e-3). 2) Unfreeze the base and RevIN weights. Slightly adjust all layers with a tiny learning rate (1e-5). In both steps, we utilize the MAE/CD-Loss [cf. (1)] and the Adam optimizer to retrain the models for up to 500 epochs with early stopping (patience 10). Step 1 leverages a larger learning rate than step 2 to mitigate the substantial loss of pretrained knowledge during fine-tuning. For datasets containing less than 100k windows, we use a batch size of 32 and 128 for larger datasets. We repeat each fine-tuning three times with varying random seeds ∈{1, 2, 3}. C. Neural Network Baselines 1) TSMixer: Since dual-view FM builds upon TSMixer, we compare our proposal with the original TSMixer architecture. The comparison model follows the structure of dual-view FM (cf. Fig. 4) with slight modifications to match the original TSMixer implementation. We replace the dual-view blocks with TSMixer blocks with feed-forward dimension 64 which is the best configuration for the electricity dataset used in [27]. For consistency, we set the dropout factor to 0.2. The head is a simple temporal projection layer [47]. Since TSMixer is not location-aware, we omit the location input. TSMixer is roughly five times smaller than dual-view FM with 98 212 (MSM) and 83 764 (CSM) trainable weights. We train TSMixer like dualview FM, including pretraining and fine-tuning. 2) Transformer: Transformers [41] are the core of FMs, such as GPT-x [11] or BERT [12]. They shine in capturing long-range dependencies within sequences. Thus, we compare dual-view FM with transformers that use the same high-level structure as dual-view FM (cf. Fig. 4). We replace the dual-view blocks with transformer encoders [41] with four attention heads and w hidden units. For consistency, the encoders in the base use dropout 0.2, while the encoders in the heads omit dropout. In addition, positional encodings [41] enrich the input signals with temporal information prior to the first encoder layer. these transformers have 4 47 950 (CSM) and 5 08 318 trainable weights (MSM) which is similar to dual-view FM. We train the transformers like dual-view FM, including pretraining and fine-tuning. D. G. Beyond Forecasting: Downstream Classification To further assess the authenticity of the forecast signals, we train an activity classifier on signals generated by the fine-tuned dual-view FMs. As the models predict only nmask time steps at a time, we introduce an auto-regressive approach (Algorithm 1) to forecast the next w time steps, ensuring that the forecasts do not overlap with the original signals. Algorithm 1 Auto-Regressive Forecasting Require: Fine-tuned model F M, input signal s ∈Rw× f, length of mask nmask with w mod nmask = 0 Ensure: Forecast sequence ˆs ∈Rw× f 1: ˆs ←s, ˆw ←0, z ←0nmask× f 2: while ˆw < w do 3: ˆs ←[ˆsnmask:w, z] ▷Shift ˆs and append zero mask z 4: ˆsw−nmask:w ←F M(ˆs) ▷Replace zeros with forecasts 5: ˆw ←ˆw + nmask 6: end while 7: return ˆs We apply Algorithm 1 to all signals in the fine-tuning train splits (cf. Section VII-A) and enlarge these splits with the forecast signals. These forecasts are included only for activities whose sample counts do not exceed p % of the samples of the activity with the most signals in the original train splits. As a result, for p = 100, the new train splits are twice the size of the original ones as all forecasts are included. For smaller values of p, the new splits double the sample counts only for activities that meet the p % criterion to ensure that activities with a larger number of samples are not disproportionately overrepresented in the new splits. p = 0 does not modify the train splits at all and thus, represents the original train splits. By keeping the validation and test splits unchanged, we maintain the original dataset properties and ensure consistency when comparing models trained under different p-configurations. While dual-view FM forecasts signals at a single sensor location (cf. Section IV-B.4), activity classifiers typically perform better with multilocation inputs [48]. Therefore, we fuse the (w, f )-shaped single-location samples into multilocation inputs with shape (|loc|w, f ), where |loc| denotes the number of sensor locations available in the current dataset. TABLE VI AVERAGE MACRO F 1-SCORES OF TINYHAR ON THE FINE-TUNING TEST SETS (BEST, 2nd BEST). THE CLASSIFIERS ARE TRAINED ON ENLARGED TRAIN SPLITS WITH VARYING p’S. N/A INDICATES THAT THE GIVEN PERCENTAGE IS NOT APPLICABLE TO A DATASET AS IT DOES NOT CONTAIN ANY ACTIVITIES THAT MEET THE p % CRITERION We train TinyHAR [6], a lightweight model for human activity classification, on the original fine-tuning splits (0 %) and the new splits (25 %, 37.5 %, 50 %, 100 %). Similar to fine-tuning, we apply early stopping and repeat the training three times with varying random seeds (cf. Section VII-B). Table VI presents the average macro F1-scores across these runs on the fine-tuning test sets (cf. Section VII-A) for each dataset and p-configuration. For seven datasets, training TinyHAR on enlarged train sets that contain forecasts of all samples (p = 100) consistently improves their macro F1-scores compared to classifiers trained on the original train sets (p = 0) only. The largest F1-score improvements (up to 0.013) are observed in DLA and ComplexHAD, which are also the datasets with the most precise forecasts (cf. Fig. 12). Only for DSADS, the scores deteriorate slightly (−0.002). These improvements are particularly valuable given that the original classifiers already achieve high performance, with four datasets approaching the maximum score of 1.0. For p = 50, TinyHAR achieves the same or better macro F1-scores than p = 0 in three of six cases. Smaller p’s do not yield improvements but still perform close to the baselines. We attribute these results to shifts in class distributions within the enlarged train sets. Overall, these findings show that signal forecasting can enhance activity classifiers and further underline the quality of dual-view FM’s forecasts. VIII. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS Dual-View FM excels in forecasting human inertial signals from previous data. It consistently outperforms benchmark architectures across diverse datasets that span a wide range of activity signal from various users. The impact of location awareness is negligible. CSM models can benefit from location awareness, whereas MSM models slightly deteriorate, indicating a need for optimized processing of such meta-information. Given the variability in wearable device placements, accurate detection of sensor placements is crucial for wearable location-aware HAR (e.g. [49]). Dual-view FM is designed to forecast inertial sensor signals from a single body location. When applied to multilocation sensing setups, signals from different locations must be WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36853 processed sequentially. A multi-input FM could address this by fusing signals from various locations directly but, on the other hand, reduces the flexibility in handling data from different sensor locations. The lack of data also limits the large-scale combination of signals from different recording modalities. IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK This article presents dual-view FM, a generative pretrained FM for signal forecasting. Dual-view FM learns global and local signal properties in the time and feature domains to build a deep understanding of human inertial signals. The global view identifies general trends in human inertial signals, while the local view addresses their spontaneous nature by individually analyzing short, sensor-specific signal frames. The evaluation demonstrates that dual-view FM excels in generating realistic signals and highlights the need for highly capable domain-specific FMs. Fine-tuning further improves the model’s generative capabilities, enabling it to outperform its pretrained counterparts and other neural networks consistently. Our findings imply that comprehensive insights into human inertial signals can contribute to more robust wearable HAR systems. Hence, we believe that research on cross-dataset generalization and FMs is crucial to enhance the robustness of future applications in pervasive real-world scenarios. Dual-view FM fuses the signals with meta-information regarding the on-body placement of sensors to get detailed insights into the interplay between human activities and body parts. In the future, the versatility of dual-view FM can be further improved by integrating more meta-information regarding the users and sensor configuration. This article also presents a large training corpus that consolidates inertial signals from eight publicly available benchmark datasets, featuring a variety of users, activities, and on-body sensor placements. While this diverse corpus is ideal for training and evaluating FMs for wearable HAR, selecting proper datasets from different sources and their alignment is tedious and time-consuming. To enable faster development of such FMs, we call for standardized presentations in future datasets, including comprehensive documentation of the data collection environment, sensor configuration (types, manufacturers), unified activity names, and unified sensor placements

## Results
evaluation on eight established datasets shows that dual-view FM accurately forecasts human inertial signals from previously unseen test datasets that involve various sensors, activities, and users. The pretrained models even outperform a production-ready FM for time series forecasting by up to 36 % in mean absolute error (MAE), demonstrating the advantages of domain-specific FMs. Fine-tuning further enhances dual-view FM’s forecasting capabilities so that it surpasses other state-of-the-art architectures by more than 7 % in MAE. Index Terms— Activity generalization, context awareness, cross-dataset, foundation model (FM), human activity recognition (HAR), inertial sensors, self-supervised learning, time series forecasting. ## Conclusion
conclusion and possibilities for future research. II. RELATED WORK This section reviews key research areas that inform the development of dual-view FM, including time series forecasting (Section II-A), cross-dataset activity generalization (Section II-B), and self-supervised learning (Section II-C). A. Time Series Forecasting TimeGPT-1 [13], TimesFM [14], and Lag-Llama [15] are transformer-based FMs for the forecasting of time series from versatile domains, such as finance, weather, or electricity. TimeGPT-1’s training set even contains IoT sensor data. However, with 200 M parameters for TimesFM and 2.5 M parameters for Lag-Llama, these models are extremely large and not suitable for wearable deployment. Furthermore, they rely on large training corpora with millions of time series. In contrast, datasets for inertial HAR are much smaller with only a few thousand signals (cf. Table I). In addition, the TABLE I EIGHT CONSIDERED DATASETS. #A: NUMBER OF ACTIVITIES, #W: NUMBER OF WINDOWS, SR: SAMPLING RATE, SI: THE UNITS OF ACCELERATION AND ANGULAR VELOCITY Fig. 1. TSMixer (adapted from [27]) mixes time series along their time and feature axes. w: window size, f: features, h: hidden dimension (a) TSMixer block. (b) Time mixing. (c) Feature mixing. resources of wearables are so limited that such large transformers cannot be realized on them. Thus, simpler architectures are required for pervasive time series forecasting. TSMixer [27] is a recent model for time series forecasting that relies solely on dense operations (Fig. 1). Its simplicity makes TSMixer an interesting alternative for wearable HAR. The TSMixer block mixes the temporal and the feature axes with its time and feature mixing layers. This structure enables TSMixer to learn temporal relationships and feature patterns within time series. However, TSMixer applies its mixing operations from a global perspective, where the mixing layers consider all values along an input dimension simultaneously. TSMixer therefore ignores essential properties of time series, such as the temporal order of the input values or important features that are located in short time frames within a signal. ActivityGAN [25] is capable of generating artificial accelerometer signals from three activities (still, walk, and jog). The generated signals improve the accuracy of several classifiers by up to 6%. However, these activities have inherently different signal shapes that are even recognizable by experienced observers. This limitation significantly simplifies signal generation and downstream activity classification with ActivityGAN. B. Cross-Dataset Activity Generalization Given the limited size and scope of datasets for wearable HAR (cf. Table I), activity generalization across multiple WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36845 datasets is essential for capturing a diverse range of motion styles from various users, activities, and sensors. For instance, SDMix [26] and CWT-CNN2D [28] conduct cross-dataset evaluations. However, they consider only up to five activities that are common among up to six datasets and ignore rare activities that provide valuable information about inertial signals and contribute to a general signal understanding. CrossHAR [29] applies cross-dataset evaluation by merging unlabeled signals from three datasets for self-supervised pretraining. Its authors evaluate this pretrained model on a fourth target dataset. Similarly, [30] pretrains LIMU-BERT on four merged and unlabeled datasets for wearable HAR. However, fine-tuning for downstream classification is performed on one of the four pretraining datasets. The results from [29] and [30] indicate that pretraining on multiple datasets enhances activity generalization, though training without domain shift still outperforms the best cross-dataset models. Other publications include [31], [32], and [33]. C. Self-Supervised Learning for Wearable HAR Strategies for the self-supervised learning of wearable HAR models leverage sophisticated pretraining objectives to identify patterns in unlabeled data [34]. Contrastive learning maximizes the similarity between positive pairs while minimizing the similarity between negative pairs of samples [31]. Masking approaches, such as span masking [30] or spatial masking [35], learn to reconstruct signals with masked values. Forecasting approaches predict future signal values based on past signals [36] or different modalities [37]. Transformation detection approaches apply random augmentations to input signals and learn to recognize the applied transformations in a multitask learning environment [38]. Combinations of different pretraining objectives can further improve the quality of the learned embeddings [36]. III. DUAL-VIEW FM FMs are necessary to handle the individualities of human activities and their sensor signals. However, current transformer-based approaches for time series forecasting are too complex for ubiquitous wearable HAR. To solve this issue, we present dual-view FM. It adapts the TSMixer architecture to the conditions of human activity signals by analyzing short, local time frames, and sensor-specific properties to better address the spontaneous nature of such signals (Section III-A). Dual-view FM also enables the integration of sensor placement for tailored signal analysis (Section III-B). A. Leveraging Global and Local Information Dual-view FM extracts global and local time and feature information from inertial signals. The Dual-view block (Fig. 2) first analyzes signals in the time dimension and then in the feature dimension. Within a dimension, each block processes signals from the local and the global view in parallel. Time mixing [Fig. 3(a)] combines global and local time mixing operations. The global time MLP (multilayer perceptron) stacks three layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). The first dense layer fuses input signals along the Fig. 2. Dual-view block differentiates between global and local information. In addition, dual-view FM can alter the temporal dimension w of an input to w′. All deviations from TSMixer are highlighted in teal color. Fig. 3. Dual-view FM’s local and global time and feature mixing. Blue: three-axis acceleration; red: three-axis angular velocity. (a) Local time mixing splits the input signal (w). (b) Local feature mixing splits the input signal (w). whole time axis and changes their dimensions from (w, f ) to (h, f ); the second dense layer returns signals with shapes (w′, f ). The local time MLP also stacks three layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). However, instead of processing the time axis globally, the local time MLP acts on st short, equally sized temporal splits with shapes (w/st, f ). Its first 36846 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 25, NO. 19, 1 OCTOBER 2025 Fig. 4. Dual-view FM’s high-level architecture. dense layer changes the split dimensions to (h, f ), while its second dense layer adjusts them to (w′/st, f ). All splits share the same local time MLP and its weights. In addition, we apply a residual connection to keep important signal features if the output length w′ is equal to the input length w. Otherwise, we disable the residual connection to prevent a shape mismatch between the input signals and the outputs of the global and local time mixing operations. Feature Mixing [Fig. 3(b)] combines global and local feature mixing operations. The global feature mixing remains functionally the same as TSMixer’s feature mixing [cf. Fig. 1(c)]. It fuses information along the whole feature axis with three stacked MLP layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). We use the term global feature mixing instead of feature mixing to highlight the receptive field of this layer. The local feature MLP also stacks three layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). However, instead of processing the feature axis globally, it acts on s f equally sized features splits with shapes (w′, f/s f ). All splits share a single local feature MLP. We set s f to the number of physical sensors. When using signals from a three-axis accelerometer and a threeaxis gyroscope, local feature mixing splits the feature axis into three-axis acceleration and three-axis angular velocity (s f = 2). The additional dense layer in global time mixing versus TSMixer’s time mixing [cf. Fig. 1(b)], the processing of focused local splits, and the ability to adjust the temporal dimensions from w to w′ grant dual-view FM advanced learning capabilities. The linear output layers ensure that dualview FM’s time mixing layers can be used as standalone outputs in time series forecasting tasks. B. Architecture Dual-view FM has a modular, highly configurable architecture (Fig. 4) that connects a base with an interchangeable head. Since dual-view FM processes multiple datasets with different data collection environments in parallel during pretraining, input signals do not always follow the same distribution (cf. Section IV). To reduce the impact of such inhomogeneous inputs, we surround base and head with reversible instance normalization (RevIN) [39]. Additionally, the model leverages information on the sensor placement loc ∈N to identify location-dependent patterns within sensor signals, where each loc represents a unique sensor location, such as wrist or ankle. The base (Fig. 5) mixes the input signal (w, f ) using Nbefore consecutive dual-view blocks and incorporates each loc as a unique (w, f )-dimensional embedding. Ultimately, the signals get further refined by Nafter dual-view blocks. The reconstruction head [Fig. 6(a)] mixes the signals further by passing the outputs of the base through Nobjective dual-view blocks. The forecasting head [Fig. 6(b)] forecasts the next w′ Fig. 5. Base transforms (w, f) with several dual-view blocks and incorporates the sensor placement. Fig. 6. (a) Reconstruction head transforms the base’s output without modifying the signal shape. (b) Forecasting head forecasts only the next w ′ time steps. time steps by passing the output of the base through Nobjective dual-view blocks. The forecasting head modifies the output shape from (w, f ) to (w′, f ); the reconstruction head keeps the output dimensions constant. IV. DATASETS AND DATA PREPARATION Pretraining FMs requires large amounts of data to ensure their generalizability on unseen inputs. However, common datasets contain only a limited amount of signals from only a few users and activities. Furthermore, they vary in available sensors and sensor characteristics. Some datasets contain normalized or preprocessed data, while others provide raw signals. Therefore, aligning signals from different sources is an extensive but important preparatory task to build comprehensive FMs for wearable HAR. We select (Section IV-A) and combine (Section IV-B) eight datasets to obtain ground truth about the trajectory of human inertial signals. A. Datasets Dual-view FM fuses accelerometer and gyroscope signals from eight daily living and sports activity datasets that differ in size, sensors, sensor locations, and activities (Table I). We have selected these datasets based on three criteria. 1) Each sensor location should contain signals from at least one accelerometer and one gyroscope. 2) Each location should be present in at least two datasets. 3) The datasets should provide raw sensor signals. Criterion (1) guarantees that dual-view FM receives comprehensive insights on the performed activities. Gyroscope signals are important since sensor placements and orientations can vary significantly between datasets. We exclude the chest data from mHealth and the wrist data from DLA from our research as they only provide acceleration. Criterion (2) ensures that dual-view FM learns differences in motion patterns at various sensor locations, while simultaneously encompassing information from several users and application scenarios. Among the eight datasets, RealWorld is the only one that provides signals from the head or upper arm. Thus, we ignore these two locations. Criterion (3) ensures the compatibility of signals from different signal collection environments. WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36847 Fig. 7. Standardized sensor placements on the body (left) and the number of six-axis sensors at these locations (right). Furthermore, the sensor placements can vary between datasets. For instance, some studies place sensors on the right wrist while others allow participants to wear them on their preferred wrist. Since location names are not standardized, we provide six common locations (Fig. 7). 1) Ankle: ankle / shin, 2) Chest: chest, 3) Hip: hip, 4) Pocket: pocket / upper leg / thigh, 5) Waist: waist, 6) Wrist: wrist / forearm. Some of the selected datasets share a subset of their activities, and other activities are unique to single datasets. However, since activity names are not standardized, datasets sometimes use different names for similar activities, for example, cycling versus bike. Furthermore, certain datasets exhibit finer granularity in distinguishing activities than others, for example, walk versus walk-circle. We have identified 40 general activities that are valid across all datasets. Therefore, dual-view FM acts on far more activities than conventional approaches, which only consider the activities of single datasets (e.g., [5], [6]). B. Data Preparation Inertial sensor signals are inherently heterogeneous across users, activities, and sensor placements. Rather than eliminating this variability, our goal is to learn from it by training a FM that generalizes across diverse sensing setups. To improve signal compatibility across datasets, we standardize basic properties such as units, sampling rates, and window sizes using lightweight alignment steps, while preserving meaningful variation between subjects and contexts. 1) Unit Alignment: The selected datasets differ in their recording units. To ensure a homogenous input distribution, we convert acceleration to m/s2 and angular velocity to rad/s. 2) Temporal Alignment Within Datasets: The sensor reading times in RealWorld vary slightly by location. To improve the generalizability, we resample these signals via linear Fig. 8. Short acceleration signal at the ankle during walking from [20]. Ten of 35 time steps are masked (red crosses). (a) MSM. (b) CSM. interpolation. Furthermore, we apply a linear interpolation to the signals in PAMAP2 to handle missing values. 3) Windowing and Temporal Alignment Between Datasets: As recommended in [24], we convert the signals into 2.56 s sliding windows with an overlap of 50 %. Due to different sampling rates, the number of time steps per window can differ between datasets. Thus, we resample the windows to 50 Hz using cubic spline interpolation. We have selected this sampling rate for several reasons: 1) common sensors support this rate; 2) this rate captures human activities effectively; 3) processing signals at this rate requires less computational resources than higher frequencies; and 4) this rate ensures that only DSADS requires upsampling. Table I lists the total number of preprocessed windows per dataset summed over the sensor locations in the #W column. 4) Model Inputs: Dual-view FM processes window-location pairs, where each pair represents a signal window (w, f ) with w = 128 readings from f = 6 sensor axes (three-axis acceleration and three-axis angular velocity) at a single sensor location loc. Thus, the model handles signals from different body locations independently and treats them as separate input streams even if a dataset provides signals from multiple locations. Fig. 1. TSMixer (adapted from [27]) mixes time series along their time and feature axes. w: window size, f: features, h: hidden dimension (a) TSMixer block. (b) Time mixing. (c) Feature mixing. resources of wearables are so limited that such large transformers cannot be realized on them. Thus, simpler architectures are required for pervasive time series forecasting. TSMixer [27] is a recent model for time series forecasting that relies solely on dense operations (Fig. 1). Its simplicity makes TSMixer an interesting alternative for wearable HAR. The TSMixer block mixes the temporal and the feature axes with its time and feature mixing layers. This structure enables TSMixer to learn temporal relationships and feature patterns within time series. However, TSMixer applies its mixing operations from a global perspective, where the mixing layers consider all values along an input dimension simultaneously. TSMixer therefore ignores essential properties of time series, such as the temporal order of the input values or important features that are located in short time frames within a signal. ActivityGAN [25] is capable of generating artificial accelerometer signals from three activities (still, walk, and jog). The generated signals improve the accuracy of several classifiers by up to 6%. However, these activities have inherently different signal shapes that are even recognizable by experienced observers. This limitation significantly simplifies signal generation and downstream activity classification with ActivityGAN. B. Cross-Dataset Activity Generalization Given the limited size and scope of datasets for wearable HAR (cf. Table I), activity generalization across multiple WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36845 datasets is essential for capturing a diverse range of motion styles from various users, activities, and sensors. For instance, SDMix [26] and CWT-CNN2D [28] conduct cross-dataset evaluations. However, they consider only up to five activities that are common among up to six datasets and ignore rare activities that provide valuable information about inertial signals and contribute to a general signal understanding. CrossHAR [29] applies cross-dataset evaluation by merging unlabeled signals from three datasets for self-supervised pretraining. Its authors evaluate this pretrained model on a fourth target dataset. Similarly, [30] pretrains LIMU-BERT on four merged and unlabeled datasets for wearable HAR. However, fine-tuning for downstream classification is performed on one of the four pretraining datasets. The results from [29] and [30] indicate that pretraining on multiple datasets enhances activity generalization, though training without domain shift still outperforms the best cross-dataset models. Other publications include [31], [32], and [33]. C. Self-Supervised Learning for Wearable HAR Strategies for the self-supervised learning of wearable HAR models leverage sophisticated pretraining objectives to identify patterns in unlabeled data [34]. Contrastive learning maximizes the similarity between positive pairs while minimizing the similarity between negative pairs of samples [31]. Masking approaches, such as span masking [30] or spatial masking [35], learn to reconstruct signals with masked values. Forecasting approaches predict future signal values based on past signals [36] or different modalities [37]. Transformation detection approaches apply random augmentations to input signals and learn to recognize the applied transformations in a multitask learning environment [38]. Combinations of different pretraining objectives can further improve the quality of the learned embeddings [36]. III. DUAL-VIEW FM FMs are necessary to handle the individualities of human activities and their sensor signals. However, current transformer-based approaches for time series forecasting are too complex for ubiquitous wearable HAR. To solve this issue, we present dual-view FM. It adapts the TSMixer architecture to the conditions of human activity signals by analyzing short, local time frames, and sensor-specific properties to better address the spontaneous nature of such signals (Section III-A). Dual-view FM also enables the integration of sensor placement for tailored signal analysis (Section III-B). A. Leveraging Global and Local Information Dual-view FM extracts global and local time and feature information from inertial signals. The Dual-view block (Fig. 2) first analyzes signals in the time dimension and then in the feature dimension. Within a dimension, each block processes signals from the local and the global view in parallel. Time mixing [Fig. 3(a)] combines global and local time mixing operations. The global time MLP (multilayer perceptron) stacks three layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). The first dense layer fuses input signals along the Fig. 2. Dual-view block differentiates between global and local information. In addition, dual-view FM can alter the temporal dimension w of an input to w′. All deviations from TSMixer are highlighted in teal color. Fig. 3. Dual-view FM’s local and global time and feature mixing. Blue: three-axis acceleration; red: three-axis angular velocity. (a) Local time mixing splits the input signal (w). (b) Local feature mixing splits the input signal (w). whole time axis and changes their dimensions from (w, f ) to (h, f ); the second dense layer returns signals with shapes (w′, f ). The local time MLP also stacks three layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). However, instead of processing the time axis globally, the local time MLP acts on st short, equally sized temporal splits with shapes (w/st, f ). Its first 36846 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 25, NO. 19, 1 OCTOBER 2025 Fig. 4. Dual-view FM’s high-level architecture. dense layer changes the split dimensions to (h, f ), while its second dense layer adjusts them to (w′/st, f ). All splits share the same local time MLP and its weights. In addition, we apply a residual connection to keep important signal features if the output length w′ is equal to the input length w. Otherwise, we disable the residual connection to prevent a shape mismatch between the input signals and the outputs of the global and local time mixing operations. Feature Mixing [Fig. 3(b)] combines global and local feature mixing operations. The global feature mixing remains functionally the same as TSMixer’s feature mixing [cf. Fig. 1(c)]. It fuses information along the whole feature axis with three stacked MLP layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). We use the term global feature mixing instead of feature mixing to highlight the receptive field of this layer. The local feature MLP also stacks three layers: dense (ReLU), dropout, dense (linear). However, instead of processing the feature axis globally, it acts on s f equally sized features splits with shapes (w′, f/s f ). All splits share a single local feature MLP. We set s f to the number of physical sensors. When using signals from a three-axis accelerometer and a threeaxis gyroscope, local feature mixing splits the feature axis into three-axis acceleration and three-axis angular velocity (s f = 2). The additional dense layer in global time mixing versus TSMixer’s time mixing [cf. Fig. 1(b)], the processing of focused local splits, and the ability to adjust the temporal dimensions from w to w′ grant dual-view FM advanced learning capabilities. The linear output layers ensure that dualview FM’s time mixing layers can be used as standalone outputs in time series forecasting tasks. B. Architecture Dual-view FM has a modular, highly configurable architecture (Fig. 4) that connects a base with an interchangeable head. Since dual-view FM processes multiple datasets with different data collection environments in parallel during pretraining, input signals do not always follow the same distribution (cf. Section IV). To reduce the impact of such inhomogeneous inputs, we surround base and head with reversible instance normalization (RevIN) [39]. Additionally, the model leverages information on the sensor placement loc ∈N to identify location-dependent patterns within sensor signals, where each loc represents a unique sensor location, such as wrist or ankle. The base (Fig. 5) mixes the input signal (w, f ) using Nbefore consecutive dual-view blocks and incorporates each loc as a unique (w, f )-dimensional embedding. Ultimately, the signals get further refined by Nafter dual-view blocks. The reconstruction head [Fig. 6(a)] mixes the signals further by passing the outputs of the base through Nobjective dual-view blocks. The forecasting head [Fig. 6(b)] forecasts the next w′ Fig. 5. Base transforms (w, f) with several dual-view blocks and incorporates the sensor placement. Fig. 6. (a) Reconstruction head transforms the base’s output without modifying the signal shape. (b) Forecasting head forecasts only the next w ′ time steps. time steps by passing the output of the base through Nobjective dual-view blocks. The forecasting head modifies the output shape from (w, f ) to (w′, f ); the reconstruction head keeps the output dimensions constant. IV. DATASETS AND DATA PREPARATION Pretraining FMs requires large amounts of data to ensure their generalizability on unseen inputs. However, common datasets contain only a limited amount of signals from only a few users and activities. Furthermore, they vary in available sensors and sensor characteristics. Some datasets contain normalized or preprocessed data, while others provide raw signals. Therefore, aligning signals from different sources is an extensive but important preparatory task to build comprehensive FMs for wearable HAR. We select (Section IV-A) and combine (Section IV-B) eight datasets to obtain ground truth about the trajectory of human inertial signals. A. Datasets Dual-view FM fuses accelerometer and gyroscope signals from eight daily living and sports activity datasets that differ in size, sensors, sensor locations, and activities (Table I). Gyroscope signals are important since sensor placements and orientations can vary significantly between datasets. We exclude the chest data from mHealth and the wrist data from DLA from our research as they only provide acceleration. Criterion (2) ensures that dual-view FM learns differences in motion patterns at various sensor locations, while simultaneously encompassing information from several users and application scenarios. Among the eight datasets, RealWorld is the only one that provides signals from the head or upper arm. Thus, we ignore these two locations. Criterion (3) ensures the compatibility of signals from different signal collection environments. WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36847 Fig. 7. V. EVALUATION—SETUP To handle large, unlabeled datasets, FMs are usually pretrained in a self-supervised fashion. This section gives an overview of different pretraining objectives (Section V-A) and model configurations (Section V-B) for dual-view FM’s selfsupervised pretraining. Furthermore, it presents the training loss and evaluation metrics (Section V-C), and the training environment (Section V-D) for the subsequent evaluation of dual-view FM (Sections VI and VII). A. Pretraining Objectives We leverage masked signal modeling (MSM) and causal signal modeling (CSM) for the self-supervised pretraining of dual-view FM (Fig. 8). Both pretraining objectives partially mask input signals and learn to reconstruct the masked time steps but differ in their masking strategies. MSM [Fig. 8(a)] randomly nullifies sensor readings at nmask time steps and trains the model to reconstruct the unmasked 36848 IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 25, NO. 19, 1 OCTOBER 2025 TABLE II MODEL PARAMETERS OF DUAL-VIEW FM FOR THE TWO PRETRAINING OBJECTIVES MSM AND CSM signals using the reconstruction head [cf. Fig. 6(a)]. During pretraining, each mini-batch generates a new random mask and applies it to all its samples. MSM learns embeddings that capture the general context of the signals. CSM [Fig. 8(b)] masks the last nmask time steps of an input sequence with zeros and trains the model to forecast the masked time steps using the forecasting head [cf. Fig. 6(b)]. CSM learns temporal dependencies from past signal features without knowing future time steps. MSM is similar to masked language modeling [12], where nmask input tokens are arbitrarily masked with placeholder tokens. CSM resembles causal language modeling [11], [41] that predicts the next token in a token sequence. B. Model Configuration We evaluate dual-view FM with the architectural parameters from Table II. These configurations result in similar-sized dual-view FMs for both pretraining objectives: the CSM models have 4 54 615 trainable weights with and about 7.86 MMACs (millions of multiply–accumulate operations); the MSM models have 4 51 673 weights and 8.16 MMACs. The number of dual-view blocks in the heads (Nobjective) differs between MSM and CSM. For MSM, we use only one dual-view block in the reconstruction head that returns the output shape (w, f ). For CSM, we use a forecasting head with three dual-view blocks where each one reduces its input length by half. This results in the CSM output shape (nmask, f ). nmask = 16 corresponds to 12.5 % of the input length w = 128. All dual-view blocks bi in the bases and heads follow the same rule for their latent dimension hi: hi = 2wi−1, where wi−1 is the output length of the previous block bi−1 and w0 = w. Thus, the blocks in the base and the reconstruction head have hi = 2w = 256, while each bi in the forecasting head reduces hi−1 by half. This configuration ensures that MSM and CSM models have similar number of trainable weights. Local time mixing splits signals in st = 4 equally sized temporal splits. This number ensures that even the last dual-view block in the forecasting head considers an adequate split size of nmask/st = 4 time steps. Local feature mixing learns sensor-specific features by splitting the feature dimension in three-axis acceleration and three-axis angular velocity (s f = 2). To improve dual-view FM’s generalizability and to avoid overfitting, we apply dropout (0.2), layer normalization [42] (ε = 0.001), and L2 regularization (l2 = 0.01) to all dual-view blocks in the base. We omit these regularization techniques in the heads to prevent them from deriving distorted signals. C. Loss Function and Evaluation Metrics We join the cosine distance CD and the mean absolute error (MAE) in the following loss function (lower values are better): MAE/CD-Loss y, ˆy  = 0.5 MAE y, ˆy  + 0.5 CD y, ˆy  (1) where y and ˆy are the actual and the predicted values. MAE ∈[0, ∞) measures the magnitude of the error between y and ˆy (lower values are better). CD ∈[0, 2] measures the similarity of y and ˆy based on their shape (lower values are better). MAE and CD are equally important for the forecasting or reconstruction of signals and are therefore equally weighted. We evaluate the models in terms of MAE and root-meansquare error RMSE ∈[0, ∞] (lower values are better). D. Training Environment We train all models on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. Furthermore, we set the PYTHONHASHSEED environment variable to 0 to obtain reproducible result [43]. VI. EVALUATION—PRETRAINING Self-supervised pretraining is an important concept of FMs. To evaluate the pretraining performance of Dual-View FM in a cross-dataset setup, we leverage the pretraining configuration and data splits from Sections VI-A and VI-B. Sections VI-C and VI-D evaluate dual-view FM’s generalizability when using CSM and MSM pretraining objectives with and without location awareness. Section VI-E analyzes the impact of pretraining sets with increasing data volumes on the model. A. Pretraining Setup We pretrain dual-view FM using the Adam optimizer [44] with learning rate 1e−3 for up to 500 epochs and early stopping with patience 10. The batch size is set to 256. To account for statistical fluctuations, we repeat each pretraining three times with varying random seeds ∈{1, 2, 3}. B. Pretraining Data Split We pretrain dual-view FM with a leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) approach that enables us to assess its cross-dataset generalizability (Fig. 9). We take seven datasets from Table I for pretraining and one for testing. Since each dataset was collected by a different research group, they leverage sensors from different manufacturers and collect signals from different activities, users, and locations. We randomly split the signals in the seven training sets into 80 % train and 20 % validation data. We ensure that both training and validation sets contain signals from all locations and activities so that dual-view FM learns from a broad context. WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36849 Fig. 9. LODO split for pretraining. TABLE III AVERAGE PRETRAINING PERFORMANCE OF THE LU CSM MODELS, THEIR LOCATION-AWARE COUNTERPARTS (LA), AND THE PRETRAINED TIMEGPT-1 [13] ON THE HOLDOUT TEST DATASETS (BEST, SECOND BEST) We repeat the LODO split eight times, with each dataset serving as the holdout test set once. For each of these eight test sets, we further split the seven remaining datasets into training and validation sets three times using different random seeds. In total, we pretrain 48 dual-view FMs [eight for each test set, three random seeds, with and without location awareness (LA)]. C. Evaluation of CSM Table III compares the average test MAE and RMSE of pretrained, location-unaware (LU) dual-view FMs with their LA counterparts and TimeGPT-1, a closed-source FM for general purpose time series forecasting that is accessible via an API [13]. TimeGPT-1’s authors claim the production-readiness of their pretrained FM across a variety of domains [45]. It therefore serves as a strong state-of-the-art benchmark for signal forecasting. However, its performance may be affected by domain differences, as TimeGPT-1 was not exclusively pretrained on sensor data. For all test sets, the small MAEs and RMSEs of the dual-view FMs indicate only a minor mismatch between the actual values and their forecasts. The RMSEs are higher than the MAEs. Thus, it is easier to forecast smooth movements than signals that exhibit abrupt changes. Nevertheless, the metrics indicate that dual-view FMs forecast time series that are close to the original signals. The LU models slightly surpass the location-aware models on seven test sets with average improvements of 0.004 (MAE) and 0.005 (RMSE). The pretrained dual-view FMs outperform TimeGPT-1 in MAE on all test sets. The LU models achieve an average MAE improvement of 0.336 over TimeGPT-1; an impressive improvement of 36.21 %. In RMSE, the dual-view FMs outperform TimeGPT-1 on seven test sets. On average, the LU models show an improvement of 0.258 points (13.18 %) over TimeGPT-1. The location-aware models also demonstrate substantial improvements in both metrics compared TABLE IV AVERAGE PRETRAINING PERFORMANCE OF THE LU MSM MODELS AND THEIR LOCATION-AWARE COUNTERPARTS (LA) ON THE HOLDOUT TEST DATASETS (BEST) to TimeGPT-1. The comparison with the production-ready TimeGPT-1 FM confirms the first-class signal forecasting qualities of dual-view FM and emphasizes the importance of domain-specific FMs. D. Evaluation of MSM Table IV compares the average metrics of the pretrained MSM dual-view FMs on the test sets with and without LA. To account for statistical deviations between different masks, we have randomly masked each sample eight times. We do not compare the MSM models with TimeGPT-1 because MSM models reconstruct signals instead of forecasting future values. The small MAEs and RMSEs show that the reconstructed signals are very similar to the original signals. However, the reconstruction of signals with sudden peaks appears to be more difficult than the reconstruction of more consistent movements. Overall, the MSM models achieve better performance indicators than the CSM models, even with the same number of missing time steps. This behavior is expected, given that the MSM models learn to reconstruct complete signals from information about past and future values while the CSM models are limited to past values. The LU models and the location-aware models achieve similar performance scores. For MAE, the LU models perform slightly better than the location-aware models with average improvements of 0.003 points. For RMSE, the location-aware models surpass the LU models by 0.009 points. The impact of location information on the MSM models is therefore negligible. E. Impact of Train Set Size To analyze the impact of the training set size on dual-view FMs, we pretrain the LU CSM models on a continuously increasing amount of data. We start with the smallest dataset and successively add further datasets with increasing cardinality until the maximum of seven training datasets is reached. We repeat this procedure three times with varying random seeds ∈{1, 2, 3}. Fig. 10 illustrates the impact of different training set sizes on the average MAEs of the models for each test set. EVALUATION—FINE-TUNING To further evaluate the generative capabilities of dual-view FM, we fine-tune our pretrained models for signal forecasting on their pretrain test sets (Sections VII-A and VII-B) and compare them with state-of-the-art TSMixer and transformer models (Sections VII-C and VII-D). We omit TimeGPT-1 [13] from the fine-tuning evaluation as it is a closed-source model with fixed parameters. Since forecasting nonperiodic signals is much harder than predicting recurring movements, we also study the forecasting performance per activity (Section VII-E) and location (Section VII-F), and leverage the forecast signals for downstream classification (Section VII-G). A. Fine-Tuning Data Split For fine-tuning, we randomly split the holdout test datasets from pretraining (cf. Section VI-B) into 60 % train, 20 % validation, and 20 % test data (Fig. 11). We make sure that all activities and all locations appear in all splits. B. Fine-Tuning for Signal Forecasting Following the pretraining parameters of the CSM models (cf. Table II), the signal forecasting task involves predicting the next w′ = nmask = 16 time steps based on the previous w −w′ = 112 time steps. The model input retains the (w, f ) shape, with the final w′ time steps masked [cf. Fig. 8(b)]. As the primary objective of MSM is to reconstruct signals with missing time steps, we adapt the MSM models to the forecasting task by replacing their pretrained reconstruction heads [cf. Fig.6(a)] with freshly initialized forecasting heads [cf. Fig.6(b)]. The CSM models remain unchanged as they perform the forecasting task by design. Following [46], we fine-tune the models in two steps. 1) Freeze the pretrained base and RevIN weights. Retrain the head with a large learning rate (1e-3). 2) Unfreeze the base and RevIN weights. Slightly adjust all layers with a tiny learning rate (1e-5). In both steps, we utilize the MAE/CD-Loss [cf. (1)] and the Adam optimizer to retrain the models for up to 500 epochs with early stopping (patience 10). Step 1 leverages a larger learning rate than step 2 to mitigate the substantial loss of pretrained knowledge during fine-tuning. For datasets containing less than 100k windows, we use a batch size of 32 and 128 for larger datasets. We repeat each fine-tuning three times with varying random seeds ∈{1, 2, 3}. C. Neural Network Baselines 1) TSMixer: Since dual-view FM builds upon TSMixer, we compare our proposal with the original TSMixer architecture. The comparison model follows the structure of dual-view FM (cf. Fig. 4) with slight modifications to match the original TSMixer implementation. We replace the dual-view blocks with TSMixer blocks with feed-forward dimension 64 which is the best configuration for the electricity dataset used in [27]. For consistency, we set the dropout factor to 0.2. The head is a simple temporal projection layer [47]. Since TSMixer is not location-aware, we omit the location input. TSMixer is roughly five times smaller than dual-view FM with 98 212 (MSM) and 83 764 (CSM) trainable weights. We train TSMixer like dualview FM, including pretraining and fine-tuning. 2) Transformer: Transformers [41] are the core of FMs, such as GPT-x [11] or BERT [12]. They shine in capturing long-range dependencies within sequences. Thus, we compare dual-view FM with transformers that use the same high-level structure as dual-view FM (cf. Fig. 4). We replace the dual-view blocks with transformer encoders [41] with four attention heads and w hidden units. For consistency, the encoders in the base use dropout 0.2, while the encoders in the heads omit dropout. In addition, positional encodings [41] enrich the input signals with temporal information prior to the first encoder layer. these transformers have 4 47 950 (CSM) and 5 08 318 trainable weights (MSM) which is similar to dual-view FM. We train the transformers like dual-view FM, including pretraining and fine-tuning. D. The fine-tuned CSM models generally perform better than their MSM counterparts. This behavior is expected, as there is a mismatch between the pretraining objective MSM and the downstream task of signal forecasting; CSM, on the other hand, already pursues the same objective as the downstream task during pretraining. For dual-view FM, however, the differences are much smaller than for transformer or TSMixer. These findings underscore the outstanding generalizability of dual-view FM and emphasize the importance of knowing the downstream tasks to select appropriate pretraining objectives. G. Beyond Forecasting: Downstream Classification To further assess the authenticity of the forecast signals, we train an activity classifier on signals generated by the fine-tuned dual-view FMs. As the models predict only nmask time steps at a time, we introduce an auto-regressive approach (Algorithm 1) to forecast the next w time steps, ensuring that the forecasts do not overlap with the original signals. Algorithm 1 Auto-Regressive Forecasting Require: Fine-tuned model F M, input signal s ∈Rw× f, length of mask nmask with w mod nmask = 0 Ensure: Forecast sequence ˆs ∈Rw× f 1: ˆs ←s, ˆw ←0, z ←0nmask× f 2: while ˆw < w do 3: ˆs ←[ˆsnmask:w, z] ▷Shift ˆs and append zero mask z 4: ˆsw−nmask:w ←F M(ˆs) ▷Replace zeros with forecasts 5: ˆw ←ˆw + nmask 6: end while 7: return ˆs We apply Algorithm 1 to all signals in the fine-tuning train splits (cf. Section VII-A) and enlarge these splits with the forecast signals. These forecasts are included only for activities whose sample counts do not exceed p % of the samples of the activity with the most signals in the original train splits. As a result, for p = 100, the new train splits are twice the size of the original ones as all forecasts are included. For smaller values of p, the new splits double the sample counts only for activities that meet the p % criterion to ensure that activities with a larger number of samples are not disproportionately overrepresented in the new splits. p = 0 does not modify the train splits at all and thus, represents the original train splits. By keeping the validation and test splits unchanged, we maintain the original dataset properties and ensure consistency when comparing models trained under different p-configurations. While dual-view FM forecasts signals at a single sensor location (cf. Section IV-B.4), activity classifiers typically perform better with multilocation inputs [48]. Therefore, we fuse the (w, f )-shaped single-location samples into multilocation inputs with shape (|loc|w, f ), where |loc| denotes the number of sensor locations available in the current dataset. TABLE VI AVERAGE MACRO F 1-SCORES OF TINYHAR ON THE FINE-TUNING TEST SETS (BEST, 2nd BEST). THE CLASSIFIERS ARE TRAINED ON ENLARGED TRAIN SPLITS WITH VARYING p’S. N/A INDICATES THAT THE GIVEN PERCENTAGE IS NOT APPLICABLE TO A DATASET AS IT DOES NOT CONTAIN ANY ACTIVITIES THAT MEET THE p % CRITERION We train TinyHAR [6], a lightweight model for human activity classification, on the original fine-tuning splits (0 %) and the new splits (25 %, 37.5 %, 50 %, 100 %). Similar to fine-tuning, we apply early stopping and repeat the training three times with varying random seeds (cf. Section VII-B). Table VI presents the average macro F1-scores across these runs on the fine-tuning test sets (cf. Section VII-A) for each dataset and p-configuration. For seven datasets, training TinyHAR on enlarged train sets that contain forecasts of all samples (p = 100) consistently improves their macro F1-scores compared to classifiers trained on the original train sets (p = 0) only. The largest F1-score improvements (up to 0.013) are observed in DLA and ComplexHAD, which are also the datasets with the most precise forecasts (cf. Fig. 12). Only for DSADS, the scores deteriorate slightly (−0.002). These improvements are particularly valuable given that the original classifiers already achieve high performance, with four datasets approaching the maximum score of 1.0. For p = 50, TinyHAR achieves the same or better macro F1-scores than p = 0 in three of six cases. Smaller p’s do not yield improvements but still perform close to the baselines. We attribute these results to shifts in class distributions within the enlarged train sets. Overall, these findings show that signal forecasting can enhance activity classifiers and further underline the quality of dual-view FM’s forecasts. VIII. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS Dual-View FM excels in forecasting human inertial signals from previous data. It consistently outperforms benchmark architectures across diverse datasets that span a wide range of activity signal from various users. The impact of location awareness is negligible. CSM models can benefit from location awareness, whereas MSM models slightly deteriorate, indicating a need for optimized processing of such meta-information. Given the variability in wearable device placements, accurate detection of sensor placements is crucial for wearable location-aware HAR (e.g. [49]). Dual-view FM is designed to forecast inertial sensor signals from a single body location. When applied to multilocation sensing setups, signals from different locations must be WIELAND AND PANKRATIUS: INERTIAL SIGNAL FORECASTING WITH FOUNDATION MODEL TECHNIQUES 36853 processed sequentially. A multi-input FM could address this by fusing signals from various locations directly but, on the other hand, reduces the flexibility in handling data from different sensor locations. The lack of data also limits the large-scale combination of signals from different recording modalities. IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK This article presents dual-view FM, a generative pretrained FM for signal forecasting. Dual-view FM learns global and local signal properties in the time and feature domains to build a deep understanding of human inertial signals. The global view identifies general trends in human inertial signals, while the local view addresses their spontaneous nature by individually analyzing short, sensor-specific signal frames. The evaluation demonstrates that dual-view FM excels in generating realistic signals and highlights the need for highly capable domain-specific FMs. Fine-tuning further improves the model’s generative capabilities, enabling it to outperform its pretrained counterparts and other neural networks consistently. Our findings imply that comprehensive insights into human inertial signals can contribute to more robust wearable HAR systems. Hence, we believe that research on cross-dataset generalization and FMs is crucial to enhance the robustness of future applications in pervasive real-world scenarios. Dual-view FM fuses the signals with meta-information regarding the on-body placement of sensors to get detailed insights into the interplay between human activities and body parts. In the future, the versatility of dual-view FM can be further improved by integrating more meta-information regarding the users and sensor configuration. This article also presents a large training corpus that consolidates inertial signals from eight publicly available benchmark datasets, featuring a variety of users, activities, and on-body sensor placements. While this diverse corpus is ideal for training and evaluating FMs for wearable HAR, selecting proper datasets from different sources and their alignment is tedious and time-consuming. To enable faster development of such FMs, we call for standardized presentations in future datasets, including comprehensive documentation of the data collection environment, sensor configuration (types, manufacturers), unified activity names, and unified sensor placements

## Abstract
Abstract Natural language processing (NLP) is a key technique for developing medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems that leverage electronic health record data to build diagnostic and prognostic models. NLP enables the conversion of unstructured clinical text into structured data that can be fed into AI algorithms. The emergence of transformer architecture and large language models (LLMs) has led to advances in NLP for various healthcare tasks, such as entity recognition, relation extraction, sentence similarity, text summarization, and question-answering. In this article, we review the major technical innovations that underpin modern NLP models and present state-of-the-art NLP applications that employ LLMs in radiation oncology research. However, it is crucial to recognize that LLMs are prone to hallucinations, biases, and ethical violations, which necessitate rigorous

## Introduction
Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare by improv­ ing patient outcomes, optimizing clinical workflows, and reduc­ ing costs.1 A key area where AI is rapidly evolving is precision medicine, which tailors personalized medical care to patients’ genes, environments, and lifestyles.2 Research in machine learning-based algorithms for the detection of disease-causing genetic mutations3 and individualized treatment protocols for patients4 is being developed and tested. Advanced AI models are being constructed within medicine for personalized disease prevention, care, and even prophylaxis. The ongoing trend of increased healthcare data collection will further aid innovative applications of these technologies in the future. Natural language processing (NLP) is a subclass of AI that enables machines to understand and interpret human language. The goal of NLP is to develop algorithms and models that are capable of processing, analysing, and generating natural lan­ guage text and speech. The history of natural language process­ ing dates back to the 1950s when early language translation programs were developed.5 However, limited computing power and lack of data slowed progress.6 The introduction of statisti­ cal

## Methodology
methods in the 1980s led to more sophisticated language models.7 The development of neural networks and deep learn­ ing in the 2010s led to significant advancements in NLP, culmi­ nating in the development of the famous transformer architecture in 2017.8 With the capabilities of the transformer architecture, a new breed of models emerged, referred to as large language models (LLMs). Notable LLMs include Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT),9 GPT-4, and ChatGPT. The development of these technologies has accelerated language processing and opened new possibilities for interacting with machines using natural language. Despite these advancements, LLMs are not without limitations, including biases that may lead to inequitable predic­ tions and hallucinations where models produce incorrect or nonsensical outputs. These issues highlight the importance of an effective evaluation framework to ensure the reliability and fairness of these models in clinical applications. The transformer architecture has paved the way for the de­ velopment of LLMs, which are now at the forefront of NLP research. ## Results
evaluation and validation prior to clinical de­ ployment. As such, we propose a comprehensive framework for assessing the NLP models based on their purpose and clinical fit, technical perfor­ mance, bias and trust, legal and ethical implications, and quality assurance prior to implementation in clinical radiation oncology. Our article aims to pro­ vide guidance and insights for researchers and clinicians who are interested in developing and using NLP models in clinical radiation oncology. Keywords: artificial intelligence; radiation oncology; natural language processing; large language models; personalized medicine.

## Conclusion
conclusions. Published NLP algo­ rithms are designed to work on specific tasks, with the em­ bedded assumption that the training and test data are generated from a similar statistical distribution. This assump­ tion may easily be violated in clinical scenarios, where input data may not match the statistical assumptions, and the algo­ rithm's stability under these inputs will be directly associated with the clinician's trust in them. To test for the predictability of outcomes, and an algorithm's stability, the concept of ad­ versarial testing can be used to estimate algorithm perfor­ mance under unstable inputs.94 There are several methods for performing adversarial testing, with the evasion method per­ haps being the most suitable for testing the edges of the NLP model.95 This testing would encompass actively modifying input data that represents the most extreme clinical scenario and analysing the algorithm output for (1) transparency— does the model explain or interpret the outputs to specific inputs? (2) predictability—does it show the same result every time? (3) fairness—does the output represent a sensible answer that is rooted in the representation of all sub-groups within the clinical setting?96 Legal and ethical considerations Legal and regulatory frameworks ensure the safe and ethical use of AI algorithms in healthcare. These address the potential risks and challenges and cover 3 main aspects of AI develop­ ment and deployment, namely, how medical devices are regu­ lated, how health data privacy is protected, and how liability is assigned for any harm caused by faulty, erroneous, or unsafe algorithm recommendations.97 Algorithm regulation strictly follows the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidelines in the United States, and significant progress has been made by the regulatory agency in defining standards and guiding principles for AI algorithms. NLP algorithms, being a subclass of AI, will fall under the category of Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). The FDA has established a regulatory frame­ work IN 2019 for these devices ( medical%20devices/published/US-FDA-Artificial-Intelligenceand-Machine-Learning-Discussion-Paper.pdf), which pro­ poses a risk-based regulation based on the intended use of the device and the patient’s risk from inaccurate output. In 2021, the FDA proposed an action plan and guiding principles in collaboration with Canada and UK to ensure safe, effective and quality SaMD use ( software-medical-device-samd/artificial-intelligence-and-ma chine-learning-software-medical-device, gov/medical-devices/software-medical-device-samd/good-ma chine-learning-practice-medical-device-development-guidingprinciples). Recent publications have discussed the regulation of LLM-based chatbots as medical devices.98 Therefore, it is critical to understand the level of regulation for the device under consideration and the regulatory implications of the FDA to ensure effective clinical use. Health data privacy is critical as LLMs become more inte­ grated into clinical workflows. While HIPAA provides a foundational framework for protecting patient health infor­ mation, it has limitations with modern AI technologies. As noted by Rezaeikhonakdar et al,99 many AI tools and chat­ bots are not classified as HIPAA-covered entities or business associates, meaning patient interactions with systems like ChatGPT or Google Gemini may fall outside HIPAA’s pro­ tections. Even when these systems claim HIPAA compliance, risks such as re-identification of de-identified data remain, as highlighted in cases like Dinerstein v. Google,100 and these risks are compounded when large tech companies crossreference extensive data resources, potentially compromising patient confidentiality.101,102 Moreover, Marks and Haupt103 emphasize that HIPAA compliance alone may not protect patient data from misuse; chatbots can prompt users to disclose sensitive information, which may then be lever­ aged for unauthorized data sharing, targeted advertising, or discriminatory practices in insurance and employment. To mitigate these risks, developers must adopt rigorous data governance and transparent practices in data usage. Clinicians also play a key role by limiting the input of sensi­ tive data into these tools and ensuring they act as responsible data stewards, understanding how these systems manage and process information. Informed consent is essential, with patients needing to know how their data will be used, stored, and protected, thereby building trust and upholding ethical principles of autonomy and respect for patients.104 Additionally, robust liability systems must be established to 8 BJR|Artificial Intelligence, 2025, Volume 2, Issue 1 Downloaded from academic.oup.com/bjrai/article/2/1/ubaf010/8233698 by guest on 21 October 2026 address any harm caused by NLP algorithms, ensuring ac­ countability and patient safety.102,105 Quality assurance The technical and clinical performance of the model is esti­ mated during the commissioning process. A Quality Management Program (QMP) details the performance tests, frequency of testing, expected outputs, and plan of action for inadequate performance. Further, it should include a quality improvement section, where the inadequate performance of the algorithm under routine use can be evaluated and dis­ cussed in detail to ensure safe and quality clinical care. As such, QMP can be divided into routine quality assurance and case-specific testing for quality improvement.106 Routine quality assurance must be performed periodically with a sta­ ble reference dataset every time to ensure the stability of out­ puts. Ideally, the reference data is a subset of the data that is utilized during the commissioning process and is representa­ tive of routine clinical data and use cases. This step should also be used for the clinical release of a device after downtime or minor changes, such as changes in computation hardware. A comprehensive data logging system is recommended for the structured collection of algorithm input, output, and stabil­ ity. This should be a pivotal piece of the quality improvement component, whereby the unexpected performance by the al­ gorithm can be traced back to the inputs, and root cause analysis can be performed to uphold safe and quality-driven clinical care. A review of case-specific performance further allows for the identification of model limitations that can fa­ cilitate future model revisions.106 We believe that new and emergent use cases for the algorithm should be evaluated fully by testing purpose, clinical fit, commissioning, and qual­ ity assurance plan as outlined in section “Framework for clin­ ical implementation” This rigorous step will ensure that the algorithm performance is suitable to ensure safe and highquality clinical care. Real-world validation of the framework for clinical implementation The proposed framework is validated by research studies employing similar methodologies. Walker et al49 developed an NLP tool to standardize free-text treatment site documen­ tation in radiation oncology EMRs, using domain-specific dictionaries and error correction to achieve superior precision and recall, thereby aligning with the framework’s emphasis on defining purpose and clinical fit. Similarly, Hong et al50 demonstrated the commissioning process with an NLP pipe­ line for automating toxicity data abstraction, achieving high accuracy for toxicities like radiation dermatitis and fatigue while addressing challenges with negated symptoms to guide iterative improvements in performance metrics, transparency, and fairness. Furthermore, Mathew et al107 integrated NLP and machine learning into an incident learning system, streamlining workflows, promoting a safety culture, and sup­ porting scalability through open-source pipelines and stan­ dard taxonomies, which reinforces the framework’s focus on routine and case-specific quality assurance. Together, these studies confirm that a structured approach encompassing purpose, clinical integration, commissioning, and quality as­ surance can successfully deploy NLP systems in radiation on­ cology, enhancing both operational efficiency and clinical outcomes while addressing key implementation challenges. Conclusion In this article, we have discussed the recent advances and applications of NLP in radiation oncology. NLP is a powerful tool that can transform unstructured clinical narratives into structured data for medical AI systems. NLP models utilizing LLMs and based on self-attention transformer architecture can perform multiple domain-specific tasks through transfer learning, which reduces the need for large annotated data sets and training burdens. These models demonstrate good per­ formance. However, before these models can be implemented and used in routine clinical care, they need to be rigorously evaluated for their validity, functionality, viability, safety, and ethical use. We have also proposed a framework that ra­ diation oncology clinicians can use to assess the suitability of NLP models for their needs. The checklist aptly discusses key areas of algorithm training, tuning, transparency and inter­ pretability, bias, and fairness, as well as legal and ethical con­ cerns. Overall, these novel NLP techniques can enable the creation of more advanced AI models, which can improve pa­ tient outcomes and expedite the progress of precision medi­ cine in radiation oncology under appropriate ethical and technical constraints. Table 1. Glossary of technical terms. Term Explanation Natural Language Processing (NLP) A field of artificial intelligence focused on enabling machines to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Large Language Models (LLMs) Advanced neural network models designed to process and generate text by analysing sequences of words, often with billions of parameters. Transformer Architecture A neural network architecture that uses self-attention mechanisms to process sequential data efficiently, allowing for parallel computation and long-range dependency modelling. Parameters (for LLMs) Numerical values in a neural network that are learned during training and define the behaviour of the model. LLMs can have billions (eg, 1B-405B) of parameters. Tokenization The process of breaking down text into smaller units, such as words or subwords, for model input. Embedding The representation of words or tokens as dense numerical vectors, capturing seman­ tic meaning. Positional Encoding Adds information about the order of tokens in a sequence, allowing transformers to process sequential data effectively. Transfer Learning A method where pre-trained models are adapted for specific tasks by fine-tuning on task-specific data. Fine-Tuning Adjusting the parameters of a pre-trained model on a smaller, domain-specific dataset to improve performance for specific tasks. Zero-Shot Learning The ability of a model to perform tasks without explicit training on them, relying on pre-trained knowledge. Few-Shot Learning The ability of a model to learn and generalize from a small amount of labelled data for a new task. Encoder-Only Models Models like BERT that analyse entire input texts at once and excel in context-based tasks. Decoder-Only Models Models like GPT that generate text by predicting the next word based on preceding words. Encoder-Decoder Models Models like T5 and BART that combine encoding and decoding capabilities for both understanding and generating text. Named Entity Recognition (NER) An NLP task where specific entities (eg, names, dates) are identified and classified in text. Self-Attention Mechanism A technique used in transformers that calculates the relevance of each word in a sequence to every other word, enabling context understanding. Scaled Dot-Product Attention A mathematical operation in transformers that calculates the importance of tokens relative to others in a sequence. Residual Connections Techniques used in neural networks to improve gradient flow and training stability by adding the input of a layer to its output. Layer Normalization A method to stabilize and accelerate training by normalizing layer inputs. Adversarial Testing A technique to evaluate model robustness by testing on edge cases or perturbed inputs. BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) A metric used to evaluate the quality of machine-generated text by comparing it to human-generated references. Rouge Metrics Metrics that evaluate the overlap between machine-generated and human-generated summaries to assess summarization quality. Hugging Face Transformers Library A popular open-source library for NLP that provides pre-trained models and tools for fine-tuning. Google TensorFlow An open-source machine learning framework for building and deploying AI models. Meta PyTorch An open-source machine learning library known for its flexibility and efficiency in building deep learning models.
