Others imagined using it to find evidence of change early in treatment (e.g., indications of more energy or better sleep) as a patient struggled with whether to continue a particular medication or therapy. One therapist gave an example of how she might, through discussion with a patient, tie a concern such as relationship anxiety to the average duration of phone use periods and then use that metric to assess whether therapy was helping with the patient’s anxiety. Several imagined using it not only for retrospective analysis but also to forecast improvement. Another envisioned use was asking the model questions during sessions to boost creativity, e.g., when challenging a patient’s worries or negative thoughts. Across these and other forms of collaborative use, some clinicians wanted their patients to be able to query the model. In addition to identifying patterns, joint use was envisioned as a way to build a more general feeling of collaboration in the therapy, something that is important for the therapeutic alliance and positive outcomes [12, 40]. 4.6.2 Identifying Issues to Explore with the Patient. Clinicians appreciated the model’s ability to list concerns with references to specific dates (e.g., days with little sleep or little movement). One clinician shared that it would be useful for GPT-4 to prioritize the questions. Clinicians suggested that they would share their observations with patients, e.g., about particular days with anomalies such as decreased sleep, as a way of opening up discussions and jogging the patient’s memory. When discussing potential concerns, clinicians wanted the model to raise questions and supply clear data. As one clinician said, the model "Could cause less harm if it provided questions for a therapist to ask instead of conclusions for a therapist to rely on" (P8). They did not want the model to apply diagnostic labels to individuals or their behaviors. 4.6.3 Generating Documentation. Clinicians varied in their thoughts on whether models would meaningfully aid in documentation. One participant appreciated the neutral boilerplate language the model used and easily imagined it as the basis for an intake summary. Another had already started using AI software to aid in documentation of sessions. Others bristled at this idea, pointing out that the LLM might miss major insights and obviate the analysis that comes from writing notes. 4.6.4 Concerns. Clinicians raised additional concerns related primarily to privacy and quality of care. From Classification to Clinical Insights • 56:13 Privacy. As clinicians considered inputs, such as patient mood logs, that would increase the model’s relevance to mental health, they grappled with privacy and other ethical concerns. One clinician worried that it could be hard to obtain meaningful informed consent. Even if a model were secure and compliant with relevant patient privacy regulations, it could be difficult for therapists to explain how the system worked and what protections it afforded. Quality of Care. Another concern pertained to relying on the model as a shortcut. Clinicians imagined the problems that could arise from overconfidence in the model’s analysis. One clinician described the possibility of missing the insights that would come from pouring over data herself: “If I was...doing this very quickly, like, before I see the client, I could totally see myself or anyone...just relying on on GPT-4. And just think... ’This is the answer. This is the knowledge,’... as mental shortcuts as opposed to pouring over the data yourself.... And I would want to ask, ‘Am I missing anything?’ (P6). Another clinician worried that not taking the time to write one’s own notes and process each session could degrade the their memory of the session and ultimately shortchange the therapy. And contrasted her efforts to examine contextual factors, such as family conflict, with a model’s narrower focus on symptoms. She noted that if relying solely on a model’s observations, a clinician could overlook important factors in assessing and treating mental health struggles. 5 DISCUSSION Our findings reveal a paradigm shift based on the value LLMs can bring to mental health care, switching from a focus of using computational tools for diagnostic classification to using them to generate clinical reasoning. Most prior ML research in mental health has focused on classification, or predicting the diagnostic category determined by a clinical interview or score on a self-report inventory such as the PHQ. While these coarse categorizations have a role in mental health care, they do not capture the specifics of a particular patient’s struggles and are insufficient to meaningfully guide treatment. Therapeutic change relies on the patient becoming aware of their patterns and options for changing them: it is an active collaboration rather than a procedure performed on a patient based on a particular diagnosis. Further, therapy is hyper-personalized, grounded in each patient’s specific concerns, goals, contexts, and dynamics. Our findings indicate that LLMs have the potential to illuminate an individual’s patterns by analyzing disparate sensor data that is otherwise unwieldy for clinicians to interpret. Unlike a diagnostic wizard used before treatment, LLMs can bring value in-session and throughout treatment. Instead of being used solely by the clinician or another professional in a care system, LLMs can be used collaboratively by the patient and clinician. In this vision, the LLM does not replace the clinician or replace dialogue between the clinician and patient. Instead, the LLM facilitates their dialogue, the alliance that supports change, and their investigation of the patient’s patterns. Below, we first discuss the challenges of using LLMs for classification followed by further steps needed to develop end-to-end tools for the proposed clinician-patient-AI collaborative therapy. 5.1 Challenges of Depression Classification This study illuminated new approaches to and challenges of screening for depression based on mobile health data. Our best-performing method for classifying depression was incorporating chain-of-thought (COT) prompting and variable explanations with the PaLM 2 model, achieving an accuracy of 61.11% on our class-balanced dataset. Although this represents a modest improvement over classical ML methods such as Random Forest and the state-of-the-art Reorder [74] method on this dataset, this level of accuracy is still far too low to be useful as a clinical screening tool. It is important to note that personalized depression forecasting approaches where model training data includes historical data from test set individuals report accuracy as high as 90.1% [35], but a reliance on extensive prior labeled data for each given individual significantly limits real-world utility. 56:14 • Englhardt and Ma, et al. In our experiments, we utilized a class-balanced dataset, as described in Section 3.1.2. This provides an indication of performance across an even distribution of individuals with potential PHQ-4 scores. With an unbalanced dataset constructed from all complete samples in the Globem dataset, the distribution would include 34.8% positive samples as opposed to 50%. With this distribution, we would expect to see a shift in the optimal prompting strategies, improving performance for direct prediction and COT prompting methods more likely to classify samples as not depressed and further decreasing performance of prompting strategies, including DSM-V depression criteria. We also attempted experiments to predict severity through a variety of methods, such as asking the LLMs to select a PHQ-4 score between 0 and 12 or options ranging from "none" to "severe" with varying degrees of additional context. In these instances, though, we notice that all three LLMs always select the middle value of the provided range. This result aligns with the findings of other works, which show that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 both require few-shot prompting with multiple labelled input examples to perform these types of regression tasks [31]. We forego few-shot prompting experiments for this work since they would require either the individual to track PHQ-4 scores as ground-truth, which is the variable we are trying to predict with the LLM in the first place, or use labelled data excerpts from other participants, which raises the challenging question of how to source representative samples from existing datasets to use for a new individual. 5.2 Managing Inaccuracy in a Clinical Context Clinicians in our study expressed a strong preference for LLMs to generate observations and insights about data relating to a patient rather than apply diagnostic labels. Such usage of LLM-based tools for generative reasoning avoids the challenges of inaccurate classification, but inaccuracies still need to be managed. In particular, welldocumented numerical inaccuracies may impact the quality of the generated reasoning. In our study, reasoning responses generated by GPT-4, based on a 448-element table (16 features x 28 days), contain at least one numerical error 25% of the time. The necessary accuracy and tolerance for inaccuracy may vary with applications of the LLM. For example, an inaccuracy in a question that is generated for the therapist to ask a patient may pose less risk than an error in a definitive statement that informs a clinician’s impressions of a patient’s mental state. These risks of inaccuracy may be mitigated by uses that prioritize the therapeutic relationship and the patient’s perspective. The clinicians in this study anticipated that they would use LLM-based tools in collaboration with patients, drawing on the tool’s observations as a starting point for discussion. They emphasized that their treatment decisions and diagnoses would be based on their direct patient interactions. 5.3 Supporting Clinician-Patient-AI Collaboration Supporting the kind of collaboration we propose between clinicians, patients, and AI will require new approaches to LLM hosting and data protection. This is due in part to the sensitivity of the data required. To inform mental health treatment and illuminate the factors associated with a particular individual’s struggles, models need to have data that are directly relevant to mental health and, ideally, personalized to individual patients. The clinicians we interviewed expected the model to have, at a minimum, daily mood and symptom tracking and ideally more in-depth data related to mood, social interactions, and behavioral routines. In addition, a clinician may want to input materials such as session notes or transcripts, manuals, or other documents describing relevant mental health issues and treatments. Much of this potentially personally identifiable data is sensitive and not appropriate as an input for existing LLM services such as ChatGPT, which may use this data to improve their models or for other commercial purposes. Privately hosted models or robust user data protections are required for this purpose. The solution to the privacy challenges of using LLMs in therapy is not as straightforward as it is for compliant medical record systems. Such record systems primarily serve providers and other employees at medical institutions, limiting patients to read-only access to elements such as test results. In this study, we heard from clinicians that From Classification to Clinical Insights • 56:15 both patients and clinicians should be able to interact with the model. This joint interaction, clinicians anticipated, could build patients’ curiosity about factors associated with their mental health and foster the collaborative alliance between patients and therapists that is associated with positive outcome [12, 40]. Such models therefore require a very different approach than that used for medical records; in this case, the patient should own their data, but both parties (the patient and therapist) should be able to generate data and actively interact with it. Meeting the computational requirements of hosting such services may be challenging for providers in smaller practices, while relying on third-party services raises questions about data ownership. Addressing these concrete privacy challenges will open the door for broader exploration. AI systems intended not just to produce a single diagnosis but rather to engage users in collaborative investigation over time will require new modes of interaction. This will pose research and design challenges in designing systems for use in mental health care and other contexts. 5.4 Limitations and Future Work 5.4.1 Dataset Generalization and Balancing. In our experiments, we utilize a class-balanced dataset confined to a subset of mobile and behavioral health data collected from undergraduate students at a single university over a three-year period. Future evaluations should seek to include both a broader range of data elements as well as data from more diverse population samples to better understand how well these approaches apply to any potential individual seeking mental health treatment. 5.4.2 Model and Prompting Bias. In addition to issues of population representation in the dataset, a growing body of work suggests that state-of-the-art LLMs are prone to producing output containing both implicit and explicit biases [20, 57]. This is further complicated by the sensitivity of classification performance to the specific information included in the prompt. For example, providing the DSM-V depression criteria results in GPT-4, which one may assume may improve depression classification, classifying 98.89% of data excerpts as depressed despite a class-balanced dataset. It is almost certain that prompt and model-specific biases exist in the generated reasoning about the provided mobile health data as well, but this is a significantly more complex problem to characterize. Benchmarking techniques are actively being explored in this area [48, 79], and further work to understand how these biases arise and can be mitigated are essential before deployment of LLMs mental health contexts. 5.4.3 Numerical Errors. Clinicians envisioned inputting both a wide range of additional features as well as a longer time period of data into LLMs for analysis. However, the maximum context window of these models is limited, and prior work has shown that the ability of LLMs to accurately recall detailed information from the entirety of the context window decreases as prompt length increases[37]. Pre-computing or summarizing portions of data could help address this technical challenge, but requiring this step could significantly reduce the ability of a tool to generalize across potential input data sources. Some errors observed by clinicians involved GPT-4 generating erroneous responses when asked follow-up questions that could not be answered based on the provided mobile health data. This challenge of grounding, or constraining LLM output to refer only to a relevant set of input text or data, is not unique to this specific application. Current approaches to improve performance in these areas include model fine-tuning[4]; augmenting a base general-purpose LLM with a smaller model optimized for a specific task[6]; and utilizing LLMs capable of querying external databases and tools to request data and perform arithmetic operations[21]. We view this third option as especially promising since enabling a model to access data from a user-controlled database may simultaneously help address the privacy challenges identified in Section 5.3. 5.4.4 Evaluation in Clinical Settings. While we find clinicians were frequently able to identify errors generated by GPT-4 when they arose during our interviews, in an actual therapy session the clinician may not be able to 56:16 • Englhardt and Ma, et al. balance the demands of critically evaluating model output while engaging with the patient. Additionally, our current work solely evaluates LLM use in therapy from the perspective of clinicians. Further evaluation in a more realistic therapeutic environment is needed to better understand how use of LLMs as part of a mental health treatment program could impact patients and their outcomes. 6 CONCLUSION This paper examines LLMs in the context of mental health care, specifically psychotherapy. While we begin our investigation by developing methods to use LLMs to output binary classifications for conditions like depression, we find instead that their greatest potential value to clinicians lies not in diagnostic classification, but rather in rigorous analysis of diverse self-tracking data to generate natural language summaries synthesizing multiple data streams and identifying potential concerns. Clinicians envisioned using those insights in a variety of ways, principally for fostering collaborative investigation with patients. This collaboration was seen as potentially valuable for strengthening the therapeutic alliance and guiding treatment. We describe a human-AI collaborative model and its requirements for secure management of personal data. These findings highlight directions for impactful future research on human-AI collaborative tools in mental health care and other contexts. Finally, different flashing paradigms have been developed to decrease trial time [12] and to improve signal classification [13]. While the P300 speller is designed to provide a means for communication, most attempts at system optimization have not taken advantage of existing knowledge about the language domain. Existing analyses treat character selections as independent elements chosen from a set with no prior information. In practice, we can use information about the domain of natural language to create a prior belief about the characters to be chosen. By adding a bias to the system based on this prior, we hypothesize that both system speed and accuracy can be improved. Statistical natural language processing (NLP) is an engineering field dedicated to achieving computer understanding of natural language. One application often used in domains such as speech recognition is to apply a language model to create probabilities for different interpretations of an input audio signal [14]. We can use this method in a BCI system by finding the probabilities of all possible continuations of the text entered in previous trials. This probability provides a prior for subsequent character selections so that text agreeing with the language model is more likely to be selected. This study exploits prior information using NLP to improve the speed and accuracy of the P300 speller. The system will determine the confidence of a classification by weighting the output of the SWLDA algorithm with prior probabilities provided by a language model. The number of flashes used to classify a character is dynamically set based on the amount of time required for the system to reach a predetermined confidence threshold. 2. Methods The subjects were six healthy male graduate students and faculty with normal or corrected to normal vision between the ages of 20 and 35. Only one subject (subject 2) had previous BCI experience. The system used a six by six character grid, row and column flashes, an ISI of 125 ms, and a flash duration that varied between 31.25 and 62.5 ms. Each subject underwent nine trials consisting of spelling a five letter word (Table 1) with 15 sets of 12 flashes (six rows and six columns) for each letter. The choice of target words for this experiment was independent of the language model used in the NLP method. BCI2000 was used for data acquisition and analysis was performed offline using MATLAB (version 7.10.0, MathWorks, Inc, Natick, MA). Three analysis methods were compared: a static method where the number of flashes is predetermined, a dynamic method that uses a threshold probability and a uniform prior, and an NLP method that incorporates a character trigram language model. 2.1. Static Method SWLDA is a classification algorithm that selects a set of signal features to include in a discriminant function [15]. Training is performed using nine-fold cross-validation where the test set is one of the trial words and the other eight are the training set. The signals in the training set are then assigned labels based on two classes: those corresponding to flashes containing the attended character and those without the attended character. Each new signal is then reduced to a score that reflects how similar it is to the attended class. The algorithm uses ordinary least-squares regression to predict class labels for the training set. It then adds the features that are most significant in the forward stepwise analysis and removes the least significant features in the backward analysis step. These steps are repeated Speier et al. Evaluation Evaluation of a BCI system must take into account two factors: the ability of the system to achieve the desired result and the amount of time required to reach that result. The efficacy of the system can be measured as the selection accuracy, which we evaluated by dividing the number of correct selections by the total number of trials. For each model we also calculated the selection rate (SR). First, the average amount of time for a selection is found by adding the gap between flashes (3.5 s) to the product of the amount of time required for a flash (.125 s), the average number of sets of flashes (s̄), and the number of flashes in each set (12). The selection rate measured in selections per minute is then the inverse of the average selection time. Since there is a tradeoff between speed and accuracy, we also use bit rate as a metric which takes both into account. The bits per symbol, B, is a measure of how much information is transmitted in a selection taking into account the accuracy and the number of possible selections [21]. Where N is the number of characters in the grid (36) and P is the selection accuracy. The bit rate (in bits/minute) can then be found by multiplying the selection rate by the bits per symbol. Significance was tested using paired two-sample t-tests with 5 degrees of freedom. Although the number of flashes was fixed for all trials, different selection rates were simulated by limiting the amount of data available for the classification algorithm. For example, if the confidence threshold is reached after six sets of flashes, the classification algorithm only uses the data from the first six sets and omits the remaining nine. 3. Results 3.1. Static Method Using the static method, all subjects were able to type with varying levels of performance. The best performer (subject 1) was able to achieve 95% accuracy after 3 sets of flashes, while the worst performer (subject 5) reached a maximum of 82% after 15 flashes. The accuracy increased with the number of flashes for all subjects and five out of six were able to exceed 90% accuracy within 15 sets of flashes (Fig. 1 and 2). The optimal number of sets of flashes varied from 3 to 8, which yielded bit rates from 12.86 to 35.10 (Table 2). In general, subjects that performed better achieved an optimal bit rate in fewer flashes (Fig. 3). On average, the subjects had a 36% accuracy after a single set of flashes which increased to about 95% after 15 sets (Fig. 1). The average selection rate for the static method was 5.91, the average accuracy was 82.97%, and the average bit rate was 22.07. Speier et al. Page 5 J Neural Eng. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2013 February 01. NIH-PA Author Manuscript NIH-PA Author Manuscript NIH-PA Author Manuscript 3.2. Dynamic Method Score distributions were found by taking the histograms of the scores from the attended and non-attended signals for each subject (Fig. 4). Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for normality were performed to verify our Gaussian assumption and none were found to be significant after Šidák correction for multiple comparisons. While the shape of the distributions was similar for all subjects, some exhibited better separation between the attended and nonattended scores (Fig. 4(a)). The maximum bit rates using dynamic classification improved by 25% overall (p=0.003), ranging from 8% (subject 5) to 36% (subject 3) compared to the static method (Table 2). On average, the accuracy and selection rate trended upward, but were not statistically significant (p=0.11 and p=0.23 respectively). In some cases, however, a decreased accuracy (subject 1) or selection rate (subject 4) was reported for the dynamic method relative to the static method because of the optimization based on bit rate. In these cases, the optimal bit rate may occur at a lower accuracy but a much higher selection rate or vice versa. 3.3. NLP method As the threshold probability varied for the NLP method, it achieved the best accuracies for any given selection rate (Fig. 2). Four of the subjects had 100% accuracies within 9 sets of flashes and subject 4 had all characters but one correct within 6 sets of flashes. Only subject 5 failed to reach 90% accuracy, but an improvement to 84% accuracy was seen within 6 sets of flashes. The overall improvement from the static method to the NLP method was between 40% and 60% for each subject. The average bit rate across subjects improved by 50% from 22.07 to 33.15 (p=0.0008). The accuracy increased from 82.97% to 93.33% (p=0.03) and the selection rate trended up from 5.91 to 7.31, but was not statistically significant (p=0.06). 4. Discussion Current BCI communication systems ignore domain knowledge when processing natural language. Most systems also use static trial lengths so that all classifications are given the same amount of input information regardless of classification difficulty. Integration of dynamic classification and NLP addresses these shortcomings, improving performance in offline analysis. 4.1. Prior Knowledge and Dynamic Classification The dynamic method was able to improve speed by rendering a decision as soon as it became confident of a classification. At the same time, it increases accuracy by analyzing additional flashes to improve confidence in more challenging classifications. There is also the potential that faster feedback afforded by the dynamic method could improve user attentiveness, but this would require online analysis to observe. The NLP method added a prior probability to the dynamic method based on the language model. This helped the system reach the threshold probability more quickly by adding additional probabilistic information from the linguistic domain rather than presuming equal a priori probabilities for all characters. It also improved accuracy as it increased the probability of selections that were consistent with natural language. 4.2. Significant Advance The static method achieved an average bit rate of 22.07 across subjects, which is consistent with previous studies [13] [22]. Our dynamic method improves the bit rate by 25% on Speier et al. Page 6 J Neural Eng. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2013 February 01. NIH-PA Author Manuscript NIH-PA Author Manuscript NIH-PA Author Manuscript average to 27.69. Using the language model for prior probabilities increased the bit rate by 40–60 percent for each subject in this study for an average of 33.15. To put this in context, Townsend et al. reported an average bit rate increase of 19.85 to 23.17 using their improved flashing paradigm [13]. 4.3. Similar Work Serby et al. implemented a maximum likelihood (ML) method which varies the number of flashes used to classify a character using a threshold as in our dynamic method [10]. Their method differs in that it makes a decision when a target score is met rather than a confidence threshold. In situations where the classifier gives high scores to multiple characters, their method makes a decision if any of them exceed the target score. Since our method converts scores into a confidence probability, it continues flashing until there is enough information to confidently choose one of the characters. Ryan et al. created a system that attempted to take advantage of the language domain by adding suggestions for word completion [22]. Their system differs in that it does not use a language model, but instead performs dictionary lookups as characters are selected. This language information is incorporated into the user interface as several of the cells in their character matrix are reserved for word completions. Their approach has several limitations. Characters are removed from their interface to make room for word completions, resulting in a smaller possible output vocabulary and a reduced system bit rate. Also, their graphical interface was more complicated resulting in a lower reported accuracy. Nevertheless, their study showed that word completion can improve the speed of a BCI system, so it could be beneficial to use it in conjunction with our method. Since our system integrates the language information into the signal processing method and their changes are exclusively in the user interface, they are essentially parallel tracks that can be integrated. 4.4. Limitations and Future Directions More advanced models that better utilize knowledge of linguistic structure will likely provide even greater improvements than the work presented here. For example, a simple improvement would be to include a model with word probabilities. The corpus used in this study contains part of speech tags which could provide additional prior information. Discourse and context information can also be integrated into this system. The corpus used in this model was chosen because it is large enough to give reliable trigram counts and because it contains text samples from a variety of domains. Clinical implementations of this system may prefer corpora that are more specific to the patients’ needs. This method is independent of system parameters, grid size, and flashing paradigm, so it can be incorporated into most other systems as well. Also, the Naive Bayes method and language model prior can be combined with any classifier that returns a likelihood probability. Studying the effects of NLP in such systems remains as future work. This study was performed to demonstrate a proof of concept for the use of a language model in BCI communication. While the results are encouraging, it remains to be seen if the improvement in bit rate translates into improved performance in a live communication system. The next step is to implement NLP in an online system and to measure the realized bit rate increase. Speier et al. Page 7 J Neural Eng. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2013 February 01. NIH-PA Author Manuscript NIH-PA Author Manuscript NIH-PA Author Manuscript 5. Conclusion Natural language contains many well-studied structures and patterns. Understanding of this domain information can greatly improve the processing and creation of language. This study showed that utilizing natural language information can dramatically increase the speed and accuracy of a BCI communication system. ## Abstract
Abstract—The current worldwide use of generative models in the field of Artificial Intelligence creates new possibilities but also new challenges and problems. In such an interconnected world, data produced by machines can become part of the training phases of new Language Models (LMs), and this can result in a problem that some scholars are starting to call “model collapse”. In this paper, we discuss the problem from three points of view. Firstly, we show how the accumulation of data can cause a given probability distribution obtained through a sampling procedure to degenerate towards a single-state-like equilibrium as the iterations of accumulations go by. The second perspective concerns the analysis through semantic, syntactic and complexity theory-related measures of texts produced through a recursive procedure involving an LSTM that is driven by its own generated data. The aim is to measure the quality of the text and the possible level of degradation. The third point concerns the synthesis of a simplified differential model that frames this scenario in which the models feed themselves with their data and which allows do estimates, albeit rough, about the future. Computational

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION Many scholars are convinced that November 30th, 2022, will be remembered as a symbolic date, not only for researchers, academics, and enthusiasts in the field of Natural Language Processing and generative models. Starting from this date, also the general public was able to finally experience the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various domains. And this date, we venture to say, will be remembered as a cognitive revolution, on par with the invention of writing. Furthermore, this paved the way towards a “modern space race”, where a (limited) number of big players are competing to develop and release more and more powerful generative AI models, not only devoted to text generation, at an impressive and unprecedented speed. In fact, at the time of writing (i.e., in less than 3 years from November 30th, 2022), generative AI-based extensions are currently integrated in a vast array of everyday-life tools, from productivity and office suites to e-mail clients, video and image editing software. Without appearing overly didactic, we can say that machines have begun to ‘master’ (to a certain degree) human language and, as such, have started to acquire a knowledge representation of the world. This knowledge is not only mediated by language as written text but is also –thanks to multimodal models [1]– synthesized from heterogeneous corpora containing data structures such as text, images, video sequences, and even more complex ones. Staying within the context of language identified by textual corpora, to say that machines dominate language –to a certain degree– means that, thanks to the Transformer architectures [2] underpinning LLMs, it is possible to model systems of increasing complexity. Language is a complex system whose instances are produced by what some scientists consider the most complex system in the universe: the brain. In fact, language and text production can be thought as activities of complexly organized brains [3] and scholars are developing ever more useful methodologies to study language within the complex system framework [4]– [7]. As stated in [8], natural language is a system functioning at the interface between biology and social interactions. This is even more true with the advent of digital communication and the Internet [9]–[12] thanks to which humanity has seen an unprecedented proliferation of written material. Also thanks to this proliferation, it has been possible, after careful selection of the training corpus, to train current LLMs that show surprising linguistic and cognitive abilities [13], [14]. But those same digital technologies that have allowed the sharing of text and other knowledge material now available for training increasingly powerful models, can become one of the most serious threats to improving model performance, which in some cases can even degrade. This phenomenon has recently been defined as “model collapse” [15] and occurs when generative AIbased models produce data that contaminates the training set of subsequent models, causing a loss of variety and relevance in their outputs. This degenerative process can have negative effects on the quality and reliability of generative models and can lead to a distortion of “reality” represented in some way in the learning dataset. In other words, model collapse can be defined as a [15]: 2025 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN) | 979-8-3315-1042-8/25/$31.00

## Methodology
methodology show the phenomenon of model collapse from a new perspective, specifically through the intertwining of the complexity of the lexical and semantic structure and the correlation structure. The recursive training generally shows a decay trend in the information arrangement of the generated text, with an increase in randomness and the deterioration of the correlation structure (obtained with the multifractal analysis). However, some counterintuitive results can be explained only through an investigation that summarizes the trend of the indices as a whole. Alongside this main study, we present a collateral experiment in which the phenomenon of model collapse is shown on a toy problem both in the case of approximation and functional errors when during the retraining phases the dataset accumulates the generated data. Finally, we present a simplified mathematical model of the performance degradation of a generative model over time given several simple assumptions about the degradation structure of the model itself. This integro-differential model mimics the iterative process and allows estimating how long after performance drops beyond a certain threshold. We anticipate that the framework presented here demonstrates that text produced by models polluted by their own data can degrade and models can drift. This problem, although serious, appears far into the future for highperformance models. The paper is organized as follows: in Sec. II is reported a description of the “model collapse” phenomenon alongside a toy experiment. In Sec. III the iterative procedure is explained together with the semantic, syntactic and complexity indices adopted for the characterization of generated text excerpts during the recursive procedure. Sec. IV deals with the simulation settings and comments on the main results while Sec. VI trance the simplified differential model that grounds on the iteration procedure. Finally in Sec. VII

## Results
results show a model drift and degradation of the text structure that evolves towards simplified forms from the lexical point of view and degraded in terms of destruction of long-term correlations (one of the main ways to generate meaning in a sentence). Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the problem exists and, although far in the future thanks to the power of the modern architectures underlying LLMs, should not be underestimated. Index Terms—LSTM, Generative Models, Text Generation, Model Collapse, Model Drift, Complex Systems, Multifractal Analysis, Hurst Exponent, Data Quality, Model Bias. I.

## Conclusion
conclusions are drown. II. BACKGROUND ON MODEL DEGRADATION Shumailov et al. in [15] define the “model collapse” as a degenerative phenomenon in generative models across generations, where produced data corrupts their own training sets, causing subsequent models to misinterpret “reality”. The study distinguishes between early and late model collapse: the former involves losing information about the distribution’s tails, and the latter is marked by the merging of different modes of the original distribution, leading to a final model output that bears little resemblance to the original, often with reduced variance. Scholars focused on the phenomenon of model collapse in generative models: they also examined the impact of sampling errors in scenarios devoid of functional approximation errors (F(p) = p) and no data accumulation during the recursive process. A critical finding of their research was the disproportionate effect of sampling errors on the probability of rare events or low-probability states in a distribution. The study demonstrated that over time, these rare events tend to diminish and eventually disappear due to their low chances of being sampled. This loss of information about low-probability events leads the distribution to converge towards a δ-function, indicating a model collapse where the output becomes overly simplistic and unvaried. Hence, we have a significant influence of sampling errors on the integrity of generative models. To exemplify the effects of recursive training in a controlled setting, we conducted an experiment using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) to simulate data accumulation over successive iterations, for a large sampling size (1000 datapoints over 1000 iterations accumulating data at each loop). Starting from an initial distribution, we iteratively estimated a new probability density function using a KDE, generated new samples and incorporated them into the dataset for subsequent iterations. At each step, we measured changes in variance, Kullback–Leibler divergence, entropy, and tail amount to quantify how the estimated distribution evolved – see Fig. 1 and related insets. The results showed a progressive distortion of the original distribution, with increasing entropy and divergence, illustrating how recursive sampling can lead to the accumulation of noise and deviation from the initial data structure. In particular, we observed a reduction in rare events, with extreme values being underrepresented over iterations, leading to a decreasing variance in the estimated distributions (classical model collapse). The increase in entropy indicates that while the overall distribution enlarged in its middle range, it became less defined in its tails. This behavior reflects how recursive estimation reinforces frequent patterns while gradually eroding the contribution of less probable events. Fig. 1. Shumailov et al. in [15] theoretically and empirically analyze model collapse for different data and models, such as Gaussian sampling, Gaussian Mixture Models and Transformers for generating text. In [23], the authors conduct an empirical and analytical analysis on generative image models of what they refer as the ”self-consuming” or ”autophaguous” loop. They conclude that without enough fresh real data at each generation, future models necessarily will have their precision or recall decrease. In [24], researchers explore scenarios involving a mix of clean image data, representative of the true distribution, and synthesized data from previous iterations of the generator. Their analysis reveals that if the data mix consists exclusively of synthesized data, the generative process is likely to degenerate over time. A steady on linguistic diversity in a recursive training loop is proposed by Guo et. al. in [25]. The authors experiment with different metrics targeting lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity, finding a consistent decrease in the diversity of the model outputs through successive iterations. To our knowledge, there are no studies that have correlated linguistic features to indices derived from complexity theory within recursive training, such as the multifractal and entropy analysis presented in the proposed investigation. In general, there is strong attention on model drift and data degradation with a need to distinguish data generated by AI systems from ”natural” data [15]. III. RECURSIVE TRAINING, TEXT GENERATION AND EVALUATION OF A LSTM NETWORK Given a text corpus C, consisting of a sequence of N tokens {w1, w2,..., wN}, the objective is to train iteratively a stateful LSTM network to generate texts that learns the style and the temporal dependencies of C. To mimic the text generation process and the phenomenon by which the generated text is fed again in the new training process, hence “polluting” the starting corpus C, we synthesized a closed-loop procedure as follows–see also Algorithm 1: • An LSTM model is initialized with parameters tailored to suit the nature of the text corpus C. This model is designed to capture the temporal dependencies and stylistic nuances present in C; • The LSTM model is trained on the original corpus C learning to predict subsequent tokens based on the current context provided by the previous tokens; • At each iteration, the LSTM model generates a new text snippet Gi. This generation is guided by a seed text or context and is constrained by parameters like the maximum length of the generated text; • The generated text Gi is then appended to the original corpus C, resulting in an augmented corpus; • The LSTM model is retrained on such augmented corpus. This retraining allows the model to adapt to the newly generated data and refine its text generation capabilities; • After each iteration of text generation and model retraining, the newly generated text Gi is evaluated using a scoring function S. This function assesses the quality of Gi in terms of various metrics, which –in our case– include linguistic and complexity figures of merit. Algorithm 1 Iterative Text Generation and Training 1: C ←Initial text corpus 2: N ←Number of tokens in C 3: n ←Number of iterations 4: model ←Initialize LSTM model 5: Train LSTM model on C 6: for i ←1 to n do 7: Gi ←Generate text using the LSTM model 8: C ←C + Gi (Append generated text to corpus) 9: Retrain LSTM model on updated corpus C 10: Si ←Compute score S for Gi 11: Store evaluation metric Si for iteration i 12: end for A. Stateful Long Short-Term Memory In text generation tasks, especially when handling long sequences, stateful LSTM models are crucial. Their key feature is the ability to maintain context over multiple batches of data [26]–[28]. Unlike traditional LSTMs, stateful LSTMs carry forward the final states (memory and cell state) from one batch Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:35:28 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. to the initial states of the next batch. This continuous flow of information is essential when full sequences can not be processed at once due to memory constraints. For example, in text generation, where the context of previous words heavily influences the next words, a stateful LSTM remembers this context across batches. This means that if a sentence is split over multiple batches, the LSTM retains the context from the first part of the sentence while processing the second part, ensuring coherent and contextually relevant text generation. This approach allows the model to produce text that is not just coherent but also rich in context, mirroring human-like continuity and thematic consistency. B. From Text to Time Series To compute metrics useful for measuring the complexity of the text and how it varies during the various eras, the text must be transformed into a time series. In this work, we use an algorithm based on Zipf’s law. The algorithm – described in Algorithm 2 – begins by tokenizing the input text into words. It then counts the frequency of each unique word and sorts these words in descending order of their frequency. For each word in this sorted list, a rank is assigned based on its position in the list. Finally, the original sequence of words is transformed into a time series where each word is replaced with its corresponding rank, resulting in a ranked sequence that reflects the frequency distribution of words in the text according to Zipf’s law. Algorithm 2 Zipf’s Law Time Series Encoding 1: procedure ENCODEWITHZIPFSLAW(text) 2: tokens ←TOKENIZE(text) 3: freqMap ←COUNTFREQUENCIES(tokens) 4: sortedFreqs ←SORTBYFREQ(freqMap) 5: zipfTS ←MAPTORANKS(tokens, sortedFreqs) 6: return zipfTS 7: end procedure C. Text Quality Evaluation Metrics Cosine similarity: Cosine similarity can be adopted to quantitatively evaluate the resemblance between texts generated by the LSTM model and a predefined baseline text. This approach involves transforming each text into a vector using word-frequencies representation, which enables a mathematical comparison. Cosine similarity, specifically, measures the cosine of the angle between these vectors, effectively capturing the degree of overlap in their word frequencies. A higher similarity score indicates a greater alignment in terms of word usage and distribution, thus reflecting how closely each iteration’s output mirrors the baseline text. Frequency of Nouns and Verbs: Analyzing the frequency of nouns and verbs in texts generated by the LSTM model offers insights into the syntactic and thematic aspects of the generated content. Nouns predominantly contribute to the thematic depth, indicating the subjects and objects, while verbs characterize the actions and states, reflecting the dynamism of the text. By tracking how the frequencies of these parts of speech change over iterations, we can discern shifts in the narrative focus or action intensity in the LSTM’s output. This analysis helps in understanding whether the model maintains a consistent thematic and syntactic structure or evolves in its linguistic expression over time. Such a measure is crucial for evaluating the model’s ability to generate coherent and contextually relevant text. Average Sentence Length and Average Word Length: This analysis provides key insights into the linguistic complexity and readability of the content. Average sentence length, measured by the number of words per sentence, indicates the syntactic complexity, with longer sentences often suggesting more complex constructions. In contrast, the average word length, typically assessed by the number of characters or syllables per word, reflects lexical complexity, where longer words might denote a higher level of vocabulary sophistication. Monitoring changes in these metrics across iterations helps evaluate the model’s consistency in sentence construction and word choice, crucial factors for assessing the readability and stylistic variation of the generated text. Type-Token Ratio and Unique Tokens: The Type-Token Ratio (TTR) and the count of unique tokens in LSTMgenerated texts are instrumental in assessing the lexical diversity and richness of the content. TTR, calculated as the ratio of unique words (types) to the total number of words (tokens), serves as an indicator of lexical variety; a higher TTR suggests a wider range of vocabulary, implying more creative or varied language use. Conversely, the count of unique tokens directly quantifies the number of distinct words used, providing a straightforward measure of the text’s lexical scope. Analyzing these metrics over successive iterations helps in understanding whether the LSTM model is diversifying its language use over time or converging towards repetitive patterns, crucial for evaluating the model’s linguistic inventiveness and potential in generating engaging and varied content. ROUGE Score [29]: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) emphasizes recall, measuring how comprehensively the generated text captures the content of the baseline corpus. It is particularly effective in assessing the inclusion of key content from the reference. A decline in the ROUGE score across epochs can suggest a gradual loss of core content elements from the original text. D. Complexity Theory Indices These indices presented below and adopted for the characterization of the texts are estimated from the time series obtained from the text according to Zipf’s encoding presented in Sec. III-B. Hurst coefficient [30]: The Hurst coefficient quantifies the long-term memory of the series, reflecting the degree of autocorrelation or memory in a system [31]. In the context of text analysis, it can be used to evaluate the predictability or roughness of a text sequence. A Hurst coefficient value close to 0.5 indicates a random series, lacking long-term memory. Instead, a value greater than 0.5 suggests a persistent series, Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:35:28 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. where high values are likely followed by high values, and low by low, indicating trends or smoothness. Lastly, a value less than 0.5 indicates an anti-persistent series, characterized by alternating high and low values, suggesting a more rugged or complex structure. This coefficient provides insight into the underlying patterns of the text, revealing whether the structure of the text is more predictable or complex. Singularity Spectrum Width ∆α [32]: The length of the singularity spectrum, commonly denoted as ∆α in multifractal analysis, quantifies the diversity or variability of singularity strengths within a process represented by a time series [31]. In text analysis, it can be useful to evaluate the complexity or richness of a text. This measure is determined by calculating the fractal dimension of subsets of a measure with identical singularity strength α, and ∆α represents the range between the maximum and minimum values of α. A wider ∆α suggests a text with higher complexity, indicating a broader range of fluctuation types and strengths, which in turn implies intricate patterns of word usage and distribution. A smaller ∆α indicates more uniformity in the text structure. Approximate Entropy (ApEn) [33]: ApEn is a statistical measure used to characterize the complexity and predictability of sequences of data. In the context of text analysis, it is applied to a time series representation of the text, where it evaluates the likelihood that similar patterns of words or phrases will reoccur. A lower ApEn value suggests more predictability and less complexity in the text, indicating repetitive or less varied use of language. Conversely, a higher ApEn value signifies a higher degree of complexity and unpredictability, reflecting more diverse and intricate use of language. This measure is particularly useful for assessing the richness and variability in language use over different texts or within a text over time. Kolmogorov Complexity [34]: the Kolmogorov Complexity, named after Soviet mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov, is a measure of the computational complexity of an object, such as a piece of text, defined as the length of the shortest possible description of the object in some fixed universal description language. It quantifies the amount of information required to describe the object exactly. For texts, this can be thought of as a measure of how much information is packed into the text. In practical terms, a text with high Kolmogorov Complexity would be one that cannot be compressed much further without losing information, indicating a high level of originality and complexity. Conversely, texts with lower complexity can be more easily compressed, suggesting more repetition or predictability. Its real value is uncomputable, but a good approximation is provided by the GZIP lossless compression algorithm1. IV. V. GENERAL OVERVIEW AND DISCUSSION The analysis of the indices computed over successive iterations of the recursive training process reveals a gradual yet structured degradation in the generated text. The cosine similarity to the baseline corpus exhibits a slow but consistent decline, indicating that while the generated text retains a general resemblance to the original dataset, it progressively diverges. This divergence is further substantiated by the decrease in noun and verb frequencies, the reduction in both sentence and word length (with sentences being more affected), and the decline in TTR and unique token count. These trends suggest a progressive loss of lexical diversity and syntactic complexity, likely driven by the model’s reinforcement of high-probability words and structures over iterations. Despite this overall simplification, the ROUGE score paradoxically increases (it is an apparent paradox indeed), suggesting that the model continues to generate words that match those found in the original corpus. However, this increase does not imply improved text quality but rather a growing tendency to rely on frequent words, leading to an overrepresentation of high-probability lexical patterns. This is corroborated by the decreasing trend of the unique token count. The decrease in the Hurst coefficient reflects a weakening of long-range dependencies, further indicating that the model loses its ability to maintain structured, coherent sequences across extended text spans, with a degradation of the order underlying the temporal structure of the word sequences. Meanwhile, the slight increase in the multifractal spectrum width suggests that while the text undergoes structural degradation, certain localized variations in complexity persist, likely due to intermittency patterns. This effect is corroborated by the increase in approximate entropy, signifying that the generated sequences become less predictable, and by the significant rise in Kolmogorov complexity, which reflects an increase in randomness and reduced compressibility of the text. These observations collectively point to a progressive form of model collapse due to the interplay of sampling and functional approximation errors, where the text retains highfrequency lexical elements but loses syntactic richness, coherence, and structured dependencies over time. The accumulation of self-generated text in the training corpus introduces a feedback loop that amplifies common patterns while diminishing linguistic diversity and structural consistency. This suggests that while the model remains lexically anchored to the original corpus, as expected, it increasingly produces shorter, repetitive, and less structured sequences. VI. A SIMPLE THEORETICAL MODEL OF THE EVOLUTION TEXT QUALITY This section presents a mathematical model designed to analyze the impact of machine-generated text on the quality Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:35:28 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. of a mixed corpus, which includes both human-generated and machine-generated content. The focus is on scenarios where machine-generated text is recursively fed back into the training data, influencing subsequent text generation iterations, akin to the LSTM-based experiment presented in the previous Section. Hence, the scenario considers both humans –that, as usual, generate new genuine texts– and machine-generated texts. These texts are fed for training new LMs within an iterative process. Specifically, we describe the dynamics of the quality degradation using a first-order model, i.e., a differential equation, that encapsulates the rate of change of a generic quality score over time. The simplified model assumes that the degradation rate is influenced by the increasing proportion of machine-generated text in the corpus. The differential model can be written as: dQ dt = −α · MPR · t H + (HPR + MPR) · t · Q, (1) where dQ dt is the rate of change of the quality score Q over time, α is a constant reflecting the sensitivity of the quality score to the proportion of machine-generated text, MPR and HPR represent the machine and human text production rates, respectively, and finally, H is the initial size of the humanwritten corpus. The differential equation can be solved with the initial condition Q(t = 0) = Q0, where Q0 is the starting quality score. Now, integrating both sides concerning t, we find the solution in the form of an exponential function: Q(t) = Q0 · exp  −α Z MPR · t H + (HPR + MPR) · tdt , (2) where the integral represents the accumulated impact of the increasing proportion of machine-generated text in the corpus over time. 0.000 0.005 0.010 0.015 0.020 0.025 0.030 Alpha Value 0 200 400 600 800 1000 Time to Reach Threshold (Years) Time to Reach Threshold Quality Score for Different Alpha Values Fig. 6. Time to reach the threshold quality score for different α values. Now let us arrange a numerical example making suitable and simplified assumptions on initial conditions: • Initial Quality Score (Q0): 0.8; • Threshold Quality Score (QT ): 0.5; • Human Text Production Rate (HPR): 106 words/year; Fig. 7. Quality score degradation over time for various α values. • Machine Text Production Rate (MPR): 5 × 106 words/year; • Initial Corpus Size (H): 107 words; • Decay Constant (α): 0.001. Under these assumptions, the model predicts that it will take approximately 566 years for the quality score to drop below the threshold of 0.5 (59 years if α is set to 0.01). This result illustrates the impact of the parameters, particularly the rate of machine text production and the decay constant, on the longevity of text quality in a corpus influenced by machinegenerated content. In Fig. 6 we plot the time to reach the threshold quality score for different α values, while Fig. 7 represents the quality score degradation over time for various α values, under the same assumptions. VII. CONCLUSION In this study, we explored in a multifaceted way the problem of “model collapse” or “model drift” from the perspective of complexity. With a simplistic experiment where a stateful LSTM model is trained recursively on text produced on preceding iteration(s), hence mimicking the accumulation over time of data produced by machine learning systems, specifically in generative contexts. This is an issue that in principle can arise considering the large and worldwide diffusion of generative models in performing daily tasks where generated data can be shared and uploaded across the Internet. Our analysis grounding on semantic, syntactic and complex system analysis on recursively generated texts demonstrated how the model tends to degrade over iterations, highlighting a problem that if not deemed serious (yet), is still to be taken into consideration. Notably, the application of multifractal indices, such as the Hurst exponent and the Singularity Spectrum width, alongside other textual measurements, proved effective in evaluating the behavior of language models during the training evolution. Specifically “model collapse” can happen if the data sampling is scarce or also if the model is showing large approximation errors. We find that the recursively-produced text became, as Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:35:28 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. iterations go by, more random and less rich in lexical structure, generating a bias towards the main content. The long-range correlation structure is slightly destroyed indicating a decrease in meaning content. The mathematical model we presented alongside the empirical study is a simplified differential tool for estimating the degradation over time and if the degradation rate is low, as expected for LLMs, problems can arise very far in the future. In any case, as is known, data quality is an essential factor for the performance of LLMs, especially concerning bias. However, we acknowledge certain limitations in our study, such as the usage of a LSTM architecture (e.g., instead of a Transformer-based one) due to computational constraints. These limitations highlight the need for more studies within heterogeneous settings comparing different (L)LM architectures. Also, the differential model is a simplified version of what can happen in reality, and more complex models can help to perform scenario analysis. In conclusion, our research provides a starting point together with other studies in the direction of studying the evolution of (L)LM when polluted with its own data generated over time. It underscores the importance of assessing the quality of models and sets the stage for future works in this area, specifically on model drift and collapse. We plan to assess the quality and the behavior within the recursive procedure of more complex and performing LLMs, testing also other quality indexes to shape the model behavior when polluted with its own generated data

They conclude that without enough fresh real data at each generation, future models necessarily will have their precision or recall decrease. In [24], researchers explore scenarios involving a mix of clean image data, representative of the true distribution, and synthesized data from previous iterations of the generator. RECURSIVE TRAINING, TEXT GENERATION AND EVALUATION OF A LSTM NETWORK Given a text corpus C, consisting of a sequence of N tokens {w1, w2,..., wN}, the objective is to train iteratively a stateful LSTM network to generate texts that learns the style and the temporal dependencies of C. To mimic the text generation process and the phenomenon by which the generated text is fed again in the new training process, hence “polluting” the starting corpus C, we synthesized a closed-loop procedure as follows–see also Algorithm 1: • An LSTM model is initialized with parameters tailored to suit the nature of the text corpus C. This model is designed to capture the temporal dependencies and stylistic nuances present in C; • The LSTM model is trained on the original corpus C learning to predict subsequent tokens based on the current context provided by the previous tokens; • At each iteration, the LSTM model generates a new text snippet Gi. This generation is guided by a seed text or context and is constrained by parameters like the maximum length of the generated text; • The generated text Gi is then appended to the original corpus C, resulting in an augmented corpus; • The LSTM model is retrained on such augmented corpus. This retraining allows the model to adapt to the newly generated data and refine its text generation capabilities; • After each iteration of text generation and model retraining, the newly generated text Gi is evaluated using a scoring function S. This function assesses the quality of Gi in terms of various metrics, which –in our case– include linguistic and complexity figures of merit. Algorithm 1 Iterative Text Generation and Training 1: C ←Initial text corpus 2: N ←Number of tokens in C 3: n ←Number of iterations 4: model ←Initialize LSTM model 5: Train LSTM model on C 6: for i ←1 to n do 7: Gi ←Generate text using the LSTM model 8: C ←C + Gi (Append generated text to corpus) 9: Retrain LSTM model on updated corpus C 10: Si ←Compute score S for Gi 11: Store evaluation metric Si for iteration i 12: end for A. Stateful Long Short-Term Memory In text generation tasks, especially when handling long sequences, stateful LSTM models are crucial. Their key feature is the ability to maintain context over multiple batches of data [26]–[28]. Unlike traditional LSTMs, stateful LSTMs carry forward the final states (memory and cell state) from one batch Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:35:28 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. to the initial states of the next batch. This continuous flow of information is essential when full sequences can not be processed at once due to memory constraints. For example, in text generation, where the context of previous words heavily influences the next words, a stateful LSTM remembers this context across batches. This means that if a sentence is split over multiple batches, the LSTM retains the context from the first part of the sentence while processing the second part, ensuring coherent and contextually relevant text generation. This approach allows the model to produce text that is not just coherent but also rich in context, mirroring human-like continuity and thematic consistency. B. From Text to Time Series To compute metrics useful for measuring the complexity of the text and how it varies during the various eras, the text must be transformed into a time series. In this work, we use an algorithm based on Zipf’s law. The algorithm – described in Algorithm 2 – begins by tokenizing the input text into words. It then counts the frequency of each unique word and sorts these words in descending order of their frequency. For each word in this sorted list, a rank is assigned based on its position in the list. Finally, the original sequence of words is transformed into a time series where each word is replaced with its corresponding rank, resulting in a ranked sequence that reflects the frequency distribution of words in the text according to Zipf’s law. Algorithm 2 Zipf’s Law Time Series Encoding 1: procedure ENCODEWITHZIPFSLAW(text) 2: tokens ←TOKENIZE(text) 3: freqMap ←COUNTFREQUENCIES(tokens) 4: sortedFreqs ←SORTBYFREQ(freqMap) 5: zipfTS ←MAPTORANKS(tokens, sortedFreqs) 6: return zipfTS 7: end procedure C. Text Quality Evaluation Metrics Cosine similarity: Cosine similarity can be adopted to quantitatively evaluate the resemblance between texts generated by the LSTM model and a predefined baseline text. This approach involves transforming each text into a vector using word-frequencies representation, which enables a mathematical comparison. Cosine similarity, specifically, measures the cosine of the angle between these vectors, effectively capturing the degree of overlap in their word frequencies. A higher similarity score indicates a greater alignment in terms of word usage and distribution, thus reflecting how closely each iteration’s output mirrors the baseline text. Frequency of Nouns and Verbs: Analyzing the frequency of nouns and verbs in texts generated by the LSTM model offers insights into the syntactic and thematic aspects of the generated content. Nouns predominantly contribute to the thematic depth, indicating the subjects and objects, while verbs characterize the actions and states, reflecting the dynamism of the text. By tracking how the frequencies of these parts of speech change over iterations, we can discern shifts in the narrative focus or action intensity in the LSTM’s output. This analysis helps in understanding whether the model maintains a consistent thematic and syntactic structure or evolves in its linguistic expression over time. Such a measure is crucial for evaluating the model’s ability to generate coherent and contextually relevant text. Average Sentence Length and Average Word Length: This analysis provides key insights into the linguistic complexity and readability of the content. Average sentence length, measured by the number of words per sentence, indicates the syntactic complexity, with longer sentences often suggesting more complex constructions. In contrast, the average word length, typically assessed by the number of characters or syllables per word, reflects lexical complexity, where longer words might denote a higher level of vocabulary sophistication. Monitoring changes in these metrics across iterations helps evaluate the model’s consistency in sentence construction and word choice, crucial factors for assessing the readability and stylistic variation of the generated text. Type-Token Ratio and Unique Tokens: The Type-Token Ratio (TTR) and the count of unique tokens in LSTMgenerated texts are instrumental in assessing the lexical diversity and richness of the content. TTR, calculated as the ratio of unique words (types) to the total number of words (tokens), serves as an indicator of lexical variety; a higher TTR suggests a wider range of vocabulary, implying more creative or varied language use. Conversely, the count of unique tokens directly quantifies the number of distinct words used, providing a straightforward measure of the text’s lexical scope. Analyzing these metrics over successive iterations helps in understanding whether the LSTM model is diversifying its language use over time or converging towards repetitive patterns, crucial for evaluating the model’s linguistic inventiveness and potential in generating engaging and varied content. ROUGE Score [29]: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) emphasizes recall, measuring how comprehensively the generated text captures the content of the baseline corpus. It is particularly effective in assessing the inclusion of key content from the reference. A decline in the ROUGE score across epochs can suggest a gradual loss of core content elements from the original text. D. Complexity Theory Indices These indices presented below and adopted for the characterization of the texts are estimated from the time series obtained from the text according to Zipf’s encoding presented in Sec. III-B. Hurst coefficient [30]: The Hurst coefficient quantifies the long-term memory of the series, reflecting the degree of autocorrelation or memory in a system [31]. In the context of text analysis, it can be used to evaluate the predictability or roughness of a text sequence. A Hurst coefficient value close to 0.5 indicates a random series, lacking long-term memory. Instead, a value greater than 0.5 suggests a persistent series, Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 21,2026 at 17:35:28 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. where high values are likely followed by high values, and low by low, indicating trends or smoothness. Lastly, a value less than 0.5 indicates an anti-persistent series, characterized by alternating high and low values, suggesting a more rugged or complex structure. This coefficient provides insight into the underlying patterns of the text, revealing whether the structure of the text is more predictable or complex. Singularity Spectrum Width ∆α [32]: The length of the singularity spectrum, commonly denoted as ∆α in multifractal analysis, quantifies the diversity or variability of singularity strengths within a process represented by a time series [31]. In text analysis, it can be useful to evaluate the complexity or richness of a text. This measure is determined by calculating the fractal dimension of subsets of a measure with identical singularity strength α, and ∆α represents the range between the maximum and minimum values of α. A wider ∆α suggests a text with higher complexity, indicating a broader range of fluctuation types and strengths, which in turn implies intricate patterns of word usage and distribution. A smaller ∆α indicates more uniformity in the text structure. This measure is particularly useful for assessing the richness and variability in language use over different texts or within a text over time. Conversely, texts with lower complexity can be more easily compressed, suggesting more repetition or predictability. V. GENERAL OVERVIEW AND DISCUSSION The analysis of the indices computed over successive iterations of the recursive training process reveals a gradual yet structured degradation in the generated text. The cosine similarity to the baseline corpus exhibits a slow but consistent decline, indicating that while the generated text retains a general resemblance to the original dataset, it progressively diverges. This divergence is further substantiated by the decrease in noun and verb frequencies, the reduction in both sentence and word length (with sentences being more affected), and the decline in TTR and unique token count. These trends suggest a progressive loss of lexical diversity and syntactic complexity, likely driven by the model’s reinforcement of high-probability words and structures over iterations. Despite this overall simplification, the ROUGE score paradoxically increases (it is an apparent paradox indeed), suggesting that the model continues to generate words that match those found in the original corpus. However, this increase does not imply improved text quality but rather a growing tendency to rely on frequent words, leading to an overrepresentation of high-probability lexical patterns. This is corroborated by the decreasing trend of the unique token count. The decrease in the Hurst coefficient reflects a weakening of long-range dependencies, further indicating that the model loses its ability to maintain structured, coherent sequences across extended text spans, with a degradation of the order underlying the temporal structure of the word sequences. Meanwhile, the slight increase in the multifractal spectrum width suggests that while the text undergoes structural degradation, certain localized variations in complexity persist, likely due to intermittency patterns. This effect is corroborated by the increase in approximate entropy, signifying that the generated sequences become less predictable, and by the significant rise in Kolmogorov complexity, which reflects an increase in randomness and reduced compressibility of the text. These observations collectively point to a progressive form of model collapse due to the interplay of sampling and functional approximation errors, where the text retains highfrequency lexical elements but loses syntactic richness, coherence, and structured dependencies over time. The accumulation of self-generated text in the training corpus introduces a feedback loop that amplifies common patterns while diminishing linguistic diversity and structural consistency. This suggests that while the model remains lexically anchored to the original corpus, as expected, it increasingly produces shorter, repetitive, and less structured sequences. VI. With a simplistic experiment where a stateful LSTM model is trained recursively on text produced on preceding iteration(s), hence mimicking the accumulation over time of data produced by machine learning systems, specifically in generative contexts. This is an issue that in principle can arise considering the large and worldwide diffusion of generative models in performing daily tasks where generated data can be shared and uploaded across the Internet. Our analysis grounding on semantic, syntactic and complex system analysis on recursively generated texts demonstrated how the model tends to degrade over iterations, highlighting a problem that if not deemed serious (yet), is still to be taken into consideration. Notably, the application of multifractal indices, such as the Hurst exponent and the Singularity Spectrum width, alongside other textual measurements, proved effective in evaluating the behavior of language models during the training evolution. Specifically “model collapse” can happen if the data sampling is scarce or also if the model is showing large approximation errors. These limitations highlight the need for more studies within heterogeneous settings comparing different (L)LM architectures. Also, the differential model is a simplified version of what can happen in reality, and more complex models can help to perform scenario analysis. In conclusion, our research provides a starting point together with other studies in the direction of studying the evolution of (L)LM when polluted with its own data generated over time. It underscores the importance of assessing the quality of models and sets the stage for future works in this area, specifically on model drift and collapse.
