## Abstract
Abstract— Preterm neonates admitted to Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICU) are at high risk of cardio-respiratory complications such as apnea, bradycardia, oxygen desaturation, hypoxemia, tachycardia. Monitoring these events generates large, time-stamped vital sign data, requiring effective temporal summarization to derive actionable insights, reduce data overload, and enable timely interventions. Hence, there is a growing need for intelligent computational frameworks that can provide interpretable insights to clinicians in real time. The objective of this work is to summarize the preterm neonate bradycardia and desaturation episodes using fine-tuned medical large language model (LLM), BioBART. The proposed work performs three key activities: Data preprocessing, LLM classification and Temporal summarization. In data preprocessing, the smoothened vital signals are annotated and segmented using threshold based sliding window segmentation

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION Preterm neonates, refers to babies born with gestational age less than 37 weeks, are highly vulnerable to health complications due to physical immaturity [1,2]. In Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs), constant monitoring of heart rate (HR), pulse rate (PR), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure (BP), and temperature is performed using specialized equipment [3]. Among neonatal complications such as hypoglycaemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and sepsis, cardio-respiratory disorders (CRDs) remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality [1,2]. Common CRDs include apnea, bradycardia, desaturation, hypoxia, and tachycardia [3]. Bradycardia occurs when HR falls below 120–160 bpm for at least 4 seconds [6,7], while desaturation refers to SpO₂ < 88% for at least 15 seconds [5]. If untreated, prolonged episodes can cause neurodevelopmental disorders, brain damage, or retinopathy [1,2,6]. Traditional CRD detection methods, such as threshold-based monitors and nurse observations, suffer from high false alarm rates and missed events, leading to delayed responses [5-7]. Recent AI advancements have improved CRD detection using machine learning and deep learning [7,8], yet challenges persist in handling unstructured clinical data such as notes, lab reports, and temporal signals [4,9,10]. To address this, Large Language Models (LLMs) like MedPaLM, BioBART, ClinicalBERT, and BioMistral have been applied to tasks such as question answering, entity recognition, and summarization [4,9,13]. Medical applications include summarization, virtual assistants, and diagnosis prediction, typically achieved through fine-tuning [10-12]. Fine-tuning strategies include transfer learning, parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, adapters, prefix/prompt tuning) [11,12], quantization for model compression, reinforcement learning–based alignment, and pruning to remove redundancy [14]. These approaches make LLMs more efficient and practical for resource-constrained medical environments. A. Outline of Contribution This work focuses on classification of bradycardia and desaturation in preterm neonates by utilizing retrospective vital signs data, specifically PR and SpO₂ recorded in temporal formats within NICU [5-7]. These data are annotated to capture the bradycardia and desaturation episode occurrences accurately, which are then used to fine-tune the BioBART model [13]. To reduce its training complexity and computational costs while maintaining accuracy, the PEFT technique [11], Low-rank Adaptation (LoRA) [12] was adopted, which makes the proposed approach effective and resource-efficient for medical deployment. II. RELATED WORKS This section presents a review on the literatures related to the proposed work. Baserdem et al., [1] addressed late preterm neonate morbidity rate and mortality rate based on various systems in human body such as respiratory system, gastrointestinal system, neurological system, and Infectious diseases and also morbidities and mortalities because of maternal risk factors and type of childbirth. Sakai et al., [9] discussed about the different LLMs used for text 2025 Fourth International Conference on Smart Technologies and Systems for Next Generation Computing (ICSTSN) | 979-8-3315-5942-7/25/$31.00

## Methodology
approach. The LLM classification is carried out with the segmented signals using fine-tuned BioBART-Base model with LowRank Adaptation (LoRA). The obtained classification model achieves an accuracy of 90.50%. The Temporal Summarization is performed by embedding classification

## Results
results with BioBART-Large model which enables concise, clinically relevant insights from temporal vital signal data. Keywords— nicu, lora, biobart, bradycardia, desaturation I.

## Conclusion
CONCLUSION Preterm neonates in the NICU are highly vulnerable to cardio-respiratory complications, demanding continuous monitoring and timely interpretation. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of fine-tuned biomedical large language models, specifically BioBART [13] with LoRA [12], for neonatal cardio-respiratory monitoring. By combining classification through window-based temporal segmentation and temporal summarization, the approach enables accurate detection and clinically meaningful interpretation of bradycardia and desaturation episodes in preterm neonates. The proposed framework not only reduces data overload but also enhances timely clinical decision making. Experimental evaluation on Level III NICU vital sign data confirms that the method achieves high classification accuracy and produces clinically validated summaries, surpassing existing state-ofthe-art approaches. Future work will focus on extending the framework to multimodal NICU data and real-time deployment for bedside decision support. All experimental procedures were conducted in compliance with relevant ethical guidelines, and the study received ethical approval from the Institutional Ethics Committee of to Dr. Mehta’s Multi Speciality Hospital. Patient data were anonymized prior to analysis to ensure confidentiality and privacy

(3) This sliding-window framework ensures that only temporally persistent bradycardia and desaturation episodes are encoded while capturing their temporal distribution across the monitoring period. Clinically, window parameters can be tuned to balance sensitivity to short events and computational efficiency. For each window segments, the following features are computed, (i) Statistical summaries, including mean, minimum, and maximum for PR and SpO₂, (ii) Event counts of bradycardia and desaturation and (iii) Temporal trends, where the linear slope of PR and SpO2 is estimated via least squares regression. Each window is encoded as a structured text string and assigned a categorical label: 0 (normal), 1 (bradycardia), 2 (desaturation), or 3 (both events present), based on the presence of bradycardia and desaturation events, which together provides an information-rich representation of neonatal vital signs that is directly compatible with machine learning pipelines and large language model input. D. Temporal BioBART Classification and Summarization This work employs the publicly available pre-trained model BioBART [13] from Hugging Face repository, which is a biomedical adaptation of the BART architecture shown in Fig 2. BioBART [13] consists of approximately 442M parameters with GeLU activation functions with encoders and decoders. The encoder learns task-specific embedding of temporal vital-sign patterns while retaining pretrained biomedical knowledge, whereas the decoder adapts crossattention to map encoder states to discrete label tokens, effectively translating clinical signal patterns into class predictions. While BioBART [13] has been pretrained on large-scale biomedical corpora, it does not exhibit specialization in detecting cardiorespiratory dysfunction (CRD) events, such as bradycardia and desaturation, in preterm neonates. Thus, domain adaptation is necessary to align the model with neonatal intensive care applications, achieved by fine-tuning using Parameter-Efficient FineTuning (PEFT). The PEFT techniques [11] designed to make the large pretrained models modified for specific tasks without updating the whole parameters. Since, LLM ranges from millions to billions of data, retraining them requires a lot of computational costs and may include redundancies, which has been overcome by using one of PEFT technique [11] called LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) [12]. LoRa addresses this issue through removing redundancies by freezing the original weights of model and converts the large parameters to lowdimensional approximation which also solves the problem of overfitting and catastrophic forgetting [13]. Fig. 2. Architecture of the base version of BART [16]. This work employs LoRA [12] to fine-tune BioBART for a clinical based text classification task, which enables effective adaptation of specialized medical data while preserving the general language understanding learned through pretraining. The proposed system achieves stable performance, efficient fine-tuning, and reduced risk of overfitting, making it a practical and robust approach for clinical text classification. In addition to classification, the framework also includes a summarization module to enhance the understanding of neonatal vital patterns for quick understanding of clinical experts through general language, which can be achieved by utilizing Bio-BART [13], a biomedical LLM pretrained and fine-tuned through various medical corpora for the tasks like summarization, information extraction, question answering, and clinical report generation. In this system, BioBART [13] was used to transform sequences of classified temporal windows into concise, clinically meaningful logs that capture both local patterns and overall trends in preterm neonates’ CRD events. In-stead of presenting window-level classifications individually, the model produces higher-level summaries that emphasize the frequency, duration, and continuity of bradycardia and desaturation episodes over time. This temporal abstraction reduces data overload, preserves the evolving nature of episodes, and provides clinicians with clear, actionable insights for rapid interpretation and timely intervention. IV. EXPERIMENTATION RESULTS The experiments were carried out using Google Colab Pro, equipped with a single NVIDIA A100 GPU and 40 GB RAM, which provided reasonable performance for fine-tuning the BioBART [13] model with LoRA [12]. The retrospective vital sign data were collected from level III NICU. This dataset consists of continuous monitoring of preterm neonates’ pulse rate (PR) and peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂) recorded at hh: mm: ss intervals in the NICU. For dataset preparation, noise removal was performed using a threshold-based median filter, and missing values in the raw signals were imputed using the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Imputation algorithm. The episodes of bradycardia and desaturation in the dataset are annotated with appropriate class labels based on clinically defined thresholds of PR and SpO2 vital signs [5-7], which are verified by clinical experts. A sliding-window segmentation strategy was then applied by dividing each signal into 300 second temporal windows with a 120 second overlap, ensuring that short-lived cardio-respiratory events were captured while preserving the continuity of evolving episodes. Each segmented window was subsequently encoded into structured textual sequences, making the data directly compatible with BioBART [13]. The dataset was split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets, with patient-level separation to avoid data leakage. The classification model is constructed using BioBART-Base model, with Adam optimizer and learning rate of 1e-5 and fine-tuned using LoRA adapters. The LoRA [12] hyper parameters are also set to lora rank of 8, lora dropout rate of 0.1, and lora alpha rate 16 with seq2seq task type to perform efficient classification. The training process demonstrated stable convergence, as shown in the loss curve depicted in Fig 3. The classification of cardiorespiratory dysfunction (CRD) events achieved promising results from five independent experiment runs with mean and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated for each metrics shown in Table 1. The summarization was performed using the BioBARTLarge model, which consists of 12 encoder and 12 decoder layers, and its performance was compared with the T5-Base model. Both models were evaluated using reference-free metrics, including readability score, relevance score, and ROUGE-C score [15]. The T5-Base model achieved scores of 0.46, 0.48, and 92.96 for ROUGE-C, relevance, and readability (Flesch Reading Ease), respectively. In contrast, the BioBART-Large model achieved scores of 0.87, 0.89, and 55.93 for the same metrics. These results indicate that the summaries generated by the BioBART-Large model were clinically meaningful, coherent, and easier to interpret. The relatively lower readability score of the BioBART-Large model reflects the use of domain-specific medical terminology, making the summaries more appropriate and understandable to clinicians. V. CONCLUSION Preterm neonates in the NICU are highly vulnerable to cardio-respiratory complications, demanding continuous monitoring and timely interpretation. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of fine-tuned biomedical large language models, specifically BioBART [13] with LoRA [12], for neonatal cardio-respiratory monitoring. By combining classification through window-based temporal segmentation and temporal summarization, the approach enables accurate detection and clinically meaningful interpretation of bradycardia and desaturation episodes in preterm neonates. The proposed framework not only reduces data overload but also enhances timely clinical decision making. Experimental evaluation on Level III NICU vital sign data confirms that the method achieves high classification accuracy and produces clinically validated summaries, surpassing existing state-ofthe-art approaches. Future work will focus on extending the framework to multimodal NICU data and real-time deployment for bedside decision support. TITULO DEL PAPER: ieee_801-multimodal sleep stage classification with llm based sleep report

Paper ID: ieee_801

Relevance Score: 0.7412

Fuente: ieee

Palabras: 5912


---


## Abstract
Abstract—Manual scoring of polysomnography (PSG), the gold standard for sleep analysis, consumes time and is subjective in nature, hence presenting a major bottleneck in clinical workflows. This research tackles such bottlenecks by proposing a full scale end to end automated sleep stage classification and intelligent report generation pipeline. The system depends on multimodal data (EEG, EOG, EMG) from the public Sleep-EDF dataset and employs an advanced machine learning(ML)

## Introduction
INTRODUCTION Sleep happens to be an important factor that concerns human health, and interrupted quality causes many chronic physiological and psychosocial illnesses [1], [2]. PSG is the clinical gold standard for evaluating sleep. This is an all night study that collects signals of multiple physiological modalities, including EEG for brain activity, EOG for eye movements, and EMG for muscular activities. The clinician’s framework in analyzing these data is manual scoring by trained technicians or clinical experts, a process so time consuming and very costly, with plenty of variation from person to person, putting a huge tunnel of obstruction in the way of the practice of sleep medicine. To address these challenges, the automated sleep stage classification using ML has emerged as a better alternative, offering the potential for fast, efficient, and scalable analysis. The main objectives of this study is, to preprocessing multimodal PSG data. Then, to engineer and select a highly effective set of features from EEG, EOG, and EMG signals through a hybrid and novel feature selection technique for accurate sleep stage discrimination. And to train, validate, and compare ML pipelines for five stages of sleep (Wake, N1, N2, N3, REM). Finally, to explore the use of LLM to automatically create a comprehensive and qualitative sleep analysis report from the model’s predictions. Ultimately, the major aim of this study is to demonstrate the potential that such a system might be automated so as to improve efficiency and standardization in scoring sleep, along with facilitating accessibility of sleep health diagnostics through a novel LLM generated clinical summaries. Sleep staging, the act of sorting 30 second PSG epochs into different sleep stages, has been a traditional manual scoring task that usually uses either the older Rechtschaffen and Kales (R&K) standard discussed in [3] or the more recent American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) standard discussed in [4]. The AASM standard that is used in this work defines five stages which are Wake (W), N1, N2, N3, and REM. In the recent studies, deep learning (DL) methods such as CNNs [8], [9], [10], [11], RNNs [12], [13], tansformers [14], and their hybrids [15], [16] have become more popular due to their capability of automatically deriving features for an end to end classification. As a result, the complexity of models has been growing along with the computational costs immensely such as SleepGPT [17] and DeepSleepNet-lite [18] for almost the same performance. These black box models do not always have the same level of interpretability as required in clinical adoption, and thus, they face some obstacles in being applied in the real world. Some researchers interpret the situation differently and claim that conventional ML presents a more feasible and interpretable option. Several studies emerge showing that a properly built pipeline, namely, deep, multi domain feature extraction from EEG and EOG signals along with efficient feature selection, is able to level with best in class DL implementations [19], [20], [21], [22]. For example, [23] one study combined a novel two phase feature selection scheme and used XGBoost classifier resulting in 87.0% accuracy. It was especially significant, as the DL models had difficulty in the N1 stage. ## Methodology
methodology. The pipeline begins with signal preprocessing, and then feature engineering takes place in all its impact, from both the time and frequency domain, ending with a novel multi metric feature selection approach aimed at resolving the paramount sleep biomarkers. Then, ML model classifies sleep into five different stages which are Wake, N1, N2, N3, and REM. The main contribution behind this work is by integrating a cutting edge Large Language Model (LLM) to generate the intelligible interpretations of quantitative classifier outputs, including parameters such as sleep efficiency, latencies, and stages. Index Terms—PSG, Sleep Staging, Machine Learning, LLM. I.

Sleep Report Generation One important transformation in the sleep report generation step is the rendering of the raw, numerical predictions of the ML model into a detailed, understandable analysis for a human user by an LLM. The method starts with producing a quantitative summary from the sleep stages that have been predicted. This summary contains key clinical metrics such as Total Sleep Time, Sleep Efficiency, Sleep Latency, and the percentage of time spent in each stage (Light, Deep, and REM) calculated based on AASM sleep scoring data [4]. The data in this summary, which is organized, is then used as the basis for a prompt that has been designed with the Gemini LLM in mind. The LLM used for report generation is gemini 1.5 flash. Gemini 1.5 flash was chosen as it offers ideal balance of performance, speed, and cost-effectiveness without compromising quality. In fact, this model is very efficient in capturing the structured sleep data and also in understanding the prompt which is quite complex as well. Baseline Comparison The detailed results from the four experimental conditions show beyond a doubt that a multi modal model that combines all features (EEG, EOG, and EMG) is decisively superior for automatic sleep stage classification. The full model obtained an overall accuracy of 90.3% and a macro average F1-score of 0.82. This is a big jump over the next best model (EEG-only, 0.75 F1-score), indicating that the signal combination is not just additive but synergistic, thus allowing the model to capture the complex physiological states that characterize sleep architecture more accurately than any single signal type can by itself. The EEG only model can be regarded as the most important single variable in the prediction of sleep stages and it can set a benchmark for the multi modal model on its own with a macro F1-score of 0.75. This is the expected result since the electroencephalogram is a direct measurement of brainwave patterns that are the main criteria for staging sleep, such as the slow delta waves of N3 and the sleep spindles of N2. Where the EEG only model is most confused is between stages that have similar low voltage, mixed frequency brainwave patterns. The same detailed results reveal this in the treatment of REM sleep, where the performance of the EEG only model is quite low with an F1-score of 0.68, as it often mistakes REM for N1 or N2 sleep. The main drawback of the multi modal approach is fixed in such a way that EOG and EMG signals are EEG dependent. The most prominent case is the REM sleep detection. The F1 score for REM increased sharply from 0.68 in the EEG only model to 0.83 in the full model. This is because the EOG features pick up the rapid eye movements while the EMG features pick up the muscle atonia, which are the two main non EEG markers for REM sleep, thus allowing the full model to make the most of these three signals for reliable predictions of N1 sleep stage and the highest F1 score (0.55) for this stage. Last of all, the EMG only model is an example of the worst standalone predictor, with a macro F1 score of only 0.44 and almost complete failure to identify N2 sleep (F1=0.26). It is clear that muscle tone alone cannot be relied on for total sleep staging. Its indispensable contribution to our identification of muscle atonia during REM sleep and high muscle tone during wakefulness is the one that enables the better performance of the multi modal model to happen.The detailed comparison of results from each feature sets is shown in Fig 5. ## Conclusion
CONCLUSION This research has successfully took the responsibility to build and prove the validity of a complete working pipeline that allows for automatic classification of the stages of sleep and the generation of an intelligent report by means of the Sleep-EDF Expanded Dataset. It is through this task of data preprocessing, extensive feature engineering, and the implementation of the multi criteria feature selection strategy that the training of a LightGBM classifier was conducted to reach a high macro F1-score of 0.79. This result shows the classifier’s potent ability to correctly identify sleep stage from the complex physiological signals. The most novel element of the present work is the transition stage in which outputs from the ML model were converted to visual, non-technical, and intuitive human output by Gemini’s LLM. ## Figures_tables_captions
Fig. 1. Sleep Staging Pipeline A. Dataset Overview The Sleep-EDF Expanded Dataset [26] consists of whole night PSG recordings, totaling 197, of which each has corresponding annotations. The selected channels for this work are two EEG channels (Fpz-Cz and Pz-Oz), one horizontal EOG channel, and one submental EMG channel. The dataset contains two different studies which are Sleep Cassette (SC) and Sleep Telemetry (ST). The SC part consist of 153 healthy subject’s recordings recorded at their homes to study the influence of age on sleep. The ST segment comprises of 44 recordings recorded from a hospital lab, which was structured to study the effect of a sleep aid on a group of individuals with mild difficulty falling asleep. The sleep stage annotations are based on the Rechtschaffen and Kales (R&K) manual and besides wake, N1, N2, N3, N4, and REM, it includes Movement stages as well. B. Signal Pre-Processing Preprocessing stage converts the original multi channel sleep data into a clean, standard format that is compatible with ML. The procedure involves first loading each subject’s PSG recording along with their corresponding hypnogram (sleep stage annotations). Each recording is adjusted to a standard frequency of 100 Hz by resampling. Wavelet denoising is being implemented as a part of preprocessing to clean the physiological signals, during which signal features are not compromised as shown in Fig 2 and 3. Traditional filters are less effective especially in the case of non-stationary signals like EEG, where the wavelet denoising technique excels [25]. There are three main steps involved in this technique and those are decomposition, thresholding, and reconstruction. Essentially the signal is decomposed into 7 frequency levels utilizing a wavelet function (db4 here). Thus the separation of the signal’s basic components from the high-frequency noise is achieved. A noise threshold is statistically derived, and the signal components that are below the threshold are either reduced in size or set to zero in the so called soft thresholding operation. The final step is the reconstruction of the cleaned signal, i.e. the noise is removed but the important features are preserved for the correct sleep stage classification. Fig. 2. Before Preprocessing Fig. 3. After Preprocessing The continuous part of the data is then cut into 30second non overlapping epochs after noise removal which is the standard for sleep stage scoring [4]. Then a per subject, per channel Z-score normalization is applied, wherein the mean and standard deviation for each channel are calculated from the data of one individual’s file only, and this is then used to scale the data. The main advantage of this method is that it effectively gets rid of the huge, most of the time irrelevant variations in signal amplitude that happen naturally between different people. Consequently, the ML model becomes capable of detecting genuine foundational patterns in the data instead of person specific baselines, thereby its capacity to generalize to new unseen subjects is enhanced considerably. Authorized licensed use limited to: Universidad Nac de Educación a Distancia (UNED). Downloaded on October 08,2026 at 20:13:21 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. C. Feature Extraction and Selection Feature extraction had a significant impact on the sleep data representation, as it managed to combine the standard metrics with several novel and advanced features that can capture complex signal dynamics. Alongside the typical time domain (e.g. mean, variance, RMS) and frequency domain features (e.g. absolute and relative band powers), the analysis has also included more advanced measures. The Hjorth parameters (mobility and complexity) were features which in a very efficient manner, represent the statistical and frequency characteristics of the EEG signal. Permutation Entropy was set as a impactful, non linear measure to outline the complexity, and predictability of EEG, thereby differentiating the various stages of brain activity. Teager-Kaiser Energy Operator (TKEO) was deployed on EOG and EMG signals for detecting transient events to calculate the instantaneous energy, which, in turn, made it very successful in locating the eye movement bursts along with the muscle twitches that are the characteristics of certain sleep stages. This multi faceted approach not only ensures that the model is getting trained on the features that depict the basic signal properties but also their complex dynamic behaviors. The feature selection step used here is a novel heterogeneous operation that aimed to judiciously trim down the original 99 features to a resilient and effective subset of 67. The stage did not depend on one metric only, but went on to use a 5 fold cross validation as an advanced ensemble strategy which takes into account of multiple metrics to reach a decision. For each feature, three different ways were used to calculate the value which are the gain of LightGBM, mutual information, and permutation importance. Then these raw scores were reprocessed by adding a stability score that accounted for the features which were ranked highly and thus in a stable manner across all the validation folds. Moreover, based on [4], the knowledge of the domain was included through the use of modality weights that gave priority to the features of EEG signals than those of EOG and EMG. The weights are as follows EEG: 0.5, EOG: 0.3 and EMG: 0.2. They were ranked by combining these metrics into one final score and then the top 80 features were picked. In the last stage, this catalog was cleansed using correlation filtering of highly correlated features (those with a correlation over 0.9) to assure that the final set was not only highly predictive but also minimally redundant. D. Machine Learning The class distribution of 5 classes is shown in Fig 4. Class 0,1,2,3 and 4 signifies to Wake, N1, N2, N3 and REM. The ML phase was a thorough comparative process which aimed to discover the best model to classify sleep stages by using the features created during the process. Two ensemble models, LightGBM and ExtraTrees Classifier, which are both strong, were systematically evaluated. As there was a significant imbalance between the classes in the dataset as shown in Fig 4, with the stage of wakefulness being the most frequent, two Fig. 4. Class Distribution different approaches were tested for each model. Firstly, the use of class weighting to penalize the errors of the minority classes more heavily and secondly, the application of a hybrid resampling pipeline that combined SMOTE for synthesizing data for the rare stages with Random Under Sampler(RUS) for reducing the majority class. The whole experiment was done with 5 fold stratified cross validation to obtain a reliable and robust evaluation. The SMOTE with RUS was applied only to the training folds within cross validation using an imblearn pipeline, ensuring no data leakage from test folds. By looking at the performance of the models using different metrics and focusing mainly on the macro F1 score and the overfitting gap between the train and test scores, it was decided that the LightGBM model combined with the SMOTE and RUS pipeline is the best way to go, thus, it got the best balance of high predictive accuracy and strong generalization. This last, optimized model was then retrained on the entire dataset and stored for the final inference and report generation pipeline. E. CONCLUSION This research has successfully took the responsibility to build and prove the validity of a complete working pipeline that allows for automatic classification of the stages of sleep and the generation of an intelligent report by means of the Sleep-EDF Expanded Dataset. It is through this task of data preprocessing, extensive feature engineering, and the implementation of the multi criteria feature selection strategy that the training of a LightGBM classifier was conducted to reach a high macro F1-score of 0.79. This result shows the classifier’s potent ability to correctly identify sleep stage from the complex physiological signals. The most novel element of the present work is the transition stage in which outputs from the ML model were converted to visual, non-technical, and intuitive human output by Gemini’s LLM. The accomplishment of this synthetic step has been quite thoroughly confirmed through a double evaluation framework, which indicated that, when compared to factual references, high factual consistency and semantic relevance were exhibited. One great thing about this kind of study is that it has the possibility to make the whole sleep field new and better. By employing ML to forecast and LLMs to interpret, this system would not only enable the clinician to do his work faster but also provide the patients with uncomplicated and easily understandable information about their sleep pattern. The feature based model implemented revealed as very efficient; the authors might consider using end to end DL strategies that could result in a better performance deriving intricate pattern from raw signals. In this regard, this study shall also be complimented on its promise of future clinical testing on different datasets. This will further facilitate its application in the real world. In general, this undertaking is an excellent illustration of the collaboration pattern between the classics of ML and the best in class generative AI paradigm in the progress of personalized medicine

## Abstract
Abstract Objective. Speech comprehension involves detecting words and interpreting their meaning according to the preceding semantic context. This process is thought to be underpinned by a predictive neural system that uses that context to anticipate upcoming words. However, previous studies relied on

## Introduction
Introduction Speech comprehension requires our brains to transform sounds into meaning [1]. As part of that process, our brains must detect speech tokens such as words and interpret their meaning according to the prior context. In turn, that context can aid speech comprehension in challenging scenarios, such as noisy multi-talker environments [2]. The predictive processing theory [3, 4] offers a neurophysiological framework explaining how prior context might contribute to speech comprehension, proposing that sensory processing is underpinned by an active process involving the continuous attempts to predict upcoming sensory events [5, 6]. Strong evidence has been gathered indicating that this phenomenon extends to word predictions [7, 8], with stronger prediction errors leading to stronger neural activations measured with electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) [9, 10]. This relationship between neural activations and word prediction error, or lexical surprise, has been studied extensively by comparing the event-related potentials (ERPs) in response to expected and unexpected words. As a result, a negative electrical deflection was measured at a post-stimulus latency of about 400 ms i.e. the N400 [7, 11]. The N400 has been studied widely by means of carefully crafted stimuli, for example impacting the contextual appropriateness (e.g. ‘I like my coffee with cream and sugar/socks’) [12]. Consequently, the N400 is typically estimated on unusual and short

## Methodology
Approach. We investigate these limitations by analyzing both simulated and actual electroencephalography (EEG) signals recorded during a speech comprehension task. We then introduce two novel assessment metrics tailored to capture the neural encoding of lexical surprise, improving upon traditional evaluation approaches. Main results. The proposed metrics demonstrated effect-sizes over 140% larger than those achieved with the conventional temporal response function (TRF) evaluation. These improvements were consistent across both simulated and real EEG datasets. Significance. Our findings substantially advance methods for evaluating lexical prediction in neural data, enabling more precise measurements and deeper insights into how the brain builds predictive representations during speech comprehension. These contributions open new avenues for research into predictive coding mechanisms in naturalistic language processing. 1.

## Conclusion
conclusions. The second key issue is that EEG/MEG prediction correlations are usually estimated by considering entire segments of data. While that is reasonable for envelope tracking studies, as the speech envelope is a continuous signal, word onset and lexical surprise are time-discrete vectors. For example, let us consider two words w1 and w2 with a very large inter-word interval of t12 = 3 s. In that case, large part of that EEG/MEG signal cannot be predicted by a lexical surprise feature, which would just inform us on the first few hundreds of milliseconds that follow w1. As a result, EEG/MEG prediction correlations would be calculated in a segment whose response is only partly affected by lexical surprise, substantially diluting the effect of interest. In other words, the intuition is that the prediction correlation metric is impacted by the word density, with slower speech leading to smaller effects of lexical surprise. The analyses that follow quantify and propose direct solutions to these issues. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Natural-speech-EEG dataset This study involves a re-analysis of a publicly available scalp EEG dataset, where neural signals were recorded as participants listened to narrative speech [13]. These data were part of a set of studies examining how human cortical signals encode acoustic and linguistic features of speech [16, 22, 23]. Nineteen participants (six female and thirteen male) aged between 19 and 38 years took part in the experiment. All participants were native English speakers, and reported normal hearing, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and no history of neurological disorders. The experiment was conducted in a single session for each participant. EEG data were recorded as participants listened to an audiobook version of a popular mid-20th century American work of fiction (‘The Old Man and the Sea’), read by a single professional male speaker. The audio stimuli were organized into 20 segments corresponding to the first chapters of the book, each with a duration of about 180 s. Segments were presented in a way that preserved the storyline, with neither repetitions nor discontinuities, and with an average speech rate of ∼210 words/min. 128-channel EEG data plus two mastoid channels were acquired at a rate of 512 Hz using a BioSemi ActiveTwo system. Triggers indicating the start of each trial were sent by the stimulus presentation computer and included in the EEG recordings to ensure synchronization. Testing was carried out in a dark, sound-attenuated room and participants were instructed to maintain visual fixation on a crosshair centred on the screen for the duration of each trial, and to minimize eye blinking and other motor activities. The present study utilized a version of the dataset that was shared according to the Continuous-event Neural Data structure (CND) [24, 25]. 2.2. Simulated EEG data One of the challenges of probing brain activity with technologies such as EEG is that the recorded neural signals are mixed with various sources of noise. Therefore, neural signatures derived by relating EEG and stimulus features likely reflect a combination of actual neural activity and EEG noise. Intuitively, a good assessment metrics would reflect how effective a model is at capturing the ground truth neural signal hidden behind the noise. However, since that ground truth signal is typically unavailable, we built a second dataset artificially with the CNSP simulation toolkit [26]. Specifically, the stimulus features used for generating the simulated EEG data were the Hilbert envelope of the speech sound and the lexical surprise vector, which was built using GPT-2 [20] (see section 2.5). Stimulus features from the NaturalSpeech-EEG dataset were convolved with predefined TRFs that were designed based on the literature. The simulated EEG data was derived by summing the two convolutions and, on top of that, EEG noise consisting of random segments of EEG data from the Natural-Speech-EEG dataset. For the artificial noise, we used a random selection of time-reversed EEG data (henceforth EEG noise), leading to simulated EEG signals that closely resemble real EEG recordings. The use of randomly selected time-reversed segments ensures that the TRF analysis would not be affected by the sensory responses in the EEG noise, as they are uncorrelated with the stimulus of interest. Several levels of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) were explored and presented i.e. SNR −25, −20, −15, −10 dB. The main analyses in the figures focussed on the intermediate SNR level −15 dB. 3 J. Please note that the outcome of our analyses on the simulated EEG dataset are insensitive to small changes in these artificial TRFs (e.g. timeshifting or scaling). Note that the resulting simulated EEG dataset has the same number of channels, trials, and participants as in the Natural-Speech-EEG dataset. 2.3. EEG preprocessing EEG data were analysed offline using MATLAB software (The MathWorks Inc.) according to the minimal preprocessing guidelines of the Cognition and Natural Sensory Processing initiative [25]. The same preprocessing pipeline and code were used for both datasets [24]. Signals were digitally filtered between 0.5 and 8 Hz using a Butterworth zero-phase filter, similar to previous studies [13, 28]. Both lowand high-pass filters had order 2 and were implemented with the function filtfilt, obtaining zero-shift phase filters. Signals were down-sampled to 128 Hz and rereferenced to the average of the mastoid channels. To identify channels with excessive noise, the time series were visually inspected, and the standard deviation of each channel was compared with that of the surrounding channels. Channels contaminated by excessive noise were recalculated by spline interpolating all the clean channels weighted by distance in EEGLAB [29]. The average number of channels interpolated across trials for each subject are shown in table S1. 2.4. TRF This study discusses evaluation metrics for TRF models, focusing on forward TRFs. A forward TRF can be described as a filter that linearly transforms a stimulus S(t) to a neural response R(t) over a specified series of time lags: R(t) = TRFw∗S(t) + ε, where TRFw are the weights of the filter at every time lag, and ε represents the residual of the prediction. Estimation of the TRF weights is done using regularized linear regression [15]. Previous studies have used this approach to investigate acoustic and linguistic processing with neural signals recorded as participants listened to continuous speech [5, 13, 28]. This approach can utilize a single stimulus feature at a time, or multiple such features simultaneously, leading to uTRF and mTRF respectively. The latter has the advantage of availing of additional information for predicting the EEG data, which can lead to an improve ability of explaining EEG variance. Furthermore, mTRFs can more clearly inform on the distinct contributions to the EEG predictions of different features in cases of multicollinearity. Here, both the uTRF and mTRF approaches were explored to determine metrics that most reliably reflect the neural encoding of lexical surprise figures 1(B) and (C). The quality of the fit of TRF models is typically assessed with two types of metrics. - The first metric is derived by building EEG predictions with cross-validation. The Pearson’s correlation of those predictions with the actual EEG data are then calculated on portions of signal that were not included in the model fit (test fold), producing correlation values for each EEG sensor, trial (e.g. chapter of an audio-book), and participant. For ease of analysis and visualization, prediction correlations are often averaged across EEG channels or calculated on selected scalp locations. This simplification comes at the cost of penalizing our assessment, in the former, and of limiting the analysis to a specific location while ignoring the others, in the latter. - Ones it is verified that the TRF model explains some of the EEG variance by studying the EEG prediction correlations, it is then possible to study the weights of the regression model. The analysis of the TRF weights can inform us on which specific stimulus-EEG latencies and scalp areas are most relevant to their relationship (e.g. ∼400 ms) [30]. This second metric is referred to as TRF weights. 2.5. Stimulus feature extraction Three speech features were used to fit TRF models: speech envelope, word onset, and lexical surprise. The broadband amplitude envelope was computed by applying the Hilbert transform, capturing a key acoustic property of the speech material [31]. Word onset was defined as a vector containing ones and zeros, where ones denote the word onset. Lexical surprise serves as a proxy for semantic processing, as it quantifies how unexpected a word is depending on the proximal context. Lexical surprise obtained with LLM for all words in the speech has been shown to relate with the non-invasively recorded brain signal, enabling the isolation of word-level predictive processes from EEG [5]. Here, lexical surprise values were derived using GPT-2 [20], an open-source transformer-based LLM, which can be employed to 4 J. Neural Eng. 22 (2025) 016004 A Chalehchaleh et al Figure 1. The second signal was the convolution of lexical surprise with an artificially-built TRF with a single negative component at a latency of 400 ms, broadly capturing previous results [5, 7, 13]. The preceding context was built based on words heard within each particular chapter of the audio-book. 2.6. TRF model fit and evaluation The neural encoding of word-level predictions can be studied with both uTRFs [13, 28, 33] and mTRFs [18, 19, 34]. To assess whether the EEG signals reflect lexical surprise, TRF results were compared when using lexical surprise vectors that did or did not match the speech material. Similar to previous TRF studies [27], mismatched surprise vectors were generated by randomly shuffling the order of the surprise values in the lexical surprise vectors, while preserving the onset times. To carry out statistical testing on individual participants, the shuffling and model-fit procedure was repeated 500 times, generating a null distribution for each participant. Note that this null distribution is stricter than simply mismatching the trial index for lexical surprise and EEG signal, as our procedure isolated the impact of the lexical surprise values, while everything else (i.e. word onset times and speech envelope) remained constant. In uTRFs, the lexical surprise vectors and their shuffled versions were used to fit uTRFs. In that case, the two only differ in the order of the surprise values, while the timing was identical. Note that the shuffled lexical surprise vectors contain meaningful word onset timing, while the surprisal values can be seen as noise, as they are unrelated with the EEG signal. In mTRFs, models were fit by considering the three features (envelope, word onsets, and lexical surprise) simultaneously. In this case, speech envelope and word onsets acted as nuisance regressors, absorbing variance related to sound acoustics and word onsets. As such, the lexical surprise regressor 5 J. Neural Eng. 22 (2025) 016004 A Chalehchaleh et al was expected to more clearly capture variance that is unique to lexical surprise (and anything correlated to it that is not envelope and word onsets). Before analysing the Natural-Speech-EEG dataset, uTRFs and mTRFs were evaluated on the simulated data, where we had full control on what information was and was not present in the EEG data (in this case, envelope and lexical surprise were encoded). For simplifying the model evaluation, EEG prediction correlations calculated on single channels were averaged across all channels and trials, leading to a single value per participant. Regarding the model weights, averaging weights across EEG channels can be problematic instead, as positive and negative deflections in different scalp areas can cancel each other out. For that reason, our analyses of the TRF weights focused on a selected Centro-Parietal EEG channel, Pz, where the relationship between wordlevel predictions and EEG is known to be particularly strong [7, 13]. 2.7. Two new metrics for evaluating word-level predictions This study proposes two new evaluation metrics for assessing the neural encoding of word-level predictions. Note that these metrics could potentially be applied for the evaluation of TRFs for other common time-discrete features, for example at the level of phonemes [17, 19] or music notes [27, 35–37]. The first metric is specifically designed for improving the evaluation of surprise-like responses from the mTRF weights. The second metric aims to increase the sensitivity of EEG prediction correlations to temporally sparse events such as words, and it applies to both uTRF and mTRF methods. ∆Time-constrained TRF weights, or ∆TC weights. The first metric relies on TRF weights and is calculated on mTRF models. The observation is that Lexical surprise uTRF weights are not particularly sensitive to the surprise values (see figure 2(A) and results section). The rationale is that the modulations relating to lexical surprise are likely small in natural speech, meaning that simple word-onset uTRFs capture most of the word responses already. To more clearly isolate the neural encoding of lexical surprise as opposed to word onsets, here we fit mTRF models by using lexical surprise and word onset features simultaneously. If the TRF model weights exhibit differences when examining the TRF weights for the two features, that would mean that the EEG signals encode correlates of lexical surprise. Otherwise, measuring undistinguishable TRF weights for lexical surprise and word onset would indicate that the specific lexical surprise is not encoded in the EEG signal. With this premise, the encoding of lexical surprise can be measured by subtracting the TRF weights for lexical surprise and word onset, and by calculating the absolute value of their difference at the latency where the major effect is expected, in this case 400 ms. Specifically, weights were averaged in the window 300–500 ms to account for latency differences between participants. Note that our conclusions did not change for small changes in the selection of that window. Time-constrained (TC) EEG prediction correlation. The second metric relies on EEG prediction correlations. Feature vectors capturing wordlevel information are typically sparse as they code the information of interest, such as lexical surprise, timelocked to the word onsets. Considering a word rate between about 100 and 260 words per minute across different speakers, speech categories and languages [38], and considering that TRF-N400 evoked component can extend approximately between 200 and 600 ms [13, 18, 28]. Under these general assumptions, the worst-case scenario would be that only 20 s every minute of EEG data would reflect lexical surprise. As such, 66% per cent of the datapoints used for calculating the EEG prediction correlation would not capture the effect of interest, substantially diluting that effect. Here, we propose to calculate the EEG prediction correlations by only considering the datapoint that might reflect the target effect. This simple modified metric is applied at the evaluation stage, and it does not affect the TRF model fit, meaning that it can be used to evaluate both uTRF and mTRF models. The code used for deriving this metric has been shared on the GitHub of the mTRF-Toolbox (function mTRFcrossval_multimetric). 2.8. Statistical analysis Statistical significance in group-level analysis was assessed through pair-wise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests applied to both EEG prediction correlations and mTRF weightsIn the single-subject level analysis (figures 3(D) and (H)), we conducted 500 permutations for each participant, systematically shuffling the values of lexical surprise in each iteration. This process generated a null distribution for each subject, allowing us to calculate statistical significance at the individual level. Wilcoxon signed rank tests were used for pair-wised comparisons. Correction for multiple comparisons was applied where necessary via the false discovery rate (FDR) approach. A two-way repeated measures ANOVA was used to assess the effects of within and between factors. The values reported use the convention F(dfnumerator, dfdenominator). Results 3.1. The challenge of probing lexical surprise in the human cortex with uTRFs The relationship between lexical surprise vectors and EEG was evaluated with uTRFs on both simulated and real EEG data. For the simulated EEG data, TRF weights were compared between the lexical surprise model and the null (shuffled lexical surprise) model. Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that there is a negative deflection for the lexical surprise model around 400 ms (figure S1(A); Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the average TRF weights in the 300–500 ms lag window: p < 0.001, d = 0.4 FDR-corrected Wilcoxon tests were carried out on individual lags with p < 0.05). Prediction correlation comparison between the lexical model and the shuffle surprise model were greater for the lexical model (figure S1(B); Wilcoxon signedrank p < 0.001, d = 9.72). Similar outcomes emerged when analysing real EEG data. TRF weights at channel Pz were compared between lexical surprise and the shuffled surprise models, showing a stronger negative deflection for the lexical surprise model at latencies close to 400 ms (figure 2(A); Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the average TRF weights in the 300–500 ms lag window p < 0.001, d = 0.22; FDR-corrected Wilcoxon tests were carried out on individual lags with p < 0.05). EEG prediction correlations were also larger for the lexical surprise model than the shuffled surprise model, leading to a statistically significant difference (figure 2(B); p < 0.001, d = 0.17). These results are in line with the literature in that a statistically significant encoding of lexical surprise is measured. As in previous work, both this result corresponded with small effect sizes (d ⪅0.2) for both TRF weights and EEG prediction correlations metrics. The analysis in section 3.3 aims at deriving evaluation metrics that are more sensitive to lexical surprise, leading to larger effect sizes. 3.2. Probing lexical surprise with mTRFs Further analyses were carried out to evaluate whether the flexibility of mTRFs can improve the evaluation of lexical surprise encoding in EEG signals. One of the advantages of mTRFs is that, by using multiple stimulus features at once, the different contributors to the prediction can be more clearly separated [18, 30]. Here, lexical surprise mTRFs were derived by including envelope, word onset, and lexical surprise features as the input, while the shuffle surprise model 7 J. While this difference captures the effect of using three speech features, envelope, word onset and lexical surprise, simultaneously rather than only lexical surprise, we also quantified the EEG variance explained by lexical surprise by subtracting the EEG prediction correlations for the lexical surprise and shuffle surprise models, where lexical surprise information was present and absent respectively. EEG prediction correlations as expected showed larger prediction correlations for the mTRF model compared to the uTRF model (p < 0.001, d = 0.83). While this difference captures the effect of using three speech features simultaneously rather than only lexical surprise, the EEG prediction gain did not show any statistically significant difference between uTRFs and mTRFs (figure 2(E); p = 0.332, d = 0.249). 3.3. Isolating robust neural metrics of lexical surprise The previous sections indicate that TRF metrics described in the literature (i.e. EEG prediction correlations and TRF weights) can be used to probe the lexical surprise generated by the human cortex during speech comprehension. However, comparing lexical surprise and shuffle surprise models exhibited small effect-sizes, when using such metrics. Further analyses were conducted to determine if that contrast (i.e. between lexical surprise and shuffle surprise models) is enhanced when considering multivariate models. While incorporating the envelope and word onset as regressors increases the prediction correlation (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001), the prediction correlation gain between surprise and shuffle models remained small (d = 0.18, figure 2(D)). However, the EEG prediction improvement did not show a statistically significant difference between uTRFs and mTRFs (figure 2(E); p = 0.332, d = 0.249). This outcome was expected, as the lexical surprise values are independent from envelope and word onset features. To magnify our ability to measure lexical prediction processes, two novel TRF metrics are introduced in the next sections. The ∆TC weights metric, which is calculated on the weights of the mTRF model, showed larger values for the lexical surprise model than the shuffle surprise model (figure 3(A); Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p < 0.001, d = 3.13) on the simulated EEG dataset. The same result also emerged on the Natural-SpeechEEG dataset (figure 3(E), p < 0.001, d = 2.09). While this effect was only evaluated on TRF weights around the 400 ms time-latency, where the impact of lexical surprise was expected to be strongest, the contrasts of TRF weights for lexical surprise and word onsets is reported in figure 3(C) for the simulated EEG dataset and figure 3(G) for the natural speech EEG across all the time-latencies in the TRF models. That visualization further highlights the value of studying that contrast, which shows statistically significant effects for the lexical surprise model but not for the shuffled lexical surprise model (FDRcorrected Wilcoxon signed rank test, p < 0.05). The ∆TC weights metric was also sensitive to lexical surprise at the level of individual participants, with 18 out of 19 of them in the simulated EEG dataset exhibiting larger values for the lexical surprise model than the shuffle surprise model (figure 3(D-left), and 14 out of 19 of them in the natural speech EEG dataset exhibiting larger values for the lexical surprise model than the shuffle surprise model (figure 3(H-left), FDR-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05); whereas the same analysis on the univariate model results showed statistically significant effects in only 9 out of 19 participants in the simulated EEG dataset (figure 3(D-right), p < 0.05) and only 8 out of 19 participants in the natural speech EEG dataset (figure 3(H-right), p < 0.05). The second novel metric, TC prediction correlation, consists of identifying time-points unrelated with the target effect by design, and then excluding those time-points when calculating the EEG prediction correlation. This time-constrained correlation metric led to a substantial enhancement of the EEG prediction correlation gain values on both the simulated EEG dataset (figure 3(B), Wilcoxon signedrank test, p < 0.001, d = 2.05) and the natural speech EEG dataset (figure 3(F), p = 0.009, d = 0.44). Correlation gain results showed a 144% increase in effect size when using TC correlation metric for model evaluation. It is noteworthy to mention that a range of SNR values were explored for the simulated EEG dataset. Given that the results were emerging similarly across different SNRs (figures S2(A) and (B)) starting from −10 dB, the main figures depict our results at −15 dB. 4. Discussion This study identified limitations with the use of TRFs with time-discrete stimulus features, such as lexical surprise. We then proposed two new metrics that tackle those issues directly. The new metrics were tested on both simulated and actual EEG data, exhibiting effect-sizes that were over 140% larger than those for the vanilla TRF evaluation. The first metric magnifies the effect on the mTRF weights by contrasting weights for word onsets and lexical surprise. The intuition lexical surprise vectors capture word onsets and surprise information. So, if the surprise values 9 J. Neural Eng. 22 (2025) 016004 A Chalehchaleh et al were meaningless (e.g. if the values were shuffled), similar TRF weights would emerge for lexical surprise and word onsets. Meaningful surprise values would instead lead to a different set of weights for the two features, which is why we expected their contrast to be representative of lexical surprise encoding. Effect sizes computed with this metric demonstrated significantly greater magnitude (d = 2.09) in comparison to univariate model evaluations utilizing the TRF weights (d = 0.22). The second metric, TC prediction correlation, improves the EEG prediction correlation metric by accounting for the temporal sparsity of the word onsets and, specifically, by only considering time-points that can be influenced by lexical surprise. Effect sizes derived from this metric also exhibited a considerably larger magnitude compared to mTRF model assessments utilizing prediction correlation for evaluation, marking a 144% increase. Indeed, this requires introducing an additional assumption on the timing of the neural response of interest, which will have to be considered when interpreting the results. So, it is up to the experimenter to determine if such an assumption is appropriate for their specific application and hypotheses. The two metrics introduced in this study improve the state-of-the-art, leading to large and medium effect sizes, despite relying on small EEG prediction correlations (r ∼0.05) and prediction correlation gains (r ∼0.01), both with values compatible in range with previous studies from other teams (e.g. [5, 39]). This is a known phenomenon that has already been reported in the literature, for example in the context of cocktail party decoding research [40] where an attended speech stream is reliably more strongly encoded than unattended speech streams, despite small measurements for either of them due to low EEG SNR. Using simulated data allowed us to better control for noise and explore different SNRs, with the one selected for the main text leading to EEG prediction correlation values of the order of what was previously measured for intracranial EEG data (r ∼0.2, 0.3; e.g. [41]). An important consideration to discuss is that our approach assumes the presence of a component such as the N400 in the EEG response at a given peristimulus latency window. However, this component may not consistently emerge in other populations, such as children, individuals with hearing loss, non-native speakers, or those with neurodevelopmental conditions, where the N400 may be absent or occur at different latencies [18, 28]. These factors must be considered when applying the metrics to diverse populations and task. It should be remembered that our metrics indeed rely on the typical linear and time-invariance assumptions of TRF methods. Relaxing such assumptions can lead to interesting developments, such as the finding that word predictability modulates both the magnitude and the latency of N400-TRFs [42]. Future research could include such considerations to further improve the TRF modelling approach and the resulting metrics. It should also be noted that the TRF results in figure 2 show some significant effects in correspondence of time-lags around and before zero. That effect may reflect anticipatory mechanisms [43– 45], whose characterization is beyond the scope of this investigation. It should be noted that that effect at negative lags appears to be a baseline effect, while the interpretation of TRF weights usually focusses on TRF components [15, 30]. One reason leading us to thread lightly on interpreting this result is that the EEG data were preprocessed with zero-phase filters, which smooth the signal in both temporal directions. While this ensures the reliability of the timing of component peaks and troughs, this can also extend the rise and fall times of a component. This smoothing can be magnified by using regularized regression to improve generalization of the TRF models. One of the key challenges when measuring linguistic level processing with EEG is that a large portion of the EEG response is explained by the acoustic changes in the sound. Lexical surprise has the advantage of producing a neurophysiological component, the TRF-N400, that is clearly distinct from the typical envelope TRF, both in terms of temporal and spatial patterns, making it possible to separate the two with mTRF models. Instead, it is less clear how effective the TRF approaches discussed here would be at determining how exactly the surprises are built. For example, it is possible to build different hypotheses by using distinct LLMs, or by altering the amount of context available for the prediction, similarly to previous music neurophysiology research with Markov chains [27] and music transformers [37]. The new metrics in the present study increase the sensitivity to lexical surprise, making that type of fine-grained comparisons more feasible. Therefore, we expect future work to explore this direction and to provide valuable insights on how context is built and used during speech processing. Recent developments have already shed some light on that question, leading to the promising result that the internal organisation of the rapidly advancing LLMs is getting progressively closer to the speech processing pathways in the human cortex [21]. The assessment metrics proposed in the present study are expected to further contribute to that line of work. The results of this study can be summarized into recommendations for future research. The first observation is that the literature is quite inconsistent in the way the TRF-N400 is evaluated, challenging the comparison and aggregation of different studies. Some studies consider word onsets and their modulation together [13], while others attempt to separate two neural signatures by relying on different approaches for calculating a baseline. In our view, the random shuffling baseline presented here, which was already used by other previous studies, could serve as a consistent baseline across different studies, as the shuffling procedure could equally applied 10 J. Neural Eng. 22 (2025) 016004 A Chalehchaleh et al to any modulated time-discrete feature. Therefore, we encourage the use of this baseline in the future. Indeed, multiple baselines can be calculated and should be considered, depending on the goals of each study. For example, it has been suggested that corrupting the model (e.g. LLM) in some ways [21] (e.g. retraining the model with random data, reducing the available context) might be a more conservative baseline than shuffling, as the latter would completely destroy the any regularity in the temporal structure. Nonetheless, that baseline and its effectiveness would depend on the specific language model and the goals of the evaluation. One final recommendation based on our results is that measuring how the lexical surprise weights are affected by a baseline, like a shuffled surprise, is insufficient and potentially deceiving in case of strong collinearities in the feature-set. The weights of other features, in fact, would also likely be affected, as measured in figure 2(B). Therefore, we recommend observing the entirety of the change in the regression weights when considering such baselines, for example by adopting the procedure proposed in figures 3(A) and (E). Figure 1. Methodological approach. (A) The simulated EEG dataset was generated by summing three signals. The first signal was the convolution of the speech envelopes from the Natural-Speech-EEG dataset [32] and a predefined impulse response, or temporal response function (TRF), with three main deflections representing the P1, N1, and P2 components of the TRF, approximating previous results on real data [13, 27]. The second signal was the convolution of lexical surprise with an artificially-built TRF with a single negative component at a latency of 400 ms, broadly capturing previous results [5, 7, 13]. The third signal was EEG noise consisting of random segments of the EEG signal from the Natural-Speech-EEG dataset. (B) Forward univariate TRF models (uTRF) were fit to describe the mapping between lexical surprise and the EEG signal. The strength of the relationship between lexical surprise and EEG was assessed by comparing the lexical surprise uTRF with a baseline model, which was derived by fitting a second uTRF after randomly shuffling the lexical surprise values, while preserving their timing. EEG prediction correlations and TRF weights were used for the evaluation. (C) Forward multivariate TRF models (mTRF) were derived by relating a multivariate feature set consisting of the concatenation of envelope, word onset, and lexical surprise with the EEG signal. mTRFs were compared with a baseline model build by shuffling the lexical surprise values. gauge the surprise of each word based on its preceding context. The preceding context was built based on words heard within each particular chapter of the audio-book. 2.6. TRF model fit and evaluation The neural encoding of word-level predictions can be studied with both uTRFs [13, 28, 33] and mTRFs [18, 19, 34]. To assess whether the EEG signals reflect lexical surprise, TRF results were compared when using lexical surprise vectors that did or did not match the speech material. Similar to previous TRF studies [27], mismatched surprise vectors were generated by randomly shuffling the order of the surprise values in the lexical surprise vectors, while preserving the onset times. To carry out statistical testing on individual participants, the shuffling and model-fit procedure was repeated 500 times, generating a null distribution for each participant. Note that this null distribution is stricter than simply mismatching the trial index for lexical surprise and EEG signal, as our procedure isolated the impact of the lexical surprise values, while everything else (i.e. word onset times and speech envelope) remained constant. In uTRFs, the lexical surprise vectors and their shuffled versions were used to fit uTRFs. In that case, the two only differ in the order of the surprise values, while the timing was identical. Note that the shuffled lexical surprise vectors contain meaningful word onset timing, while the surprisal values can be seen as noise, as they are unrelated with the EEG signal. In mTRFs, models were fit by considering the three features (envelope, word onsets, and lexical surprise) simultaneously. In this case, speech envelope and word onsets acted as nuisance regressors, absorbing variance related to sound acoustics and word onsets. As such, the lexical surprise regressor 5 J. Neural Eng. 22 (2025) 016004 A Chalehchaleh et al was expected to more clearly capture variance that is unique to lexical surprise (and anything correlated to it that is not envelope and word onsets). Before analysing the Natural-Speech-EEG dataset, uTRFs and mTRFs were evaluated on the simulated data, where we had full control on what information was and was not present in the EEG data (in this case, envelope and lexical surprise were encoded). For simplifying the model evaluation, EEG prediction correlations calculated on single channels were averaged across all channels and trials, leading to a single value per participant. Regarding the model weights, averaging weights across EEG channels can be problematic instead, as positive and negative deflections in different scalp areas can cancel each other out. For that reason, our analyses of the TRF weights focused on a selected Centro-Parietal EEG channel, Pz, where the relationship between wordlevel predictions and EEG is known to be particularly strong [7, 13]. 2.7. Two new metrics for evaluating word-level predictions This study proposes two new evaluation metrics for assessing the neural encoding of word-level predictions. Note that these metrics could potentially be applied for the evaluation of TRFs for other common time-discrete features, for example at the level of phonemes [17, 19] or music notes [27, 35–37]. The first metric is specifically designed for improving the evaluation of surprise-like responses from the mTRF weights. The second metric aims to increase the sensitivity of EEG prediction correlations to temporally sparse events such as words, and it applies to both uTRF and mTRF methods. ∆Time-constrained TRF weights, or ∆TC weights. The first metric relies on TRF weights and is calculated on mTRF models. The observation is that Lexical surprise uTRF weights are not particularly sensitive to the surprise values (see figure 2(A) and results section). The rationale is that the modulations relating to lexical surprise are likely small in natural speech, meaning that simple word-onset uTRFs capture most of the word responses already. To more clearly isolate the neural encoding of lexical surprise as opposed to word onsets, here we fit mTRF models by using lexical surprise and word onset features simultaneously. If the TRF model weights exhibit differences when examining the TRF weights for the two features, that would mean that the EEG signals encode correlates of lexical surprise. Otherwise, measuring undistinguishable TRF weights for lexical surprise and word onset would indicate that the specific lexical surprise is not encoded in the EEG signal. With this premise, the encoding of lexical surprise can be measured by subtracting the TRF weights for lexical surprise and word onset, and by calculating the absolute value of their difference at the latency where the major effect is expected, in this case 400 ms. Specifically, weights were averaged in the window 300–500 ms to account for latency differences between participants. Note that our conclusions did not change for small changes in the selection of that window. Time-constrained (TC) EEG prediction correlation. The second metric relies on EEG prediction correlations. Feature vectors capturing wordlevel information are typically sparse as they code the information of interest, such as lexical surprise, timelocked to the word onsets. Considering a word rate between about 100 and 260 words per minute across different speakers, speech categories and languages [38], and considering that TRF-N400 evoked component can extend approximately between 200 and 600 ms [13, 18, 28]. Under these general assumptions, the worst-case scenario would be that only 20 s every minute of EEG data would reflect lexical surprise. As such, 66% per cent of the datapoints used for calculating the EEG prediction correlation would not capture the effect of interest, substantially diluting that effect. Here, we propose to calculate the EEG prediction correlations by only considering the datapoint that might reflect the target effect. This simple modified metric is applied at the evaluation stage, and it does not affect the TRF model fit, meaning that it can be used to evaluate both uTRF and mTRF models. The code used for deriving this metric has been shared on the GitHub of the mTRF-Toolbox (function mTRFcrossval_multimetric). 2.8. Statistical analysis Statistical significance in group-level analysis was assessed through pair-wise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests applied to both EEG prediction correlations and mTRF weightsIn the single-subject level analysis (figures 3(D) and (H)), we conducted 500 permutations for each participant, systematically shuffling the values of lexical surprise in each iteration. This process generated a null distribution for each subject, allowing us to calculate statistical significance at the individual level. Wilcoxon signed rank tests were used for pair-wised comparisons. Correction for multiple comparisons was applied where necessary via the false discovery rate (FDR) approach. A two-way repeated measures ANOVA was used to assess the effects of within and between factors. The values reported use the convention F(dfnumerator, dfdenominator). Results 3.1. The challenge of probing lexical surprise in the human cortex with uTRFs The relationship between lexical surprise vectors and EEG was evaluated with uTRFs on both simulated and real EEG data. For the simulated EEG data, TRF weights were compared between the lexical surprise model and the null (shuffled lexical surprise) model. Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that there is a negative deflection for the lexical surprise model around 400 ms (figure S1(A); Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the average TRF weights in the 300–500 ms lag window: p < 0.001, d = 0.4 FDR-corrected Wilcoxon tests were carried out on individual lags with p < 0.05). Prediction correlation comparison between the lexical model and the shuffle surprise model were greater for the lexical model (figure S1(B); Wilcoxon signedrank p < 0.001, d = 9.72). Similar outcomes emerged when analysing real EEG data. TRF weights at channel Pz were compared between lexical surprise and the shuffled surprise models, showing a stronger negative deflection for the lexical surprise model at latencies close to 400 ms (figure 2(A); Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the average TRF weights in the 300–500 ms lag window p < 0.001, d = 0.22; FDR-corrected Wilcoxon tests were carried out on individual lags with p < 0.05). EEG prediction correlations were also larger for the lexical surprise model than the shuffled surprise model, leading to a statistically significant difference (figure 2(B); p < 0.001, d = 0.17). These results are in line with the literature in that a statistically significant encoding of lexical surprise is measured. As in previous work, both this result corresponded with small effect sizes (d ⪅0.2) for both TRF weights and EEG prediction correlations metrics. The analysis in section 3.3 aims at deriving evaluation metrics that are more sensitive to lexical surprise, leading to larger effect sizes. 3.2. Probing lexical surprise with mTRFs Further analyses were carried out to evaluate whether the flexibility of mTRFs can improve the evaluation of lexical surprise encoding in EEG signals. One of the advantages of mTRFs is that, by using multiple stimulus features at once, the different contributors to the prediction can be more clearly separated [18, 30]. Here, lexical surprise mTRFs were derived by including envelope, word onset, and lexical surprise features as the input, while the shuffle surprise model 7 J. The intuition is that lexical surprise and word onset feature vectors would capture different EEG variance only when the surprise values are meaningful and encoded in the EEG signal. Results on the simulated EEG data showed main effects of feature, model, and their interaction (repeated measures ANOVA, feature: F(1,18) = 0.50, p = 0.48; model: F(1,18) = 4.81, p < 0.05; feature∗model: F(1,18) = 68.73, p < 0.001, with statistically significant differences between lexical surprise and word onset (p < 0.001, d = 3.50) and between shuffled surprise and word onset (p < 0.001, d = 2.57). For the real EEG dataset, we found main effects of feature, model, and their interaction (repeated measures ANOVA, feature: F(1,18) = 20.68, p < 0.001; model: F(1,18) = 5.22, ∗p < 0.05; feature∗model: F(1,18) = 22.98, p < 0.001, with statistically significant differences between lexical surprise and word onset (p < 0.001, d = 2.57) but not between shuffled surprise and word onset in the shuffle surprise model (p = 0.104, d = 0.49). TRF weights corresponding to lexical surprise in the lexical surprise and shuffle surprise model showed statistically significant differences at individual lags (figure 2(C-left); FDR-corrected Wilcoxon signed rank test, p < 0.05). Also, TRF weights related to word onset in lexical surprise and shuffle surprise showed statistically significant differences at individual lags (figure 2(C-right); FDR-corrected Wilcoxon signed rank test, p < 0.05). EEG prediction correlations for the simulated EEG dataset were larger for the lexical surprise model than the shuffle surprise model (figure S1(D); Wilcoxon signed rank test; p < 0.001, d = 3.64). EEG prediction correlations were also compared between 8 J.
